News.title: Face of suffering: Vladimir Putin's war on Ukraine's civilians with overnight barrage of missiles
News.content:
Face of suffering: Vladimir Putin's war on Ukraine's civilians with overnight barrage of missiles

As Ukraine suffers multiple ballistic missile targetin of its capital President Zelensky defies Trump demands to stop deep strike operations against Russia, launching major attack on Moscow

View 6 Images A woman with a bloodied face and bandaged head following a Russian strike on a residential apartment building in Kyiv (Image: Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

Shocked and bloodied a wounded Ukrainian woman is one of the latest victims of Vladimir Putin's brutal war on Kyiv's civilians following overnight strikes against the capital.

‌



‌



She was lucky to survive after a ballistic missile and drone attack on her apartment block in one of the capital's residential areas.

‌



This is the face of war in Ukraine, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may have followed up on his threat to ditch intelligence sharing with Kyiv.

‌



Shelling is cruelly targeting non combatants - a repeated and vile pattern in Putin's attacks on Ukraine's cities and villages as he tries to force Kyiv to bend to his will.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 6 Images The woman kneels in the street after the attack (Image: Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

‌



NATO commander warns of bloody retaliation if Russia attacks READ MORE :

As many as five of Kyiv's districts experienced blackouts and water supply issues, and public transport operates with disruptions.

The latest attacks left at least three dead and 22 more people injured as rescue teams battle to save other survivors of Putin's latest brutality.

In response Ukraine fired close to 1,000 drones at Russia overnight after another night of strikes on Kyiv - amid suspicions America stopped sharing intelligence.

‌



At least 500 of the weapons targeted Moscow region, aimed at data centres and oil installations in defiance of US President Donald Trump ’s orders against energy firms.

View 6 Images Ukrainian rescuers and paramedics carry a wounded resident (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

It followed claims by Ukrainian President Zelensky that the US stopped life-saving intelligence sharing on Russian attacks that gives civilians time to take shelter.

‌



America had warned it might cease sharing vital intelligence if Ukraine failed to stop its deep strike operations against Russian energy supplies, earlier in the week.

The latest Ukraine attack also marked Kyiv’s defiance of Trumps’s claims his negotiators had struck an energy ceasefire deal between Russia and Ukraine.

View 6 Images Russian airstrike on a Kyiv apartment (Image: Getty Images)

‌



On Tuesday evening Kyiv locals were not warned of incoming missile attacks on homes and a power plant, killing a suspected three people and injuring another 13.

The attack hit the capital at around 10:40 p.m., sparking fires across several districts.

In Desnianskyi district, a fire spread across apartments on the first through eighth floors before firefighters extinguished it.

‌



View 6 Images Ukrainian firefighters extinguish a blaze at the site of a Russian missile strike at an apartment building in Kyiv (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Rescuers recovered two bodies from the building and evacuated 16 residents, while other strikes caused fires and casualties throughout the capital.

Mr Zelensky stormed: “Once again, ‌no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure.”

‌



He had said of an earlier strike: “Advance intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches is critical to saving lives.

View 6 Images Russian drone strike in Kharkiv (Image: Jam Press)

“Early warnings give people time to seek shelter and help prevent casualties. Normally, we receive advance warnings from our partners, which are crucial for our defense.”

‌



Ukraine’s attacks on Moscow temporarily closed four airports in the region as Mr Zelensky flew into the UK for meetings at 10 Downing Street.

Moscow’s defence ministry said at least 902 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Russia overnight.

President Trump claimed earlier this week that intelligence sharing had not stopped as he said:

‌



“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and Russia on getting the war to end.”

He had claimed an energy ceasefire was in place between Ukraine and Russia, although it was broken within hours by the Kremlin attacking Ukraine’s infrastructure.

Trump has tried to blame Ukraine for the sharp rise in fuel prices across America and has signed a deal with Russia to import diesel, whilst dropping sanctions.

Article continues below

Today Mr Zelensky said Russia has launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones against critical infrastructure in Kyiv city, Kyiv region and Kharkiv.

He said: “Russia does not view the US President’s statements as strong.”

He also reasserted Ukraine’s determination to continue to defy Vladimir Putin ’s full-scale invasion of his country, adding: “Peace can only be achieved through strength.”

News.title: Paris fire - live: Huge blaze erupts near Austerlitz train station with flames seen for miles
News.content:
Rescue crews descended on as area near Gare d'Austerlitz in the French capital's 13th arrondissement with firefighters battled the flames and police established a huge security cordon

Paris fire - live: Huge blaze erupts near Austerlitz train station with flames seen for miles

A plume of smoke was visible for miles above Paris this morning after a massive fire erupted near Austerlitz train station.

The blaze broke out on Wednesday morning close to Gare d'Austerlitz in the 13th arrondissement neighbourhood of the French capital.

Emergency crews descended on the area, with firefighters battling the flames and police establishing a huge security cordon nearby.

Access to Boulevard de l'Hôpital, which runs alongside the station, has also been blocked as the emergency response continues.

News.title: Top energy boss says households 'seriously struggling' even before winter price surge
News.content:
Top energy boss says households 'seriously struggling' even before winter price surge

The chief executive of one of the UK's biggest energy companies has issued a warning about prices and debts ahead of this month's Budget

View 3 Images An estimated 1.7 million households won't use any heating this winter because of the cost, research has suggested (Image: Getty Images)

The boss of one of Britain's biggest energy firms has warned many households are already “seriously struggling” even before what he warned would be a “bad” price hike in the depths of winter.

‌



‌



Keith Anderson, chief executive of Scottish Power, said the scale of crisis meant the government would need to consider emergency support in this month’s Budget.

‌



It comes as Ofgem’s price cap is set to surge by a forecast 16% to more than £2,000 a year in January, driven by an energy shock caused by the Middle East war.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Energy bills are forecast to spike in January - just when many households use the most heating (Image: PA)

Radiators will be warmer this winter with 1 simple bedroom item READ MORE :

Mr Anderson said all the indications were that there would be "another huge rise in bills" in January, "we can see how that is going to be."

‌



He added: "The reality is that the most vulnerable people in our country need further support and they need that support this winter. Many of them are genuinely seriously struggling to pay what is due."

View 3 Images Scottish Power CEO Keith Anderson used a speech in London to warn about the threat to energy suppliers of ever rising customer debts (Image: Getty Images)

Tim Jarvis, chief executive of Ofgem, told trade body Energy UK's conference in London: "It is going to be a difficult winter. People are going to struggle without help."

‌



The comments come amid growing expectations Chancellor John Healey will unveil targeted help - rather than support for all households - in his Budget on October 28. The most likely option is extending the £150 Warm Home Discount to more people who are on means-tested benefits. Another possibility is that the temporary £45 a year saving for all households through axing VAT on electricity bills will be extended.

Dhara Vyas, Energy UK's chief executive, said “tackling the cost of energy for households and businesses has to be a priority” and that, despite the Government’s fiscal challenges, “failing to act risks greater long-term costs for households, businesses and the economy”.

The threatened price spike comes against the backdrop of a customer debt mountain, which already stands at £6billion and is heading towards £7billion.

‌



Mr Anderson called it "one of the biggest challenges facing the industry", with debts owed to suppliers meaning he was "more worried than I have ever been" about the sustainability of such firms.

"We are reaching a point now where the debt owed is neither fair to those who are having to pay it, and is not sustainable for the companies carrying it," he told Energy UK's conference.

He said it was time to separate those customers who genuinely "can't pay" from those who "choose not not to pay". "We are heading into a doom loop where we are asking today's billpayers to pick up the cost of others," Mr Anderson added. "We are getting to the point where we can'y wait any longer."

Article continues below

Speaking to the Mirror later, Mr Anderson said as much as 35% to 40% of the debt was owed by tenants in rented accommodation who use energy but leave before suppliers are able to properly bill them for what they use. One solution he said could be speeding up the process of tenants registering with a supplier by, for instance, giving them a few days to do so after moving in. Another problem he said was being able to identify households who would benefit from having a prepayment meter fitted.

Another of Mr Anderson's suggestions would be to bundle up a chunk of the debt - potentially up to £4billion - which is then sold on and recovered from billpayers over a much longer period, 10 years or longer.

News.title: Ruth Ellis: Family of last woman to be executed in UK finally get headstone for grave 70 years after death
News.content:
Ruth Ellis: Family of last woman to be executed in UK finally get headstone for grave 70 years after death

Ruth Ellis' family will finally have a headstone to mark her grave in Amersham after she was granted a posthumous conditional pardon earlier this year 'to recognise a profound injustice in this exceptional case'

View 5 Images Just two years after Ellis was executed, legal changes introduced diminished responsibility as a partial defence to murder, allowing a conviction to be reduced to manslaughter. (Image: Facebook/YOURAmersham)

More than seven decades after her death, a headstone has been installed for the last woman executed in the UK.

‌



‌



Ruth Ellis was just 28 when she was hanged at London’s Holloway Prison in 1955. She was sentenced to death after being convicted of fatally shooting David Blakely, with whom she had been in a relationship. Earlier this year was granted a posthumous conditional pardon after a campaign by her family which argued she was a victim of abuse at Blakely's hands.

‌



After her execution, her body was buried in an unmarked grave within the prison grounds, but her remains were later exhumed during redevelopment work, and she was reburied in Amersham in 1971. Previous memorials at her grave had since been vandalised.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Hero Brit doctor saves stranger's life on airport floor after landing in Miami for holiday READ MORE :

911 call after Christa Pike failed lethal injection execution reveals confusion that delayed medical help READ MORE :

View 5 Images Ellis was granted a conditional pardon in July 2026 (Image: PA)

The request for the new headstone came from her grandson Scott Walker, who said he was determined to have something “poignant and punchy” in place at St Mary’s Cemetery, Amersham, to mark what would have been his late grandmother’s 100th birthday. The idea came after Scott visited the cemetery with his daughters in 2024.

‌



He described Ellis as “sort of lying in an unmarked grave”. He added: “People kept pinching stuff off it. A wooden cross went missing and it just looked a bit sad”.

He contacted Amersham Town Council, which was pleased to support a memorial that would see "people stop and think". The plans were discussed by a family committee made up of relatives living in Dubai, Spain and Canada, and the headstone has since been installed.

View 5 Images The grave was previously unmarked (Image: Wiki Comms)

‌



Ellis’s grandchildren Laura Enston, James Enston, Stephen Beard and Chloe Beard had called for a posthumous pardon for their grandmother. Their application presented Ellis as a victim of domestic, physical and emotional abuse at the hands of Blakely. They said her case was profoundly shaped by circumstances and trauma that were not adequately recognised at her trial.

David Lammy confirmed Ellis had been granted a conditional pardon in July. He said: “While the pardon does not claim she was innocent of killing David Blakely, it replaces the death penalty with a sentence of life imprisonment to recognise a profound injustice in this exceptional case.”

Speaking on the day, Laura said: “This pardon does not undo what happened 71 years ago. It does not restore the lives that were broken - the children left behind, the years lost. But it says, formally and finally, that Ruth should not have been executed; that the justice system failed her. That acknowledgement matters profoundly to our family.”

‌



View 5 Images Laura Enston and Stephen Beard making a statement outside the Houses of Parliament (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

She added: “Ruth was a victim of sustained and brutal abuse. Her children - our mother and uncle - never recovered. My uncle took his own life; my mother’s trauma left her unable to be the parent we needed. The shadow of Ruth’s execution has fallen across two generations. We have carried shame that was never ours to bear.”

She previously said: “We are determined to do what we can to right this historic injustice and honour not only Ruth but all victims of domestic abuse who have been let down by the criminal justice system.”

‌



Ellis’s case has provoked public outrage since her execution. At her trial, the jury was instructed that the abuse she had endured did not amount to a defence of provocation under the law at the time. Her murder conviction carried a mandatory death sentence. A petition that called for the execution to be called off reached 50,000 signatures but was denied.

View 5 Images A crowd of 500 - 1,000 protestors gathered outside the court on the day of her execution (Image: Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

Just two years later, legal changes introduced diminished responsibility as a partial defence to murder, allowing a conviction to be reduced to manslaughter. Ten years after her execution, the death penalty for murder was abolished in Great Britain in 1965.

Article continues below

Ellis’s case helped fuel the campaign for abolition, alongside those of Timothy Evans, executed in 1950, and Derek Bentley, executed in 1953, who also received posthumous pardons. In 2015, section 76 of the Serious Crime Act introduced the offence of controlling or coercive behaviour.

Kelly Thornton, the deputy mayor of Amersham, said: “Honouring [Ellis’] memory means supporting women’s rights and public services that understand trauma, recognise coercive control, safeguard children and help survivors find safety. It also means respecting her family’s privacy and wishes concerning her resting place.”

News.title: New 'soft and cosy' £10 Lidl jacket like £98 Next version - in stores Thursday
News.content:
New 'soft and cosy' £10 Lidl jacket like £98 Next version - in stores Thursday

Lidl has a new addition to its fashion range that could rival a pricier alternative on sale at Next

View 3 Images Lidl has roughly 1,000 stores across the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Temperatures are dropping as autumn tightens its grip with winter just around the corner, prompting people to look for affordable ways to keep warm outdoors. Lidl may have just the solution without stretching the budget.

‌



‌



The major supermarket, which has over 1,000 stores nationwide, is renowned for its 'Middle of Lidl Aisle' that boasts a selection of deals on homeware, garden accessories, seasonal items, fashion and much more. One of its latest additions could steal the show - and it looks almost identical to a higher-end alternative on sale elsewhere.

‌



Shoppers can grab the Men's Black Thermal Fleece Jacket in-store only for £9.99 from Thursday, October 15 while stocks last. Anyone hoping for home delivery will be disappointed, so to avoid a wasted trip on launch day, make sure to double check stock levels at your local branch via the online store finder.

‌



The jacket has a versatile black design with orange accents, making it easy to pair with a range of outdoor outfits. Made from 100 per cent polyester fleece, it is designed to help retain warmth and keep the chill at bay.

Full list of product features

View 3 Images The new Men's Black Thermal Fleece Jacket at Lidl (Image: Lidl)

Soft and cosy fleece

Full zip with chin guard

With high collar

With side pockets

Anti-pilling finish helps prevent bobbles

Embroidered detail on the chest

Sizes: M-XL

Contains 100% GRS*-certified recycled polyester

‌



Shoppers hoping to find out more are urged to visit the Lidl website. It could be considered a budget alternative to a premium piece available at a rival retailer.

Next, for instance, is stocking the Reiss Navy Meros McLaren Racing Fleece Half-Zip for £98 - nearly 10-times the price of Lidl's offering. While it's not marketed as a jacket, it boasts an almost identical look but with the iconic McLaren branding normally associated with motorsport, Formula 1 racing and luxury supercars.

View 3 Images The Reiss Navy Meros McLaren Racing Fleece Half-Zip at Next (Image: Next)

Article continues below

Describing the product, Next said: "The Navy Meros top is crafted from soft fleece with McLaren Racing and Reiss embroidery on the chest and additional branding to the back. The half-zip style is finished with a motorsport sleeve badge."

A half-zip jumper is a versatile wardrobe staple that helps keep you warm while allowing you to adjust your temperature throughout the day. The zip can be opened for extra ventilation when you're feeling warm or pulled up to help trap heat when the temperature drops, making it ideal for layering over a T-shirt or under a coat.

One of the biggest differences between the two is that customers can order the half-zip for home delivery. Next offers next-day home delivery for £4.95 per order when placed before 11pm, subject to availability. Its Nextunlimited annual pass costs £24.50 and includes unlimited home and ParcelShop deliveries, while oversized furniture deliveries incur a £30 fee.

News.title: Pope Leo surgery - latest: Vatican issues updated after pontiff's cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Pope Leo XIV (C) arrives at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital in Rome yesterday

Pope Leo XIV has undergone a 90-minute operation at the Policlinico A. Gemelli hospital in Rome which saw surgeons remove the lower lobe of the 71-year-old’s right lung after finding a cancerous nodule

Pope Leo XIV has spent a peaceful night in hospital after an operation following his diagnosis with lung cancer, the Vatican has said.

The diagnosis came after an operation which saw doctors remove a growth from the 71-year-old’s right lung.

An examination of the nodule during the operation led doctors to confirm that the religious leader had adenocarcinoma.

"The surgery was successful, and there were no further complications, the statement said. The Vatican said there were currently no plans for the Pope to begin chemotherapy or other therapies.

Messages of support and well wishes have flooded in after the surgery, which was performed at a hospital in Rome, the Policlinico A. Gemelli. The Vatican previously said Leo will spend about a week in hospital recovering from the operation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was among those who took to X to offer his best wishes.

News.title: HSBC cuts cost for customers 'from Thursday' in 'welcome move'
News.content:
HSBC cuts cost for customers 'from Thursday' in 'welcome move'

Experts said it was good news

View 3 Images Other big names could follow, experts said (Image: Octavian Lazar via Getty Images)

HSBC has made an announcement this morning confirming a cost cut for customers from tomorrow.

‌



‌



It has announced that it is set to cut its mortgage rates from Thursday in a "welcome move" for borrowers. Actual rates will be available to review from Thursday, but the downward trend will be comforting for both brokers and borrowers.

‌



Brokers told Newspage that some of its fixed-rate deals could fall below 5%. HSBC currently offers a two-year fix at 5.01% and a five-year fix at 5.03%.

‌



Experts said the reduction could encourage competing lenders to follow, providing relief for homebuyers and borrowers approaching the end of fixed deals. But they cautioned that one lender cutting rates does not prove the market has stabilised, particularly while swap rates and gilt yields remain elevated.

Others may follow with cost cuts

Justin Moy, managing director of Chelmsford-based EHF Mortgages, said HSBC's move will encourage other lenders to follow suit.

He added: "While we are awaiting news of the new rates, the mere whiff of improvement is enough to put a bounce in the step of borrowers and brokers. The market feels like it has plateaued over the last week or so, still around 1% more than we were just a few months ago, but to see HSBC move will encourage other lenders to follow over the coming days.”

‌



View 3 Images Justin Moy (Image: Justin Moy)

Tracey Dixon, buy-to-let mortgage specialist and owner of Cardiff-based Pure Mortgage and Protection, said it was “encouraging”.

She added: "A welcome move from HSBC, particularly for borrowers approaching the end of their fixed deal. We’ll need to see the new rates and fees before judging the overall value, but any improvement in monthly payments will be welcome. One lender’s reduction doesn’t confirm the market has stabilised, although it’s an encouraging sign.”

‌



Back below 5%

Aaron Strutt, product and communications director at London-based Trinity Financial, said HSBC would now likely have deals below 5% once again.

He added: "It looks like HSBC will be offering sub-5% fixes from tomorrow which is another step in the right direction. HSBC currently has a 5.01% two-year and a 5.03% five-year fix. It has been an unusually quiet week with very few changes from the big banks and building societies bringing some welcome stability.

“With so much talk of base rate rises and the war in Iran dragging on it seems unlikely fixed rates will get a huge amount cheaper but the mortgage market is notoriously hard to predict. Yorkshire Building Society currently has a 4.83% two-year fix and 4.95% five-year fix, while Santander has a 4.92% two-year fix and a 4.93%. Thankfully there are lots of rates to choose from well below 6%.”

‌



Waiting for details

David Stirling, Independent Financial Adviser at Belfast-based Mint Wealth, said he would be waiting for the details to come out tomorrow.

He added: "HSBC is the latest lender to nudge rates down, which is much better than watching them head the other way. We’ll reserve judgement until we see the actual numbers tomorrow, but borrowers and brokers will take comfort from the direction of travel.

"In the mortgage market, boringly cheaper is exactly the sort of excitement we like. The champagne can stay in the fridge until tomorrow."

‌



View 3 Images Harry Goodliffe (Image: Newspage)

Harry Goodliffe, director of Winchester-based HTG Mortgages, said it was good news.

He added: “HSBC being one of the first to cut rates is a welcome piece of news for borrowers and hopefully a sign of where the market is heading. Lenders are currently fighting hard for business, and even a small reduction can make a real difference to monthly payments.

Article continues below

"Let’s hope more lenders follow suit, or will swap rates and current market uncertainty put the brakes on any further cuts. Either way, competition between lenders is good news for borrowers.”

Michelle Lawson, director of Fareham-based Lawson Financial, added: “HSBC's latest reduction today is welcomed but yet to be celebrated. Swaps and Gilt rates are still increasing and the market is still volatile so the storm isn't subsiding yet.”

News.title: Woman told she 'looked too good' to be disabled as businesses deny her assistance dog entry
News.content:
Woman told she 'looked too good' to be disabled as businesses deny her assistance dog entry

Rachel O'Connor, who has a rare neurological condition, said she has been turned away from businesses and public buildings while with her assistance dog Justin

View Image Rachel O'Connor claimed she has been discriminated against while with her assistance dog Justin (Image: Facebook)

A woman said she was told that she looked "too good" to be disabled when her assistance dog was denied entry into a building.

‌



‌



Rachel O'Connor was diagnosed with Ataxia - a rare neurological condition that affects co-ordination, speech and balance - when she was a child and faced misconceptions and hurdles most of her life. The woman however has revealed she now faces a new challenge and claims she has been discriminated against while trying to enter some businesses and buildings with her assistance dog.

‌



Rachel, from Kerry, Ireland, said she has been refused entry from places several times while with her assistance dog, named Justin.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

The woman said she has been turned away due to policies prohibiting dogs, despite Justin being a trained assistance animal. Rachel, who works for the disability non-profit Enable Ireland, also claimed someone even shockingly said she looked "too good to have an assistance dog".

‌



The charity worker, speaking to the Irish Independent, said: "It is happening to me in a few places in Tralee. It's really frustrating when all I'm trying to do is go about my day. They will usually say to me, 'No dogs are allowed.' When I tell them he is an assistance dog, some will leave it at that, but there are others who don’t.

"One person in a premises asked me why I needed an assistance dog. When I told him I had a disability, he said I looked too good to have an assistance dog. I was really surprised when he said that."

Rachel, who did not share the name of these businesses, said she had emailed to complain but said they are yet to respond. The woman added that staff should be better trained in 2026 to avoid these situations.

Article continues below

The dog was given to Rachel by the Cork-based charity Dogs for the Disabled, which provides assistance dogs to disabled adults and kids for free. Rachel, who has had her dog for eight years, claimed "this discrimination has been happening over the last two years" since she started work.

She said: "It's becoming more frequent. To be honest, I'm sick of it. I've tried to explain things to people and give them some leeway, but it keeps happening."

Rachel is also a member of the Independent Living Movement Ireland - an organisation whose aim is that "disabled people achieved Independent Living, choice and control over their lives and full participation in society as equal citizens", according to the ILMI website.

News.title: Watch: What we know about Russia's overnight strikes on Ukraine
News.content:
A key energy facility and a residential building in the outskirts of Kyiv have been hit by overnight Russian missile and drone strikes.

In the capital, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said. At least 600,000 people across the country are without electricity after strikes hit critical infrastructure in the Kyiv region and the north-eastern city of Kharkiv.

The strikes come after US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.

Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes had targeted communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.

BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson explains.

News.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
News.content:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed. A reopening date has not been confirmed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers.

An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster Coroner's Court on Thursday.

Footage of the incident has been widely shared on social media, including on Tuesday evening by US President Donald Trump.

News.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
News.content:
Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.

The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.

Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.

The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.

On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at Â£300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately Â£699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a Â£150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun, but the BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

News.title: One stolen every four minutes - inside the police battle against vehicle thieves
News.content:
It is 01:00 on a Thursday and we are in the back of an unmarked police car on the hunt for vehicle thieves in east London.

A call comes in over the radio about a stolen Ford Transit van. Within 25 minutes officers have found it, chased it down and arrested a suspect.

Officers tell us the night has been successful, with further arrests made, yet across the UK a car is stolen every four minutes.

Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to Home Office data. Last year, just 3% of vehicle theft offences resulted in a charge or summons.

As well as spending time on the front line in London and Sussex, we have privately spoken to 20 police officers from six forces.

They told us while they have the skills and experience to tackle vehicle crime, they are overstretched, under-resourced and struggling to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminal networks.

Thieves are becoming more confident. A man who claims he receives stolen vehicles and breaks them into parts at a so-called "chop shop" told the BBC he does not fear the authorities, because they "couldn't catch a cold".

Once the preserve of joyriders and opportunists, vehicle theft is now a lucrative global criminal business. Cars are stolen to order, and moved across the country or dismantled within hours, say police, making them difficult to recover and suspects hard to track. Many vehicles are sent overseas to places like the United Arab Emirates, The Democratic Republic of Congo and Jamaica.

Victims of car theft have told us they feel frustrated and helpless. One woman said it took car thieves just 35 seconds to steal her BMW, yet police only began investigating a day later. Another man said he feared for his life when masked thieves broke into his home demanding his car keys.

The success criminals are having is also hitting motorists more widely, with insurance quotes having risen by 82% since 2021, according to security think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).

News.title: Watch: BBC joins police on front line against car theft
News.content:
Vehicle thefts have risen by almost 50% in a decade, yet just 3% of offences resulted in a charge or summons last year, BBC analysis has found.

Organised crime groups are using increasingly sophisticated technology to steal cars to order, while police and manufacturers look to keep pace.

Criminals, the BBC has been told, are able to work out how to steal a car within weeks of a model being launched.

Investigations reporter NJ Convery has been out with police as they hunt for thieves.

Watch Stolen: Chasing Britain's Car Thieves on iPlayer now

News.title: Shipwreck thought to be 4,700 years old found off coast of Turkey
News.content:
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.

They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.

The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.

The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.

"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Ãniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.

News.title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
News.content:
Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined Â£6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics â with some customers set to receive refunds.

The online furniture retailer was fined Â£4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined Â£1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said.

Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined Â£48,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships.

It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of Â£440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate.

Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment.

Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of Â£25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to Â£50, according to the CMA.

The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds.

Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March.

The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added.

The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%.

The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing.

News.title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery felt like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
News.content:
TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.

Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024.

"After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith.

"When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."

The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after a colloid cyst was found in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.

In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.

She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.

Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there.

"I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."

A year ago, for the first time since the surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.

News.title: Pastor died when festival arch fell, inquest told
News.content:
A pastor died from "multiple severe injuries" when a large wooden arch fell on him at a Christian event in West Sussex, an inquest opening heard.

Robert Guanco, 41, was a pastor at Jesus the Living Water Church in Eastbourne, East Sussex, and attended the Big Church Festival, near Steyning, on 28 August.

An inquest opening at Woodvale Coroner's Court in Brighton on Wednesday heard that Guanco suffered multiple severe injuries and blunt force trauma.

Speaking afterwards, his widow Isaeli said she hoped learning the truth about what happened to her husband would "help us grieve" and "prevent other families going through the same thing".

Six others were injured, four of whom were taken to hospital for treatment.

After a post-mortem examination, a provisional cause of Guanco's death was given as "1a multiple severe injuries and 1b blunt force trauma", the inquest was told.

Area Coroner Joseph Turner offered his "sincere condolences" to the family and adjourned the inquest until a pre-inquest review on 9 March.

Guanco's widow added: "Suddenly losing Robert has been a huge challenge - I've gone from planning our daughter's birthday party a few weeks ago to organising his funeral.

"It brings a deep pain to my heart."

News.title: Gales and heavy rain to impact UK as yellow wind warning issued
News.content:
A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK this week.

The centre of the low, and its most significant impacts, will stay hundreds of miles from UK shores but north-west Scotland will see a spell of gales.

A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places.

Heavy rain will also affect parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland but much of England and Wales will remain largely dry with spells of sunshine.

The area of low pressure will also send a renewed surge of warm air across the country bringing above-average temperatures for many.

News.title: Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans
News.content:
About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.

The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.

The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.

Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.

Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.

It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.

But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.

"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."

A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.

News.title: One man dead and two missing as search goes on for fishing boat off Lewis
News.content:
Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised at about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat was overdue from Lewis.

It said a plane and two helicopters were making searches off the Port of Ness in north Lewis.

Six coastguard rescue teams, two RNLI lifeboats, a local boat and Police Scotland have also been involved.

News.title: Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow boss
News.content:
Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned.

Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion.

The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year.

The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps".

A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment".

They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around Â£40 billion in economic benefits across the country".

Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation.

"If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said.

"It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country."

A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost Â£33bn to build.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners".

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month.

Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions.

News.title: Home of oldest restaurant given to National Trust
News.content:
The home of London's oldest restaurant, which has hosted famous faces from Charles Dickens to Madonna over the past two centuries, has been given to the National Trust.

Rules originally opened in 1798 at 34-35 Maiden Lane in Covent Garden and has outlasted empires, survived the Blitz and fought off development plans.

The Â£11m freehold gift of the restaurant building along with its historic collection such as visitor books, menus, and photographs will now be protected for future generations, the National Trust said.

Rules restaurant will continue to trade, while becoming a commercial tenant of the charity. Under the deal, the rent payments will go towards conserving the building.

News.title: Swimmer Archie Goodburn to meet prime minister over cancer funding
News.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn is to meet the prime minister later after making a tearful plea for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, said the Downing Street meeting offered a "unique opportunity for change".

He previously called for Andy Burnham to introduce a brain cancer lead to give patients a chance to "fight for their lives" during an appearance on BBC Breakfast.

Goodburn, 25, cried while looking down the camera, saying he was "on my knees begging" for help to ease the "unbearable suffering" of patients and their families.

Burnham later contacted Goodburn on social media to set up the meeting at Downing Street.

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born swimmer underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.

News.title: Amputee told he needs more proof for blue badge
News.content:
For amputee Nigel Ward, the evidence is undeniable.

The 71-year-old from King's Lynn assumed that providing photos showing his missing leg would be enough proof to get his blue badge renewed by Norfolk County Council.

But Ward has been asked to verify his disability further, with one council worker suggesting amputees can run marathons - a level of physical endurance he insists he does not have.

Norfolk County Council has insisted it is following correct procedures. But Ward, who lost his leg following a medical incident on a cruise three years ago, has been left "very disheartened" and says he worries it will affect his independence.

He added: "I am a genuine applicant, not a benefits cheat and I need a blue badge."

News.title: The King will write to Pope Leo after the pontiff’s lung cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The King will write privately to the Pope to pass on his well-wishes after the pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer, the Press Association understands.

Pope Leo XIV’s condition was confirmed on Tuesday after the Vatican said he had undergone a “successful” planned surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung.

King Charles III and Pope Leo XIV met for the first time earlier last year during a state visit to Vatican City.

The pair made history – marking the first time a reigning British monarch and a pope had prayed together in public since the 16th-century Reformation.

News.title: Ship carrying  2,500 containers sinks after hitting mine in Strait of Hormuz, claim Iran’s Guards
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Iran’s stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route that usually carries one-fifth of global oil supplies, continues as a container ship is reported to have hit a naval mine.

According to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy, a vessel carrying more than 2,500 containers on Wednesday attempted to transit what it described as an “unauthorised and dangerous” route. The ship caught fire after hitting a naval mine and has sunk in the south of the Strait.

In a statement, Iran’s Guards have warned local vessels and fishermen to take care.

It comes as the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) received a report of an incident where a container ship was struck by an unknown projectile - although it is currently unclear whether the two incidents are linked.

Iran’s stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz

Before the war on Iran, around 125 to 140 large commercial vessels including oil tankers, gas carriers, bunkers and container ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz every day. This came to an effective standstill on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched coordinated military airstrikes across Iran.

While traffic on the 24-mile Strait appeared to be increasing over recent months, two senior Iranian officials say that Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the passage as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections.

open image in gallery A vessel transits the Gulf of Oman off the coast of Khor Fakkan in the emirate of Sharjah in the east of the UAE. ( AFP/Getty )

“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials said.

As part of the new strategy, Tehran will expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.

Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.

The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.

“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. “Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz.”

News.title: Eufy’s new budget security camera solves a common problem faced by renters
News.content:
Get the Independent Home newsletter for home improvement inspiration, expert tips and offers Get our Independent Home email Get our Independent Home email Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Installing an outdoor security camera isn’t always simple. Drilling holes for mounts and running power cables, or ensuring the location is suitable for solar charging, adds complexity, while for renters it can be a non-starter.

Eufy claims to have a solution with its new window camera E10. The budget camera costs £69.99 and plugs into a wall socket inside your home and sticks to a window to capture a view of the outside.

This will appeal to anyone who has struggled to get good security footage from a camera sitting on a windowsill, since the E10’s window mount should cut down significantly on reflections and glare.

The camera records at 2.5K resolution (2,688px x 1,520px) and has a 125-degree field of view, while the lens can be manually tilted up and down by 25 degrees. There’s also the option for colour night vision without the assistance of a spotlight, dual-band wifi and support for Alexa and Google Assistant.

The tool-free installation requires new screws and no drilling, so could be a good option for renters. ( Eufy )

And since this is a mains-powered security camera, it can be set to record 24/7. This is unlike most outdoor cameras, where continuous recording would quickly drain the battery. For that, you’ll need to install your own microSD card or connect the E10 to one of Eufy’s security camera hubs, like the HomeBase S380. Using the latter also unlocks a 24/7 snapshot function.

Tool-free installation is also a major selling point, especially for renters, since the E10’s window mount uses a peel-off adhesive pad to stick to any window. The camera can be stuck to any glass surface, such as a window, a door or a cupboard.

There’s also AI-powered motion detection to help the camera tell the difference between humans, vehicles and pets, a pre-roll function where a few seconds of footage is saved from before motion is detected, and optional cloud video storage available with a subscription.

This is an interesting camera from Eufy, especially given the price. It gives homeowners and renters another way to monitor the outside of their property, without installing a conventional outdoor camera or dealing with the reflections usually created when recording through a window.

News.title: Golf clubs and private schools among businesses facing severe water use restrictions in ongoing drought
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Businesses including golf clubs, car washes, and private schools could face severe restrictions over water use as drought conditions persist across much of England.

The potential ban could prevent businesses from using mains supplies to irrigate playing fields and halt car washes under “non-essential use” bans sought by three water companies.

It comes as 11 regions of England and Wales remain in drought status following an exceptionally hot and dry summer that left reservoir levels severely depleted. Yorkshire was the latest to move from prolonged dry weather - the stage before drought - into drought status, on 9 October.

open image in gallery Reservoir levels remain low despite recent rainfall ( Getty )

It follows an unusually dry September, with the ongoing lack of rainfall into the autumn months causing the flow in rivers and groundwater levels to reach very low levels in parts of Yorkshire, officials said.

Rainfall was 80 per cent lower than average across the country in September in some areas, raising concerns over dwindling water supplies.

Research by the Environment Agency shows England needs 20 per cent more rainfall than average until the end of April for all of the areas to emerge from drought status.

South East Water, South West Water, and Southern Water have all made non-essential use ban applications for parts of their regions to the department for environment, food, and rural affairs (Defra), who have yet to make a decision on the potential bans.

If approved, household customers would remain unaffected, although huge swathes of the country including London and much of the south of England are already under hosepipe bans.

Almost all reservoirs in England except two are classed as below normal or lower for the time of year, while eight reservoirs or reservoir groups now have levels now classed as exceptionally low.

Earlier this week, executives warned Ardingly Reservoir, which serves 280,000 people in the West Sussex, could run dry within weeks. The reservoir has fallen from 22.8 per cent full a week ago to just 20.2 per cent full now.

open image in gallery An exceptionally hot and dry summer left England parched ( Getty )

The remains of prehistoric villages have also been uncovered in Devon, after huge drops in reserves at Fernworthy Reservoir.

Sam Bottomley, South West Water’s director for drinking water services said the non-essential use application is “a responsible step to help protect the environment and preserve the water we have available”.

He urged customers to “continue to take steps to reduce their water use” adding the company is doing “everything we can to protect water supplies”.

Water minister Emma Hardy previously said: “The recent rainfall is not yet enough to replenish all the water we’ve used over the spring and summer, and the Yorkshire drought declaration highlights the situation is still serious.

“Long-term resilience against our changing climate is a priority for this Government.

“Our strengthened Water Bill will start a decade-long journey to a very different water system, including nine new major reservoirs to secure supplies.”

What areas are in drought?

East Anglia

Hertfordshire and North London

Thames

Devon, Cornwall and Isles of Scilly

West Midlands

Wessex

Kent and South London

Solent and South Downs

East Midlands

Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire

Yorkshire (from 9 October)

How low are water levels in England’s reservoirs?

Almost all reservoirs except two are classed as below normal or lower for the time of year, while eight reservoirs or reservoir groups now have levels now classed as exceptionally low.

Just four reservoirs recorded an increase in storage in the week ending 6 October 2026, whilst all others decline. Overall, England storage was 54 per cent, having fallen by 1.3 per cent, and is now 21 per cent below average for the time of year.

The following eight reservoirs are classed as exceptionally low:

• Abberton reservoir operated by Essex and Suffolk Water

•Ardingly reservoir operated by South East Water Clatworthy reservoir operated by Wessex Water

• Colliford Reservoir operated by South West Water Dove Group operated by Severn Trent Water, where winter refill was impacted by water quality and operational issues

• Hanningfield reservoir operated by Essex and Suffolk Water Pennines Group operated by United Utilities Water Wimbleball reservoir operated by South West Water

News.title: Russell Brand trial latest: Celebrity told friends he wanted to ‘bed 5,000 women in his lifetime’, court hears
