Rooney: Martinez has gone too far, his performances aren't good enough

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Danyal Khan provides insight on three things we learnt from Manchester United's 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League

Martinez's comments also drew criticism from former Manchester United captain Wayne Rooney, who agreed with Carragher that the Argentina defender's performances have not been good enough to make such an outburst.

Rooney also feels Martinez's comments are disrespectful to the other United players.

"It's a difficult one because I always used to think I was outspoken as a player and you want to have your opinion," Rooney told Amazon Prime.

"I think he has maybe gone a bit too far. That's for the manager, and that should really stay internal.

"The fans want to hear the players speak; they want to hear the players care, so you can clearly see he cares and he wants the team to invest more money, and more players, and to do that he is probably one of the players who is out the door through his performances. His performances haven't been good enough.

"But I think in some ways he is right in terms of the club needs to invest more, at the top end of the pitch and in defence as well.

"But it looks like that was a bit of an agenda; he's wanted to say that, because that doesn't mirror the performance. I thought the performance was better.

"It's a bit disrespectful to his team-mates as well. He is disrespecting his team-mates because he's saying the team isn't good enough.

"Bruno (Fernandes) is the only one who has any right to come out and say anything like that as captain. And even then it should be behind closed doors if there are issues, which does happen.

"Players have conversations with the manager, the manager has conversations with the board, but that interview is not going to help the situation the club are in at the minute.

"That's going to bring a greater noise around it; the players are not happy, they're not settled, they don't trust in their team-mates. That's not going to help at all."

What is the makeup of the Man Utd hierarchy?

The Glazer Family & Sir Jim Ratcliffe [owners]: The Glazers retain majority ownership and corporate oversight, while Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the INEOS group are in charge of the day-to-day football operations and investments in the team.

Image: Sir Jim Ratcliffe, owner of Ineos and co-owner of Manchester United and CEO Omar Berrada [right]

Omar Berrada [CEO]: Poached from Man City in 2024, the Moroccan sits directly below the co-owners and serves as the bridge between the boardroom and football matters.

Jason Wilcox [Director of Football]: After hanging up his boots, the one-time Blackburn Rovers, Leeds United and England winger became academy director at Man City and Southampton, before joining United in April 2024.

Image: Man Utd Director of Football Jason Wilcox

However, when Dan Ashworth left Old Trafford in December 2024, Wilcox took on his role as sporting director, before being promoted to Director of Football after Sir Dave Brailsford's departure in June.

Christopher Vivell [Director of Recruitment]: Joined from Chelsea for the 2024-25 campaign having served as their technical director, the 39-year-old German was made the club's Director of Recruitment on a full-time basis in February 2025 where he manages scouting, data analytics and transfer shortlists, reporting to Wilcox.

Sports.title: Millwall boss Neil criticises decision to pause game after alleged racist chanting
Sports.content:
Swansea's 1-0 win over Millwall at The Den was held up for almost seven minutes after an allegation of racist abuse from the crowd towards Swans substitute Eom Ji-Sung; "Stopping the game doesn't deal with anything. All it does is kill the momentum," said Lions boss Alex Neil

Millwall: Alex Neil criticises decision to pause game against Swansea after alleged racist chanting towards Eom Ji-Sung

Millwall's Alex Neil criticised the decision to pause the game against Swansea after alleged racist chanting

Millwall manager Alex Neil criticised the decision to pause Tuesday night's game against Swansea due to alleged racist chanting.

The match - which Championship leaders Swansea won 1-0 - was held up for almost seven minutes after an allegation of racist abuse from the crowd towards Swans substitute Eom Ji-Sung was reported by the Welsh club to officials.

Referee Edward Duckworth halted the game in the 65th minute and walked to the dugouts to speak with Lions boss Neil, Swans counterpart Vitor Matos and fourth official Ruebyn Ricardo.

Image: The game at The Den was held up for almost seven minutes

A security guard was also on the scene with referee Duckworth seeming to point to an area in the stands behind the Swansea dugout.

When play eventually resumed it was announced in the stadium that there had been a report of racist chanting, adding that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.

Matos confirmed the player in question was South Korea winger Eom, who was warming up.

Speaking to the BBC after the game, Neil said: "I don't see the point.

"It needs to get dealt with, absolutely, but stopping the game doesn't deal with anything. All it does is kill the momentum.

Image: Swansea's Eom Ji-Sung was warming up at the time of the alleged chanting

"Listen, if we score I probably don't feel this way, but that's how I feel just now."

Millwall later released a statement, which said: "Millwall Football Club is aware of an alleged, individual incident of discriminatory abuse towards a Swansea City player during the second-half of Tuesday evening's Sky Bet Championship match.

"The club operates a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of discriminatory abuse. Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action.

"The club is working alongside the relevant authorities to establish the facts and is unable to comment further as tonight's alleged incident is the subject of an ongoing police investigation, which the club fully supports."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Sky Bet Championship match between Millwall and Swansea.

Swansea added: "The club wants to place on record its thanks for the swift and decisive manner in which the match officials, Millwall Football Club and the police dealt with the incident.

"We will now follow all protocols and processes and provide whatever assistance we can to all parties as the incident is investigated.

"We stand with Ji-Sung, and he has our unstinting love and support."

Sports.title: Manchester United teammates widely share Martínez view that Wilcox is failing
Sports.content:
Lisandro Martínez’s view that Jason Wilcox is failing as Manchester United’s director of football reflects the dressing room’s general frustration at recruitment and squad depth, although the outburst is also regarded as a push by the defender to secure a move because he is out of contract next summer.

Martínez’s comments came after Tuesday’s 2-0 Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid. This left United with two wins all season, having taken six points from their first six Premier League matches, the club’s poorest league start for 40 years.

The run of form has placed Michael Carrick’s position under pressure, but Martínez zoned in on Wilcox and the rest of the hierarchy. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas,” he said, pointing upwards.

“I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more, but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”

Wilcox, the executive in charge of transfers, oversaw a £155m spend in the last window on Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. The decision to recruit three midfielders and not strengthen other areas has been met with puzzlement within the squad, particularly as Wilcox sought a left-back, with Newcastle’s Lewis Hall the prime target.

Luke Shaw is United’s only senior player in that position and his 12-year career at the club has been plagued by injury. The 31-year-old missed the Atlético defeat and Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham owing to a muscular problem. The lack of depth at left-back reflects the prevailing view among players that Carrick has been left without the resources to challenge. United were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton after making eight changes.

Although Carrick led United to third last season, this came after he took over as caretaker in mid-January with only 17 league games to play with the team out of all the other competitions.

Sports.title: Joining Shakhtar as they make base in London: ‘We’re here to show the world that we are alive’
Sports.content:
The morning has thinned out into low, wispy cloud. Beneath it, Shakhtar Donetsk’s players are going through their paces. It is a light session for those who did not start against Veres Rivne the previous day; that means Arda Turan observes from the side, watching with the director of football, Darijo Srna. A stray ball zips towards them and Srna, after juggling it up, bends it into the goal with a familiar right-footed arc. “Modric!” exclaims Turan. But the two men are football legends in their own right and, as they continue to joke before Srna dashes away to take another phone call, the thought occurs that this happy scene could be played out almost anywhere else. Nearby, just beyond the team’s accommodation, a lake shimmers under the emerging sun.

It masks the fact that, around dawn, air raid sirens disrupted the peace for everyone in view. Even here, in Shakhtar’s bucolic spa hotel base 15 minutes outside Lviv, nobody is safe from the threat of Russian rockets and drones. In Rivne, three hours’ drive to the north-east, another alarm had sent the players and staff down to the stadium’s shelter. The second half was delayed by 20 minutes and that, no matter the corner of the country or the vividness of the autumn colours, is a weekly reality.

So is a travel schedule any other Champions League club would recoil at. Shakhtar are about to hit the road yet again, because there remains no chance of playing European games in Ukraine. This season they will host matches in England for the first time, Stamford Bridge the winner in a beauty contest of three venues in the capital. If the border crossing into Poland is unforgiving, the journey could take anything up to 18 hours. The Guardian has been invited to join their trip to London for Wednesday’s game “at home” to AEK Athens.

“It has good feelings for me and inshallah it will for our players too,” a beaming Turan says, a few hours before making a journey that starts via a convoy of people carriers. He has wrought a transformation at Shakhtar since his appointment as head coach in May 2025 and has been reminding anyone who will listen of his semi-final goal against Chelsea in 2014, when an Atlético Madrid side at the peak of their powers produced a classic away performance. Alisson, one of Shakhtar’s forwards, was unaware of Arda’s heroics and has been made to learn quickly. But there is always a serious point. “It’s an iconic stadium but it’s not our home,” Turan says. “If you don’t have a home stadium at this level it’s very difficult, ask any other club. But we have a dream and inside we have great power.”

They will need all of it for the trip. Shakhtar have become used to packing up, regrouping and taking their roadshow to locations in Poland, Germany and Slovakia for their “home” matches on the continent. But it does not become easier and, with parts of Ukraine under intensified attack from Russia, there is no immediate prospect of a happy ending.

View image in fullscreen Newertton, one of Shakhtar’s many Brazilians, is unfazed by the journey at Rzeszow airport. Photograph: Courtesy of Shakhtar Donetsk

“In the first year playing games away we felt more enthusiastic,” says Vitaliy Khlivnyuk, Shakhtar’s director of sports management. “And we continue, but with each year it becomes harder and harder for everyone. It’s like if you didn’t sleep for one day, you can recover. You didn’t sleep for two, you already feel worse. The third, it’s something else. It accumulates. Physically you can get over it but mentally it’s really tough.”

Khlivnyuk half-jokes that his office has become a “panic room” for the endless last-minute hitches and logistical challenges of running a club in wartime. Today’s quandary is a case in point: Shakhtar need new residency permits for their foreign players and staff, but the application system has been taken offline by Russian bombs in Kyiv. According to the rules, there is little time for a workaround.

Kyiv, where Shakhtar were based more regularly until three years ago, is an increasingly dangerous place. “Now it has the kind of atmosphere where the birds don’t sing,” says Khlivnyuk, drawing an unhappy parallel with the early days of the invasion of Donetsk in 2014. Domestic matches are still played in Kyiv but the entire league may soon need relocating to the country’s west.

At lunch one of Shakhtar’s bus drivers, Oleksandr, readies himself for the task ahead. He has long since lost count of the miles accrued during two and a half years on the payroll, but remembers travelling 930 miles to Slovenia for a Conference League game last season. On one trip, Shakhtar were held up at the border for eight hours. He has set today’s departure time for 1pm. Three of the squad play-fight by the dessert buffet and then, realising time is tight, hurry downstairs to collect their belongings.

The players and coaching staff travel in a group of smaller vehicles, four or five to each. Shakhtar introduced that extra concession to comfort a year ago, receiving a favourable response. Other club employees follow on a larger coach, the vehicles winding through low‑slung villages and past glinting domed churches. Crumbling Soviet signs are reminders of a complex past; a couple of modest cemeteries bring the present starkly into view.

Passengers’ names are taken before arrival at the Krakovets border crossing, which is reached in just under two hours. Many of the players leap out to stretch their legs. Kauã Elias, among the brightest talents in Shakhtar’s modern crop of exciting Brazilians, has been playing Fifa video games with a carload of his compatriots. “Before I came here I didn’t know about this travel situation, but it’s just something we have to do,” he says. “It’s normal now. My friends always want to know how it is for me playing in a country with a war, but this bus travel is the only real difference. Having so many other Brazilians for company helps a lot.”

In Lviv they all meet once a week to cook churrasco; Marlon Gomes has the best knack for it, according to Elias. The prospect of Stamford Bridge is plenty to chew on. Wednesday’s match is, at least in part, the culmination of a lifelong ambition. “Since I was a kid I dreamed of playing there for Chelsea,” Elias says. “So going there with Shakhtar is a dream in the same way. We’re very happy to play in London this year.”

Border formalities on the Ukrainian and Polish sides take an hour and a quarter. It rarely gets smoother on this particular crossing. On one occasion, an overenthusiastic young immigration official demanded that all of Shakhtar’s vehicles were emptied and their contents searched one by one. The buses begin coursing through the corn fields of south-east Poland; 10 minutes later a vast snake of lorries, led by a police escort, passes in the opposite direction. All of life, and life support, must take the slow road to enter Ukraine now.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Shakhtar’s head coach, Arda Turan, says of the club: ‘I feel 100% part of this family and this story.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Shakhtar Donetsk

Shakhtar arrive at Rzeszow airport four hours after leaving Lviv. There are shirts to sign with a handful of fans who have caught wind of their presence. As usual, late administrative dramas have materialised too. One player has discovered that his electronic travel authorisation to enter the UK did not work; the system had seemingly misread the name on his passport. A rushed reapplication later, and his safe passage is ensured with half an hour to spare before boarding.

Turan makes a video call while waiting for the flight; one of his assistants is watching Chelsea play Bournemouth and another is clipping up action from the 3-0 win at Veres. “There’s time to do it all on these trips,” Turan says. He is working through episodes of Mobland when downtime is called for.

This magnetic, emotional figure has thrown himself into Shakhtar. “I feel 100% part of this family and this story,” Turan says. “Sometimes when I see children smiling at us I can tell they have home, and if I feel I’ve helped that then it’s the greatest thing for me. It’s something more important than football. I want to raise the voice of the people here. We live in war but we will never accept it and I will always continue bringing it up. Football is sometimes everything in life, but sometimes it’s nothing.”

London, or at least Gatwick airport, is only two and a half hours away when Shakhtar’s chartered plane departs. Srna sits across the aisle from Turan in row one. “We now have nine games in 29 days, three of them in the Champions League, and have to travel home too,” he says. “It’s a very difficult thing to understand if you don’t experience it with us.”

Shakhtar hope at least 25,000 fans will attend the AEK game, perhaps the lowest-profile home match of a quartet that will conclude with Real Madrid’s visit in January. The club’s connections with London extend beyond football: Metinvest, its sister company, provided 5,000 tonnes of steel that built the Shard, the capital’s tallest building. On the pitch, they will wear shirts highlighting the “Invest in Ukraine” campaign driven by their owner and sponsor SCM.

There is hope of progress to the playoff round after a useful draw at PSV Eindhoven on the opening matchday. “If you come along and support Shakhtar, you’re supporting Ukraine,” Srna says. “This team need support and need emotion, because we are living under sirens and bombs. We’re here to show the world that we are alive, strong, united and will fight to the end.”

At the back of the plane, Shakhtar’s Ukrainian contingent are playing cards. “On some of these long trips I feel like a squished lemon by the end of the day,” says the midfielder Dmytro Kryskiv, turning away from the pack. “But there are others that are easier and this feels like one of them, travelling to Stamford Bridge for the Champions League.”

Kriskiv thinks there is “something special connecting the team”, driven by the mercurial Turan. They disembark after a nine-hour expedition and, within 90 more minutes, will be settled into their west London hotel. For modern-day Shakhtar it gets no easier than this. On Thursday they must make the return journey before preparing for Saturday’s league game with Kolos Kovalivka.

“But we have to continue to play,” Khlivnyuk concludes. “Many of our citizens are struggling more than us. When you know that a win or draw can be a spot of light in this darkness, you will always do it.”

Sports.title: Hong Kong club hope David Silva can be their hero – but just for one day
Sports.content:
Hong Kong, China (as is the official football name), has long tried to follow the advice of Han Solo in Return of the Jedi: keeping their distance from China while trying not to look like they are keeping their distance. It is all about maintaining an independent football association and the trappings and privilege that come with it. There was some talk a few years ago about getting a Hong Kong team in the Chinese Super League, when the spending was in full flow, and although that did not happen the local Premier League has belatedly got in on the act – kind of.

This glittering city is not known as a football hotbed but has a long history in the sport that started when it was a British colony and has continued since it became a special administrative region of China in 1997. George Best, Peter Shilton, Arie Haan, Bobby Moore, Diego Forlán, Nicky Butt, René van de Kerkhof, Tony Morley, Gordon McQueen and Craig Foster have played in the territory and soon David Silva will too.

Shortly after the trophies Silva helped Manchester City to win between 2011 and 2018 were tainted by the findings of the Premier League’s independent commission, the 40-year-old picked up the boots that thrilled the Etihad Stadium for so long and is returning to action, though there is confusion as to how long he will be in action for.

Last week it was announced that Silva had joined the Hong Kong Premier League club Supreme Sha Tin, more than three years after retiring owing to an anterior cruciate ligament injury picked up during pre-season training for Real Sociedad. There had been three seasons in San Sebastián after his decade with City, with whom he won four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and five League Cups. Add 125 caps for Spain, the 2010 World Cup triumph and the Euros on either side and it was quite the career – and it is not quite over.

Supreme Sha Tin were promoted last season and tried to sign Juan Mata but have landed a bigger name. “I am very happy to join Supreme Sha Tin for this experience,” Silva said. “I am really looking forward to going to Hong Kong to enjoy the culture, the people and the food.”

That was the video posted on the club’s Instagram account with Silva’s introduction. “Our founders struck it big with this deal!” was the reaction and there were promises made to fans of special perks of behind-the-scenes access to training.

“We are officially announcing that the legendary Spanish No 21 midfielder, David Silva, has officially joined Supreme Sha Tin!” The post then added: “David Silva will be in Hong Kong soon to settle in, link up with squad training, and build up to peak match fitness before making his pitch debut. Stay tuned!”

View image in fullscreen David Silva playing for a World Legends XI in Hong Kong in 2025. Photograph: Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

It sounded as if Silva would be with the club for the remainder of the season, 17 games for the team to try to climb the table after a slowish start. It made headlines around the world, much to the confusion of the player. “I am surprised because in the end it is only to play one match,” Silva said. “The news made it look like I had signed for a season and it has kept me busy all afternoon. It is a league match, but it is still just one match.”

Whether it is good for Hong Kong football to bring a 40-year-old out of retirement for only one game is not a question for Silva to answer. He is not doing it for the money either.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Silva said: “It is in Hong Kong, a city I love very much … Some have expressed concern about the financial side for me … But that is not the case here. Thanks to my father and my adviser, with whom I have been investing well for years, I have achieved great success.”

Investing well and achieving success are precisely what the ambitious Sha Tin owner, Jim Wong Chi-chuen, who also plays for the team, wants after taking over three years ago. Along the way, the club have been rebranded and before this new season he appointed the girl group Collar as club ambassadors.

A change of image was necessary because the coach who delivered promotion, Lo Kwan-yee, a former Hong Kong footballer of the year, was reportedly arrested in June in relation to match-fixing allegations. Local media reported that the allegations relate to the period before Lo joined Sha Tin but Wong said the club had been affected. “We’ve lost some sponsors and, financially, they haven’t been replaced,” he told the South China Morning Post. “The financial pressure on me is greater than I expected, but I want to push this forward and make it work. I’m trying to do something very pure.”

When scandals and sham contracts are making the headlines, the sight of Silva in full flow is as pure as it gets. If he can be a hero, even if for just one day, it could be the talk of Hong Kong for years to come.

Sports.title: Have any footballers ended their career with more own goals than goals? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“How many professional players have ended their senior careers with more own goals than goals for their own team?” wonders Peter Clark.

In the past we’ve looked at the players with the most own goals, but we haven’t looked at those who ended their professional career in debit. “Southampton cult hero Francis Benali scored only one ‘positive’ goal in his career and was legendary for banging in goal-of-the-month contenders at his own end, most notably a bullet header against Oldham in the 1993-94 season,” writes Daz Pearce. We could only find a couple of OGs for Benali, the other being against Manchester United in 1999-2000. But we were unable to find a comprehensive Southampton database, so there’s a chance we’ve missed some beauties.

Another unsentimental defender, Riccardo Ferri, the formidable stopper in Internazionale’s title-winning side of 1988-89, scored six goals and eight own goals in Serie A. He may be in credit overall – he scored three more goals in cup competitions, but we only have his OG data for Serie A. “Jamie Carragher finished his career with four goals and seven own goals,” writes Dean Whearty. “He even managed to score two in one match against Manchester United in 1999!”

And another in the FA Cup final of 2006, though that had a happier ending for Liverpool. Some sources credit Carragher with five goals at the right end, including an equaliser against Middlesbrough in August 2008. But the official Premier League site puts that down as an Emmanuel Pogatetz own goal.

“Sven van Beek is the all-time leading own-goal scorer for the Eredivisie, with eight in a career at Feyenoord, Willem II and Heerenveen, over the course of 12 seasons and 193 matches,” writes Rob de Hair. “He only managed to score five goals for his own team in those matches. ESPN provided a ‘highlight’ reel here.” Van Beek is still playing in Qatar, and appears to have netted five goals at the right end for Al-Shahania.

Another player on minus three is Luigi Zannier, a defender who played for several Italian clubs, including Milan, in the 1950s and 1960s. In Serie A matches, he scored three and put in six at the wrong end.

Zannier and co have nothing on Everton’s Billy Balmer, however. “At the turn of the 20th century he netted eight goals during open play; all, unfortunately, at the wrong end of the pitch,” writes Gavin Buckland. “In more than 300 appearances for the Toffees his only goal at the right end was a single penalty in 1899.”

Un-Brescia-dented

“What is the earliest point in a season a team in the top flight has been confirmed as having a trophyless season?” asks Matt Walker.

The concept of a trophy has changed in the last 15 years, particularly since Arsène Wenger referred to fourth place – and Champions League qualification – as a trophy. But this is The Knowledge, not La Vibe, so we are only referring to actual shiny things you can lift above your head in triumph.

In England, the flicker of a trophy is often extinguished at the start of January, when Premier League teams play in the third round of the FA Cup. Tom Reed cites the example of Bournemouth last season. “They were knocked out of both domestic cup competitions by 10 January. Despite having a good season, they had no realistic expectation of winning the Premier League, and weren’t in Europe either.”

But, as Tom points out, Bournemouth were not mathematically out of the title race at that time. Tom has calculated that Derby County, who finished the 2007-08 season with only 11 points, are the earliest case of an English top-flight team being mathematically unable to win a trophy. “They were knocked out of the League Cup on 28 August and the FA Cup in the fourth round on 26 January. Their inability to win the Premier League was officially confirmed in their 26th league match of the season, on 9 February, when a 3-0 defeat by Tottenham – coupled with a victory for the leaders Arsenal – made the gap between top and bottom insurmountable.”

View image in fullscreen Derby County’s Roy Carroll is put under pressure by Olof Mellberg resulting in the first of six Aston Villa goals at Pride Park in April 2008. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

Other countries start their main cup competition earlier in the season, which means many clubs have been forced to embrace their trophyless-ness before Christmas (realistically, if not mathematically). “The early rounds of the Coppa Italia are played at the start of the season,” writes Daz Pearce, “and therefore the weaker Serie A teams could easily crash out of it in September. That’s what happened to Lecce in 1993-94 and Brescia in 1994-95. They were never in contention for the title – Lecce won one of their first 23 games, Brescia none of their first 14. They also tumbled out of the Coppa Italia in round two, the earliest possible stage for a Serie A club at the time. I’m sure at some point, they would have clocked that the Scudetto was probably beyond them.”

We’ve looked into it and think that Lecce and Brescia were both mathematically out of contention after 22 of the 34 Serie A games. In Lecce’s case, that was 6 February 1994; in Brescia’s, 5 March 1995.

Bum luck (part II)

In last week’s Knowledge, we looked at players who ended their scoring droughts with a goal off their backside. Tom Clarke has one more to add to the list.

“I think there is in fact a case of a usually prolific striker enduring a barren run with a goal off their bum, at least partially,” he writes. “Late in the 2023-24 Championship season, Leeds’ automatic promotion push was stumbling due in part to Patrick Bamford’s goals drying up. He needed one to go in off his derrière, which is pretty much what happened during a 4-3 win at Middlesbrough. You could say it’s partly hip, partly backside, but surely it’s sufficiently rear-end to count! I recall saying to a fellow Leeds-supporting friend during the match how funny it was that he’d literally got one to go in off his backside and fulfilled the cliche.”

Knowledge archive

“Where and when was the term ‘shithousery’ first used, and do other languages have a word for it?” asked Brian in 2022.

Before we consider the contemporary phenomenon, we should probably look at how the word from which it is derived became part of the English language. According to our own John Ashdown, who wrote about the S-word during the 2018 World Cup, it can be traced back to Scouse slang used in the 1960s. The Concise New Partridge Dictionary of Slang has an entry for “shithouse”, with definitions “an extremely unpleasant individual” and “a coward”.

It had certainly reached the east Midlands by the 1970s. In Duncan Hamilton’s wonderful book Provided You Don’t Kiss Me, he talks about Brian Clough’s penchant for using the word. “The phone rang. ‘Where are you, shithouse?’ asked Clough. (He used the word ‘shithouse’ as frequently as other people use ‘please’ and ‘thank you’. ‘It’s an affectionate term,’ he’d explain – though he didn’t always use it that way)”. It also appears in most of the Clough stories told by Mark Crossley in his hilarious Undr the Cosh interview.

Jack Charlton was equally fond of the phrase. In 1990, during a prescient observation about how the media might ruin Paul Gascoigne, he said: “Journalists … they’re all shithouses, them”. A couple of years earlier, he said during an interview there was no room for “shithouses” in his Republic of Ireland squad.

View image in fullscreen Jack Charlton issues a few choice words to his Republic of Ireland team at the 1994 World Cup. Photograph: Peter Robinson/Alamy/PA Images

John Hartson, then at Arsenal, was sent off against Middlesbrough in January 1997 after calling the referee, Mike Reed, “a shithouse”. But the neologism of shithousery only emerged in the 21st century. “The word does not (yet) feature in the Oxford English Dictionary,” writes the lexicographer John Williams, “but taking the ever-excellent Jonathon Green’s Dictionary of Slang as a baseline, we see that his earliest citation is from 2014, with Nicolás Otamendi as the alleged culprit.

“As this is a Twitter citation, I looked back further. The first football personality accused appears to be Arsène Wenger in 2011, the accusation coming from the Guardian’s own Daniel Harris.”

It started to become a wider part of the football lexicon in the 2010s, most notably when, according to one Arsenal fan, Crystal Palace “bantered us off for 90 minutes with shithousery”. Arsenal actually won 2-1, so goodness knows what he’d have said had they lost.

Can you help?

“AIK and Brommapojkarna contested an 11-goal thriller in the Allsvenskan league, with Brommapojkarna winning 6-5. Remarkably, all goals came in the second half. Is this the highest-scoring match where every goal was scored in the same half?” asks Kári Tulinius.

“As a Maidenhead United fan (National League South, the sixth tier of English football, since you ask), I was delighted when our marauding wing-back Jordon Ragguette recently received an international call-up for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines,” writes Adie Bradshaw. “Jordon was on the winning side in all four of their recent Concacaf Nations League games, which gives him a 100% win record in international football. This made me wonder: are there any players with 10 or more international caps who have a 100% win record?”

“In a Vietnamese league match against Nam Dinh in 2022, the home side Hai Phong had a goal ruled out for handball by video replay – even though VAR wouldn’t come to Vietnam until 2023. There was a giant TV screen in the stadium, and the referee happened to see an instant replay of the goal. Has there ever been another situation like this, where the referee didn’t have VAR, but another source of video replay helped them to reverse a decision?” asks Duc Tran Anh.

Sports.title: Tottenham’s forgotten man Richarlison scores for under-21s: ‘I was missing it’
Sports.content:
Tottenham’s forgotten man Richarlison has been hailed for his “immaculate” attitude after he scored for the club’s under-21s on Tuesday night. Richarlison has not played for Spurs’ senior side since an opening-day defeat at Brentford on 22 August after he was left out of the 25-man Premier League squad list, having been told he was not part of first-team plans for this season.

Failed moves to Trabzonspor and Vasco da Gama, after talks with Everton collapsed in the final days before the transfer window in England shut, have left Richarlison in limbo for the first half of the campaign. However, the Brazil international earned himself fans after he made a surprise appearance in the Jersey Mike’s (EFL) Trophy tie at Cheltenham. Richarlison, 29, scored after 56 minutes in a 2-2 draw and converted a spot-kick in a 7-6 penalty shootout loss for Wayne Burnett’s side.

The Cheltenham manager, Steve Cotterill, as quoted by Gloucestershire Live, said: “We weren’t expecting it, but it was good. When I found out he was on the team sheet, I was actually chuffed with that. I was really pleased. It gives our lads a glimpse of what it’s like at that top level.

“To be fair to him, with a lot of talk about our lads playing against him, Richarlison’s attitude was immaculate tonight. He was really, really good and his attitude was great. He could have easily come down here and thought: ‘I am not too bothered about tonight.’ We had a decent crowd here, but he’s used to playing in front of 60,000 every week – when he gets picked anyway! It was great for our lads to play against someone of his stature. It’s good and I really enjoyed tonight.”

After Richarlison’s fine first-time finish in the 56th minute, Tottenham’s academy players joined the Brazilian in performing his pigeon celebration. He later posted on Instagram: “Happy to do what I love the most in life. I was missing it!” Roberto De Zerbi and the rest of the Spurs squad are in Marbella for warm weather training.

Sports.title: Timber’s touch of class and supersub Saka secure Arsenal win against Lille
Sports.content:
Twelve wins in a row and counting. On a night when Arsenal remembered Ken Friar – the club’s life president who was instrumental in their move from Highbury to the Emirates in 2006 – it was fitting that Mikel Arteta’s side should rack up yet another Champions League milestone at their home that has become a fortress.

Such has Arsenal’s dominance been here in recent seasons that when Bukayo Saka slotted home their third against a dogged Lille side, it was the 36th goal they have scored at the Emirates in the league or group stage since returning to Europe’s top table under Arteta three years ago. In those 12 wins, they have remarkably conceded only three times.

Arsenal have also now racked up 14 successive league-stage victories in this competition – three short of Bayern Munich’s record – even if Arteta’s side were made to work for this one and had to wait until the 64th minute to find the breakthrough. That came from the unlikely source of Jurriën Timber after Arsenal’s second-string attack – and Viktor Gyökeres in particular – had looked laboured. But while Arteta may be concerned that it needed the introduction of Saka from the bench along with Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz to put this game to bed as Eberechi Eze added a second before Saka rounded off the scoring with a third in the space of seven minutes, they never looked in any danger of losing their proud record as Olivier Giroud received a standing ovation on his return to north London.

“I’m sure he is very happy to see how the boys played. But not only that, because I know how proud he felt about what we built,” said Arteta of Friar. “It’s a really sad day for everyone who loves football. The legacy that Ken is going to leave for this club is going to be for ever.”

Arsenal had earlier paid tribute to Friar, who worked his way up from the box office to club secretary before becoming managing director in the 1980s, when his death at the age of 92 was confirmed. The players wore black armbands as a mark of respect. Friar would have been especially proud of their formidable record here under Arteta in this competition that stretches back to the 2023-24 season, when they returned to the tournament after an absence of six years. It is little wonder that Arteta was so reluctant for redevelopment plans to go ahead given the disruption any temporary move away to Wembley or elsewhere would have caused.

Despite the absence of Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi after they were both injured during the warm-down after the victory over Leeds on Saturday, the Arsenal manager was still able to make five changes. Lille’s manager, Davide Ancelotti, who worked under his father, Carlo, at Everton and Real Madrid among others before being appointed during the summer in only his second senior role, resisted the temptation to start with 40-year-old Giroud against his former club.

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka slots home Arsenal’s third goal from close range. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Restored to his favoured right flank after excelling on the left against Leeds, it had not been saying much that Noni Madueke had once again been Arsenal’s most dangerous outlet in a first half in which they struggled to create much against a deep-lying defence.

Bruno Guimarães and then Mikel Merino spurned decent chances, while Ayase Ueda had the ball in David Raya’s net after Nabil Bentaleb’s shot deflected off Timber and hit Hákon Haraldsson on the way through, with the video assistant referee confirming the Japan striker was marginally offside.

But Arsenal lacked creativity without Ødegaard and Gyökeres showing plenty of hustle and bustle yet making little real impact.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It summed Arsenal’s first half up when he could not get out of the way after Eze forced Berke Ozer into his first proper save and was promptly flagged offside. Ozer then had to scramble the ball away from the feet of the Sweden striker after spilling a shot from Guimarães on the stroke of half-time.

The referee, Felix Zwayer, waved away appeals at the start of the second half when Guimarães went down in the area under pressure from Alexsandro but the Arsenal midfielder seemed to be looking for the contact. A wayward effort that almost made it into the upper tier from Madueke was the signal for Arteta to summon Ødegaard, Saka and Havertz to get ready.

Before they had time to be introduced, Arsenal finally found the breakthrough when Madueke picked out Timber to apply a deft finish with his right foot after a brilliant first touch. Saka made an immediate impact by setting up Eze to dispatch the second with his left foot – possibly with the help of a deflection – less than three minutes later, before adding a third after combining with Havertz and Ødegaard. Lille must have wondered what had hit them.

As well as the chance to pay their respects to Giroud, the Arsenal fans were treated to a late cameo from the dazzling Max Dowman to round off another very satisfying evening that has become the norm.

Sports.title: Championship roundup: Swansea’s win at Millwall marred by alleged racist abuse of Eom Ji-sung
Sports.content:
Swansea’s last-gasp 1-0 win at Millwall was held up for almost seven minutes after an allegation of racist abuse from the crowd towards Eom Ji-sung was reported by Swansea to officials.

The referee, Edward Duckworth, halted the match in the 65th minute and walked to the dugouts to speak with Alex Neil, the Millwall’s manager, Swansea’s manager, Vítor Matos, and the fourth official, Ruebyn Ricardo. A security guard was also on the scene, with Duckworth seeming to point to an area in the stands behind the Swansea dugout.

When play resumed it was announced in the stadium that there had been a report of racist chanting and that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.

Matos confirmed the player in question was the South Korean Eom, who was warming up. Neil said: “It’s been reported and it’s not acceptable.”

“As a club we condemn racism and discrimination in all forms, and there is no place for such behaviour in football or in society,” Swansea said. “The club wants to place on record its thanks for the swift and decisive manner in which the match officials, Millwall Football Club and the police dealt with the incident. We will now follow all protocols and processes and provide whatever assistance we can to all parties as the incident is investigated. We stand with Ji-sung, and he has our unstinting love and support.”

Millwall said: “Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action. [We are] working alongside the relevant authorities to establish the facts and unable to comment further as [the] alleged incident is the subject of an ongoing police investigation, which the club fully supports.”

View image in fullscreen Ronald (left) celebrates scoring a late winner for Swansea in their game at Millwall, which was suspended for almost seven minutes. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA

The substitute Ronald scored a last-minute winner to keep Swansea top of the Championship.

The Brazilian defender Neto Borges scored in injury-time after earlier scoring an own goal as Middlesbrough secured a 3-2 victory over Stoke. It was his first league goal for 18 months and Boro stay second in the table after stretching their unbeaten run to five games.

Callum Brittain had fired the visitors ahead three minutes into the second half before Junior Tchamadeu’s shot deflected in off Borges for an unfortunate own goal soon afterwards.

The England Under-21 striker Will Lankshear restored the visitors’ lead with his eighth league goal in 10 games after the Stoke keeper, Viktor Johansson, spilled Amario Cozier-Duberry’s left-foot strike from the edge of the area. It took the striker to the top of the Championship scoring charts.

Substitute Robert Bozenik looked to have earned the home side a point, slotting home after Luke Ayling’s poor clearance with five minutes left, but Borges scored from close range in the first of four minutes of stoppage time.

View image in fullscreen Neto Borges fires in Middlesbrough’s winner. Photograph: Nigel French/PA

Watford’s woeful season took another turn for the worse as they conceded four first-half goals in a 5-1 defeat at Cardiff to drop into the relegation zone.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Jack Moylan scored twice in the first half, winning and converting an 11th-minute penalty and then picking his spot to beat Federico Ravaglia in a one-on one in the 35th.

Mattie Pollock had brought down Moylan for the penalty and then headed into his own net from a corner in the 41st minute before Ollie Tanner added the fourth in the fifth minute of first-half added time.

Birmingham underlined their growing promotion credentials with a commanding 4-0 victory over 10-man Preston at St Andrew’s. Two goals from August Priske and one each for Liam Millar and Demarai Gray gave them a third win in four games. Preston, who played most of the second half with 10 men, remain rooted to the bottom of the table.

Ivan Mesik scored a last-gasp leveller for Charlton to clinch a 2-2 draw at Burnley, extending the hosts’ 360-day wait for a home league win. Largie Ramazani’s 57th-minute goal put Burnley into a 2-1 lead at Turf Moor, but Mesik equalised with virtually the last kick of an absorbing contest.

West Brom staged a late revival to beat Wrexham 2-1 at Stōk Cae Ras. Kieffer Moore’s stunning second-half strike gave Wrexham hope they could claim back-to-back home wins for the first time since February. But West Brom scored twice in five minutes through Isaac Price and Aune Heggebo to stop the rot after derby defeats to Wolves and Birmingham.

Wolves suffered their first home league defeat of the season as Bolton won 3-1 at Molineux. Atsuki Ito gave the visitors a deserved 28th-minute lead and although Jean-Ricner Bellegarde equalised five minutes after the break, substitute Sam Dalby and Josh Sheehan struck in the last 20 minutes to seal victory.

A magnificent goalkeeping display from Balazs Toth inspired Blackburn to a 1-0 victory over Bristol City at Ashton Gate. Toth made a string of outstanding saves, particularly in the first half. Oladapo Afolayan rifled home the only goal in the 38th minute.

Sports.title: Potter helps England find magic but World Cup playoff format needs rethink | Tom Garry
Sports.content:
If there had been a vidiprinter at the King Power Stadium displaying the aggregate scorelines from the night’s Women’s World Cup qualifying playoffs around Europe, it might have looked more at home on the cricket scoreboard just over a mile further south at Leicestershire’s Grace Road. Sweden 15-0 against Lithuania. Republic of Ireland 12-0 against Kazakhstan. Netherlands 11-0 against Hungary.

How much, therefore, could be gleaned from England’s 8-1 aggregate win against Greece? It was, irrefutably, a significantly better performance from England, on a night when they got some of their mojo back, they played with a zip and panache, but overall there was plenty to observe but very little new information. After 180 minutes of football and more than 3,000 miles travelled, to all who correctly guessed the outcome a week ago, congratulations, you were correct: the European champions were able to beat a team ranked outside the world’s top 50 over two legs.

It is tempting to wax lyrical about Lauren James’ first-half display and how she relished in her free role, finding space, driving England up the pitch and toying with the defenders – truly, she can be the difference-maker in this Lionesses side next summer – but, when Greece aren’t attempting to mark one of the best forwards in the world, should we be surprised that she delivered two goals and an assist?

It is similarly tempting to eulogise about the impressive debut of Lexi Potter, who looked at home in the midfield to such an extent that you could be forgiven for thinking it was her 50th cap rather than her first. The 20-year-old, whose intelligent positional awareness, tidy passing and steady tempo allowed those around her to flourish higher up the pitch, can be proud of her display and deserves another start in the next round of the playoffs against Ukraine. But anyone who has watched the Women’s Super League this season already knew Potter would be a terrific addition to this team.

We could also spend the next 24 hours praising the effectiveness of England’s new wingback system, comment on how adeptly Maya Le Tissier covered for the injured Lucy Bronze, praise the energy of Alessia Russo, rejoice in the debut handed to the London City Lionesses winger Freya Godfrey, who deserved her chance, or hail the ever-reliable goalscoring record of Georgia Stanway – even scoring with her head, at 5ft 5in – and examine how she fared in a higher role.

All of it, though, had to be taken with a great pinch of salt because the opponents were competing against the Faroe Islands and Georgia in League C of the qualifying groups, while England have won five games out of six in League A and must have wished they could have tested themselves against stronger opposition to try to prepare for next summer’s tournament.

Even the locals seemed to realise this was all something of a formality; more than 22,000 tickets were issued but the eventual attendance looked far lower, perhaps with lack of jeopardy surrounding the occasion playing a role in that.

View image in fullscreen Lauren James relished her free role, finding space, driving England up the pitch and toying with the defenders. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

The DJ at the King Power, one of the night’s star performers, tried their best to create a party atmosphere, as did the pitchside flameflowers pre-match and the exuberance of England’s forward line, but this was a tie that really did very little for the growth of the women’s game.

It was a rather good advert for the one-legged playoff ties used by men’s football in European qualification paths, single‑night matches with tension, competitiveness and a real edge to proceedings, as well as an efficient feel – it takes the men’s game a window to get through two rounds of playoffs, and the women’s game has another two matches still to go.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The meetings in November and December with Ukraine – a side whom England beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in this qualifying process – are unlikely to feel any more challenging.

That is no fault of England, Greece, nor Ukraine, but rather that of a growing sport still trying to figure out how to develop a qualification system with real balance. When qualifying for the 2023 World Cup, England cruised to 20-0 and 10-0 wins over Latvia.

The group stage this time, mirroring the new Nations League format, felt much improved, but as the home fans at the King Power felt the need to break into a Mexican wave after just 22 minutes of this second leg, it became clear that the playoffs still need further thought.

Sports.title: ‘Passenger’ – Michael Carrick urged to make seismic decision and drop Man United star
Sports.content:
Manchester United cannot afford to 'carry' Bruno Fernandes against Leeds United on Sunday.

That is according to talkSPORT's chief football correspondent Alex Crook following the Red Devils' latest defeat.

3 United have been warned they cannot continue to 'carry' Fernandes Credit: Getty

United were beaten 2-0 by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday night.

Michael Carrick has now been urged to drop his captain for their upcoming trip to Elland Road.

His side are winless in their last five off the back of their latest reverse, which also saw Leny Yoro sent off in the second half.

The Red Devils have not tasted victory since beating Sabah at Old Trafford on September 10.

United urged to drop Fernandes

Crook believes it is now time to take Fernandes out of the side in order for the midfielder to regain full fitness.

Speaking to Adrian Durham on Kick Off after the defeat to Atletico, he explained: "I don’t think he’s fit.

"He missed games for Portugal during the international break. He hasn’t looked himself.

"I think the biggest call that Michael Carrick could make right now and it would be huge to leave his captain out.

"Apart from the game against Ipswich, he’s not putting numbers on the board. I would take him out of the team against Leeds at the weekend."

Fernandes picked up an injury on international duty with Portugal last month which caused him to miss their win over Norway.

3 Crook believes Fernandes is not fully fit amid his recent United form Credit: Getty

However, he returned to the side just four days later against Denmark, a match in which he provided two assists.

Meanwhile, his only Premier League goal contributions this season came against Ipswich Town in August.

Crook continued: "They’re losing games with him in the team and, as I say, at the moment it seems to me like they’re carrying a passenger.

"Credit to Bruno Fernandes, he rarely misses games through injury, but he doesn’t look fit and if he’s not fit I just don’t think they can afford to carry him."

Fernandes has four goals and an assist to his name in all competitions this term.

Outside of his hat-trick against Ipswich, though, he has yet to find the target in the Premier League.

3 Fernandes has not scored in any of his last five United appearances Credit: Getty

The 32-year-old once again started in the Spanish capital on Tuesday, playing 80 minutes before being replaced by Matheus Cunha.

Fernandes is into the final year of his current United deal, although his contract includes the option of a further 12 months.

His slow start to the new season follows a record-breaking campaign last term.

The playmaker's 21 Premier League assists represented the most in a single campaign by a player along with nine goals across his 35 appearances as United finished third in the table.

Sports.title: Ex-Manchester United striker secures emergency transfer eight games into season
Sports.content:
Doncaster Rovers have secured the signing of former Manchester United striker Will Keane after special approval from the FA and EFL.

The League One side were granted special dispensation from the governing bodies to replace a current striker on their 22-man squad list.

2 Keane was a part of the Man United academy from the age of 11 Credit: Getty

Frankie Okoronkwo suffered a back injury and is now expected to be sidelined until January.

Manager Grant McCann had to move quickly to ensure he was strengthening his attacking options after the former Everton player was ruled out.

Keane brings a wealth of experience to the club having played in the Championship with the likes of Ipswich Town, Preston, and Sheffield Wednesday.

The forward has signed as a free agent after he was released from Preston this summer following a loan spell at Reading. The striker netted twice in 14 appearances last season.

The 33-year-old holds an impressive goalscoring record, scoring 26 league goals at Wigan in the 2021/22 season which helped the team to the League One title. He also claimed the division's Golden Boot.

Keane said: “I’m really excited for the challenge. It's been a long, long couple of months really waiting, so just really eager to get going now and looking forward to it.

“I had a really good chat with the gaffer last week. Obviously just speaking to him about how he sees me fitting into the team, what I can add.

“It's been great to see the team doing well of late and hopefully I can add to that and bring that experience to the group. I've been around for a while now, so I can add that and hopefully bring my quality and add goals to the team.”

Doncaster manager McCann added: "Will is a proven goalscorer at this level, having won the Golden Boot at Wigan and he’s also played in the Championship.

"He’s hungry to come in, play football and prove himself, and we’re really pleased to have him here. He’s been working hard to maintain his fitness, including completing a 12-week camp with the PFA.

2 Keane only made three appearances for the Man United first team during his time at Old Trafford Credit: Getty

"He’s continued training since then, and we’re looking forward to getting him working with the group. He’s a good option for us.

"Frankie has unfortunately suffered a setback just as he was getting close to returning, but we believe in him and see him as an important part of our long-term plans.

"We don’t need to rush him back. The priority is making sure he has the time and support he needs to recover fully, and this gives him the opportunity to focus on that without any added pressure.

"Will’s arrival gives us another option in attack. He’s a good character and a good footballer, and we believe he can make a positive contribution between now and January."

The Yorkshire-based outfit travel to Leicester City in League One on Saturday, with both sides currently sat on nine points.

Life at Man United

Keane's twin brother Michael Keane currently plays for Everton and is an England international.

Will became a Republic of Ireland international after a youth career with England.

Both brothers worked their way through the Man United academy, and were awarded three-year scholarships in July 2009.

Will made his senior debut in 2011 in a 3-2 defeat to Blackburn Rovers in the Premier League, coming on as a late substitute for Rafael.

He suffered a knee ligament injury during international duty with England Under-19s and was out for the entire 2012/13 season.

The striker had various loans over the next three years, including at Wigan, Queens Park Rangers, Sheffield Wednesday, and Preston North End until he eventually signed a permanent deal with Hull City.

Sports.title: Premier League star has weekend red card rescinded for ‘wrongful dismissal’
Sports.content:
The Football Association have announced that Pascal Struijk has had his red card for Brighton rescinded.

Struijk was sent off in the 57th minute of their 2-0 win at Sunderland on Saturday for denying Wilson Isidor a goal-scoring opportunity.

2 Struijk initially faced a one-match ban for his dismissal against Sunderland, but this has now been rescinded amid wrongful dismissal Credit: Getty

It meant he was set to miss the derby clash against Crystal Palace in the Premier League this weekend as part of a one-match ban.

However, this has now been overturned and Struijk is free to play for Brighton.

FA statement on Struijk red card

"An independent Regulatory Commission has upheld a claim of wrongful dismissal in relation to Pascal Struijk and moved his one-match suspension," a statement said.

"The Brighton & Hove Albion defender was sent off during the Premier League fixture against Sunderland on Saturday 10 October for denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity."

The Premier League's explanation for the dismissal was: "After VAR review, the referee issued a red card to Struijk for denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity (DOGSO).

"REF: 'After review, there is a foul by Brighton No.4, which denies Sunderland a goal-scoring opportunity. The final decision is a red card and a direct free-kick.'"

Despite having a one-man disadvantage, Brighton still went on to win all three points at Sunderland.

Maxim De Cuyper gave them the lead just four minutes before Struijk, who joined from Leeds United this summer, was dismissed.

Jaouen Hadjam then added the second in stoppage time as Brighton won their fourth match of the season.

Only Chelsea have beaten them in the 2026/27 campaign, whilst Leeds picked up a 1-1 draw at the beginning of September.

2 Brighton will now have Struijk available for selection for the visit of Palace in the derby on Sunday afternoon Credit: Getty

Victories have also come against Aston Villa, Coventry City, as well as reigning champions Arsenal.

Speaking after their win at Sunderland, head coach Fabian Hurzeler said: "I have to praise my players. I think it was a different performance (to Arsenal) because we had different circumstances.

"We had to face different adversities, but overall the players reacted really well. They defended really good as a team. Also, after the red card we had a really good defensive mindset.

"And on top of that, we had really good subs who made an impact when they came into the game.

"We showed that togetherness, and I think it was a deserved win.

"They really stick together, and they face adversity no matter how tough it is."

Sports.title: Millwall manager vents frustration over stoppage in play after racism allegation
Sports.content:
Swansea City's win at Millwall on Tuesday was marred by allegations of racist chants aimed at winger Eom Ji-sung.

The Championship match was stopped for around seven minutes following the incident.



4 Eom was subjected to alleged racist chants during Swansea's win at Millwall Credit: Getty

Eom had been warming up with his fellow substitutes when he was allegedly targeted by the home crowd.

Referee Richard Duckworth immediately stopped play once made aware of the complaint before speaking to both sets of coaches.

An announcement was subsequently made over the PA system inside The Den informing supporters that police were working to identify any offenders using CCTV.



Alex Neil frustrated with delay

Millwall manager Alex Neil spoke to talkSPORT after the match, venting his frustration over the length of the stoppage in play.

It is not clear whether Neil was aware the complaint was about racist chanting at the time of his interview.



He told talkSPORT's Ian Abrahams: "There are rules in place, obviously, because there was an incident reported.

"The referee tells me he needs to speak to the safety officer and the safety officer comes down. By the time he speaks to the safety officer, the game restarts.



"My frustration is that nothing is getting dealt with at that point. We know there has been a complaint. The fourth official has got these documents and all that sort of stuff. Why stop the game for 15 minutes [sic]?

"You’re not going to solve it then. Once it’s been reported, I understand them coming over. Tell the fourth official, note that down, ‘this is what happened, blah, blah, blah.’ Get on with the game.

"That’s what I think should have happened. If we had won later on, I might not feel that way right now, let’s be honest, but as it stands just now, it’s frustrating.

4 Neil was left frustrated by the length of the stoppage in play Credit: Getty



"We had good momentum in the game. That incident now takes all the momentum out of the game, basically."

When asked which team the alleged abuse had been aimed at, Neil asked: "Who's saying racist chanting?" before adding: "I don't know," when informed it had been displayed on the stadium's big screen.

Millwall statement

Meanwhile, Millwall released a statement on social media following the match.

Writing on X, the club said: "Millwall Football Club is aware of an alleged, individual incident of discriminatory abuse towards a Swansea City player during the second-half of Tuesday evening's Sky Bet Championship match.



"The club operates a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of discriminatory abuse. Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action.

"The club is working alongside the relevant authorities to establish the facts and is unable to comment further as tonight’s alleged incident is the subject of an ongoing police investigation, which the club fully supports."

4 Both sets of coaches were spoken to by the officials during the delay Credit: Getty

Swansea boss Vitor Matos praised the referee and Millwall for their handling of the incident at full-time.



Speaking to Abrahams, he explained: "The main thing is what the players felt in that moment and what the people around him felt in that moment.

"I think that made the referee follow the protocol, which is important in this type of case.

"Millwall did as well what a good club needs to do, that is announcing and then trying to make everyone aware of the situation."

Eom remained an unused substitute, but this was not as a result of the alleged chants, Matos confirmed.



The Portuguese added: "There’s nothing related with if the player is coming on or not.

4 Matos has praised the officials and Millwall for their handling of the incident Credit: Getty

"This is a situation that should not happen in this society. We stand with that. It’s nothing to do with the game."

He continued: "I think we should have already stopped, but football is a big, big part of the society and a big show for the world.



"Like in all parts of society there are still these situations, unfortunately for all of us.

"So when that happened we are here to stand with for the right things and the right thing today was to make the complaint, follow the protocol and then evaluate the situation."

Swansea went on to claim a 1-0 victory thanks to Ronald's 90th minute winner.

The win leaves the Swans a point clear of Middlesbrough at the top of the table having lost just one of their opening 10 matches.



Matos' side will go in search of a fifth successive victory at home to West Ham United on Saturday.

Sports.title: Man United board rocked as senior players side with Lisandro Martinez over explosive outburst
Sports.content:
Senior Manchester United players share Lisandro Martinez's frustrations with the hierarchy, talkSPORT understands.

Martinez called out sporting director Jason Wilcox over a lack of squad strengthening following Tuesday's 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid in a bombshell post-match interview.



2 Martinez did not hold back on his assessment of United as he called out the board for their transfer business Credit: Getty

2 Wilcox [left] is the man chiefly responsible for Man United's transfer business and finds himself in the firing line from senior stars Credit: Getty

talkSPORT has been told the Argentine is by no means the only United star unhappy with a perceived lack of ambition at board level with sporting director Wilcox firmly in their firing line.

There is a sense Wilcox missed the opportunity to build on the momentum of the second half of last season by only bringing in three midfielders in the summer when other areas of the squad were in need of additions.



Caption Bruno Fernandes has been visibly frustrated during United's poor recent run and doubts remain over his long-term future at the club.

What did Martinez say?

"It was really poor, really poor," Martinez told Amazon Prime minutes after the full-time whistle in Madrid.



"I have to control myself a lot. But sometimes it's a reflection of our club at the moment. We did it last season and now we expect more from the top.

"To bring more players, to compete. Other teams bring in many more players. I expect more from everyone… 100 per cent I expected more from our technical director.



"I have to be honest and also the players have to do more but it's just important when you make a strong squad for this type of night."

Martinez added: "Last season we created a base to build an amazing team. It's annoying and disappointing to come here and I'm not seeing my team get an amazing result here."
