World.title: Ruto wades into growing ODM-UDA conflict
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto marks Mazingira Day by planting trees in Elgon downs, Trans-Nzoia County. [PCS]

President William Ruto delved into the growing tension among Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) and United Democratic Alliance (UDA) contenders in the Coast and asked them to tone it down during his recent tour of the region.

Speaking hours before he wound up his eight-day tour, Ruto appeared to notice the widening cracks and told politicians within the two parties to embrace a ceasefire and unite against the opposition.

The head of state, who is facing a formidable challenge from the united opposition, warned that divisions in the ODM and UDA could weaken their team, whose union gives it a chance to win the 2027 general election.

“ODM and UDA are one team, and you should accommodate each other under a broad-based government. We should not allow divisions in ODM and UDA to undermine our unity of purpose,” he stated.

His statement appeared to be directed at the growing tensions among contenders, particularly in Kwale, Mombasa and Kilifi counties where prominent politicians face challengers within the ODM and UDA political union.

President Ruto’s earlier attempt to zone the region in favour of sitting governors is also blamed for the cracks in the broad-based team at the Coast.

In Mombasa County, UDA secretary general Mr Hassan Omar has already rejected a plan by the so-called broad-based team to support governor Abdulswamd Nassir’s re-election.

Omar, who is also a member of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) insisted that he will challenge Mr Nassir.

Already, businessman and EALA member Mr Suleiman Shahbal has quit ODM after he left he could not get the party ticket as the president's allies favour Nassir, a deputy party leader.

Shhabal has since aligned himself to former Laikipia governor Mr Murithi Nderitu’s Kenya Reform Party even as he insisted that he will be on the ballot.

In Mombasa, Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Mr Hassan Joho and governor Nassir appeared to be handing over Coast which was the ODM leader late Raila Odinga’s political turf, to President Ruto.

“This region stands with Ruto because he has dignified us with title deeds and many other development projects. We however expect him to support us when we seek the presidential seat in 2032,” Joho said.

Joho’s elder brother Abubakar Joho, who is a prominent businessman, has also joined the campaign for President Ruto.

While touring Kwale, Ruto addressed the growing noise among the main contenders, Governor Fatuma Achani (UDA), Prof Hamadi Boga and Engineer Lung’anzi Chai (ODM) after the broad-based leaders appeared to settle for Ms Achani who has the backing of Sports CS and former Kwale governor Salim Mvurya.

After witnessing the rising political tension, Ruto changed tone and told the three contenders to directly seek support from the voters rather than relying on external political backing.

In a complete change of heart and political tact, Ruto emphasised that the power to choose leaders ultimately belongs to the electorate, who will evaluate candidates based on their track record and development agenda for the region.

“You should all seek votes from the people and not rely on external backing. What I need from all of you is your support,” he stated.

For long, Governor Achani has enjoyed unwavering backing of President Ruto, Mvurya and recently Joho, who had preferred Kwale to be zoned in favour of the governor and UDA.

But Prof Boga, who has been Mr Joho’s ally, described the broad-based government’s zoning arrangement as undemocratic and a coercion to the Kwale electorate who he said should be allowed to choose their leaders without external interference.

Boga has been critical about the attempt to stop some aspirants from contesting seats in the broad-based government, noting that it was possible to zone candidates and difficult to do so for the voters.

In a statement, Boga noted that former Gender CS and Kilifi governor aspirant Ms Aisha Jumwa’s recent departure from UDA to Wiper Patriotic Front (WPF) reflected a growing sense among a segment of coastal leaders that decisions about their political future are increasingly being made elsewhere, then handed down as settled outcomes rather than negotiated realities.

“Zoning at the Coast is a fantasy: You can zone candidates but you cannot zone the voters,” Boga had warned.

“And if UDA and ODM are not paying attention to that signal, they may be underestimating the political consequences of their emerging arrangements at the Coast. “There is a dangerous assumption taking root in the broad-based arrangement: that coastal politics can be settled around a table in Nairobi and then delivered to voters as a finished political package. You take this seat, we take that one, and the voters will follow,” he added.

Boga, who came second in the 2022 governor poll, warned that if the Coast is mishandled, the problem will not necessarily be that voters have suddenly embraced another political formation, but the greater danger is that voters may decide that none of the established arrangements speak for them, creating either a rebellion or apathy.

In Kilifi County, the broad-based team publicly worked with Governor Gideon Mung’aro, forcing Ms Jumwa, his main challenger, to quit the government team in protest.

Kilifi Senate aspirant Mr Stephen Kahocho and Ganze parliamentary aspirant Ms Zawadi Kingi have publicly warned that they might be forced to quit UDA and vie as independent candidates or join other political formations.

This is after it emerged that the broad-based arrangement was behind Mung’aro (ODM), Kilifi senator Stewart Madzayo (ODM) and Ganze MP Kenneth Kazungu Tungule of Pamoja African Alliance (PAA), an affiliate of UDA.

World.title: Kalonzo to Ruto: You have no numbers
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka speaks during launch of economic empowerment equipment distribution at Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos town on October 9, 2026. [John Muia, Standard]

The united opposition will deal President William Ruto a humiliating defeat in next year’s general election, Wiper Party leader Kalonzo Musyoka has predicted.

Speaking Friday in his Ukambani backyard during an empowerment equipment handover ceremony hosted by Governor Wavinya Ndeti at the Kenyatta Stadium in Machakos, Kalonzo declared the opposition will defeat Ruto at the ballot ‘no matter what magic he (Ruto) deploys.

“Ruto has been cornered. We have heard him suggesting that they will import foreigners from neighboring countries to vote for him but even so, he will not secure the numbers. We in the united opposition have committed to produce a single candidate that will face Ruto at the ballot,” Kalonzo said.

Recognizing the need to consolidate his lower Eastern vote bloc, Kalonzo rallied the Akamba community to come out in huge numbers to register as voters in the upcoming voter listing initiative by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).

“It is the time to redeem this country. The IEBC will as from next month undertake the final leg of voter registration and I urge all eligible voters to apply for national identity cards and register as voters,” he said, vowing he will defeat Ruto in Luo Nyanza.

Kalonzo called out Ruto over what he termed as the president’s habit of making empty promises to Kenyans. “The other day I heard Ruto promising thousands of dams across the country. He should come for benchmarking in Machakos. Retired President Mwai Kibaki and I secured African Development Bank (ADB) funding for the construction of Yatta Dam and now he has ten months left in office. When will he build?” he posed.

Former Attorney General Justin Muturi, who flanked Kalonzo, declared time was fast running out for the opposition to identify and name its presidential flag bearer for the next year’s general election.

The DP party leader, who has gone public declaring his choice of Kalonzo as the presidential ticket bearer for the opposition expressed his frustrations for the opposition’s dillydallying in naming its flag bearer.

“We (the opposition) are tired of singing one song for years that we will produce and name one person to face Ruto. When you see us here another day, do not entertain such kind of talk. Demand that it is Kalonzo for State House,” said Muturi.

During the ceremony, Governor Wavinya Ndeti unveiled assorted empowerment equipment targeting about 6000 beneficiaries across the county.

Addressing residents during the forum, Wavinya jeered at UDA-allied politicians who have been dishing out cash handouts to residents, terming it untenable.

“It is time to demonstrate to those who are approaching our people with cheap hand-outs that when the people of Machakos are given the tools to work, they produce real wealth. My commitment is that I will continue allocating resources to asset-based empowerment until every household in Machakos enjoys economic dignity,” Wavinya said.

World.title: Revealed: 84 Kenyans killed, 52 missing in Russia-Ukraine war
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi. [File,Standard]

The government has records of 354 Kenyans linked to the Russia-Ukraine war, including 84 classified as killed or missing in action and five being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine.

Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi gave the updated figures in a response to Parliament on the recruitment of Kenyans into the Russian military and the detention of Kenyans in Ukraine on Thursday, October 8.

The records show that 77 Kenyans remain on the front lines, 38 are in camps, 52 have an unknown or unclassified location and 34 are hospitalised.

Another 62 Kenyans have been repatriated, while one is in detention and another has completed a military contract.

The government said Russia has stopped the enlistment of additional Kenyans after Kenya secured the country’s placement on Russia’s ‘Stop List’ during Mudavadi’s visit to Moscow in March.

“The Embassy of Kenya in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyan nationals have been enlisted in the Special Military Operation following the implementation of the Stop List,” Mudavadi said.

Russian authorities have told Kenya that requests to terminate military contracts will be considered on a case-by-case basis by individual military unit commanders.

Mudavadi said Kenya continues to engage Russian authorities and affected families over the burial, cremation or repatriation of remains after Russia said its Defence Ministry could not meet the cost of repatriating the remains of deceased Kenyans.

Five Kenyans held in Ukraine

Five Kenyan nationals are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, according to information sent to Kenya by the Ukrainian Embassy in Vienna on September 3.

The government identified them as Evans Kibet, detained since May 2025; Willi Muniu Macharia, detained since November 2025; Haron Kibet Pachenge, detained since March 2026; Joseph, detained since April 2026; and Francis Ndarua Ndungu.

Kenya’s Honorary Consul in Ukraine visited the Zakhid 1 prisoner-of-war camp and reported that the detainees were being held in humane conditions, had access to medical services and were being treated under rules governing prisoners of war.

The government also said Ukraine was holding the remains of four other Kenyans.

They are Simon Gitau, Clinton Nyapara Mogesa, Dennis Bagaka Obwori and Eric Mwangi Nyambura.

Kenya is seeking the release and repatriation of the affected Kenyans through diplomatic channels, including engagement with Ukraine and the International Committee of the Red Cross.

The government wants Kenyans held as prisoners of war to be considered as possible victims of international human trafficking.

Mudavadi said many of the affected Kenyans reported that recruiters lured them with promises of employment before they ended up in military service.

The government says the circumstances surrounding their recruitment could fit the definition of trafficking under Article 3(a) of the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, also known as the Palermo Protocol.

It wants the issue considered during negotiations over their repatriation so the Kenyans can access assistance available to trafficking victims.

President William Ruto has also raised the matter directly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a telephone conversation, according to the government.

Kenya has further received approval from Kyiv for its ambassador to Ukraine, with the government saying this will improve its ability to respond to cases involving Kenyans in the country.

The State Department for Diaspora Affairs said families should report cases to the government as soon as communication with relatives in Russia is disrupted.

Once a family reports a case, the department collects identification details, travel information and next-of-kin contacts before referring the case to the Kenyan Embassy in Moscow for verification.

The government has also facilitated the return of 62 Kenyans who had been involved in Russia’s military operations.

It has provided affected families with updates from diplomatic missions, information on compensation processes, psychosocial support and guidance on the repatriation or burial of remains.

The government said it is also expanding measures to prevent deceptive recruitment by providing pre-departure information, urging Kenyans to verify recruitment agencies and employment offers and strengthening emergency assistance through Kenyan diplomatic missions.

The scale of the recruitment first emerged publicly in February when Parliament was told that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been recruited to fight for Russia.

The National Intelligence Service report presented to lawmakers said recruiters targeted former security personnel and civilians with promises of lucrative employment, salaries and bonuses.

The figures at the time included 89 Kenyans on the frontline, 39 hospitalised, 28 missing in action, 35 in camps or bases, 30 repatriated, one detained and one who had completed a contract.

The government then stepped up diplomatic efforts. In March, Kenya announced an agreement with Russia to stop further enlistment of Kenyans into its military operations and to facilitate consular support and voluntary disengagement for Kenyans already serving.

The issue remains unresolved for many families. More than 30 families affected by the recruitment were reported this week to be seeking a meeting with President Ruto before Kenya's delegation travels to Moscow for the Russia-Africa Summit, demanding answers on missing relatives, repatriation of survivors and the return of remains.

World.title: Al-Azhar condemns Riyadh Airport attack, targeting of civilians, Umrah pilgrims
World.content:
Al-Azhar has strongly condemned the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which left civilians and Umrah pilgrims dead and injured, stressing that attacks on civilian infrastructure and pilgrims visiting Islam’s two holiest mosques constitute a grave provocation to Muslims, a violation of humanitarian values and international norms, and a direct threat to Saudi Arabia’s security and territorial integrity.

In a statement, Al-Azhar reiterated its unequivocal rejection of repeated attacks that have claimed innocent civilian lives and undermined the Kingdom’s security and stability.

It warned of the consequences of continued aggression, emphasizing that safeguarding regional security requires an immediate halt to such attacks and full respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states.

Grand Imam of Al-Azhar Ahmed al-Tayyeb extended his heartfelt condolences to Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz, Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques; Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; the Saudi people; and the families of the victims.

He prayed for the victims to be granted Allah’s mercy and forgiveness, wished the injured a speedy recovery, and asked Allah Almighty to protect the Kingdom of the Two Holy Mosques and all Muslim countries from harm and adversity, and to ensure the continued security, peace and stability of their peoples.

World.title: FM calls for further efforts to prevent regional conflict from widening
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty emphasized the importance of intensifying efforts to achieve de-escalation, contain regional tensions and prevent the conflict from widening, in a way that safeguards regional security and stability.

In an interview with Sky News Arabia, Abdelatty also discussed developments in the Iranian file and their implications for regional security.

He addressed key regional issues, including Egypt-Gulf relations and ways to strengthen coordination and consultation on current challenges.

The interview also covered developments in the Gaza Strip, Egyptian water security as an existential issue and the situation in Sudan.

World.title: FM highlights Egypt’s efforts to de-escalate US-Iran tensions
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty outlined Egypt’s efforts to de-escalate regional tensions and create conditions for an agreement between the United States and Iran, as well as the conflict’s economic repercussions for the global economy, supply chains and energy markets.

In an interview with Thailand’s CNA television channel, Abdelatty discussed prospects for Egyptian-Thai relations and ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation across various fields, during his visit to Thailand — the first by an Egyptian foreign minister in 30 years — as Egypt seeks to expand its partnerships with Asian countries.

The minister also outlined Egypt’s assessment of the challenges facing the global economy amid mounting pressures, stressing the importance of stronger international cooperation and a greater role for international financial institutions in providing concessional financing.

Such financing would support developing countries’ efforts to achieve sustainable development and address current economic challenges, he said.

World.title: FM highlights expats’ role in strengthening Egypt’s global standing
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty said Egyptians living abroad represent an extension of their homeland and contribute their expertise and skills to enhancing Egypt’s image and standing internationally.

Abdelatty made the remarks during a meeting with members of the Egyptian community in Thailand on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of his visit to Bangkok. The meeting was attended by Egyptian Ambassador to Thailand Hala Youssef.

The minister praised the role of Egyptians residing in Thailand in strengthening ties and communication between the two countries.

He reaffirmed the Foreign Ministry’s commitment to maintaining contact with Egyptian communities abroad, protecting their interests, addressing their needs and facilitating access to consular services.

In this regard, Abdelatty outlined the ministry’s efforts to modernize consular services and expand digital service delivery to simplify procedures and improve efficiency. He also highlighted initiatives for Egyptians abroad, including “Your Home in Egypt” and “Open Your Account in Egypt.”

The minister praised the Egyptian community’s participation in the seventh edition of the Conference of Egyptians Abroad, held in August 2026, and expressed hope that they would continue to participate actively in future editions.

He described the conference as a platform for direct dialogue and the exchange of views between Egyptians abroad and state institutions.

Abdelatty also listened to community members’ views and proposals on issues affecting their interests, stressing the importance of sustaining dialogue and developing communication channels to address their demands and aspirations.

World.title: Why billions spent on defense haven’t shielded Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
World.content:
Saudi Arabia spends tens of billions of dollars on defense every year, but is struggling to protect key assets such as airports, refineries and pipelines from missiles and drones fired by Houthi militants from Yemen.

Despite acquiring state-of-the-art weapons systems from the United States and Europe and possessing multi-layered air defenses, the kingdom has seen deadly attacks on the main airport serving the capital, Riyadh, over the past week.

Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.

But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides.

From the east, Iran fired about 1,000 missiles and drones at Saudi targets during the most intense part of the conflict this year. From the north, Iranian-backed militias in Iraq have sent drones to attack the country’s critical East-West oil pipeline. And from the south, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels fire missiles at the kingdom from shelters and mobile launchers in the mountains of Yemen.

Satellite imagery shows damage to the Saudi Arabia East-West pipeline following a drone attack, on September 22. Vantor/Reuters

Defending Saudi Arabia means protecting a vast network of targets, not just Riyadh or a single refinery. Its defenses must detect incoming threats, decide which to intercept and warn civilians, all within moments, according to Vision2030.ai, an independent website analyzing the kingdom’s economic transformation.

The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through. The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack, according to a Saudi source.

Houthi capabilities

The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses. The approach resembles Russia’s playbook: Moscow has frequently used a mass of drones along with cruise and ballistic missiles in barrages against Ukraine.

Cruise missiles fly at lower altitudes, making them harder to identify and track. The Houthis have also introduced a new generation of ballistic missiles that they claim are maneuverable.

No single air defense system can guarantee that every incoming threat will be intercepted.

But the Houthis have not done this alone.

Eight years ago, UN experts “identified missile remnants, related military equipment and military unmanned aerial vehicles that are of Iranian origin and were introduced into Yemen” despite an international arms embargo.

That same panel said two years ago that “the scale, nature and extent of transfers of diverse military material and technology provided to the Houthis from external sources, including financial support and training of its combatants, is unprecedented.”

Experts note that the latest Houthi missiles, such as the Hatem-2 and the Palestine-2, are very similar in design to Iranian weapons. They are fast and accurate.

Last year, a Houthi missile evaded Israel’s vaunted air defenses and impacted near Ben Gurion airport. Analyst Amir Bar Shalom told CNN at the time: “They were very accurate, and to be very accurate if you’re launching from 2,000 kilometers, it’s impressive.”

Yemen’s Houthi group hold a military parade in Sana’a, Yemen, on September 21, 2023. Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images

The Houthis have also modified Iranian air defense weapons to strike aircraft and cruise missiles, according to Brigadier General Majed al-Nazili, spokesperson for the Yemeni government forces.

“These missiles move around for a period of up to 25 minutes per missile and operate using a thermal-tracking system,” he said last month.

Will they listen to Tehran?

The Houthis have long been part of Iran’s ‘axis of resistance.’ While other allied groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and militias in Iraq have been significantly degraded, the Houthis have gone from strength to strength.

They continue to have a strong relationship with Tehran and sent a delegation to the funeral of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. But they also have their own agenda.

Seven years of conflict with Saudi Arabia between 2015 and 2022 caused immense suffering in Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, and an economic and transport embargo has continued since.

Ultimately, that led the Houthis in July to declare they would attack Saudi shipping in the Red Sea – and the campaign of missile strikes began soon afterwards, initially targeting an Aramco oil refinery on the Red Sea coast and Saudi airbases.

Smoke rises from the site of the Saudi Aramco refinery after reported Houthi attacks, south of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in this satellite image taken on October 3. European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-3/Reuters

The Houthis are demanding an end to Saudi airstrikes in support of government forces in Yemen, as well as billions of dollars in compensation from Saudi Arabia.

Whether in good faith or not, Iran has offered to mediate between Riyadh and the Houthis. On Monday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was ready to provide “any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen,” meaning the Houthis.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, claimed Monday that Riyadh had accepted mediation but the group had rejected truce proposals of two weeks and of one month.

“The battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena,” al-Bukhaiti said. “Every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow.”

Kingdom faces tough choices

Saudi Arabia has tried to project an image of “business as usual” even as the conflict with the Houthis intensified. Its civil defense authority stopped issuing public alerts by phone of incoming missiles and drones last week – before the series of deadly strikes on Riyadh airport.

Alerts have since resumed, according to several residents of Riyadh who spoke with CNN. Saudi authorities say three ballistic missiles were intercepted on Monday.

An expatriate resident of Riyadh told CNN their children were being schooled at home this week. The resident was upset on Saturday by the lack of automatic alerts for incoming missiles in the preceding days but said phone alerts were working effectively by Monday. They also expressed frustration at the Saudi authorities’ silence over the weekend about the strikes on Riyadh airport.

CNN has asked the Saudi authorities for a response on the absence of alerts.

Going forward, the kingdom faces tough choices. Accommodation with the Houthis after more than a dozen civilians were killed in the airport attacks would be unpalatable.

This image from CCTV video released by Saudi Arabia’s Media Ministry shows passengers taking cover as flames and smoke fill part of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday. Saudi Media Ministry/AP

Escalation, through even more intense airstrikes, would bring the risk of further missile attacks that would undermine the goal of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to make Saudi Arabia a world-class destination for investment, technology and tourism.

The stakes extend beyond the oil industry. Data centers, desalination plants and airports underpin the kingdom’s technology ambitions, water supply and tourism economy. The crown prince’s marquee investment event in Riyadh later this month will put his pitch to international investors in the spotlight.

But major corporations shied away this week from the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh.

Defeating the Houthi rebels through a ground offensive involving Yemeni government forces seems highly unlikely. The Houthis are entrenched, battle-hardened and know the mountainous terrain. They have inflicted heavy losses on government forces in the last month.

Last year, the US spent more than $1 billion on a seven-week campaign of air-strikes against the Houthis. The Houthis eventually agreed not to attack US shipping in the Red Sea but remained very much in place – and in the meantime shot down a number of highly advanced US Reaper drones.

Neither US nor Israeli strikes eliminated members of the Houthi leadership, even if commanders and technocrats were killed.

If anything, the Houthis, who may have as many as 350,000 men under arms, are on the front foot. They have now encircled the government-held city of Taiz, Yemen’s third largest and a vital logistical hub, the Institute for the Study of War said on Monday.

Saudi Arabia seeks support

Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud and Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, as well as ministers and military leaders from Turkey and Pakistan, attend the Mecca defense pact meeting between the three countries in Riyadh, on October 5. Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

The Saudis are seeking to mobilize an international coalition against the Houthis. Regional allies have offered help in the way of defensive systems. Pakistan has sent thousands of troops to help defend the kingdom. Egypt has offered whatever support is asked for.

The Saudis may also be able to procure more air defense systems from Europe and the US, after running down shipments delivered at the start of the conflict with Iran.

But the US itself is short of such systems. A report by the US Defense Department’s Inspector-General said the campaign against Iran had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”

And with mid-term elections three weeks away, US President Donald Trump is wary of yet another entanglement in the Middle East. He has been non-committal about direct US strikes against the Houthis, while not ruling them out.

“US reluctance to get involved stokes the perception that the United States has abandoned a partner at its moment of greatest need,” according to Michael Ratney at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

Writing before the airport strikes, Ratney – a former US ambassador in Riyadh – added: “The kingdom is under attack, and as a political matter, it has to retaliate. But ultimately, we should expect a return to diplomacy – imperfect, unsatisfying diplomacy that nonetheless deescalates the conflict.”

That may leave the Houthis in place, and in a stronger position inside Yemen.

CNN’s Nic Robertson contributed to this article.

World.title: Headquarters of Saudi Aramco hit as Houthis and Riyadh trade strikes
World.content:
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis traded fresh strikes on energy infrastructure, with the Iran-backed group again targeting the Saudi capital and appearing to hit the headquarters of Saudi state oil giant Aramco.

An administrative building belonging to Aramco in the Eastern Province city of Dhahran, where the company is headquartered, was targeted, according to Saudi authorities. It caused a limited fire, but it’s not clear if this was due to a direct hit or to falling debris. No injuries were reported.

The Saudi-led coalition also said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles and two drones targeting the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia. At least four people were injured from falling debris, according to Saudi authorities.

CNN has reached out to Aramco for comment.

It marked the latest escalation between the two sides, following a week of deadly Houthi missile and drone attacks that shut Riyadh’s main international airport.

The strikes also came just hours after Saudi Arabia attacked a key fuel depot on Tuesday, which it claims was being used by Houthi rebels to support strikes on the kingdom’s airports and energy facilities – as well as attacks on shipping in the Red Sea.

Earlier, the Houthi-controlled Yemen Oil Company had said that the facility held no stocks of petroleum products, and that an attack would not affect fuel reserves or supplies.

The strikes killed two civilians and injured two, according to the Houthis, though the Saudi-led coalition insisted it had warned civilians to leave the area beforehand.

“This operation focused on neutralizing the capabilities the Houthi militia uses to threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and maritime corridors,” coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.

Tuesday’s exchange comes amid signs the long-running conflict, which reignited this summer and intensified last month after years of relative calm, is continuing to escalate.

Earlier Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward its eastern province, and another aimed at Haradh near the Yemeni border. It also reported intercepting three Houthi drones north of Riyadh.

Meanwhile, Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that artillery fire by the Saudi-led coalition in Saada province wounded three Yemenis and two African residents in Baqim district. It later reported that two civilians were killed and two others wounded by artillery fire on residential villages in the border district of Shada in Sadaa, and also reported strikes in Sanaa and several other provinces. CNN cannot independently verify the reports.

The conflict has been intensifying since the Houthis announced in July that — in response to what they say is retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital — they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as well as infrastructure inside the kingdom.

Those attacks have stepped up in recent days, including with repeated strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded on Saturday in what was the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries now warning their citizens against using the airport. Meanwhile, the US State Department on Tuesday expanded travel restrictions for US government personnel in the kingdom, saying employees now require special authorization from the chief of mission to use any airport in Saudi Arabia.

The attacks have also exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages its air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.

On Tuesday, the Yemeni government forces claimed to have made continued advances in the military operation, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen.” It said that in the past 24 hours its forces had carried out 2,200 strikes against Houthi positions, killing about 1,200 fighters and destroying or disabling more than 440 military vehicles and other assets. CNN could not independently verify the figures.

Meanwhile, the Houthis vowed further attacks against economic and aviation targets within Saudi Arabia, warning that they would target facilities belonging to Aramco as well as the King Khalid International Airport if Saudi forces continued attacking them.

World.title: Trump admin silent as Russia hits American businesses with ‘drones and missiles’ in Ukraine
World.content:
As President Donald Trump and his administration have ratcheted up pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, citing harm to American consumers, they have remained silent on recent Russian strikes on US businesses in Ukraine.

Russia has escalated its attacks on facilities tied to American corporations – and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine writ large – over the past several months.

According to Andy Hunder, the President of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine, Russian missiles and drones have damaged facilities belonging to some of America’s most notable brands, including Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, McDonalds and Oreo.

Although Russia has tried to deter successful American business in the past, it’s “nothing we’ve seen like over the last months,” Hunder told CNN.

“This is a direct hit with drones and missiles, and they keep hitting them. It’s sending a message that they’re targeting American business. We’re not seeing any response from the White House,” he said.

“We need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors that are being hit and are being targeted,” he said.

Firefighters work at the site of a warehouse, used by McDonald’s, that was hit by a Russian drone strike, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine in Kyiv region, Ukraine, on September 25, 2026. Sergiy Chalyi/Reuters

When a Russia drone struck a Coca-Cola factory outside Kyiv in early September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attack was a “clear signal” to the US.

“Today, the Russians struck a Coca-Cola plant with a drone. Coca-Cola has become such an enemy to them that they’re burning it down with their Shaheds,” Zelensky said in his nightly video address on September 3, referring to “Iranian-designed ​drones.”

“This is a clear signal from Russia to America. The Russians cannot possibly be unaware that this is an American enterprise,” Zelensky added.

Later that month, the Russians used “an attack drone” to destroy a warehouse used by McDonald’s, Zelensky said in a post on X. McDonald’s Ukraine confirmed in a statement that “a warehouse operated by one of our logistics partners in the Kyiv region was damaged in a drone attack on 25 September.”

“An attack drone – against ordinary food products,” he wrote. “The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers – for Russia, ordinary life in and of itself is simply a target.”

Mcdonald’s offering a reduced menu

McDonald’s Ukraine said that as a result of the damage, its restaurants are offering a reduced menu.

PepsiCo acknowledged in a statement in late August that a production facility in the Mykolaiv region was damaged, but there were no casualties.

There is not a consensus among the US businesses on the ground about how much they want to talk publicly about being hit “or disclose the fact that they’ve been targeted multiple times,” a former senior State Department official told CNN.

“Some businesses do want us to raise this,” Hunder echoed, but others “are treading very carefully.”

However, several Democratic US lawmakers have publicly called on the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and to call out Moscow’s actions. Ukraine has highlighted the attacks as another reason to step up defense support, so that they can sufficiently shield American companies on the ground.

The Chamber of Commerce meets with visiting US lawmakers from both parties when they visit Kyiv, and Hunder told CNN they have asked them to raise the matter with the White House.

This photograph shows a McDonald’s logo displayed on the facade of one of its restaurants, damaged and melted by Russian strikes near the Lukianivska metro station in Kyiv on May 27, 2026. Roman Pilipey/AFP/Getty Images

President Donald Trump spoke out publicly when asked in August 2025 about a Russian strike on a US electronics factory, saying he told Russian President Vladimir Putin that he was “not happy about it.”

A White House official said Trump “wants the war to stop entirely so the senseless killing ends.”

“The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done,” the official said, arguing that the US is “the only country in the world” that can “play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end.”

Admin has condemned Ukraine’s energy strikes

Still, the relative lack of condemnation on the strikes from the Trump administration stands in contrast to the admonishments to the Ukrainian government about striking Russian energy infrastructure. In February, CNN reported the administration had warned Kyiv that its strikes on a Russian Black Sea oil facility late last year had impacted US investments in Kazakhstan. In recent weeks, Trump has blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian diesel facilities for rising fuel prices, which have been driven up by the US-Iran war.

Last Friday, he announced a deal to waive sanctions and purchase diesel from Russia, in defiance of US law. The US has also threatened to restrict intel sharing and munitions for Ukraine if Kyiv does not stop those strikes, sources told CNN.

Hunder told CNN he has struggled to understand the administration’s relative silence on the matter, particularly given how much they’ve portrayed themselves as pro-US business.

“Any company, any business, wants to have some sort of protection. You would expect your government to stand up in your corner and fight the fight with you, especially if it’s a foreign military that is attacking the American companies,” he said.

The former senior State Department official noted that “there’s an awful lot of people in ‘official Washington’ who think the only people who can talk about Ukraine are Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and if it’s not one of the two of them, then we need to stay out of it.” As such, it is a challenge to even draw attention to the attacks on US businesses.

“The idea that you would get a rationale back” on why the US was silent about the attacks “is not something that people can expect,” they told CNN.

Hunder said the American Chamber of Commerce sent a message seeking a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner last month to update them on the state of US business in Ukraine, including the latest hits on American business.

“We didn’t get any response on that,” he said.

World.title: Trump says ‘massive’ oil and gas drilling is about to begin in Greenland
World.content:
President Donald Trump claimed early Wednesday that “massive oil, gas and mineral exploitation is getting ready to begin” in Greenland, without providing further detail about the operation.

“There are experts that are saying that the amount of easily available oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the world,” he wrote on Truth Social just after midnight.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has repeatedly threatened to take control of Greenland, an autonomous part of Denmark, or to access its natural resources – including its vast and untapped minerals, angering close European and NATO partners.

Researchers have previously suggested it would be extremely difficult and expensive to extract Greenland’s minerals because many of the island’s deposits are located in remote areas above the Arctic Circle, where there is a mile-thick polar ice sheet. Approximately 80 percent of the island is covered in ice.

Vehicles on a narrow road in Nuuk, Greenland, on January 21, 2026. Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images/File

Last month the US, Denmark, and Greenland reached an agreement intended to help resolve tensions following Trump’s threats to annex the strategically located island.

The agreement, which Trump claimed at the time gave the US “permanent control” over Greenland’s security, begins with an acknowledgment of Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.

The agreement, which makes small changes to a 1951 treaty that gives the US permission to station troops in Greenland as part of NATO’s defense, makes no explicit mention of oil or gas, but acknowledges “minerals cooperation” and “cooperation on economic development and business promotion,” with no further specifics, according a text of the agreement published on the White House’s website.

It also paves the way for additional US bases, and an assurance of US military access if Greenland becomes independent from Denmark.

In his post on Wednesday, Trump said, “Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived.”

CNN has reached out to the White House, to the Danish Prime Minister’s Office, and to Greenland’s government and Mineral Resources Authority for comment.

World.title: Liberia’s Council of Churches warns justice “must not become political revenge” as ex-ministers convicted in Saudi aid case and Chief Justice floats scrapping jury trials
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s most influential Christian body has called on the government, the courts and the country’s political class to keep politics out of the courtroom, days after a jury convicted a former foreign minister and other ex-officials of stealing rice donated by Saudi Arabia for disaster victims.

By Rodney D Sieh

In a statement issued Tuesday titled “Justice Without Political Interference; Reconciliation Without Impunity,” the Liberia Council of Churches (LCC) said it “neither determines guilt nor dictates the outcome” of the case, but insisted that justice be “governed by evidence and law, free from political interference, intimidation, and public pressure.”



“No one should be prosecuted because of personal hatred or political opposition, or escape lawful accountability through political influence,” said the Council, which is led by Rev. Dr. Samuel Broomfield Reeves, Jr., who also serves as vice president of the Inter-Religious Council of Liberia.

A verdict that split the jury, and the country

The statement follows a mixed verdict delivered Friday, October 9, at Criminal Court “C” in Monrovia. According to the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce (AREPT), which prosecuted the case, the jury found eight of the 13 defendants guilty, including former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf. Three were acquitted, and verdicts on two others were inconclusive.

Kemayah was reported guilty on all five counts: theft of property, economic sabotage, misapplication of entrusted property, abuse of office and criminal conspiracy. But the jury was far from united. Four of the 12 jurors reportedly voted to acquit him of theft, and four voted against conviction on both economic sabotage and conspiracy; only the abuse-of-office count was unanimous.

Former National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) chief Henry O. Williams was reported not guilty on all charges, a notable outcome given that his agency was responsible for storing and distributing the rice. Charges against Mary Broh, the former head of the General Services Agency and one-time acting mayor of Monrovia, were dropped by the Justice Ministry in August.

Jurors were reportedly seen wearing masks to hide their identities during the trial, an indication of the pressure surrounding a case involving some of the most recognizable figures from Liberia’s previous government.

Rice meant for the vulnerable

The case centers on a humanitarian gift. In 2023, Saudi Arabia donated 29,412 bags of rice, valued at about US$500,000, for disaster victims and vulnerable Liberians. The indictment alleged that 25,054 of those bags were unlawfully diverted or misapplied. Rice is Liberia’s staple food, and the alleged diversion of aid in one of West Africa’s poorest nations has made the case a lightning rod for public anger over corruption.

Kemayah, who helped secure the donation while serving as foreign minister, has consistently denied stealing, receiving or misappropriating the rice. His defense argued that the financial side of the donation was handled directly by Saudi humanitarian authorities and the supplier, not by him.

The prosecution grew out of President Joseph Boakai’s anti-corruption drive after he defeated incumbent George Weah in the 2023 election. Kemayah and Sirleaf both served in Weah’s cabinet, and supporters of the defendants have increasingly cast the trials as politically motivated.

‘Score-settling masquerading as justice’

That charge was sharpened on Monday when one of the convicted officials, former NDMA official and ordained Baptist minister Rev. Rosetta L. Gbassay Bowah, rejected her verdict on Facebook. She alleged that prosecutors had persistently pressed her to become a state witness, a claim her post offered no evidence for and which has not been independently verified. She warned that Liberia risks a cycle of vengeance, political persecution and “score-settling masquerading as justice.”

The government sees it differently. AREPT welcomed the verdicts as a significant milestone in the fight against corruption, and its chairman, Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin, said the taskforce was ready to defend the convictions if defendants appeal to the Supreme Court.

Chief Justice questions jury system

The Council’s call for judicial independence also lands amid a fresh controversy over how Liberia’s courts reach verdicts. Opening the Supreme Court’s October Term on Monday, Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. said jury manipulation was eroding justice in civil and criminal cases, declaring that “a corrupt jury is worse than no jury at all.” He cited suspected interference in proceedings at Criminal Court “C,” the same court that heard the rice case.

The Liberia National Bar Association condemned tampering but said its participation in any review should not be read as support for abolition, while Senator Darius Dillon argued that removing jury trials would require a national referendum.

Reconciliation ‘not a shield’

The LCC’s statement reaches beyond the courtroom to a sensitive national theme. Liberia is still grappling with the legacy of civil wars that killed an estimated 250,000 people between 1989 and 2003, and debates over accountability and forgiveness remain raw.

“Reconciliation must not become a shield for wrongdoing,” the Council said. “Forgiveness cannot erase the need for accountability, and accountability must never become an instrument of revenge.”

Recalling the country’s “painful history,” the churches warned that “justice pursued without fairness can deepen division, while peace pursued without accountability can preserve injustice.”

The Council urged public officials, political parties, the media and citizens not to prejudge the case or pressure the courts. “Public scrutiny is legitimate; political interference is not,” it said, and called on congregations to “reject hateful rhetoric” and encourage peaceful dialogue.

“Let the courts follow the evidence, the Government respect the law, and the Church speak the truth,” the statement concluded.

World.title: Liberia’s Charlyne Brumskine Elected President of ECOWAS Court of Justice
World.content:
ABUJA, Nigeria — Liberian lawyer and law professor Charlyne M. Brumskine was elected president of the Community Court of Justice of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) on Tuesday, a week after she was sworn in as one of five new judges on the regional bench.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Her fellow judges chose her on 13 October 2026 to lead the Abuja-based court, the judicial arm of the West African bloc, for a two-year term. The election makes Justice Brumskine, the first Liberian woman to sit on the court, the head of an institution that rules on disputes between member states, ECOWAS institutions and individuals, including human rights complaints brought by ordinary citizens of the region.



“With profound humility and a deep sense of duty, I address you as the newly elected President of this distinguished judicial institution,” she said in her acceptance address.

“I am sincerely grateful to my esteemed colleagues for the confidence they have each reposed in me. I accept this responsibility fully conscious of the obligations it entails and the expectations that accompany leading a regional judicial institution entrusted with interpreting and applying community law and protecting human rights.”

She said she saw the presidency as a duty rather than an honour. “I regard this office not as a personal distinction, but as an opportunity to serve the courts, the ECOWAS community, and ultimately the people of West Africa,” she said.

What the president does

As president, Justice Brumskine presides over the court’s hearings and deliberations and directs its judicial business, including assigning cases and scheduling proceedings.

She also chairs the Bureau of the Court, which sets its strategic direction, work programme and budget priorities, and she oversees the Registry and the court’s administration.

Beyond the courtroom, she is the court’s public face. She represents it externally, presents its activity report and budget to the statutory bodies of ECOWAS, and works with national judiciaries, other regional and continental courts, bar associations and civil society groups to widen access to justice.

A central part of that role is persuading member states to comply with and enforce the court’s judgments, a long-standing challenge for the institution, which has no enforcement arm of its own and depends on national governments to carry out its rulings.

A court open to citizens

Established under ECOWAS treaty provisions and operational since 2001, the court interprets and applies the bloc’s laws and settles disputes over them. Its reach widened significantly in 2005, when a supplementary protocol allowed individuals to bring human rights cases directly before it without first exhausting remedies in their national courts.

That feature has made the court one of the most accessible regional human rights forums in Africa. Citizens, journalists and civil society groups have used it to challenge arbitrary detention, restrictions on free expression and other alleged abuses by their own governments.

Justice Brumskine takes office at a delicate moment for the bloc. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, formally withdrew from ECOWAS in January 2025, placing their citizens outside the court’s jurisdiction and testing the community’s cohesion.

Five new judges sworn in

Justice Brumskine was among five judges inducted on Tuesday, 6 October, at the ECOWAS Commission headquarters in Abuja for the 2026–2030 term. Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, chairman of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, administered the oath of office.

The other new judges are Désiré Henri Aihou of Benin, Awa Bah of The Gambia, Henrietta Uzoamaka Didigu of Nigeria and Yaouza Ouro-Sama of Togo.

They replace five judges whose four-year mandates have ended: Ricardo Cláudio Monteiro Gonçalves of Cape Verde, Sengu Mohamed Koroma of Sierra Leone, Dupe Atoki of Nigeria, Gberi-Bè Ouattara of Côte d’Ivoire and Edward Amoako Asante of Ghana.

The judges elect a president and a vice-president from among themselves, each serving a two-year term.

‘Institutions endure’

In her address, Justice Brumskine described the handover from the outgoing to the incoming judges as a moment of “continuity, renewal and collective responsibility.” She said the new leadership must build on the foundations laid by its predecessors rather than start afresh.

“Today’s transition reminds us that the institutions endure beyond the individuals who serve them,” she said.

She paid tribute to past presidents and outgoing judges, saying their experience and contribution to the court’s case law would underpin the work ahead.

The incoming judges have received handover notes, reports on the state of the court and legal and administrative records, which she said would be reviewed carefully to ensure continuity in governance and operations.

“These documents represent more than formal records. They provide a basis of understanding the institution’s current position, ongoing responsibilities, operational challenges, and priorities requiring our attention,” she said.

She pledged to lead with “seriousness, openness and a commitment to responsible institutional stewardship.”

‘Liberia can reciprocate’

For Liberians, the appointment carries particular weight. ECOWAS sent its ECOMOG peacekeeping force into Liberia in 1990, during the country’s civil war, and helped broker the 2003 Accra peace agreement that ended 14 years of conflict.

Justice Brumskine drew on that history in her remarks.

“The concept of regional justice and rule of law is not new to Liberia. ECOWAS played a role in Liberia’s recovery to peace. Now Liberia has the opportunity to reciprocate justice by sending one of its own to the Court,” she said.

“This distinction is not about me but the collective good of the region. I am proud that Liberia has been given the opportunity to lead this regional judicial institution. I will serve with excellence.”

Lawyer, teacher, politician

Justice Brumskine brings more than two decades of legal experience to the post. She founded the Monrovia-based CMB Law Group, is licensed to practise in Liberia, New York and Washington, D.C., and has taught at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law at the University of Liberia.

She has also worked on public policy, including an anti-human trafficking framework with Liberia’s Ministry of Justice and the country’s accession to the World Trade Organization.

In 2023, she was the vice-presidential running mate of opposition leader Alexander Cummings of the Collaborating Political Parties. She is the daughter of the late Charles Walker Brumskine, a prominent lawyer and four-time presidential candidate who died in 2019.

Two Liberian men, Micah Wilkins Wright and Yussif D. Kaba, have previously served on the ECOWAS Court.

For Liberia, her election places the country at the head of a regional institution whose credibility rests on its independence, the quality of its judgments and, above all, on whether member states respect them.

World.title: Liberia: Dagoseh Aide Accuses Senate Pro Tempore, Dillon of Orchestrating Ouster, Alleges US$80k Payoff, Lawmakers Deny Allegation
World.content:
MONROVIA — Two senior Liberian lawmakers, Senate Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Montserrado County Senator Abraham Darius Dillon, have been accused of allegedly orchestrating the dismissal of former Commerce Minister Magdalene Dagoseh, with a representative of her foundation claiming that the lawmakers offered US$80,000 to officials in the Office of the President to influence the decision.

By Obediah Johnson

The allegations were made Tuesday, October 13, by Cyrus Julius Jones, head of Media, Policy and Communication Management Professional at the Magdalene Ellen Dagoseh Foundation (MEDF).



Jones alleged that the lawmakers sought Dagoseh’s removal because of her growing political influence in Grand Bassa County and concerns that she could challenge Karnga-Lawrence in the 2029 general and presidential elections.

Both lawmakers have rejected the allegations. Karnga-Lawrence, through her media attaché, described the claims as unfounded, while Dillon responded dismissively when contacted by FrontPage Africa.

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai dismissed Dagoseh as Minister of Commerce on Friday, September 11, replacing her with Stephen Yekeson Jr. An Executive Mansion release announcing the decision stated that Dagoseh had been relieved of her duties to be reassigned to another government position.

The circumstances surrounding her removal have since generated political controversy, with some of her supporters alleging that the decision was linked to her anticipated political ambitions in Grand Bassa County.

Alleged US$80,000 payment

In a statement issued in Monrovia, Jones alleged that Karnga-Lawrence initially provided US$50,000 to Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel A. Stevquoah and Presidential Legal Adviser Cllr. Bushuben M. Keita in an effort to influence Boakai to remove Dagoseh from the Commerce Ministry. The Executive Mansion did not respond up to the time of publication.

Jones further alleged that Dillon subsequently provided an additional amount exceeding US$30,000 to Stevquoah as part of the alleged effort.

Jones did not provide publicly verifiable documentary evidence in the statement to substantiate the alleged payments.

According to him, Dagoseh’s increasing visibility through her humanitarian activities and the work of her foundation had become a source of political concern for Karnga-Lawrence, who represents Grand Bassa County in the Senate.

Jones claimed that the former minister’s position in the government could have enhanced her capacity to organize and finance a potential senatorial campaign against the Senate Pro Tempore in 2029.

“The activities of the Magdalene Ellen Dagoseh Foundation had increased the former minister’s visibility, creating political anxiety ahead of the 2029 elections,” Jones said in the statement.

He further alleged that Karnga-Lawrence had repeatedly expressed concerns to President Boakai about the possibility of Dagoseh challenging her politically.

The allegations have not been independently verified by FrontPage Africa.

Jones alleges closed-door meeting

Jones also claimed that a closed-door meeting was arranged involving Karnga-Lawrence, Dillon, Stevquoah, Keita and two unidentified employees of the Ministry of State.

According to him, the meeting followed delays in the alleged initial arrangements to influence the President’s decision regarding Dagoseh’s removal.

The statement did not establish when the meeting allegedly took place or provide independent confirmation of its participants or the purported financial transactions.

Jones also challenged Karnga-Lawrence’s previous assertion that she had been consulted by Boakai before Dagoseh was appointed Commerce Minister.

He maintained that the Senate Pro Tempore did not know the circumstances surrounding Dagoseh’s appointment, arguing that the former minister’s longstanding service to the Unity Party and Liberia contributed to her selection by the President.

Jones further accused the two lawmakers of attempting to undermine Dagoseh’s political standing in Grand Bassa County because of her humanitarian activities.

Despite her removal from the Commerce Ministry, he said, Dagoseh remained committed to supporting vulnerable people and communities through the foundation.

“Madam Dagoseh remains committed to expanding humanitarian programs through the Magdalene Ellen Dagoseh Foundation,” he said.

He assured beneficiaries that the foundation’s programs would continue despite the controversy surrounding her departure from the government.

Dillon dismisses allegations

When contacted via WhatsApp for a response, Senator Dillon dismissed the allegations in a brief message.

“If this nonsense makes sense to you… go publish it,” Dillon responded.

He did not provide further details in the response.

Karnga-Lawrence denies involvement

Meanwhile, Rolay Glay, media attaché in the Office of Senate Pro Tempore Karnga-Lawrence, denied that his principal orchestrated or attempted to influence Dagoseh’s dismissal.

Glay argued that the President has the constitutional authority to appoint and dismiss members of his administration, maintaining that the Senate Pro Tempore had no reason to interfere with an executive decision.

“I want to call on Cyrus Jones to go and do his civics very well to understand the functions of the three branches of government. The Pro Tempore is part of the Legislature; she will not interfere into the Executive,” Glay said.

He insisted that Karnga-Lawrence had neither orchestrated Dagoseh’s removal nor sought to influence Boakai to dismiss a presidential appointee.

According to Glay, the Senate Pro Tempore exercises her legislative responsibilities through the Senate, including participating in decisions on the confirmation of presidential nominees, rather than offering money to executive officials.

He also maintained that Karnga-Lawrence had played a significant role in working with her colleagues to secure Dagoseh’s confirmation when she was nominated to head the Commerce Ministry.

Glay questioned the plausibility of the alleged payment, asking why Karnga-Lawrence would offer money to influence a decision that constitutionally rests with the President.

“It makes not sense (for the Pro Temp to offer money). How can someone offer US$50,000? Are you saying the President took a bribe of US$50,000 because it is the president who makes the decision?” he said.

He did not provide evidence to independently establish the circumstances surrounding Dagoseh’s dismissal.

Glay further dismissed suggestions that the Senate Pro Tempore was concerned about Dagoseh’s possible political challenge in 2029, insisting that Karnga-Lawrence remained focused on serving the Liberian people.

Political implications

The allegations place the dismissal of the former Commerce Minister against the backdrop of emerging political calculations ahead of the 2029 elections, when Grand Bassa County voters will again elect their representatives to the Senate.

However, the claims that the lawmakers financed an effort to secure Dagoseh’s removal remain allegations, and no independent evidence presented in Jones’s statement establishes that the purported payments occurred or that they influenced Boakai’s decision.

The Executive Mansion’s earlier announcement said Dagoseh would be reassigned to another government position, but the statement cited in this account did not specify the position or explain the reasons for her removal.

The dispute also raises questions about the basis for the competing accounts of Dagoseh’s dismissal, particularly the allegations of financial inducement and the denials from the lawmakers’ representatives.

FrontPage Africa’s account of the controversy is based on Jones’s statement and responses from Dillon and Karnga-Lawrence’s media attaché. The allegations concerning payments to presidential officials have not been independently confirmed.

As of publication, the responses cited above did not include separate comments from Stevquoah or Keita addressing the specific allegations that they received money in connection with Dagoseh’s dismissal.

The former minister’s promised reassignment, as announced by the Executive Mansion, also remains a key outstanding issue in the controversy.

World.title: Liberia: Koon Faces Lawmakers’ Revolt, Then Draws 62 Members as House Resumes Business
World.content:
CAPITOL HILL, Monrovia — Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon presided over a House of Representatives session attended by 62 lawmakers on Tuesday, October 13, as the chamber resumed legislative business days after a boycott by more than 40 members exposed growing discontent over the leadership’s handling of lawmakers’ benefits and district support.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The turnout offered a contrast to the House’s reopening on Friday, October 9, when dozens of lawmakers stayed away from the formal proceedings and convened separately to discuss grievances against the chamber’s leadership.



The aggrieved lawmakers, operating under the banner of the “Reformists,” demanded benefits, legislative support funds and other resources they allege have been withheld under the current leadership.

Although Tuesday’s attendance suggested that the boycott had not carried over into the latest sitting on the same scale, it did not establish whether the lawmakers’ grievances had been resolved.

The session instead provided an opportunity for Koon to address the disagreements, caution members against taking internal disputes into the public domain and outline his priorities for the final quarter of the Third Session of the 55th Legislature.

The House is also preparing for deliberations on the national budget, placing additional pressure on lawmakers to sustain legislative business amid the leadership dispute.

Lawmakers Cite Benefits and District Support

The dispute came into public view last Friday when more than 40 lawmakers reportedly boycotted the House’s reopening and held a separate meeting in Margibi County to discuss their concerns.

The grievances reportedly center on benefits, legislative support funds and other resources that the lawmakers say have not been made available to them under the current leadership.

Several members of the Reformists who spoke about the meeting indicated that their objective was to engage the relevant authorities and press for the fulfillment of their demands.

Representative Samuel Enders of Montserrado County District No. 6 also said the discussions focused on benefits and district support.

Enders added that he was not aware of any effort to remove the House leadership, distinguishing the group’s stated concerns from speculation about a possible attempt to unseat the Speaker.

The boycott nevertheless raised questions about the level of support for Koon’s leadership and whether the grievances could disrupt the chamber’s legislative agenda.

Tuesday’s attendance of 62 members provided a different picture, although the number alone does not establish whether the disagreements have been settled or whether all aggrieved lawmakers have withdrawn their demands.

The House’s latest sitting unfolded against two competing realities: a return to legislative business and unresolved questions about the distribution of benefits and resources among lawmakers.

Koon Warns Against Public Disputes

In his opening remarks, Speaker Koon cautioned lawmakers against taking nearly every disagreement within the institution into the public domain before exhausting opportunities for dialogue and consultation.

He said internal disputes should be addressed through established procedures and mechanisms, warning that public disagreements could damage the reputation of the Legislature and weaken public confidence in the institution.

“Honorable Members, we must understand that every internal disagreement that becomes a public spectacle has consequences beyond the individuals involved. It affects the image of the entire House and further erodes the confidence of our citizens in the institution we have all sworn to serve,” Koon said.

According to the Speaker, members of the public do not always distinguish between individual lawmakers and the institution they represent.

He argued that when lawmakers publicly undermine one another or portray disagreements as an institutional crisis, the credibility of the entire House suffers.

However, Koon acknowledged that lawmakers have the right to express their views, question decisions and hold the leadership accountable.

“I am not suggesting that members should surrender their convictions, remain silent in the face of wrongdoing, or abandon their constitutional responsibilities. Every member has a right to speak, to question, to criticize, and to hold leadership accountable. But we must exercise this right with responsibility, professionalism, and respect for this institution,” he said.

His remarks came days after the Reformists’ boycott brought their complaints into public view, placing the House leadership under pressure to respond to concerns about lawmakers’ benefits and institutional support.

While Koon urged members to exercise restraint in their public engagements, the outstanding question remains whether the leadership and the aggrieved lawmakers can reach an agreement on the issues that triggered the protest.

Speaker Pledges to Hear Members’ Concerns

Koon said his leadership remained committed to listening to lawmakers, respecting differing opinions and providing an environment where concerns could be raised and addressed fairly.

He acknowledged that unity within the House could not be achieved by leadership alone, stressing that every member had a responsibility to contribute to the institution’s cohesion.

The Speaker also reminded lawmakers that they had entered the final quarter of the current legislative session, leaving limited time to address pending legislative responsibilities and restore public confidence.

While the turnout signaled a return to legislative business, Koon urged lawmakers to resolve internal disputes through established channels, warned against publicizing disagreements, and called for greater accountability as the Legislature prepares to consider the national budget.

“We have entered the final quarter of this session and time is not on our side. We have legislative responsibilities to discharge, constituencies to serve, and public confidence to restore and sustain. We must therefore be deliberate about how we use the remaining months of this session,” Koon said.

He urged members to make the final quarter one of greater productivity, stronger collaboration and responsible public engagement.

“Let us make this quarter one of greater productivity, stronger collaboration, responsible public engagement, and renewed commitment to the ideals of democracy that we truly represent — especially as we deliberate on the National Budget that is expected,” he added.

The Speaker’s appeal places particular emphasis on cooperation as lawmakers prepare to consider the national budget, a process that will require sustained participation from members of the chamber.

However, whether the leadership’s assurances will satisfy the Reformists remains unclear, as no resolution of their reported demands was announced during Tuesday’s proceedings.

Lawmakers Ordered to Submit Constituency Reports

Beyond the leadership dispute, Koon called on lawmakers to account for their activities during the recent constituency break, directing each member to prepare and submit a comprehensive report to his office.

He said the reports should document engagements with constituents, progress made in addressing local concerns, challenges encountered and issues requiring intervention from the House leadership.

“Please ensure that this report is submitted to my office for review and action where necessary,” Koon said.

He explained that lawmakers were subject to public assessment by civil society organizations, journalists and citizens, making it necessary for members to document their work and communicate their activities to the public.

“We cannot complain about negative assessments or negative reports if we have not documented our own activities or adequately communicated the work we are doing,” he said.

Koon argued that properly documented constituency reports would provide evidence of lawmakers’ engagements with the people they represent and give the House a factual basis to respond to criticism.

He said the reports could also help the institution correct inaccuracies and respond to what members consider unfair or misleading assessments of their performance.

The Speaker, however, distinguished documentation from shielding lawmakers from scrutiny, stressing that accountability must remain central to their responsibilities.

“It is not about shielding anyone from accountability. Rather, it is about ensuring that public judgments are informed by facts and that the contributions of members are properly recorded,” he said.

He urged lawmakers to take the directive seriously, adding that their responsibilities to constituents did not end when they left Monrovia for their respective districts.

The directive comes as lawmakers face questions about their performance, use of public resources and responsiveness to constituency needs. It also adds a reporting requirement at a time when the House leadership is seeking greater cooperation among members.

Rehabilitation of Legislative Facilities Nears Completion

Koon also informed lawmakers that rehabilitation and refurbishment work on several offices and sections of the main chamber was nearing completion.

He described the work as part of broader efforts to restore the dignity, functionality and working environment of the Legislature.

Beyond the ongoing work, the Speaker disclosed that plans were being developed to begin the rehabilitation and reconstruction of the Joint Chamber, which was gutted by fire on December 18, 2024.

Koon appealed to lawmakers to support the proposed undertaking, describing the restoration of the facility as a shared institutional responsibility.

“The Joint Chamber is not just a sitting hall. It is the venue where the President of the Republic of Liberia formally delivers his Annual State of the Nation Address to the Legislature. It is also the largest seating and event space within the Legislature, providing the capacity to host major national functions, institutional engagements, and distinguished guests,” he said.

Since the fire, the absence of the facility has limited the Legislature’s ability to host major events on its premises, forcing lawmakers to seek external venues for functions that would ordinarily take place within the Joint Chamber.

The proposed reconstruction would restore a key facility used for major legislative and national engagements, although Koon did not provide a specific commencement date or completion timeline for the planned work.

Unresolved Grievances Loom Over Final Quarter

Tuesday’s sitting demonstrated that the House had resumed business despite the boycott that marked the opening of the quarter. Yet the larger question of whether Koon’s leadership has addressed the grievances of the Reformists remains unanswered.

The lawmakers’ reported demands for benefits and district support have exposed tensions within the chamber at a time when members are expected to focus on pending legislation and the national budget.

Koon has called for dialogue, responsible public engagement and unity, while also asking lawmakers to document their constituency work and support the rehabilitation of legislative facilities.

For the House leadership, the challenge will be to translate Tuesday’s attendance into sustained cooperation while addressing the concerns that prompted the boycott.

Whether the Reformists’ demands will be met, and whether the current tensions will affect the chamber’s remaining legislative business, remains to be seen.
