And the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), also teed up over $46 million in battleground races.

"This pity pitch from Chuck Schumer is a testament to the enthusiasm of Republican grassroots donors who are re-engaging in full force to stop Democrats’ socialist march," NRSC spokeswoman Bernadette Breslin told Fox News Digital. "Unfortunately for Schumer, the DNC’s debt crisis is symptomatic of a dying Democratic brand, with approval ratings in the toilet and donors doubting their own chances of flipping the Senate."

World.title: What’s fueling inflation? Fuel.
World.content:
Inflation in America is being powered by diesel.

The price of the fuel, used by farmers and truckers, is up more than 75% since the start of the Iran war in late winter. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for economists, who say higher diesel fuel costs trickle down into “just about everything.”

And the final government inflation report before November’s pivotal midterm elections will most likely reflect how much of a headache it has become for businesses and consumers.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics is set to release its September consumer price index report at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday. It’s expected to show the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.7% from 3.4%, according to a survey of economists from Dow Jones. From August to September, prices are expected to have risen by 0.6%. The monthly jump, if it is confirmed, would also be one of the largest in years.

Since August, oil prices have risen to more than $105 per barrel from about $80. The price of regular gas, which most consumers buy, also remains elevated by more than 45% since late February, when the Iran war was launched.

As early voting kicks off this week, a higher inflation reading would come at a precarious moment for Republicans defending majorities in the House and the Senate. Polls consistently find that inflation and the high cost of living are top issues this year for voters in both parties.

Higher diesel prices this summer and fall have hit agricultural states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas especially hard. Long viewed as Republican strongholds, all three states have Democrats outperforming in Senate races with campaigns focused on the high cost of living.

In response to the outcry over the high cost of gas and diesel, President Donald Trump has pulled several policy levers in recent weeks aimed at pushing down prices. But so far, none of them has made much of a dent.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order to lower the cost of diesel fuel at a campaign rally in Nebraska this month. Win McNamee / Getty

The Trump administration has pressured Group of Seven allies to release more diesel stocks, issued an order to allow more widespread use of tax-free diesel and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin under which Russia would release some diesel supplies and drop some of its export restrictions.

The latest action has drawn global backlash after Trump also eased some sanctions on Russia to facilitate the Russian diesel deal.

Core concerns

Consumers’ wages are still lagging behind the rate of inflation. As of September, wage growth was 3%, and it has not grown faster than inflation since March.

Still, despite the pressure on prices and wages, consumers continue to spend. The CEOs of the nation’s largest banks reported Tuesday that consumers continue to spend at a steady pace.

“While various headwinds, most recently higher energy prices, and tighter monetary policies have been challenging, the global economy has held up remarkably well in the U.S.,” Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said. “While much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much” of the economy’s momentum, she added.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said, “Our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well.” JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the economy “continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending” over the last three months.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices and is more closely watched by the Federal Reserve, is expected to rise, as well, to 2.5%. If it is confirmed, that would be its highest level since June.

Planes take off from Hollywood Burbank Airport on Tuesday. Myung J. Chun / L.A. Times via Getty

One key sector fueling higher core inflation is airfare. “Airfares remain the core category most directly affected by higher oil prices,” said economists at Morgan Stanley. “Airfare CPI is already up 23% y/y, which raises the question of how much further prices can increase.”

They noted that jet fuel prices have risen 90% since this time last year “and typically account for roughly 20-30% of airline operating costs.” As a result, airlines “may already be approaching full pass-through of the increase in fuel costs to consumers.”

iPhones and interest rates

Another major consumer item that could affect September’s inflation rate: pricier iPhones.

Apple’s latest iPhone began selling Sept. 12, and Morgan Stanley’s economists said, “Price increases were generally in the 10%-14% range across models.”

00:00 00:00 Why laptops, tablets and phones are skyrocketing in price 01:45

“Given Apple’s roughly 50% share of the U.S. smartphone market,” that could translate into what they said could be a small upside impact on overall inflation.

But while the higher iPhone prices are likely to be contributing to September’s inflation, they are also the product of inflation earlier this year — inflation that traces back to the ever-expanding buildout of AI data centers.

The race to build data centers and chips for AI has triggered a scramble for memory, in particular. Given that the supply of memory chips is limited, prices have soared at an unprecedented pace.

In June, Apple told NBC News that it has “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly.”

Economists at Goldman Sachs also expect to see a jump in September in other key consumer categories.

“We expect a pickup in autos inflation, reflecting a 0.5% increase in used car prices, a 0.2% increase in new car prices, and a 0.2% increase in the car insurance category,” they wrote in a note.

Wednesday’s data could also “determine whether the Fed’s next hike is imminent, or simply still ahead,” said economists at UBS. Already, the Federal Reserve has raised interest rates once this year to try to slow inflation. A number of top Fed officials have also spoken about the need to raise rates even higher.

“If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our two percent goal,” Federal Reserve governor Christoper Waller said Thursday. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.”

The Fed is expected to raise rates one more time this year, most likely in December. But an inflation reading Wednesday that comes in hotter than expected could increase that urgency and lead to a pre-Election Day rate hike at the central bank’s Oct. 27-28 meeting.

World.title: Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028 during heated Georgia debate
World.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028.

Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term.

“I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”

Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do.

After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week. Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club.

Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America.

The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media.

Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.”

“I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.”

The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files. Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate.

Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts.

“How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.”

Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.

“I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.”

Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges.

Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to help overturn the 2020 election.

“You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said.

World.title: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
World.content:
A federal judge issued an order late Tuesday blocking the Trump administration from banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House complex while the organizations’ lawsuit over access proceeds.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly of Washington, D.C., issued the preliminary injunction in the wake of a hearing Thursday at which the administration contended it imposed the ban in part because of national security concerns; media organizations said it was because of “viewpoint discrimination.”

Kelly sided with the news outlets, noting that Trump used national security as a reason for the ban after their press passes had already been revoked and ruling that it also likely violated reporters’ freedom of speech and due process rights.

“There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer,” Kelly wrote in his 26-page opinion.

His order will give the outlets access to the White House until the underlying lawsuit challenging the ban is resolved. But it doesn’t require the administration to allow reporters from the outlets access to the Oval Office or Air Force One — locations where the administration has blocked reporters from CNN and Politico in recent weeks.

Trump vowed to appeal on Truth Social before the ruling was handed down. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment following the ruling.

Kelly had issued a temporary restraining order lifting the ban while he weighed whether to issue an injunction.

Trump announced the bans of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on social media on Sept. 18, saying they were a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he wrote on Truth Social.

In court filings, the three news organizations said the ban affected 78 journalists who had “hard passes,” meaning they had been previously screened and credentialed to work at the White House.

The outlets filed a lawsuit alleging Trump’s action violated their due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit said.

The White House and Trump then began arguing that the ban was intended to address national security concerns, with Trump saying in another post that the outlets’ reporting was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

The judge was unmoved by that argument.

Kelly said it was clear from Trump’s announcement of the ban and from subsequent remarks that his motivation was content.

“President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly wrote, finding this decision violated the journalists’ First and Fifth amendment rights.

He noted, however, that his decision doesn’t concede that Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness are unfounded or that the government is “powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”

Kelly cited Trump’s recent remarks to Time magazine that he didn’t like “bad story after bad story” coming from CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. It was, Ted Boutrous, the news outlets’ attorney, had argued ahead of the decision, “a confession of what amounts to viewpoint discrimination.”

“President Trump, I’ll give him credit,” Boutrous said. “He’s not hiding it.”

In his previous decision, Kelly also found that the administration had denied the outlets due process under settled law from several cases that have made their way to the D.C. federal appeals court.

The White House argued that the appeals court decisions were wrong.

“Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote.

At a hearing on the injunction Thursday, the Justice Department lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik, asked Kelly to lift his restraining order, calling the White House a “sacred place” that shouldn’t have to give people access just because they “identify as a reporter.”

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” Velchik said.

Boutrous argued that the administration was engaging in impermissible and unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination” because the ban was based on Trump’s dislike of the outlets’ reporting and because he has said he hoped the ban would force journalists to “straighten themselves out.”

In court filings, Boutrous urged Kelly to ignore the national security arguments, saying they were manufactured and not what the case is really about.

Boutrous argued that “the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories,’ as he ‘won the election’ and has ‘done great things.’”

After Tuesday night’s ruling, Boutrous said he and his clients were grateful to the court for securing their access anew.

“The President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” he said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban.’”

Separately, the Justice Department said last week that it was investigating five major TV networks, including CNN and NBC, for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump as a result of the ban against the three news outlets.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording a president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The on-duty network then distributes information and media, such as video and audio, to other outlets for their use.

World.title: Pope Leo spends a peaceful night in the hospital after cancer surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in the hospital after successful surgery that saw part of his right lung removed and a confirmed cancer diagnosis, the Vatican said early Wednesday.

It said more information would follow later in the day.

The 71-year-old American pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer which accounts for 80% of all cases, according to the American Lung Association.

The 90-minute operation to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating theatre for nearly three hours, it said.

The Vatican did not offer details on planned treatment moving forward or whether the cancer might have spread.

The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer.

Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli hospital as he entered on Tuesday.

The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.

The surgery saw the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung removed using a “video-assisted technique,” according to the Vatican.

Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations.

The pope’s cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although he is not known to ever have been a smoker.

The cancer diagnosis could complicate the pontiff’s busy schedule.

Just weeks earlier hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence.

The pope was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead.

Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news.

“We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife Jeanette were praying for the pope, who was born in Chicago.

“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, German Catholic news agency KNA reported.

“The pope‘s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying.

World.title: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
World.content:
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday.

“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News.

Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot.

Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston.

“My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. Raquel Natalicchio / Houston Chronicle via Getty

Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group.

Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation.

On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers.

ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco.

Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”

But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away.

He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said.

ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it.

“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.”

Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses.

“I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said.

Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said.

According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic.

A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said.

Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza.

Miguel Parra Hernandez. Noticias Telemundo

In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles.

Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.

The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status.

“All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.

World.title: Bank of America ordered to pay historic $1.2 billion over alleged sanctions law violations
World.content:
Bank of America was ordered Tuesday to pay $1.2 billion to the Treasury Department, which said it violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

00:20 Bank of America ordered to pay historic $1.2 billion fine 00:00 00:00

The penalty is the third largest ever issued in Treasury history, the agency said. As part of that total, the bank was ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine it has ever levied.

“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

As the second-largest bank in the country, Bank of America has more than 70 million clients and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for individual customers every year.

In addition, the bank handles $450 trillion in payments for corporate customers, including payrolls, corporate credit cards and supplier payments.

The Treasury Department said Bank of America “admits that it willfully violated” the Bank Secrecy Act and “failed to maintain” an anti-money laundering program that met minimum requirements under the law. The bank also admitted having failed to file mandatory Suspicious Activity Reports.

“Bank of America failed to timely report to FinCEN over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions, with over $1 billion of this activity implicating national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in a statement.

FinCEN is the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which combats money laundering, illicit financial activities and terrorist financing networks around the world.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” Bank of America said in a statement to NBC News.

“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.”

“We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.”

In addition to the FinCEN violations, the Treasury Department said Bank of America is also settling “its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs” with the Office of Foreign Assets Control, which oversees sprawling U.S. sanctions.

The company “processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism,” the Treasury Department said.

Bessent said, “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”

Bank of America will report its third-quarter earnings shortly before 7 a.m. ET Wednesday.

World.title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
World.content:
For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.

Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

Sens. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., and Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn. Getty

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.

I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened. -Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.

Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”

Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.

Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the first nine months of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.

The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”

Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began.

Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.”

“They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”

World.title: Trump pardons two vehicle repair shop owners during Alaska rally
World.content: During his rally in Alaska, President Trump pardoned Zachary Czuback and Patrick Fleming, co-owners of a vehicle repair shop in Anchorage. Both pleaded guilty in 2022 to violating the Clean Air Act by tampering with federally mandated and monitored devices that tracked vehicles’ diesel emissions.Oct. 14, 2026

World.title: Grad student allegedly poisoned her colleague, tried to flee U.S.
World.content:
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she didn't get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.

Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment - research similar to work she'd done in China.

Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim's wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.

U.S. officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.

The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.

"It's been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student's life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that," Gomelsky told The Associated Press. "That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career."

This photo provided by Mark Gomelsky shows University of Wyoming microbiology graduate student Aili Wang at the university in Laramie, Wyo., May 2, 2024. Mark Gomelsky via AP

Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

Amateur sleuthing helps campus cops develop case

The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as "K.T.," began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.

Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through the alleged victim's desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded "taking photos and manipulating notebooks" on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer's affidavit said.

Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.

During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she "had not used acrylamide in years." A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of "multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials," according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to "significantly increase" her $200,000 bond upon extradition.

Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved "new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment," according to the affidavit.

Wang "was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.," the affidavit alleges.

Alleged victim is a high-achieving student

Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.

Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague's success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.

The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.

He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.

Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.

Wang had not been doing lab work since June while she worked on her dissertation, he said.

Suspect faces return to Wyoming to face charges

Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

It's not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors' request and raised bond to $1.5 million cash-only.

Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

Best known as a carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide can be acutely toxic in high doses. It's used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.

Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is "not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere," Sumaya said.

The alleged victim was working on "a pretty promising cancer therapy method," Sumaya said. Wang, Sumaya added, took photos of every page of a notebook the alleged victim left on his desk.

"You wouldn't do that with like your office or lab mate's notebook unless there's a really good reason, and there wasn't," Sumaya said.



Professor says the victim is still experiencing symptoms

The alleged victim went to the campus health clinic in August with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness. Suspicion led his wife and others to boil away coffee maker water from the shared office to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit.

The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.

The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.

"Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it's unclear if he'll fully recover or not," the professor said.



Similar case in California

A chemical engineer in Berkeley, California, suffered years of unexplained illness until she purchased a spy camera and caught her coworker, David Xu, poisoning her food and water with cadmium. He struck a plea deal and served two years of probation for one felony count of poisoning.

According to court records, in October of 2017, Xu began trying to poison a female fellow engineer, Rong Yuan, by mixing "a poison and harmful substance with food, drink, medicine, and pharmaceutical product" that belonged to Yuan.

Yuan allegedly "noted a strange taste or smell from her water and food left unattended in her office," according to the criminal complaint. She later began experiencing "immediate and significant health problems after consuming this water and food, at times requiring emergency care at a hospital.

World.title: AI linked to 84% of ransomware attacks, new report finds
World.content:
Cybercriminals exploited artificial intelligence in ransomware attacks experienced by 84% of surveyed victims, according to a sweeping new global cybersecurity report, while 44% reported that attackers exploited their own AI systems.

The 2026 Ransomware Risk Report by cybersecurity firm Semperis polled 1,200 IT and security professionals across nine countries and eight industry sectors, revealing an evolved picture of cybercriminal enterprise—one that increasingly leverages AI to magnify its technical capabilities and escalate pressure on targets.

But the findings also underscored ransomware's human toll. According to the report, more than a third of surveyed victims faced psychological or physical threats against employees, and 14% of surveyed organizations even reported employees or family members forced to change jobs, office locations or residences as a result of sustained ransomware threats.

In all, 69% of surveyed ransomware victims experienced multiple successful attacks sometime in the previous year, with 59% of respondents paying a ransom at least once, and 87% experienced attacks targeting their identity systems, or the digital infrastructure that controls access to their networks.

For Chris Inglis, former White House National Cyber Director under former President Joe Biden, artificial intelligence represents a turning point in the capabilities ripe for cybercriminals' exploit —and he warns that a particularly consequential development is already underway: autonomous ransomware attacks.

"AI actually increases the capacity, scope, scale of attackers in understanding what perhaps might be the weaknesses in your system or perhaps increase the sophistication of their approach to you if they're trying to get you to do something you shouldn't do, that gives them an advantage, lets them in," Inglis said in an interview about the report.

The cybersecurity expert and Semperis board member previously spent three decades watching technologies mature at the National Security Agency watching as attacks required substantially less direct human involvement – no longer simply a theoretical possibility.

"AI is an inflection point in their capacities to hold the same things at risk," Inglis said. He later added, "I think we're already seeing autonomous attacks. Autonomous ransomware attacks are included in the mix."

Inglis described how a person lacking the technical expertise to penetrate an organization's networks could turn to AI to write the necessary code, effectively instructing an AI system to target a company and hold its data hostage without a sophisticated understanding of how digital infrastructure operates.

"We have democratized AI to the point where even low level models can allow that to happen," Inglis said, noting that the technology compounds the number of criminals capable of launching more technical attacks, while inviting experienced cybercriminals to penetrate networks more efficiently and on a much greater scale.

AI is changing the ransomware playbook

For years, criminals have relied on a familiar playbook: exploiting vulnerabilities, penetrating corporate networks, encrypting data and demanding a ransom payment in exchange for restored access or withholding sensitive information. Now, in more than eight out of 10 attacks, AI has been incorporated into that process.

AI has also enabled attackers to quickly identify weaknesses, tailor social engineering schemes to specific employees, automate an intrusion and readjust tactics as defenders try to react, according to Inglis.

"What's not changed is the things that people or organizations had that is of value that they would pay money or time or energy to protect," Inglis said. "And those things are still the object of a broad swath of criminals attention. They want to use whatever tools they can to try to hold those at risk so they can get you to pay them money, sometimes time, but really it's about money."

By lowering technical barriers, AI risks enabling a wider range of actors to attempt intrusions that previously demanded a wide swath of resources and more specialized training or know-how.

Tomer Bar, Semperis's associate vice president of security research, warns that AI could enable ransomware developers to produce more sophisticated malicious code, reduce development time and make investigations more challenging.

"We're starting to see more attacks with more rapid development, and attribution of these attacks will be more difficult for law enforcement," Bar says in the report.

"We'll also be less likely to see mistakes in attack encryption algorithms because attackers can test their code with [large language models.]"

When a company's own AI becomes a weapon against it

One of the report's most striking revelations is that 44% of surveyed victims experienced ransomware attacks exploiting their own AI agents or systems, a finding that raises an uncomfortable question for businesses and government agencies racing to integrate the technology into its networks.

Courtney Guss, Semperis's associate vice president of crisis management, warns that autonomous AI agents can create security risks when they seek additional permissions or interact with sensitive corporate systems.

"If your company is adopting AI agents, you should consider that at some point, those agents will try to compromise your identity systems — even if that action isn't meant to be malicious," Guss writes in the report.

"That's just how they operate. AI agents typically try to accomplish their assigned tasks by any means they can." Guss continued. "One way they can gain more ability to operate in the environment is by getting permissions to other systems. The fastest path to get those permissions is to compromise your identity system, which effectively puts the agent into 'god mode,' enabling it to grant itself whichever permissions it needs to accomplish its task. Unfortunately, the agent then becomes a ticking time bomb."

Unlike conventional software operating, some AI agents possess the ability to use multiple applications at once and make educated decisions on behalf of their users.

If an attacker manipulates just one of those agents—or compromises the credentials and permissions it relies upon—the attacker gains another way of moving deeper into an organization's systems.

Still, Inglis cautions against assumptions that AI necessarily makes an organization more vulnerable to outside intruders.

"Many attackers already do what's called living off the land – they'll move into your digital infrastructure, onto your property or digital property, and they'll use the tools that you have there or the insights or the data set," Inglis said. "To blend in, to navigate the landscape, they try not to stand out, and they do that by using your tools. If AI is one of your tools, they'll use those, but the weakness that let them in is probably the same weakness that existed before."

Inglis argues that the fundamental vulnerability often lies within a company's failure to control access to its networks or digital infrastructure in the first place. Rather than abandon AI out of fear, Inglis argues that organizations must embrace its defensive potential.

"I would turn that around. Flip the script," he said. "You must use AI in order to counter that threat, and you must use AI for affirmative purposes."

Julia Kimani-Burnham contributed to this report.

World.title: Trump says Greenland oil, gas and mineral exploration "getting ready to begin"
World.content:
President Trump said Wednesday that "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is preparing to begin in Greenland.

In a statement posted on his Truth Social platform, Mr. Trump said "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland," but did not give more details.

The president added that "there are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World."

Mr. Trump also touted Greenland's role in the defense of the United States in Europe, saying that "any future attack" on the U.S. would have to come across the semi-autonomous island, "where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet conceived."

"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" Mr. Trump added.

Prime Minister of Greenland, Prime Minister of Denmark and President Trump sign a security pact on September 22, 2026 in New York City. Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images

The announcement comes more than four weeks after the U.S., Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the territory, signed a new security agreement to bolster American military and security presence on the island.

That agreement, which gives the U.S. broad access to the island's airspace and territory, largely focuses on using Greenland for military purposes, but also mentions resource extraction and "minerals cooperation" between the two countries, without specifying any details.

The plan allows the U.S. to expand the existing Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation which serves as an early-warning system for incoming missiles. The agreement also says the U.S. can establish additional bases at the sites known as Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, which are roughly 950 miles apart. Any of the three parties can propose more "defense areas" as needed, subject to approval by the others.

Map showing main deposits of selected critical minerals in Greenland, according to the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland. Jonathan Walter, Valentina Breschi/AFP via Getty Images

The deal, which has no expiration date, also blocks non-NATO countries from establishing bases on the island without agreement from the parties.

Since his first term, Mr. Trump had cited Greenland's strategic location as one of the reasons for greater U.S. control over the semi-autonomous island, and even suggested purchasing the island from Denmark or using military force.

Some industry experts believe mineral resources in Greenland have only been lightly explored and up until now the cost of extraction has not made economic sense for private companies.

World.title: Trump pardons 2 auto workers on stage during rally in Alaska
World.content:
President Trump during a political rally in the state late Tuesday granted onstage pardons to two Alaska auto shop owners who pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act — an unusually public use of the president's clemency power.

The president said the two men — Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming — were "wrongly charged," and cast the charges against the two men as an example of how the Biden-era Justice Department "viciously targeted the Alaskan way of life."

Czubak, Fleming and a third man named Michael Hanzuk owned an auto shop that specialized in diesel vehicles called Arm Rippin Toys, according to court records. Federal prosecutors say they offered to remove the emission control systems in customers' vehicles for a fee of $1,140 to $5,445, in part by modifying their physical components and preventing their diagnostics systems from noticing a problem, causing the vehicles to spew more pollutants.

All three men pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Clean Air Act in 2022. They were each sentenced to five years of probation, $66,000 in fines and community service.

During Tuesday's pre-midterm election rally in Wasilla, Mr. Trump called Czubak and Fleming onto the stage and said to an aide: "Bring me the pardons!"

"Think of it: They want to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine. How sick?" the president said. "Now if you murder somebody, no problem. Unless a Republican does the murdering. Then it's, you know, the electric chair, right?"

Mr. Trump signed the pardons at the podium and handed them to Czubak and Fleming, drawing cheers from rallygoers as the president held one of the pardons up to the crowd.

The president said he was also "taking care of" a third person. He did not name the other person, but the third co-owner of Arm Rippin Toys, Hanzuk, received a pardon last month.

"When you give somebody a pardon, they say that means, and I don't know how this works and why it's an expression, but it's well-used, that means you're as clean as a newborn baby's ass," the president said. "I never understood that. Why is that so clean?"

Czubak and Fleming briefly addressed the crowd, with Fleming saying the charges against the three "really did destroy us."

"We're not criminals. We're not trying to hurt anybody," he said. "We want to help Alaskans. We want to help people with diesel trucks, with vehicles, across the world."

CBS News has reached out to Czubak, Fleming and Hanzuk's attorneys for comment.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump granted a pardon to Mac Spurlock, another diesel mechanic who was also charged with violating the Clean Air Act by removing pollution control systems — a case that the president mentioned during Tuesday's rally.

Spurlock and his supporters, including GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, argue the engine modifications that he performed were necessary to prevent emissions systems from malfunctioning due to Alaska's frigid weather.

Sullivan applauded Spurlock's pardon in July, calling the charges the work of "overzealous federal prosecutors" and arguing the Environmental Protection Agency's rules should be modified to account for cold-weather states. Tuesday's rally was held in part to help Sullivan fend off a challenge from Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.

The Justice Department announced in January it would "no longer pursue criminal charges under the Clean Air Act based on allegations of tampering with onboard diagnostic devices."

During the Biden administration, officials took a different tack, warning in a statement on the Arm Rippin Toys charges that cutting out emissions controls "results in a massive increase in air pollution from even a single vehicle." Scot Adair, former special agent in charge of the EPA's Criminal Investigation Division in Alaska vowed to "hold accountable those who jeopardize human health and the environment for the sake of profit."

Mr. Trump and members of his administration have railed against other environmental regulations, relaxing fuel economy standards and ending an EPA policy that gave credits to car manufacturers that installed start-stop emissions systems.

The president has also frequently used his pardon power to grant clemency to political allies and people who — like him — argue they were wrongly prosecuted.

World.title: Judge blocks Trump's White House ban targeting CNN, MS NOW and Politico
World.content:
Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday blocked President Trump's attempt to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, maintaining access to the grounds for reporters from the three news organizations indefinitely.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Mr. Trump, granted the outlets' request for a preliminary injunction, which will remain in place while the case moves forward. In a 26-page decision, Kelly found that the revocation of their journalists' hard passes likely violated their Fifth and First Amendment rights.

"It is likely that President Trump's revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes is the sort of action that would deter a reasonable reporter or news organization from publishing stories to which he objects," Kelly wrote in his decision. "The revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes matters a lot as to how, whether, and to what extent they can do their jobs."

The judge said Mr. Trump's comments "suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before."

Mr. Trump had anticipated that his administration would lose in court to CNN, MS NOW and Politico. He said on Truth Social last month that if Kelly ruled against him, the Justice Department would appeal.

Theodore Boutrous, lawyer for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, said the court was right to block the White House from enforcing Mr. Trump's ban.

"When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement. "Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers. The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound."

The president announced last month his decision to ban journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds because of what he said was their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS." Reporters from the three outlets who showed up at the White House the day after the ban was announced were turned away and had their press credentials taken by the U.S. Secret Service.

The news organizations filed their lawsuit on Sept. 21 and argued the president's ban retaliated against them because of their news coverage, in violation of the First Amendment. CNN, MS NOW and Politico also argued their reporters were denied their Fifth Amendment right to due process because they were not provided notice that their reporting could lead to their White House access being revoked or the opportunity to respond.

The day after the outlets filed their suit, the White House Press Office sent them letters informing them of the president's initial decision to revoke their journalists' press credentials and setting a Sept. 25 deadline for them to respond. The White House argued that reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico violated standards of professionalism and published articles that raised national security concerns.

The White House provided the outlets with lists of pieces that it said "threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods." But most of the articles were written by journalists who do not have White House hard passes. One of the flagged stories from Politico, which was published in June, was based on a press call organized by the White House. During the call, reporters were instructed to attribute quotes to a "senior administration official," according to court records.

The news outlets asked Kelly to grant them temporary relief and restore their journalists' access to the White House, which the judge agreed to do late last month.

His decision then was based on the press organizations' due process argument. Kelly did not address their First Amendment claims.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico also asked Kelly to grant them longer-term relief, which would remain in place as the litigation plays out.

In a hearing last week, the judge pressed a Justice Department lawyer on the Trump administration's justifications for the ban and why the government's argument in court appeared to differ from Mr. Trump's public justification.

The Justice Department has argued that the president determined the outlets should be denied access to the White House because they violated standards of professionalism and threatened national security. But Mr. Trump has repeatedly attacked the outlets for "negative" coverage of his administration and for publishing "constantly bad stories."

Mr. Trump "seems to have said publicly and on several occasions" that he was taking action "because of X and Y, and now the government is coming to court saying no, it was actually Z," Kelly said.

The judge also said the due-process concerns were "the biggest hurdle" for the Justice Department to surmount.

In his decision, Kelly said the Trump administration failed to put forward evidence that Mr. Trump's decision to revoke hard passes for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists initially was based on national security grounds, and reiterated that the reporting cited by the White House as raising issues is "commonplace, for better or worse."

"When he announced the ban with his post on September 18, he did not mention national security. When he was asked later that day about the 'particular reason' for his action, he did not mention national security. And while it is true, days later, that he used the phrase 'national security' in subsequent social media posts about the ban, that expression appears to have been simply another way for him to describe Plaintiffs' alleged inaccuracies and unfairness in their reporting about topics like his achievements or electoral success," he wrote.

Addressing the letters the White House sent to each of the outlets informing them of the ban, Kelly wrote that they "appear to conflate concerns about otherwise protected speech ('trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about ... other issues') with national security concerns."

Mr. Trump has for years denounced the media over coverage that he dislikes, calling news outlets "fake news" and lobbing attacks against individual reporters. The president stopped the Associated Press from attending certain events at the White House over its refusal to use the name "Gulf of America" after his executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico.

The AP sued and a federal appeals court allowed Mr. Trump to restrict its access to the Oval Office and Air Force One, places where only a subset of the White House press corps goes. But the appeals court has not yet ruled on the legal merits of the White House's ban targeting AP journalists.

Mr. Trump's decision to keep CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists from the entire White House campus marked an escalation of his yearslong feud with the press. When he announced the ban targeting the three outlets, the president warned he could revoke access for "other Fake News Media Outlets."

CNN and CBS News are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.

World.title: Dolly Parton's nephew pushes back on restraining order
World.content:
Dolly Parton's nephew and longtime head of security said in a Tennessee court filing Tuesday that he was a close friend and ally of Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell before Nozell took out a restraining order accusing him of threatening to do violence and destroy Parton's legacy and business empire.

In an affidavit opposing the temporary order becoming permanent, Bryan Seaver said text messages Nozell cited as evidence against him were a "private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy." The text messages were sent shortly before and after Parton's Aug. 25 death.

Seaver said he never sent threatening messages to any of Parton's businesses or business partners or their employees.

A Tennessee judge last month granted the temporary restraining order filed by She's Alive — an entity run by Nozell and founded to manage Parton's estate — against Seaver and his private security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services.

As part of the order, Seaver and SAPS must refrain from talking with or being within 1,000 feet of She's Alive employees, attorneys and business partners. The order is also meant to keep Seaver from interfering with its business relationships.

Tuesday's filings represent Seaver's first public defense of himself since a serious rift opened up in the country music legend's circle and spilled into public view shortly after her death.

Seaver's court filing says Nozell did not react with alarm to his text messages at the time and that he agreed with or reacted positively to some of them. Seaver says Nozell encouraged him to publicly tout the military and arms aspect of SAPS as a smart business-promotion move, then turned around and used them as evidence of Seaver's capacity for dangerous violence.

She's Alive terminated Seaver and SAPS in early September, and the following week petitioned for the restraining order against him, arguing that his "terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable."

In granting the temporary restraining order, Chancellor I'Ashea L. Myles cited Seaver's "claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate."

The two sides will make their cases to Myles at a hearing on Oct. 20. Emails from The Associated Press seeking comment were sent to lawyers for She's Alive and Nozell.

The complaint filed last month alleged that Seaver and his company used "terroristic threats, harassment, and intimidation" against She's Alive.

"Those means are especially improper because they have been deployed as part of a calculated campaign by a trained military/private-security operative with access to an arsenal of military-grade weaponry, rather than through any legitimate commercial or legal process," the complaint read.

Seaver said he was blindsided by the order, which was granted while he was doing contract security work in Haiti.

In one message written Sept. 1 that was cited by She's Alive, Seaver said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or f****** pay me."

It also accused Seaver of being "emboldened" and "relentless" in his threats against She's Alive since Parton's death.

"He has individually, and through his associates, made repeated written threats to Ms. Parton's staff, legal and business advisers, and others," the complaint read. "These were not ordinary workplace disputes or heated words; they were deliberate threats from a self-proclaimed heavily armed, former security operative with a military-contractor background."

In another text message, Seaver alleged that he "just sold 29 million dollars worth of ammo to Haiti."

Seaver argued in his response Tuesday that the order is so broad, and Parton's business reach so great, that much of Nashville and even his own relatives are off-limits to him.

Seaver said his anger and the demand were only over more than $250,000 that his company was owed for completed work by Herschend Family Entertainment, which operates Parton's amusement park Dollywood and her Songteller Hotel, which opened after her death.

Seaver acknowledged being overly crude and profane in his messages to Nozell. He said allegations that he had "menaced and intimidated" HFE employees were simply false. He said in his filing that he had "never threatened physical harm" to Nozell or any She's Alive employee.

He included as an exhibit a 2024 letter from Parton praising him and his company. Parton had handpicked Seaver to announce her death once she succumbed to cancer.

"I have declined to speak with the media about this case and have asked my attorneys to handle all media communications," Seaver wrote in his affidavit. "I care about Ms. Parton, her music, her legacy, and her family. I do not want this dispute to harm her legacy."

In a prerecorded video announcing Parton's death last month, Seaver said that his video was "something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality."

He described it as "an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus."

Parton was a widely beloved country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon who wrote hundreds of songs, including classics such as "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors" and "I Will Always Love You." Her music earned a total of more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

World.title: These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs
World.content:
These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs

Faven Mulugeta for NPR

KARUR, India — Three men stride across a cavernous textile factory floor of Texworth in the southern Indian city of Karur, handing GoPros and smart glasses to workers, including 40-year-old Shoba Kirubakaran. She's packing yellow aprons decorated with chickens into plastic wrapping for the brand Designs By Danica. It's the third time Kirubakaran says she's been told to don a GoPro.

It's recording her every hand gesture, to train AI robots to take over this job — a fact that she says the company did not share with her. NPR informed her when they interviewed her on a recent day. "Nobody told me anything about it," she says.

Sponsor Message

Kirubakaran has worked in the factory for 10 years, six days a week, from around 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. She makes $90 a month. With that money, she's helped her husband, a rickshaw driver, raise their two sons. And she adds, "I only know how to do this job."

Scenes like these shook the Indian public in April after a video went viral showing rows of textile factory workers wearing these headsets. "This is not a scene from a science fiction film," warned one news anchor from outlet News9Live. "That is happening right now on factory floors across India." Another outlet, AsiaNet News warned: "Indian workers are training AI robots to take their jobs."

Seeking "egocentric data"

India is emerging as one key place to record this kind of footage because of its large population, relatively low wages and relative openness to new tech. And developers need millions of hours of this footage, what the industry calls egocentric data — data gathered from the perspective of a human with a camera to train AI robots.

"That can be obtained only by emulating or collecting data from real human beings that does the job," says Prathosh A.P., a professor at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru. Like many other Indians, he uses initials to refer to his family name. "Think of today's AIs as brains without a body," he says. "Now you have to give them all motor skills ... to do all kinds of intricate motions that we do using a physical body."

Sponsor Message

Some workers are signing up because they're paid by the hour for the data. But it appears many others, like Kirubakaran, are simply made to record herself working without any explanation. "Call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor," says Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, which studies the impact of technology on people.

What will the impact be for India's workforce — the world's second largest, with 600 million people working or seeking work? "Training workers, retraining workers, absorbing them into new occupations," says Amit Basole, economics professor at Azim Premji University. "Do we have the policy agility to do that? I doubt it."

The power question

But that vision of a future full of factory and domestic robots isn't exactly around the corner, say some experts. AI robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India — in the near future at least — because they cost a lot of money and consume a lot of power, which is both unreliable and costly across parts of India. "We may be able to make the robots, but they're bloody expensive to run, right?" says Kapoor of the Aapti Institute. "Humans are cheaper to run than robots."

That power crisis is evident even in Karur, where an Indian tech company, Objectways, gathers egocentric data to sell onto AI developers. Massive generators loudly rumble to ensure seamless electricity in the buildings it powers. The company appears to be one of the town's biggest white-collar employers, occupying at least four building blocks in the town.

The CEO, Ravi Shankar, is a Karur native who migrated to Arizona decades ago. He's in perhaps unlikely agreement with Kapoor about the deployment of AI robots in India. "I think it will be more expensive," he says of AI robots, in comparison to human labor. "I don't think it's going to be cheaper."

Sponsor Message

He says his Indian clients want help designing AI robots for jobs that they can't find people to do, like tapping rubber from rubber trees; jobs that are geographically isolated, like dusting off solar panels in rural areas, and jobs that are physically grueling, like destemming chiles for processing.

Inside Objectways, employee Rajeshkumar Ramaswamy shows us how they are training other robots to do repetitive industrial jobs for foreign clients, through what he calls collecting exocentric data — that's data collected from the point of view of a robot. Instead of filming hands of actual workers, young men with GoPro cameras strapped to their heads record themselves doing jobs while holding and manipulating what look like grippy robot claws. One man records himself using the claws to screw bottle lids off and on.

There are dozens of bottles — big, small, plastic, metallic. Ramaswamy says it's to teach robots how to identify all the different shapes and sizes of this thing called a water bottle. The "robot needs to learn what is [a] water bottle," he says.

Ramaswamy says they'll repeat this process of screwing bottle tops about 100 times and feed that data into an AI robot, so it can see for itself how to use its own grippy hands to do the job.

"The robot is like a child," Ramaswamy says. "We are the humans. We are teaching the robots what needs to be done."

The company also trains robots to do household tasks — like folding towels, putting away books and unpacking bags. It sells that data to AI companies hoping to create domestic robots — there's already a few on the market, including one prominent model that looks like a faceless servant and retails for $20,000.

Working in a fake kitchen

Up a few flights of stairs, Ramaswamy shows us where they have humans recording themselves doing domestic jobs, on a floor kitted out to look like an Ikea-style three-bedroom house. In a fake kitchen, a woman, Rani N., records herself chopping onions.

Sponsor Message

Most clients who want first-person recordings of domestic chores are in the U.S., so Ramaswamy says they also pay Americans to record themselves doing housework — so their clients can train AI robots on American-specific data.

For instance, in India, many folks use stainless steel plates to eat. A robot trained to pick up a stainless steel plate could use a lot of pressure to grip it, and could drop it — no harm done. But if the same robot tried to pick up a ceramic plate, which is what many Americans use, the same pressure would cause it to "be separated into minute particles," Ramaswamy says — that is, smashed to bits.
