World.title: Canada paused Black Hawk helicopter deal over Trump's trade war: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Liberal government quietly ordered a pause on a modest, but important purchase of 16 U.S.-made UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters just before trade negotiations began last summer with the Trump administration, CBC News and Radio-Canada have learned.

The aircraft, which are intended for use by Canada's special forces, are manufactured by Sikorsky, a subsidiary of the U.S. defence giant Lockheed Martin.

The decision to suspend the acquisition is linked to trade and diplomatic tensions with the Trump administration, according to several sources within the government and defence industry.

The purchase had been signed off by the U.S. State Department agency that handles foreign military sales and was headed for congressional approval when the halt was ordered before trade negotiators met in Washington, according to two confidential sources.

The decision, the sources said, was partially related to the trade talks, which ultimately failed. It was also part of a wider effort by federal officials to inventory what the Canadian military planned to purchase from the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly questioned Canadian sovereignty since being re-elected. He has also launched a major trade war with Canada, imposing tariffs on key sectors such as steel, aluminum and automotive manufacturing.

As Canada seeks to reduce its military reliance on the United States, the government decided that the timing was not right to purchase American helicopters without a competitive bidding process, several sources said.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Since being elected in the spring of 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney has made it a priority to boost domestic defence industrial production, establish partnerships with foreign firms operating in Canada and — only as a last resort — purchase directly from abroad.

The pause on the Black Hawk purchase comes as the Carney government continues to review whether it will purchase a full order of F-35 stealth fighters, which are also manufactured by Lockheed Martin.

The government ordered a review of that plan in the late winter of 2025 and has yet to decide whether it will buy all 88 fighters as originally planned.

Canada has committed to buy 16 F-35s, but has also ordered the parts for more than a dozen others.

Government 'continues to evaluate options'

Whenever Canada — or other countries — buy U.S. military gear, the purchaser is required to request permission through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program.

Once reviewed by officials, the deal is sent to American lawmakers who have 15 days to object before it becomes official.

A spokesperson for the agency overseeing Canada's military procurement suggested options other than the Black Hawks could be considered.

"The government of Canada continues to evaluate options to meet the needs of the special operations forces," said Sofiya Sapeha, spokesperson for Stephen Fuhr, the parliamentary secretary responsible for military procurement.

"Canada remains in contact with the relevant partners and continues to review all information necessary for decision-making."

A Black Hawk helicopter is seen on display in Kielce, Poland, last month. A defence expert tells CBC News that the U.S.-made helicopter is well suited for Arctic operations. (Kacper Pempel/Reuters)

The Black Hawks are intended to replace the special forces' use of the CH-146 Griffon, which is more than three decades old and significantly inferior in terms of military operations.

One of the reasons Canada's commandos were keen on the Black Hawk was because of its range and robustness for operations over vast distances in the Arctic.

The UH-60 has a typical combat radius of about 595 kilometres, which can be extended by air-to-air refuelling. In that case, its range goes out to 2,250 kilometres. The Griffon's normal combat range is up to 656 kilometres, but can be fitted with external fuel tanks that take it up to 909 kilometres.

Special forces have been using the Griffon since their inception as a separate unit within the Canadian military in the early 1990s. The helicopter is currently flown by 427 Special Operations Aviation Squadron.

Retired major-general Denis Thompson, who commanded special operations troops, said the difference between the two helicopters is stark.

"In some ways you're comparing apples and oranges because a Griffon is a small, agile helicopter better suited for temperate climates and frankly better suited for urban operations than something as large as a Black Hawk," Thompson said.

"Range is important and the fact that it's a military design, a helicopter designed expressly for the military, means that it is just more robust and it can stand up to more punishment than the Griffon."

Thompson questioned the political calculus, but said he understands the way Canadians feel about the Trump administration.

"When we buy a piece of equipment, we're not hanging on to it for the two years that are left in Mr. Trump's mandate," Thompson said. "We're hanging on to them for 20, 30 years. And so what's important is to make sure that we buy the equipment that Canadian Armed Forces need and that we look to the long-term and not short-term political gain."

Low public support for buying American

Earlier this year, Policy Magazine published the results of a poll that indicated that 62 per cent of Canadians disagree with purchasing military equipment from the United States. Similarly, Abacus Data found that 64 per cent support an immediate halt to U.S. military purchases.

"I know it's difficult to explain that to the public, but that's what needs to be done," said Thompson.

He said equipment like the Black Hawk and F-35 weren't selected "for political reasons, at least not from the military standpoint. They were selected because they are the best piece, the most suitable piece, of equipment to fulfil the task that the military believes it might have to fill."

Defence analyst Justin Massie said the government is also clearly grappling with military procurement projects that were set in motion before the trade tensions began.

WATCH | Canada-U.S. trade minister on state of negotiations: Canada not 'desperate' to get a U.S. trade deal 'at any cost,' says minister | Duration closed caption 1:27 Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says comments from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the Trump administration is not in a rush to make a deal with Canada are 'consistent with the conversations' he's had with his U.S. counterpart. LeBlanc says the government will keep working to reach an agreement, but 'we're not waiting by the phone.'

"What is changing is not so much the strategy as the political discomfort of publicly announcing purchases of American military equipment." said Massie, a political science professor at Université du Québec à Montréal.

A spokesperson for Lockheed Martin highlighted the firm's willingness to continue working with the Canadian Armed Forces, without commenting on the status of the acquisition process.

"We are ready to support international customers wishing to acquire the latest-generation UH-60M Black Hawk helicopter through the Foreign Military Sales program," said the spokesperson, Amanda Hauck.

Other projects stalled

According to government and defence industry sources, Ottawa is hesitating to approve further military purchases from the United States, or even announce contracts already signed with American firms.

For instance, a recent Department of National Defence contract for specialized cloud computing services with California-based Google has not yet been announced. This contract involves storing and protecting classified information related to national security.

Another contract for a ground vehicle crew training system is reportedly slated for the U.S. firm Raytheon but has not been announced, sources say.

Earlier this year, the government waited months before confirming a contract to purchase M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from Lockheed Martin.

World.title: Charlottetown police lost the evidence in a P.E.I. cold-case murder. How did it happen?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The case against the man accused of murdering a P.E.I. teacher in 1988 has unravelled after Charlottetown police revealed the evidence crucial to securing a conviction was missing. How did police lose key evidence, and what does that mean for the case?

All charges against Todd Joseph Irving, 59, were dropped on Tuesday. He had been charged with first-degree murder and interfering with human remains in the killing of Byron Carr, a teacher found strangled and stabbed in his home.

According to the P.E.I. Crown Attorney's Office, moving forward with prosecution wasn’t an option because Charlottetown Police Services lost key evidence, leaving no chance of a conviction at the trial that was scheduled to begin in November.

Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, told CBC News on Tuesday that the agency knew when the cold case was reopened in 2007 — long before Irving was charged in early 2024 — that the knife left at the scene and the towel used to strangle Carr were missing.

“This was 1988. It was a different time in policing, the standards were far different than they are today,” MacDougall said.

So police instead built their case on DNA found at the scene.

“What we did in 2007 was we endeavoured to look at what we had, realize the challenges, and look forward to what was available to us as far as tools were concerned to identify the offender," MacDougall said.

Police hoped forensic evidence would be enough

When police announced Irving’s arrest in early 2024, they said the break in the case came thanks to advances in investigative genetic genealogy that linked Irving to one of the DNA samples found at the crime scene.

At a pre-trial hearing, police said Irving's DNA was found on Carr’s body, on a pair of underwear left at the scene and on an extinguished cigarette butt placed in Carr’s navel.

His DNA was not found on the towel used to strangle Carr, nor or on a sock left at the crime scene that police said was likely used as a glove to prevent leaving fingerprints behind.

"I certainly hoped that the forensic evidence would be enough to carry the day,” said former Charlottetown police chief Brad MacConnell, who led the investigation for years and now works as the city's chief administrative officer.

“It became apparent over the last several months as we worked through this that the challenges were too much to overcome."

WATCH | The man police accused of murdering Byron Carr in 1988 is now free. Here's what happened: The man police accused of murdering Byron Carr in 1988 is now free. Here's what happened | Duration closed caption 7:20 Todd Joseph Irving walked into court Tuesday facing charges of first-degree murder and interfering with human remains in the 1988 killing of P.E.I. teacher Byron Carr. After a two-minute hearing, he walked out a free man after the Crown dropped all the charges because the police lost crucial evidence. CBC's Wayne Thibodeau explains.

But the Crown's office didn’t know about the missing evidence until July — years after Irving’s arrest and just months before the trial was set to begin.

Crown attorney Christopher White said he’s disappointed the case won’t go to trial.

“This was a matter of personal and public significance,” he said.

“I think that everyone involved viewed that it was important that it be adjudicated in a public venue, so for that not to be able to take place, it’s disappointing and I cannot image what it would be like for Mr. Carr’s family.”

Byron Carr was 36 years old when he was murdered in his Charlottetown home in 1988. This poster was displayed at a 2024 news conference when police announced they'd made an arrest in relation to the case. (Wayne Thibodeau/CBC)

Charlottetown police say they haven’t ruled out a third-party review into how evidence is handled, but MacDougall said he’s confident something like this wouldn’t happen now.

The Crown said it won’t reopen the case against Irving.

Despite the outcome, both police and Carr’s family say they’re confident that while there isn’t enough evidence to bring him to trial, the right person was arrested.

“There’s no justice when someone is killed,” said John Carr, Byron’s brother.

“Nothing he could be sentenced to would ever bring Byron back or give us any more satisfaction. We’re not out to get anyone for it, but you know, he’s the one that’s got to live with himself.”

World.title: A Brexit scholar travelled to an Alberta separatist meeting. Here’s what he took away
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ten years ago, after the Brexit vote, a research institute was set up in Dublin.

Its goal? To study the ripple effects of the United Kingdom’s withdrawal from the European Union.

Ian Cooper, who was born in Saskatchewan and grew up in Alberta, works at that institute — the Brexit Institute at Dublin City University — as a senior research fellow, mapping out the vote’s political and economic fallout.

In recent months, he’s said he can’t help but feel a sense of “déjà vu.”

Much of what has transpired in Alberta as the referendum approaches reminds him of the lead-up to Brexit, Cooper has said. Compelled to vocalize what he saw as parallels, he hopped on a flight.

LISTEN | Brexit's lessons for Alberta, from CBC's Front Burner: Front Burner 21:03 Brexit's lessons for Alberta

He made the journey in August to Rimbey in central Alberta, where a free town hall was hosted by the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent pro-independence organization.

He noted the many farmers in the crowd, who naturally had questions about agricultural policy in an independent Alberta. The atmosphere was “respectful but not raucous,” he said.

WATCH | Ian Cooper talks parallels between the Alberta referendum and Brexit: CBC speaks with Senior research fellow at Dublin City University's Brexit Institute, Ian Cooper | Duration closed caption 8:18

He also listened to speeches, including one from Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project.

“I'll give him this. He's a talented public speaker, and he has got a certain kind of gruff public charm as a public speaker,” Cooper told CBC News Network Tuesday .

Cooper also saw parallels in the messaging to the "Leave" campaign in Britain.

“They can make all kinds of wild promises about how everything’s going to be wonderful if you vote for independence, and if Alberta becomes an independent country, it’ll be all upsides and no downsides,” Cooper said.

“That was also true of the ‘Leave’ campaign in Britain … only after the referendum passed did people see just how difficult Brexit was going to be.”

WATCH | 10 years after Brexit, is anybody happy?: 10 years after Brexit: Is anybody happy? | Duration closed caption 4:51 Ten years after the Brexit vote, few Britons have anything good to say about its unintended consequences. For The National, CBC's Chris Brown examines the Brexit fallout and its lessons for Alberta's independence movement. [Note: The title of this video has been edited to adhere to CBC’s Journalistic Standards and Practices.]

Sylvestre told CBC News Tuesday that he didn’t see the Brexit vote as analogous to Alberta’s referendum vote.

“We’re very resource-rich here. And as long as there’s a market for what we produce, we’ll keep producing it,” he said. “With what we have here, we’re pretty much self-sufficient … so, you know, I think we’ll be fine.”

Unlike the Brexit vote, which led to the U.K. leaving the European Union, Albertans will be asked Oct. 19 to choose one of two options: for the province to stay in Canada, or to hold a second binding referendum on separating from the country.

Various groups have attempted to put numbers to what it would mean in practice if Albertans ultimately choose to leave Canada and successfully negotiate independence with Ottawa and the other provinces.

In September, the University of Calgary School of Public Policy estimated the cost of establishing a new country between $50 billion and $170 billion over a five-year period, adding that it would be highly unpredictable over the long term.

Separatist groups have also offered up projections.

In September, the pro-independence Alberta Transition Council estimated about $5 billion in one-time expenses, while predicting an independent Alberta would have a potential budget surplus of between $22.2 billion to $32.1 billion each year.

Lawyer Keith Wilson with the Alberta Transition Council has rejected comparisons to Brexit, arguing Brexit was about the U.K. moving away from its largest market, Europe.

"Alberta independence is about Alberta moving closer to its largest market and the largest market in the world, the United States,” he said earlier this year .

Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, said there are lessons to be drawn from how things were handled in the U.K. after the Brexit vote.

“If you get to the point of a positive vote, your work is far from over,” he said.

“They got the vote, then took their hands off the steering wheel.”

WATCH | Why this Alberta separatist leader says it's time to leave Canada: Why this Alberta separatist leader says it’s time to leave Canada | Duration closed caption 8:52 As Alberta gets set to vote on pursuing a referendum to leave Canada, CBC’s Julia Wong goes to Bonnyville to meet the man behind one of the most prominent separatist organizations and others who believe the province is better off going it alone.

Former British PM dismissed comparison

David Cameron, who led the U.K. leading up to the Brexit vote, visited an energy conference in Calgary in September.

As part of his remarks, Cameron dismissed comparisons between Brexit and Alberta’s referendum, arguing Alberta’s vote is tied to the future of a country, rather than the U.K.’s membership in a trade association.

Former prime minister of the United Kingdom Lord David Cameron speaks at the Energy Disruptors: UNITE conference in Calgary on Sept. 28, 2026. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Cooper with the Brexit Institute said he agreed with Cameron that there is a fundamental structural difference, given Alberta is a province of a sovereign state.

But he said in his view, Cameron was “missing the point” tied to roles that political leaders play.

He noted that Cameron promised a referendum on Brexit to keep certain backbenchers in his party happy, though he himself campaigned against Brexit.

“You can see the same kind of thing happening in Alberta. Danielle Smith, she herself is campaigning in favour of remaining in Canada … but she’s trying to appease the hardcore, pro-separatist wing of her own party,” he said.

WATCH | Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she's 'public enemy number one' to some separatists: Smith says she's ‘public enemy No. 1’ to some separatists | Duration closed caption 0:37 In an interview with CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she is not in contact with separatist leaders, some of whom, she says may view her as “public enemy No. 1” because of her position to keep the province in Canada.

Britain ended up voting to leave, with 52 per cent in favour.

Polls tied to Alberta’s referendum have suggested a less competitive race. A recent poll suggested 23 per cent of respondents would vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum, while 72 per cent said they wanted to remain in Canada.

But polling suggests a very different picture among those who said they’d vote for the UCP, with 53 per cent saying they’d vote for the separation option, while 40 per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.

Smith was a frequent critic of federal policies that she argued disadvantaged Alberta. But under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Smith has argued that “Canada is working better than it ever has,” citing developments like the West Coast pipeline , officially known as Pacific Link.

Quite the 'political stew'

Cooper said that in the wake of the Brexit vote, the “Leave” and “Remain” camps became entrenched in the United Kingdom’s political landscape.

“To start this process … could lead to a very, very acrimonious debate within Alberta,” he said.

Morgan with Pathway to Independence said there is going to be quite the “political stew going on,” no matter which way the vote goes.

“If the vote goes 'yes,' she’s in dire trouble, because she’s going to be expected by the [UCP] members and a lot of Albertans to get moving on it. If she drags her feet, that could lead to a lot of political turmoil,” Morgan said.

“Likewise, if there’s a 'no' vote, she’s got to figure out then how to keep the discontented faction of her party from marching off to start another party.”

World.title: Russian strikes kill at least 3, as Ukraine reports intelligence, Starlink disruptions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Russian strikes killed three people in Kyiv and plunged hundreds of thousands into darkness overnight, authorities said Wednesday, in an attack Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump's peace effort.

The hours-long missile and drone attack primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, and damaged 30 energy facilities, Zelenskyy said. At least 600,000 people were left without power, he added.

"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale — Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"Russia does not consider the American president's statements strong."

Ukraine received no warnings from partners about missile attacks | Duration 2:24 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv received no intelligence from its partners about incoming ballistic missile attacks that struck the capital. While Zelenskyy did not specifically accuse the United States of withholding intelligence, several media outlets have reported that U.S. officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine if Kyiv does not halt deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Zelenskyy had earlier said Ukraine had received no warning from Western partners before a previous overnight attack on the capital. Trump said Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.

Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. threatened to cut off intelligence used for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine unless Kyiv stops attacking Russian oil refineries.

Trump, who lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week in a bid to lower politically sensitive fuel prices, has said that both sides agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, though neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed it.

Starlink questions

Ukrainian officials also said Wednesday that SpaceX had introduced a limit ‌on some Starlink services within the country, disrupting combat drone missions for which the technology is crucial.

The satellite internet terminals from Elon Musk's company are vital for guiding Ukraine's longer-range drone strikes in occupied ​southern and eastern Ukraine, which have wreaked ​havoc on Russian logistics.

"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential ​adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.

A firefighter battles a blaze at an apartment building in Kyiv damaged by a Russian missile strike on Tuesday. (Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters)

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular U.S. business hours.

Zelenskyy is due in London on Wednesday for talks with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Kyiv and its European supporters are racing to shore up Ukrainian defences amid Russia's escalating bombardment and doubts about the Trump administration's commitment to helping Ukraine to fend off Moscow's invasion, which began in February 2022.

Burnham's office said the U.K. government will provide "urgent support" for Kyiv in the coming weeks and will accelerate delivery of air defence missiles that Ukraine desperately needs before the bitter winter sets in.

Russia's Defence Ministry said Wednesday it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets.

Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defence against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.

Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of winter as it struggles on the battlefield, sparking fears of widespread power and heating outages across the country.

Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly been attacking Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs in recent months, in what it views as one of the few ways it can respond to more than four-and-a-half years of Russian bombardment.

Wednesday's Russian attacks also targeted state railway facilities in five regions across Ukraine, said Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi.

Trump blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for the rise in fuel costs, especially of diesel, which has hit record prices since his war against Iran disrupted global oil supplies.

World.title: A man's death on a U.S. roller-coaster triggered closures in Canada. Are the rides safe?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians can still feel safe riding roller-coasters after Tuesday's death at a Six Flags amusement park in the U.S., experts tell CBC News, because such accidents are "stunningly rare."

Police say a 42-year-old man killed while riding the Goliath roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, in Mableton, Ga., was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Several others were injured.

Nine similar roller-coasters at six North American parks have been closed "out of an abundance of caution," according to a Six Flags Entertainment Corp. spokesperson, including two at Canada's Wonderland near Toronto and one at Montreal's La Ronde amusement park.

Doug Perovic, a professor in materials science and engineering at the University of Toronto, says he's ridden the same Goliath coaster at California's Six Flags Magic Mountain "many times" with his son and would still feel safe getting back on.

"When you look at the safety record for roller-coasters, I mean, the numbers of these incidents are so, so small," he said.

"There are systems in place, if they're done properly, to inspect and do maintenance on a regular basis. And that is all documented and recorded. So that's why these types of failures are very rare."

What went wrong?

Experts say it's hard to know what might have gone wrong on the Goliath, given how little information has been released, but Perovic says his first thought, from a forensic engineering perspective, is that the restraint system failed.

He says investigators will look at whether there was a manufacturing problem with the restraint that became a defect over time, or a deficiency in the inspection protocols — for example, if someone missed a crack or other problem that was worsening over time.

"There are a number of different possibilities that are going to be looked at," he said.

WATCH | Canadian parks suspend some rides: Wonderland, La Ronde suspend some rides after Six Flags death | Duration 1:54 One man is dead and several riders were injured after a passenger was thrown from a roller-coaster at the Six Flags amusement park in Austell, Ga., on Oct. 12. At least two theme parks in Canada have temporarily shut down roller-coasters similar to the one at the U.S. theme park 'out of an abundance of caution,' according to a Six Flags Entertainment Corporation spokesperson.

Kathryn Woodcock, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University's School of Occupational and Public Health and director of the Tools for Holistic Ride Inspection Learning and Leadership lab, says these systems are complex and people will have to wait for answers.

Woodcock said in an email that roller-coasters are typically designed to an internationally recognized standard, and manufacturers establish inspection programs for specific things based on how often they fail and how detectable they are.

Plus, "the ride itself has built-in testing, in the automation system, with hundreds of sensors, and considerable redundancy," she said.

"So if any components have failed, it will have required the improbable event that multiple components failed at the same time."

'No competitive secrets'

But accidents do happen. The most infamous roller-coaster accident in Canada was 40 years ago on the West Edmonton Mall's Mindbender when a car derailed, killing three people and injuring 19. It was blamed on design and manufacturing flaws.

In 2013, in an incident similar to this week's death, a woman riding the Texas Giant roller-coaster died after she was thrown from her seat, fell 23 metres and struck a metal beam at Six Flags Over Texas. Six Flags redesigned its restraints before reopening the coaster two months later, and the park and the ride manufacturer settled a lawsuit with the woman's family.

WATCH | CBC coverage of the Mindbender deaths: From the archives: 3 killed in Mindbender derailment | Duration 1:59 It's been 30 years this week since a car on the Minderbender roller-coaster at West Edmonton Mall derailed, killing three.

But while accidents like these dominate headlines, they are extremely rare.

The National Safety Council said in its 2024 report for the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions that there were an estimated 118 serious injuries across North American fixed-site amusement rides that year and 1,360 injuries overall, though parks attributed two-thirds of those to guest-related factors, like medical conditions and behaviour.

The association's website pegs the likelihood of being seriously injured in a fixed-site ride at a U.S. amusement park at one in 15.5 million rides taken.

Woodcock says it is "stunningly rare" for someone to be ejected from a roller-coaster, and adds that people can take some reassurance from other Six Flags operators temporarily closing similar rides for safety reviews.

"We should also be aware of the regulatory authorities in Canadian provinces being well connected to each other and to their counterparts internationally to help communicate about safety," she said.

"The attractions industry has no competitive secrets when it comes to safety."

Extreme rides raise risk

Perovic cautions, however, that there could be a growing danger for some riders even when roller-coasters are working properly.

Six Flags Magic Mountain said last month it would retire its famously extreme X2 coaster following multiple lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious injuries — including a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old rider who was rushed to hospital in 2022 with severe brain bleeding and died a day later.

Last year, a medical examiner concluded that a man in his 30s — who was found unresponsive after riding Stardust Racers at Universal Orlando Resort — had died from blunt impact injuries, perhaps related to previous injuries. The man's family settled a wrongful death claim with Universal and the park updated its operational procedures and safety signage before reopening the ride two weeks later.

Six Flags has temporarily closed two roller-coasters at Canada's Wonderland, north of Toronto, out of an 'abundance of caution.' (Ken Townsend/CBC)

Perovic says people may want to consult their doctor before jumping on some extreme rides.

"These coaster manufacturers and these operators in the parks, they're all trying to one-up each other. They all want to be higher and faster and so on and keep breaking the world records," he said.

"Well, that comes at a cost. The forces could be too high and excessive. Not everybody's as fit as everyone else."

World.title: N.S. couple cycles through their grief as hospital tests vaccine to save other babies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The pregnancy, the birth and the early days of parenthood were the fulfilment of their dreams.

“She was pretty lively,” said Alexandre Genest, remembering his daughter, Lupine, as an infant. “She had long hair already.”

“And big, sparkly eyes,” added his wife, Carly Wedge, Lupine’s mom.

But after just three weeks with their "perfectly healthy" baby, the new parents were plunged into their worst nightmare. At their home on Nova Scotia’s South Shore, Lupine suddenly turned ill, and her parents took her to the nearby regional hospital. Doctors ordered that she be sent to Halifax’s children’s hospital, where she was taken into intensive care.

Five days later, she was gone.

A picture of Lupine Genest follows her dad's bicycle as he travels around Nova Scotia's highways and trails. (Paul Poirier/CBC)

Lupine was infected by Group B Streptococcus, or GBS, which led to sepsis and meningitis. GBS is a common bacterium that many adults carry without symptoms, but it causes life-threatening illness in babies.

Pregnant women are often screened for GBS, and if they test positive, they’re given a preventative round of antibiotics during labour. The antibiotics can protect newborns during the first week of life, but not beyond. For cases that begin later in infancy, such as Lupine’s, there is no means of prevention — yet.

Now, as Lupine would be turning six months old, Wedge and Genest are touring around Nova Scotia on their bicycles — working through their grief, raising money for the hospital that tried to save her, and spreading the word about a vaccine that’s in development.

“It's a rare thing, what happened to Lupine, but I think when it happens to you, it doesn't really matter that it's rare and you just want something to change,” said Wedge.

“A cure,” added Genest.

A vaccine on the horizon

What makes GBS so dangerous is that it escalates very quickly, said Dr. Joanne Langley, pediatric infectious disease specialist at the IWK Health Centre — the children's hospital where Lupine was treated.

“By the time you get the baby to care and start care, the baby has often become very unwell. And so even our best treatment will not catch up, in some cases.

"Preventing this disease is the best strategy,” she said.

Dr. Joanne Langley is an infectious disease specialist at the IWK Health Centre and investigator at the Canadian Center for Vaccinology. (Galen McRae/CBC)

Langley is an investigator at the Canadian Center for Vaccinology, and she’s working on a Phase 3 clinical trial for a maternal GBS vaccine.

Researchers have been trying to develop a vaccine against GBS since the 1970s, but Langley said no attempt has advanced as far as the current one, by Pfizer. Depending on how the current trial progresses, and on regulatory approvals, she said the vaccine could be widely available in the next few years.

“This will be just an overwhelming advance in the care of women and babies,” said Langley.

The World Health Organization says GBS causes about 150,000 stillbirths and infant deaths globally, each year, and vaccines could prevent more than 50 per cent of infant GBS cases. GBS can also lead to preterm birth, and a vaccine may lower that risk, too, according to the WHO.

Wedge and Genest say their baby girl, Lupine, was perfectly healthy for the first three weeks of her life. Then she suddenly turned severely ill. (Martha Wedge/Submitted)

In addition to preventing illness and death, Langley said the vaccine could also reduce the use of antibiotics in pregnant women who screen positive.

“That's a good thing, because the normal bacteria that mom has on her skin and her vagina are all healthy and part of the newborn's eventual microbiome,” she said.

Pfizer is testing the vaccine at more than 200 locations across the globe, including four in Canada.

Wedge said it feels like serendipity that the clinical trial started in Nova Scotia shortly after Lupine’s death.

"The more I learn about GBS, the more passionate I feel about making sure something is done to hopefully prevent other families from going through what we went through," she said.

Alexandre Genest and Carly Wedge stand by their bicycles at Summerville Beach Provincial Park, N.S., in early October 2026. (Jake Foley/Submitted)

As she and Genest cycle along Nova Scotia's rural roads and trails, they’re pulling a small trailer displaying Lupine’s picture, and sharing their journey on social media.

They said it’s been healing, talking to people about their daughter. At the same time, they’re trying to get people interested in the vaccine; they want to see the clinical trial get all the participants it needs.

“We're trying to get the word out to as many people who might be interested as possible, to help them push the science forward,” said Wedge.

Langley said because of the newness of the vaccine, the risks are unknown. The current study is specifically meant to test its safety.

Langley said investigators have not seen any serious events associated with the shot, so far. She said another trial may be needed to test the vaccine's efficacy in preventing disease.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Why Zelenskyy's claims that Ukraine drone attack halted Russian bot traffic don't hold up
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Ukraine struck three data centres owned by the Russian technology and AI company Yandex over the weekend, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy initially said the attacks had resulted in a sudden drop in pro-Russia bot activity.

"It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms," Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum Monday via video link. "A lot of people noticed it. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations. Because there were fewer bots.

"And it's pretty clear where those bots were coming from — if they disappeared when Yandex went offline."

When we started responding to Russia’s operation against our data centers, and when our strikes reached Yandex’s data centers, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms. A lot of people noticed it. There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations. Because there were fewer bots. And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from – if they disappeared when Yandex went offline. This proves, again and again, that Europe is not the source of the problems. Europe is not the one making everything more difficult. Most importantly, we need people in America, every morning, when the day in Europe is already moving toward evening, to really see what is happening. To see the truth. From a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum. (3/3) —ZelenskyyUa

The Ukrainian president's assertions that the strikes had curtailed the spread of pro-Russia disinformation were also repeated and spread on various social media forums. But some experts are casting doubt on his claims and instead suggest that people are misinterpreting data collected about bot traffic following the drone attacks.

'A dangerous misconception'

"It's a dangerous misconception," L ukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at the Department of War Studies at Kings College London, posted on X.

"The 'bots went silent' story is misinforma tion," he wrote. "Believing it is plainly dangerous. It tells people the threat is gone while influence operations keep going."

Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in the development of Russian artificial intelligence.

The airstrikes on the data centres caused outages across Yandex's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities as well as those in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

In an interview with CBC News, Samuel Woolley, who studies disinformation at the University of Pittsburgh, agreed it was an "an overstatement" to suggest propaganda bot traffic declined following Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centres.

"I haven't seen any research or data that tracks all of the propaganda bots," he said. "It's a misconception to say that all the Russian propaganda bots went down because of this."

Russia is alleged to have created a vast network or army of bots — automated software programs on the internet — to spread disinformation, particu larly about Ukraine and the war.

Flawed interpretation of data

Following the strikes on the data centres, some on social media were quick to cite a chart from Cloudflare, a U.S. company that monitors global internet traffic, claiming that it showed Russian bot activity had dropped to nearly zero.

Olejnik said in an email to CBC News that while the data from Cloudflare is reliable, it just showed a decline in automated traffic activity from Yandex's search engine crawler, which he explained is different from automated bots used to spread disinformation by posting on social media sites.

"The problem is how these figures were interpreted," Olejnik said, noting the Cloudflare data does not measure propaganda infrastructure activity on social networks.

"The strikes disrupted Yandex's infrastructure, but no significant general decline in pro-Kremlin activity is confirmed," he told CBC via email.

Woolley says most people associate the word "bot" with fake accounts online, however, it's a generic term to describe any kind of software that completes automated tasks on the internet. Including the kind Yandex uses to scour the web.

"So it makes total sense if you attack Yandex, that automated traffic online would go down," he said.

Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development. (Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters)

"Basically, bot traffic generally dropped, but everyone is so focused on the internet being so rife with disinformation and propaganda, people relate the word bot to a manipulative social media account."

Woolley says it's estimated that over half of online traffic is automated, but "that doesn't mean that half of online traffic is malicious bots."

He also says it's unlikely that Russian propaganda networks were entirely reliant on the Yandex data centres hit in the strikes.

Olejnik says Russian influence operations involve thousands of accounts across various platforms, and that "taking down a few data centres" won't solve the whole problem.

"Troll farms hide behind proxies, hijacked devices and Western clouds," he wrote on X. "They're still operating."

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy appeared to be backtracking a bit on his initial claim. The Ukrainian president's office told BBC he was "talking about the atmosphere on social media" rather than a decline in bot activity.

The office noted that it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.

World.title: Mark Norman: Canada’s defence-spending quagmire
World.content:
Article content

To make this more complicated, we are not starting with a clean-sheet design for the CAF. The “force in being” — which is a product of decades of previous decisions — has an enormous impact on both current decisions and future options and it often constrains how we transition to any future force. This is in part why the impacts of new spending are not necessarily immediately measurable or impactful. It takes time and effort to divest of old stuff (and all of its attendant procedures, logistics support, etc.) and “onboard” new capability. Without sufficient people, training, doctrine, spare parts or a plan, new equipment is not necessarily any more “ready for operations” than what it replaced despite its relative “newness.” This also assumes that the new capability is actually delivered before it becomes operationally irrelevant, unsustainable or no longer fit for purpose. That assumption is sadly not always true given the protracted timelines of our traditional procurement processes.

World.title: The end of Quebec’s left-wing consensus
World.content:
Article content

The Parti Québécois may have won a minority government, but the biggest winners in last week’s election might just have been the Quebec Conservative Party. Under the leadership of Éric Duhaime, the Quebec Conservatives came from nowhere to capture 19 seats in the Quebec National Assembly after a campaign where the Conservatives drove much of the policy agenda. In this interview, Rob Breakenridge is joined by former Quebec Conservative Leader Adrien Pouliot for a closer look at how the party finally made its big breakthrough and burst Quebec’s long-standing consensus around big government and left-of-centre policies. Pouliot says that Quebec Conservatives ran and succeeded with a campaign focused on ideas, including tax cuts, cutting government waste, health care reform, and better control of immigration — an approach that offers lessons for conservative parties across Canada.
