PERU · TRADE

Key Facts The country Peru is a major copper and gold exporter in South America with a free-trade agreement with the United States since 2009.

What happened Peru’s Association of Exporters blamed extra US tariffs on Tuesday, 13 October, for a 5.7% fall in Peru clothing exports from January to August.

The numbers Clothing exports fell to US$764.1 million from US$810.6 million a year earlier, and the United States bought US$490.4 million, or 64.2%.

US imports US clothing imports from Peru fell 10.4% in the first eight months of 2026, leaving Peru in 19th place among suppliers.

Jobs Jobs tied to clothing exports fell 14.6% through July, a loss of 33,487 direct, indirect and induced posts, and 49 fewer firms exported.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open How much of the slide comes from tariffs rather than a stronger sol and high logistics costs, and when the government’s recovery plan arrives.

Peru clothing exports fell 5.7% to US$764.1 million in the first eight months of 2026, and the country’s exporters blame US tariffs. The United States buys almost two-thirds of the clothing Peru sells abroad, from cotton T-shirts to knit shirts.

The Asociación de Exportadores (ADEX), a Lima business group that speaks for Peruvian exporters, released the market breakdown on Tuesday, 13 October. It said extra US duties of 10% since April 2025 and 12.5% since July 2026 leave Peruvian clothing less competitive.

What the Exporters Reported

ADEX said Peru clothing exports totalled US$764.1 million between January and August, down from US$810.6 million in the same months of 2025. It said the fall came mainly from the tariffs imposed by the United States, the sector’s main market.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

César Tello Ramírez, the association’s president, said the extra duties weaken Peru against suppliers from Asia and Central America. “These are factors that hinder the momentum of this activity,” he said, pointing to a world market ever more sensitive to costs.

ADEX’s overall export report on Tuesday, 6 October, already showed the 5.7% clothing decline, while high metal prices lifted total exports 34.3%. The new statement added the breakdown by market and tied the slide directly to Washington’s tariffs.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the US Market Matters

The United States took 64.2% of Peru clothing exports from January to August, worth US$490.4 million, according to ADEX. Brazil came a distant second at US$57.6 million, up 15.2%, out of 85 markets in all.

Chile, Canada, Germany, Colombia, Venezuela, China, Mexico and Argentina completed the top ten buyers. The best-selling products were cotton T-shirts for men and women, single-colour cotton T-shirts and knit shirts of synthetic fibres.

ADEX also cited the Office of Textiles and Apparel (OTEXA), the US Commerce Department unit that tracks American clothing imports. By that count, US clothing imports from Peru fell 10.4% from January to August, placing Peru 19th among suppliers.

Total US clothing imports slipped 2.5% over the same months by OTEXA’s count, with shipments from China down 29.4%. Only three of the ten largest suppliers grew: Cambodia by 6.9%, Italy by 6.1% and Indonesia by 2.6%.

Jobs and the Government’s Emergency Plan

The slump is hitting a labour-heavy industry, which generated more than 411,000 direct jobs in 2025, according to the Ministry of Production. Through July, the number of companies exporting clothing fell 5.6%, or 49 firms, and jobs tied to clothing exports fell 14.6%, ADEX said.

That equals 33,487 lost jobs, counting direct, indirect and induced positions. Tello welcomed a government decree, announced on Thursday, 1 October, that put the textile and clothing chain under emergency for 120 calendar days.

The decree, Supreme Decree 014-2026-PRODUCE, orders the Ministry of Production to approve a recovery plan within 15 working days. The plan is aimed mainly at small firms, and the decree sets out four lines of action.

The four are easier financing, training and productivity, state purchases from small firms through the Compras a MYPErú programme, and trade promotion in new markets. Tello said a full recovery also requires fixing problems tied to exports.

He listed high logistics costs, a shortage of skilled workers and a stronger sol, Peru’s currency, which makes exports dearer abroad. He also called for faster digital change and more automation in factories.

What It Means for You

For American retailers and shoppers, Peruvian clothing now carries an extra 12.5% US duty, despite a free-trade agreement in force since 2009. The same US order spares textiles and clothing that enter duty-free from Central America and the Dominican Republic under their own trade pact.

For US brands that source in Peru, the emergency plan promises financing and support for small firms, but it cannot change US duties. ADEX itself urges exporters to sell more elsewhere, since heavy reliance on a few markets raises their exposure to trade shocks.

For investors, clothing earned US$764.1 million in eight months, a small sum next to Peru’s copper and gold sales. The next test lies with the people who run Peru’s economy, since the Ministry of Production must now deliver its plan.

What Is Not Known

ADEX did not put a figure on how much of the fall in Peru clothing exports came from tariffs rather than other costs. It also did not say how many of the 33,487 lost jobs were direct factory posts rather than indirect or induced ones.

ADEX did not say when the Ministry of Production will present the recovery plan the decree requires. ADEX has not yet published clothing export figures for September, which would show more of the higher duty’s effect.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Peru’s clothing exports falling?

Peru clothing exports fell 5.7% from January to August, and the exporters’ association ADEX mainly blames extra US tariffs. It also points to high logistics costs, a shortage of skilled workers and a stronger sol.

How much Peruvian clothing does the United States buy?

The United States bought US$490.4 million of Peruvian clothing from January to August 2026, or 64.2% of the total. Brazil was a distant second at US$57.6 million.

Does Peru have a free-trade agreement with the United States?

Yes, the US-Peru Trade Promotion Agreement has been in force since 1 February 2009. Even so, a US Trade Representative order has added a 12.5% duty on most Peruvian goods since 24 July 2026.

What is Peru doing to help its clothing industry?

A government decree declared the textile and clothing chain in emergency for 120 calendar days. It orders the Ministry of Production to approve a recovery plan, aimed mainly at small firms, within 15 working days.

World.content:

PERU · RELIGION

Key Facts The country Peru, a largely Catholic Andean nation, is where Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV spent years as a missionary and later as a bishop.

What happened The Archdiocese of Lima postponed a second preparatory meeting for clergy and religious orders ahead of Pope Leo’s visit, with no new date.

Why now On Tuesday 13 October, surgeons in Rome removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung and confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, a type of cancer.

The trip The Vatican programme has the pope in Peru from Wednesday 11 to Monday 16 November, with stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa.

Prediction markets Kalshi gives an 86% chance that Pope Leo visits Peru this year, down from 93% a day earlier (14 October, 4:12 a.m. ET).

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open Whether doctors clear a 12-day, three-country tour that begins 24 days after the operation.

Lima’s Catholic Church has postponed a planning meeting for Pope Leo XIV’s November visit to Peru, hours after his lung cancer surgery in Rome. For American Catholics and US travellers booked for the trip, it is a sign that the diagnosis is already touching preparations on the ground.

Auxiliary Bishop Guillermo Elías, head of the organising commission, announced the delay on Tuesday in a written statement to clergy. Infobae Perú reported it that evening, and archdiocese spokesman Juan José Dioses told Lima broadcaster RPP that “so far the apostolic trip is confirmed”.

What the Lima Church Put Off

The postponed event was the second preparatory meeting for priests and members of religious orders in the Lima ecclesiastical province, which includes neighbouring dioceses. Elías wrote that the new date, time and place will be announced later, according to Infobae Perú.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In the same statement, he said organisers “continue working” so that every activity planned for the encounter with Pope Leo takes place. Dioses told Infobae Perú that the delay affects only the clergy meeting and does not cancel or delay the papal trip.

He added that the church can “only wait calmly and prudently” for official announcements expected this week. He did not say who would make them, but the Holy See, the Catholic Church’s central government, sets the pope’s travel.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Doctors in Rome Found

The Vatican said surgeons at Rome’s Gemelli hospital removed the lower lobe of Pope Leo’s right lung on Tuesday 13 October. A tissue test during the operation confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer, as earlier scans had suggested.

He spent about three hours in the operating room, and the procedure itself took around 90 minutes, according to Vatican News. The Vatican said the planned one-week hospital stay had not changed and that further tests on the removed tissue would follow.

Pope Leo, 71, was born in Chicago and became the first US-born pope in May 2025, as the 13 October report on his diagnosis explains. He spent years in Peru as a missionary and later served as bishop of Chiclayo, a city in the country’s north.

How Peru Is Reacting

Peru’s conservative president, Keiko Fujimori, responded to the diagnosis with a call to “unite our faith in a great chain of prayer”. El Comercio and Infobae Perú carried her words, and Dioses told RPP that the faithful have started a prayer chain for the pope.

The pope’s personal secretary, Edgard Iván Rimaycuna, a 36-year-old priest from Chiclayo, has described him as “very calm” about the diagnosis. Chiclayo parish priest Carlos Samamé received that reply in a message and repeated it at a Mass on Tuesday, Infobae Perú reported.

Elías also called a day of prayer for the pope’s health on Wednesday 14 October in all parishes and communities of the archdiocese. He entrusted the pope’s recovery to the Lord of Miracles, the Lima devotion whose sanctuary is the Las Nazarenas church.

The Peru Programme at Stake

The Holy See’s programme, published on 21 September, runs from 6 to 17 November across Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. Pope Leo is due to land at the Callao air base, next to Lima, at 5:30 p.m. on Wednesday 11 November.

He would then fly to Chiclayo on Friday 13 November and on to Cusco and the Amazon city of Pucallpa on Sunday 15 November. The Peru leg ends with a Mass at Las Palmas Air Base in Lima and a flight to Rome on Monday 16 November.

Dioses told RPP the tour spans 14 cities and 35 speeches, calling it the pope’s longest apostolic trip. He said Peru is the most demanding stop geographically, because the pope must travel to a city at high altitude.

What It Means for You

US pilgrims and tour groups booked for Lima, Chiclayo or Cusco can keep their plans for now but should check refund terms. Lima’s archdiocese says the trip stands, and Peru’s government said on 11 October that the programme had not changed.

A lung specialist quoted by La República, Dennis Valer Ugarte, said recovery from this kind of planned keyhole surgery takes about 10 to 14 days. He added that an exhausting visit on top of the stress of surgery is “definitely not the healthiest” choice for the pope.

The Peru leg alone includes four domestic flights between 13 and 15 November, plus a return helicopter trip from Chiclayo on 14 November. Until the Vatican speaks, travellers should treat the dates as planned but not certain, and our Lima city guide covers the capital.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), bettors give an 86% chance that Pope Leo visits Peru this year. That price stood at 93% a day earlier, before the Vatican confirmed the cancer (14 October, 4:12 a.m. ET).

The same Kalshi series puts Uruguay at 84% and Argentina at 81%, with about 217,000 contracts traded across all countries. These are bets on an outcome, not polls and not forecasts by the church.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether doctors will clear the pope for a 12-day tour that starts less than four weeks after surgery. The Vatican has not said whether he needs further cancer treatment, pending tests on the removed tissue.

Lima’s archdiocese has not set a new date for the postponed clergy meeting. It has also not said whether any other preparatory events for the papal visit will move.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Pope Leo’s visit to Peru cancelled?

No, the Archdiocese of Lima says the apostolic trip remains confirmed for now, and the Holy See had announced no change by Wednesday morning. Only a preparatory meeting for clergy in Lima has been postponed.

When is Pope Leo due in Peru?

The Vatican programme has him landing in Lima on Wednesday 11 November and leaving for Rome on Monday 16 November. In between, he is scheduled to visit Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa.

What surgery did the pope have?

On 13 October, surgeons in Rome removed the lower lobe of his right lung, and tests confirmed lung adenocarcinoma. The Vatican said the operation went without complications and the planned one-week hospital stay is unchanged.

Should US travellers change their plans?

The Archdiocese of Lima says the trip stands for now, so travellers can keep bookings while checking refund and change terms. The archdiocese expects official announcements later this week.

World.title: Peru Senate Panel to Vote on Crime Powers
World.content:
Save Share In short Contents Listen Aa

PERU · POLITICS

Key Facts The country Peru, a US free-trade partner and major copper exporter, led since July by conservative President Keiko Fujimori.

What happened The Peru Senate’s Constitution Committee held a hearing on Tuesday 13 October, and its chair expects a vote on Thursday 15 October.

The scope 20 measures on citizen security and El Niño for 90 calendar days, out of 66 the government had requested.

Lower house vote Deputies passed the bill on Tuesday 6 October by 66 votes to 34, with 24 abstentions.

Next step The full Senate is expected to debate the committee’s text on Monday 19 October.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open Whether senators add measures back, and whether the committee votes on Thursday as planned.

A Peru Senate committee plans to vote on Thursday 15 October on 90 days of decree powers for President Keiko Fujimori. The bill would let her government change laws on crime and on the El Niño weather pattern without new votes in Congress.

For US companies, travellers and investors, the vote will shape how fast Peru can rewrite its rules on extortion and organised crime. Fujimori, a conservative who took office on 28 July, saw the lower house reject the trimmed plan once before passing it on a second vote.

What Happened at Tuesday’s Hearing

The Peru Senate’s Constitution Committee met on Tuesday 13 October to review the bill, which the lower house passed a week earlier. Its chair, Carlos Mesía, is a senator for Fuerza Popular, Fujimori’s conservative party.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Mesía said the committee had declared itself in permanent session and would vote on Thursday. He added that the full Senate would debate the approved text on Monday 19 October, El Comercio, a leading Lima daily, reported.

Senator Patricia Iturregui of Buen Gobierno, a party that wants the deputies’ text kept intact, asked first to settle the Senate’s room for changes. Mesía replied that there was no time, because “the committee only has seven working days to issue its report.”

The session was suspended shortly after 1 p.m. without a vote, and no time to resume had been set by late Tuesday. It followed Saturday’s sitting, which broke down after the clash described in Peru Senate Clash Interrupts 90-Day Powers Hearing.

Before the break, committee chairs, business groups and a constitutional lawyer spoke, the Congress news service said. Defence committee chair Francisco Calisto proposed clearer rules for troops when police are overwhelmed, and a stronger national intelligence system.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Small Businesses Say They Pay Gangs

Representatives of small and micro businesses told senators what crime already costs them. “We small businesses pay protection money all the time,” they said, according to El Comercio.

Alfonso López Chau, who leads the opposition Ahora Nación party, said dropped measures could return to Congress as urgent bills. Business speaker Rebeca Antezana Díaz replied that firms could not wait.

The groups also asked for a tax reform and a law to promote Peruvian cuisine, which the bill does not cover. Simpler rules to bring small firms into the formal economy were among the measures the deputies dropped, El Comercio’s tally shows.

The text passed by the lower house lists extortion, contract killings, organised crime and cybercrime among the areas open to decrees. It also covers migration control, weapons oversight, prison reform and identifying and blocking illicit communications, the Congress news service said.

What the Lower House Already Approved

Peru’s Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, approved the bill late on Tuesday 6 October by 66 votes to 34, with 24 abstentions. It had failed at a first vote, before a motion to reconsider passed by 75 votes to 33.

Deputies kept only 20 of the 66 measures the government had asked for, all on citizen security and El Niño weather risks. Our earlier report, Peru Deputies Back 90-Day Decree Powers for Fujimori, covers that vote in detail.

On El Niño, a Pacific warming that can flood Peru’s coast, the bill covers direct civil defence aid in an emergency’s first 15 days. It also covers support for farmers and simpler procedures for infrastructure, housing, water and sanitation.

A Peru Senate Split Over Changing the Bill

Members of the Peru Senate disagree on whether they may add back measures the deputies dropped. Víctor Flores, another Fuerza Popular senator, ruled out restoring all 66, Infobae Perú reported: “No, no, by no means.”

Flores said senators could add some points, but only within the two subjects the lower house approved. He also said the government’s plan would go ahead “with powers and without powers.”

Mesía said the Peru Senate would respect the lower-house text but adjust its parts on El Niño and security, Correo, a Lima daily, reported. On the TV programme Panorama, he complained that deputies had refused to let the government label criminal organisations “hostile groups.”

Héctor Ventura, a third Fuerza Popular senator, wants the Senate to add work by the armed forces in support of the police. Iturregui and Senator Iber Maraví of the opposition Juntos por el Perú party oppose adding subjects the lower house left out.

Juntos por el Perú is the left-wing party of Roberto Sánchez, whom Fujimori beat in this year’s presidential runoff. Víctor García Toma, a constitutional lawyer, told the committee the Senate may reshape the two subjects but cannot add matters such as insurance or banking.

Oscar Reto of Buen Gobierno, who presides over the Chamber of Deputies, has said the Peru Senate has no right to distort the deputies’ text. Mesía told El Comercio in an interview that Reto was “mistaken.”

Fuerza Popular and Renovación Popular, the conservative party of Rafael López Aliaga, hold six committee votes, matching the opposition, El Comercio reported. In a tie, Mesía as chair has the casting vote.

What It Means for You

For Americans living in or visiting Peru, the decrees could bring tougher policing, migration checks and prison rules soon after a final vote. Investors in Peruvian mines, banks and ports will watch how fast the government can act on extortion.

The El Niño measures matter for anyone who buys Peruvian fruit, fish or minerals, because floods can cut roads and ports. A long fight in the Peru Senate would leave less time to prepare before the summer rains on Peru’s coast.

What Comes Next

If the committee approves a text on Thursday 15 October, Mesía expects the full Peru Senate to debate it on Monday 19 October. Once the law is in force, the government would have 90 calendar days to issue its decrees.

What Is Not Known

It is not known when the suspended committee session will resume or which measures senators will add. Mesía said on Tuesday that members still had to decide what goes into the text.

It is also unclear whether the government will send the dropped measures to Congress as separate urgent bills, as Flores and López Chau suggested. The government has not said which decrees it would issue first.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are decree powers in Peru?

Peru’s Congress can let the government issue laws by decree on specific subjects for a set period. The current bill would allow 90 calendar days of decrees on citizen security and El Niño.

When will the Peru Senate vote?

The committee chair, Carlos Mesía, expects a committee vote on Thursday 15 October. He said the full Senate would debate the text on Monday 19 October.

Why did the government get fewer powers than it asked for?

The government asked for 66 measures, but the lower house kept only 20, on citizen security and El Niño weather risks. Items left out include some housing measures, simpler rules for small firms and a plan to label criminal organisations hostile groups.

Does this change anything for travellers to Peru yet?

No new rules apply yet, because Congress has not finished the process. If the law passes, decrees on migration control, weapons and policing could follow within 90 days.

BRAZIL · TRAVEL

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest economy, draws many US visitors to Rio de Janeiro, whose main international gateway is Galeão airport.

What happened Aena, the Spanish airport group that took over Galeão on 6 October, presented plans for more international flights on Tuesday, 13 October.

US routes The plan adds service to New York, Dallas, Miami and Atlanta, alongside Toronto and Montreal in Canada, by January 2027.

Investment Partners plan R$1 billion (about US$200 million) of projects over three years, including a hotel and an airline hangar.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open Airlines set the final dates and frequencies, and the cost and timetable of works inside the terminals are not yet public.

We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Galeão, the main Rio airport for international travel, plans more flights to New York, Dallas, Miami and Atlanta under its new operator, Spain’s Aena. The company presented the plan on Tuesday, 13 October, one week after it took control of the airport on 6 October.

For US travellers, it promises more direct ways into the city of Copacabana beach and the Christ the Redeemer statue as the southern summer approaches. Airlines, not the airport, will set the exact dates and the number of flights on each route.

What Aena Announced in Rio

Aena, a Madrid-listed airport group controlled by the Spanish state, presented the plan at a press conference at the airport. Brazil’s Minister of Ports and Airports, Tomé Franca, attended and backed the push for more foreign visitors.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Agência Brasil, the federal government’s news agency, reported more than 50 extra weekly flights to nine foreign cities by January 2027. Those nine are Paris, Miami, Frankfurt, Lisbon, Porto, Santiago, Córdoba, Atlanta and Panama City.

The agency listed nine more foreign cities for resumed or new flights in the same period. They are New York, Dallas, Toronto, Montreal, Asunción, Salta, Mendoza, Rosario and Lima.

Brazil’s Ministry of Ports and Airports said the Rio airport handled 12.67 million passengers from January to August, up 10.9% on a year earlier. International travellers rose 13.8% to 4.32 million in the same period, the ministry added.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

When the New Flights Start

Diário do Rio, a Rio news site, laid out a timeline for the first changes, starting in October 2026. More service to New York and Toronto and more flights to Paris and Miami come first.

In November, flights to Asunción in Paraguay are due to resume, with more to Frankfurt, Lisbon and Porto. December brings more service to Dallas, Montreal, Mendoza in Argentina and Lima in Peru.

The travel site Passageiro de Primeira published the route list Aena presented, which puts American Airlines on the New York, Miami and Dallas routes. Delta Air Lines adds New York in November and more Atlanta flights in December, the list shows.

Air Canada and Air Transat are listed for the Canadian routes, Lufthansa for Frankfurt and TAP Air Portugal for extra Lisbon and Porto flights. Panama’s Copa Airlines and the Chilean airlines LATAM, SKY and JetSMART add flights on Latin American routes.

Diário do Rio stressed that the dates and frequencies of each route depend on the airlines’ own schedules. Flights to 18 Brazilian destinations, including Porto Alegre, Fortaleza and Manaus, also increase in the summer high season, O Dia and Passageiro de Primeira reported.

What It Means for You

For a traveller in the United States, the plan means more ways to fly into the Rio airport from New York, Dallas, Miami and Atlanta. No fares were announced, so the effect on ticket prices is not known.

Gol, a Brazilian low-cost airline, has flown between Rio and New York’s JFK airport since July. Anyone planning a trip should check each route’s start date with the airline before booking.

Investors in Aena’s shares in Madrid also have a stake, since the company now runs the Rio airport as well as São Paulo’s Congonhas. The Rio contract runs until May 2039, the Ministry of Ports and Airports said.

A Hotel, a Hangar and New Jobs

Aena also presented R$1 billion (about US$200 million) of investments over three years, at about 5.02 reais to the US dollar on 14 October 2026. Agência Brasil reported that partners will put in that money, with Aena coordinating the projects.

The projects include a hotel of at least 232 rooms between the terminals, a test centre for Chinese carmaker BYD and a logistics warehouse. Gol plans a maintenance hangar for its aircraft at the Rio airport.

Aena expects the projects to create about 3,860 jobs over the three years, the Ministry of Ports and Airports said. Diário do Rio and O Dia, two Rio newspapers, reported the same figure.

Terminal 1, closed for ten years, will only be reconsidered if demand for new flights grows, Agência Brasil reported. Repairs to lifts and baggage belts are planned, but Aena did not say how much it will spend inside the terminals.

Limits on Rio’s Downtown Airport End in 2029

Santos Dumont, the smaller downtown Rio airport, has had a passenger cap since 2023 to push flights back to the Galeão airport. The limit stands at 6.5 million passengers a year, Agência Brasil reported.

Franca said the agreement lets the cap rise to 8.5 million in 2027 and 9.5 million in 2028, with no limit in 2029. If the government keeps a tighter cap, he said, Galeão’s contract will be rebalanced against the operator.

“Brazil needs more airports geared to international tourism,” Franca said, naming Galeão alongside São Paulo’s Guarulhos airport. Diário do Rio reported that he also argued for new airlines in Brazil and closer air links among South American countries.

What Is Not Known

Airlines can still change dates and frequencies before the new flights start. Whether Terminal 1 will ever reopen depends on new demand, and no date was given.

How many extra seats each route out of the Rio airport will get is not yet public. The timetable for the investment package and the works inside the terminals are also still to come.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which US cities get more flights to Galeão, the Rio airport?

Aena’s plan lists New York, Dallas, Miami and Atlanta, with American Airlines and Delta, for new, resumed or extra service by January 2027. The exact dates and frequencies depend on each airline’s own schedule.

Who runs Rio de Janeiro’s Galeão airport now?

Spanish airport group Aena took over Galeão on 6 October 2026 and holds the concession until May 2039. It also runs São Paulo’s Congonhas airport.

When do the first new flights to Rio start?

Diário do Rio reports that the first changes are planned for October 2026, starting with New York, Toronto, Paris and Miami. Dallas and Montreal follow in December, according to the same report.

Will the new flights make tickets to Rio cheaper?

No fare changes were announced, so the effect on prices is not known. That depends on how many seats airlines actually add on each route.

World.content:

COLOMBIA · SAFETY

Key Facts The country Colombia, a close US security partner in South America, is led by President Abelardo de la Espriella.

What happened A 51-year-old British cancer doctor who lived in the United States died on Monday, 12 October, after falling ill at a Medellín music festival.

The festival EDC, a brand of the US company Insomniac, held its first Colombian edition on 10 and 11 October at Medellín’s main sports complex.

Earlier death A Costa Rican man died early on Sunday, 11 October, after falling ill on the festival’s opening night.

Medical cases Medellín’s health department counted 193 medical cases at the festival, 107 of them linked to intoxication, and seven hospital transfers.

Cause of death No official cause has been published for either man, and forensic results are still pending.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

A 51-year-old British cancer doctor living in the US has died after falling ill at EDC, a Medellín festival of electronic music in Colombia. He is the second foreigner to die after the Medellín festival, held on 10 and 11 October by a US festival brand.

Colombian outlets including El Espectador and La FM reported on Tuesday, 13 October, that he died the previous afternoon in a clinic. Local media have linked his death to drug and alcohol use, but no official cause of death has been published.

What Happened to the Doctor

El Tiempo reported the death early on Tuesday, describing the man as an English oncologist based in the United States who specialised in prostate cancer. El Espectador and Vanguardia later said he had co-founded a prostate cancer institute in Arizona in 2002.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

He fell ill at the Medellín festival on Sunday, 11 October, and was taken to the El Rosario clinic, Publimetro and Vanguardia report. He died there at about 5 p.m. on Monday, 12 October, a public holiday in Colombia.

La FM reported that Medellín’s security department linked his condition to a high intake of amphetamines and alcohol. El Espectador stressed that the exact circumstances are still under investigation and that the official cause must await the relevant procedures.

The paper also cautioned that drug use inside the Medellín festival should not be assumed without official information to back it up. Colombia’s state forensic institute, known as Medicina Legal, normally establishes the cause of death in such cases.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Colombia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The First Death on Opening Night

The first victim was a Costa Rican man who fell ill on the festival’s opening night, Saturday, 10 October. El Colombiano, Publimetro and Vanguardia report that he was found unconscious and died early on Sunday at the Pablo Tobón Uribe hospital.

Investigators are looking into a possible overdose, which has not been confirmed. His father has told El Colombiano and Noticias Caracol that his son was not an addict.

The Rio Times reported the Costa Rican’s death on 11 October, when it was the only death linked to the Medellín festival. Authorities have not said whether the two deaths are connected.

What Medellín’s Health Department Reported

Natalia López, the city’s health secretary, reported 193 medical cases at the Medellín festival’s care points over the two days. Of those, 107 were linked to some kind of intoxication, and seven people were taken to hospitals in the city.

López urged people at large events to look after their health and to use the medical points when they need help. “Above any celebration is life,” she said, according to Telemedellín and La FM.

A Stabbing After the Festival

In a separate case, an Australian man staying in Medellín’s Laureles district was found with 25 stab wounds early on Sunday, 11 October. El Colombiano and Semana both reported the attack, and El Colombiano said he had likely attended the festival that night.

El Colombiano said investigators were reviewing security cameras and treating robbery as one line of inquiry, with no arrests reported. The Rio Times covered the attack on 12 October, and nothing published so far ties it to the two deaths.

Medellín’s Big Night Out

EDC, short for Electric Daisy Carnival, is a large electronic dance music festival brand owned by the US events company Insomniac. The Rio Times previewed the Colombian debut before the event.

The festival used the Atanasio Girardot sports complex, home to the city’s main football stadium, in the Laureles-Estadio area. The two deaths and the stabbing all came during the long holiday weekend of the Medellín festival.

What It Means for You

The US State Department rates Colombia at Level 3, “Reconsider travel,” in an advisory issued on 31 March 2026. It lists drugging among the crimes visitors face and warns: “Never leave food or drinks unattended at a bar or restaurant.”

At any big Medellín festival or night out, stay with friends, watch your drink and find the medical point when you arrive. Carry insurance that covers emergency hospital care abroad, and read The Rio Times guide to staying safe in Colombia.

What Is Not Known

No official cause of death has been published for either man, and no public forensic report backs the drug findings described in the press. It is also not known what, if anything, either man took inside the festival grounds.

Authorities have not said whether the two deaths are linked or where any drugs were obtained. It is also not known whether Medellín will change its rules for future large festivals at the sports complex.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who died after the EDC Medellín festival?

Two foreign visitors died: a Costa Rican man who fell ill on the opening night and a British cancer doctor who lived in the US. The doctor, 51, died on Monday, 12 October, a day after he fell ill at the festival.

What caused the deaths?

No official cause has been published for either death. Press reports point to drug and alcohol use, and the authorities are investigating both cases.

How many people needed medical help at the festival?

Medellín’s health department reported 193 medical cases at the festival’s care points, 107 of them linked to intoxication. Seven people were taken to hospitals in the city.

Is Medellín safe for US travellers?

The US State Department advises Americans to reconsider travel to Colombia and warns of drugging and robberies, including through dating apps. Travellers should watch their drinks, stay with people they trust and avoid meeting strangers alone.

COLOMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Colombia is Latin America’s fourth-largest economy, and the United States took 28.3% of its exports from January to August 2026.

What happened The International Monetary Fund (IMF) cut its Colombia growth forecast for 2026 to 2.2%, from 2.3% in April, in its October World Economic Outlook.

Next year The IMF now sees growth of 2.3% in 2027, down from 2.5%, and unemployment rising from 8% in 2025 to 10% in 2027.

Inflation The IMF expects average consumer prices to rise 6% in 2026 and 5.7% in 2027, well above the central bank’s 3% target.

Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 65.5% chance Colombia’s central bank holds its 12.25% rate in October (14 October, 4:08 a.m. ET).

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open The finance ministry has not yet published its planned debt law, and the terms of any IMF support are not known.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has cut its Colombia growth forecast to 2.2% for 2026, just below the 2.3% it expects for Latin America. The Washington-based lender set out the figures in its October World Economic Outlook this week and lowered its 2027 forecast to 2.3%.

For US investors in Colombian bonds and shares, the cut follows a rise in the central bank’s key rate from 9.25% to 12.25% this year. The IMF also expects inflation to average about 6% this year, twice the central bank’s 3% target.

What the IMF Forecast Says

The IMF now expects Colombia’s economy to grow 2.2% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027, after growth of 2.6% in 2025. In its April outlook, the IMF’s Colombia growth forecast was 2.3% for this year and 2.5% for next year.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The new Colombia growth forecast comes with a worse inflation picture. The IMF sees average consumer prices rising 6% in 2026 and 5.7% in 2027, up from 5.9% and 5.2% in April.

Unemployment is expected to climb from 8% in 2025 to 9% this year and 10% in 2027, the same path the IMF drew in April. The fund also sees the current-account deficit, the gap in Colombia’s trade and income with the world, widening to 3.4% of economic output in 2027.

Portafolio, a Bogotá business daily, reported the figures early on Tuesday, 13 October. It noted that growth in 2027 would be only 0.1 percentage point faster than this year.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Colombia Compares With the Region

The IMF expects Latin America and the Caribbean to grow 2.3% this year and 2.5% in 2027. Its Colombia growth forecast of 2.2% puts the country level with Brazil and ahead of Mexico at 1.5% and Chile at 0.6%.

Peru, its Andean neighbour, is forecast to grow 3% this year, while the United States is seen at 2.3%. Colombia’s inflation forecast of 6% for 2026 is higher than the IMF’s figures for Brazil, Mexico, Chile and Peru.

That mix of slow growth and stubborn prices keeps borrowing costs high for families and companies. It also makes it harder for the central bank to cut rates soon.

Debt, Interest Rates and the Talks With the IMF

Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República, raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 12.25% on 30 September. The rate stood at 9.25% at the end of 2025, according to the Bogotá daily El Tiempo.

Annual inflation reached 6.29% in September, the national statistics office DANE reported on 7 October. Governor Leonardo Villar said inflation may not return to the bank’s 3% target until 2028, El Tiempo and the news site Valora Analitik reported.

Deputy finance minister Juan Sebastián Betancur told a Senate committee the government will present its “rescue law” on debt within days, El Tiempo reported. Its aim, he said, is to make sure “the bathtub does not overflow with debt”.

The IMF’s own tables show general government debt rising from 59.5% of economic output this year to 62.9% in 2027 and 65.1% in 2028. It puts the overall government deficit at 6.9% of output in 2026.

The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative in office since August, asked the IMF in late September to review the economy. A finance ministry team led by Betancur was due to meet the fund in Washington on 6 October to seek financing, Valora Analitik reported.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bettors give a 65.5% chance that the central bank holds its 12.25% rate in October (14 October, 4:08 a.m. ET). They put a quarter-point hike at 31.5% and a half-point hike or more at 5%.

About US$35,900 has been bet on that market, and the quarter-point hike gained one point over the past day. On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US by the CFTC, a hold is priced at 62% and a quarter-point hike at 28%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For US holders of Colombian bonds, slower growth and rising debt keep the focus on the government’s coming rescue law and any IMF deal. Both will show how far the new government is willing to cut spending or raise revenue.

For travellers and expats paid in dollars, the official exchange rate was about 3,182 pesos to the US dollar on 14 October. Local prices keep rising, with restaurants and hotels up 9.44% in the year to September, according to DANE.

For US companies that buy Colombian coffee, flowers or oil, the lower Colombia growth forecast changes little in the short term. Harvests, the peso and US trade policy matter more for those prices than a 0.1-point change in growth.

What Is Not Known

The IMF report gives no specific reason for trimming its Colombia growth forecast. The finance ministry has not published the text of the rescue law or listed the cuts it will contain.

It is not known what form any IMF financing would take or how large it could be. The central bank’s next rate decision is due on Friday 30 October and will depend on inflation data still to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the IMF’s new Colombia growth forecast?

The IMF expects Colombia’s economy to grow 2.2% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. In April it had forecast 2.3% and 2.5%.

Why are interest rates so high in Colombia?

Annual inflation was 6.29% in September, more than double the central bank’s 3% target. The bank raised its benchmark rate to 12.25% on 30 September to bring prices down.

Is Colombia asking the IMF for money?

The government asked the IMF in late September to review Colombia’s economy, and officials planned financing talks in Washington on 6 October. The form and size of any IMF support have not been announced.

What does the forecast mean for the Colombian peso?

The official rate was about 3,182 pesos to the US dollar on 14 October. A weaker growth outlook and high debt can weigh on the currency, while high interest rates tend to support it.

PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts The country Peru is an Andean nation on South America’s Pacific coast and a leading exporter of copper and gold.

What happened Police broke up an alleged Tren de Aragua extortion cell in Puente Piedra, a district on Lima’s northern edge, and detained six Venezuelans.

The suspects Six Venezuelans aged 23 to 32, including a 28-year-old named as the alleged leader; all are presumed innocent.

What was seized A mini Uzi, a rifle, a hand grenade, 85 rounds of ammunition, six phones, a car and four motorcycles.

The alleged scheme A seized notebook allegedly lists four bus companies and a fee of 80 soles (about US$23) a vehicle each week.

The US angle Washington has listed Tren de Aragua as a Foreign Terrorist Organization since 20 February 2025.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Police in Peru have broken up an alleged Tren de Aragua extortion cell in Lima and detained six Venezuelans. Tren de Aragua, a gang born in a Venezuelan prison, has been on the US list of terrorist organizations since February 2025.

Peru’s Interior Ministry announced the raid on Tuesday, 13 October, in Puente Piedra, a district on Lima’s northern edge. Officers seized a mini Uzi, a rifle, a grenade and a notebook that allegedly lists weekly payments demanded from bus companies.

What Police Found in Puente Piedra

The raid targeted a house in the Villa Los Olivos housing association that police say served as the gang’s base of operations. RPP, a leading Peruvian radio network, quoted General José Antonio Zavala, head of the police’s criminal investigation directorate, saying so.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The six detained Venezuelans are aged 23 to 32, the Interior Ministry said. Police name Iam Gael León Díaz, 28, as the alleged leader of the group.

The group calls itself “Los Remanentes del Tren de Aragua”, Spanish for “the Tren de Aragua Remnants”. The unit that made the arrests specialises in extortion and organised crime cases.

Officers seized a mini Uzi submachine gun, a rifle, a hand grenade, three magazines and 85 unfired rounds of 9 mm ammunition. A police bomb squad destroyed the grenade in a controlled blast outside the house, RPP reported.

Police also took six mobile phones, a white Chevrolet car, four motorcycles and four licence plates. They found construction-worker uniforms and clothing bearing the logos of several companies.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Six Venezuelans Are Accused Of

The six are under investigation for extortion, membership of a criminal gang and crimes against public safety. The ministry says investigators must still identify possible victims and the full scope of the alleged extortion.

The seized notebook allegedly records Tren de Aragua extortion payments from public transport companies on the Puente Piedra route. It names four bus firms, including El Chino and Virgen de la Puerta.

General Zavala said the suspects acknowledged in preliminary statements that they extorted public transport and construction workers, according to RPP.

“According to their own words, they say they have to go and put pressure,” Zavala said. He also said all six appear to have entered Peru irregularly, RPP reported.

Correo, a national daily, reports that the uniforms are under examination because detectives want to know whether the gang extorted other businesses. The phones will be examined for threats, demands for money and messages between gang members.

Why Tren de Aragua Matters to the United States

Tren de Aragua began as a prison gang in Venezuela, with its base in Tocorón prison, and now also operates in Colombia, Peru and Chile. The US State Department lists it as a Foreign Terrorist Organization, with a listing date of 20 February 2025.

That label makes it a crime for anyone in the United States to knowingly give the gang material support, including money. US banks that find funds in which the gang has an interest must also freeze them and report them to the Treasury.

On Friday, 12 June 2026, President Donald Trump announced that a US military strike had killed the gang’s leader, Héctor Guerrero Flores. Washington and Caracas called it a joint operation against “Niño Guerrero”, as he was known, and Venezuela confirmed his death that night.

El Comercio, a leading Lima daily, reported in May that the US Justice Department had charged more than 260 members and associates since January 2025. The department said many suspects in one of those operations were undocumented migrants from Venezuela, Colombia and Honduras.

Lima’s Extortion Wave Hits Transport Workers

The Puente Piedra raid fell under the Unified Command for the Fight Against Crime, which Peru’s conservative president, Keiko Fujimori, launched on 7 October. It brings Peru’s armed forces and the National Police under one command to confront criminal organisations.

On Sunday, 11 October, motorcycle-taxi drivers blocked the Pan-American Highway North in Puente Piedra after one of their colleagues was attacked. They told RPP that four gangs had extorted them since May, and one driver said threats demanded 50,000 soles (about US$14,500).

On Monday, 12 October, prosecutors and police broke up another Lima gang that allegedly charged informal shared taxis 120 soles (about US$35) a week. The raids took place in the Rímac and San Juan de Lurigancho districts, according to the Public Ministry, Peru’s prosecution service.

On Saturday, 10 October, the Interior Ministry announced seven arrests in an alleged Tren de Aragua extortion case against traders in Piura, northern Peru. In one case, the suspects allegedly demanded 100 soles (about US$29) a week from a trader.

The government is also setting up a committee with banks and the telecom regulator to fight extortion. Prime Minister Luis Galarreta announced it on Monday, 12 October, to give investigators faster access to information in extortion and illegal mining cases.

What It Means for You

The US State Department rates Peru at Level 2, “Exercise increased caution”, in its current travel advisory. It warns that crime is common in Peru and that muggings and other violent crime often happen even in daylight.

Puente Piedra lies on Lima’s northern edge, far from Miraflores and Barranco, the seaside districts popular with visitors. The gangs in these cases target bus operators, motorcycle-taxi drivers, traders and builders, according to officials and the drivers themselves.

For US readers, the case shows groups using the Tren de Aragua name still active in Lima after the June strike on its leader. Companies with partners in Peru’s transport or construction trades should note that Tren de Aragua extortion in this case allegedly targeted exactly those sectors.

What Is Not Known

The Interior Ministry has not said on which day the raid took place or how many bus operators paid the cell. Police have also not said how much money the group allegedly collected in total.

It is not yet known whether prosecutors will ask a judge to hold the six in pretrial detention. Investigators have not shown whether this Tren de Aragua extortion cell takes orders from the gang’s wider leadership or only uses its name.

No court has ruled on the case, and all six suspects are presumed innocent. The ministry says the investigation will continue with the competent authorities to establish each suspect’s role.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Tren de Aragua?

Tren de Aragua is a criminal gang that began in a Venezuelan prison and now operates in several Latin American countries. The United States listed it as a Foreign Terrorist Organization on 20 February 2025.

Who was arrested in Puente Piedra?

Police detained six Venezuelans aged 23 to 32, including a 28-year-old they describe as the cell’s alleged leader. All six are presumed innocent until a court rules otherwise.

How much did the gang allegedly demand?

A notebook seized in the raid allegedly lists Tren de Aragua extortion fees of 80 soles (about US$23) a vehicle each week. Police have not said how many vehicles paid or how much money was collected.

Is Lima safe for American visitors?

The US State Department asks visitors to exercise increased caution in Peru, its Level 2 rating, because crime is common. The extortion cases in this story targeted local transport workers, traders and builders.
