World.title: Cousin charged after allegedly drinking out $50 worth of money meant for bathroom repairs
World.content:
Cousin charged after allegedly drinking out $50 worth of money meant for bathroom repairs

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 34-year-old Belize City construction worker has been charged with theft after allegedly taking money from his cousin meant to purchase building materials, only to spend part of it on alcohol.

A park ranger residing on West Canal, reported that her cousin, Kashief Myvette, visited her home on Saturday, October 10, and asked whether she had any construction work available.

The woman reportedly agreed to hire him to cement her bathroom floor and handed him $100 to purchase cement blocks, sand and plumbing materials. She also allowed him to borrow her bicycle to make the purchases.

However, after approximately two hours passed without Myvette returning, the woman contacted his brother and learned that he was at the family residence in Yabra.

She subsequently went there and confronted Myvette, who allegedly admitted that he had spent some of the money and considered part of it payment for the job.

According to the woman, Myvette told her, “I done drink it out I noh got no more money.”

The woman reportedly recovered $50 but demanded the remaining money, explaining that the two had not agreed on a labour fee and that no work had been completed.

Police were called, and the woman requested court action.

On Monday, October 12, Myvette was formally arrested and charged with theft of $50.

World.title: Woman trying to help her friend with dead car battery struck by passing van on roadside
World.content:
Woman trying to help her friend with dead car battery struck by passing van on roadside

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 35-year-old Santa Elena woman was injured after being struck by a passing van while attempting to assist a friend whose vehicle battery had died.

The woman reported that she arrived near Rustic Roast along the George Price Highway early Saturday morning, October 10, after receiving a call for assistance from her friend.

According to the woman, her friend had opened her vehicle’s hood and was attempting to disconnect the battery when the woman stepped onto the roadway to see what she was doing.

At that moment, a passing white Coaster van reportedly struck her hand, causing her to fall onto the pavement.

The woman complained of lower back pain following the incident. She told police the van continued along the George Price Highway before turning onto Mabel Pitts Street.

Emergency personnel transported the woman to the San Ignacio Community Hospital, where she received medical attention. A doctor subsequently classified her injuries as harm.

Police are investigating the incident as negligent harm.

World.title: Police are investigating a shooting incident in Belize City after two people on a motorcycle allegedly opened fire toward a couple near Pregnant Alley and Cemetery Road on Saturday night
World.content:
Police are investigating a shooting incident in Belize City after two people on a motorcycle allegedly opened fire toward a couple near Pregnant Alley and Cemetery Road on Saturday night

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting incident in Belize City after two people on a motorcycle allegedly opened fire toward a couple near Pregnant Alley and Cemetery Road on Saturday night.

According to police, a 27-year-old woman and her boyfriend were heading to purchase food around 10:32 p.m. on October 10 when they noticed a motorcycle approaching from the direction of the Taylor’s Alley checkpoint.

The woman reported that the passenger, who was not wearing a helmet, pointed what appeared to be a firearm in their direction and fired a shot.

She reportedly shouted a warning to her boyfriend, and both ran into Pregnant Alley. Moments later, another gunshot rang out as the motorcycle sped away toward Albert Street.

Police recovered one expended 9mm shell casing from the scene. No injuries or property damage were reported.

Investigators attempted to obtain surveillance footage but were unsuccessful. The woman subsequently declined to provide a formal statement.

No suspects have been detained, and the investigation continues.

World.title: Seven injured after wooden verandah collapses during family wake in Belize City
World.content:
Seven injured after wooden verandah collapses during family wake in Belize City

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Seven people, including children, were injured when a wooden verandah collapsed during a family wake on Curl Thompson Street in Belize City on Friday night.

The incident occurred around 9:30 p.m. on October 9, while relatives and friends were gathered at a residence to mourn the death of a family member.

According to police, several people were socializing on the verandah while others were standing in the yard underneath the structure when it suddenly collapsed.

The injured included five adults and two teenagers and a five-year-old child, according to the ages listed in the police report. They were transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital suffering from injuries to their legs, feet and backs.

Police confirmed that all seven were in stable condition following the incident. Several remained under observation into the early morning hours of Saturday.

Family members reportedly declined to pursue police action, explaining that the collapse was accidental.

Scenes of Crime personnel documented the location, and the incident remains under investigation.

World.title: Man accuses uncle of stealing phone while he slept drunk on verandah during the middle of the day
World.content:
Man accuses uncle of stealing phone while he slept drunk on verandah during the middle of the day

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A family dispute over a missing cellphone has reached the police in San Jose Succotz, Cayo, after a 24-year-old construction worker accused his uncle of stealing the device while he slept.

The man reported that he returned home intoxicated and fell asleep on his front verandah around midday. When he awoke several hours later, he discovered that his Redmi 5 cellphone, valued at $300, was missing from his pocket.

The man told police that his aunt had informed him that his uncle allegedly took the phone while he was asleep.

Officers subsequently located and questioned the uncle, who denied taking the device.

Police also spoke with family members but were unable to obtain eyewitness evidence supporting the allegation. One relative clarified that she had not personally witnessed the alleged theft.

The uncle was released without charges due to insufficient evidence. Investigators indicated that an arrest could not be made based solely on hearsay.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Thief steals pickup battery and damages windshield in Belize City
World.content:
Thief steals pickup battery and damages windshield in Belize City

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City welder is reporting losses of approximately $950 after someone allegedly stole the battery from his pickup truck and damaged its rear windshield.

The 20-year-old vehicle owner told police he parked his green 1995 Ford Ranger on Vasquez Avenue around 10:00 p.m. on Sunday, October 11.

When he approached the vehicle around 4:00 p.m. the following afternoon, he noticed that the hood had been left fully open.

Upon inspecting the pickup, the owner discovered that its battery, valued at $450, was missing. He also observed that the rear windshield had been broken, causing an estimated $500 in damage.

He subsequently filed a report at the Queen Street Police Station. The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Motorcycle stolen from Lords Bank yard; owner says it was worth $400
World.content:
Motorcycle stolen from Lords Bank yard; owner says it was worth $400

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Lords Bank resident has reported the theft of his motorcycle from his yard sometime between Sunday evening and Monday morning.

The 35-year-old cycle owner told police he last saw his black 2019 Lifan LF110-7A motorcycle around 7:45 p.m. on October 11, when he picked it up from the ground and secured it.

When he checked the following morning, the motorcycle was missing.

The man explained that the vehicle had not been in use because its insurance and licence had expired. He valued the motorcycle at $400 and said it could be identified by its broken left handle, damaged seat and missing front fender.

The motorcycle bears licence plate MC-5766. Police are investigating the reported theft.

World.title: Thief caught on camera stealing $2,000 motorcycle in Santa Elena
World.content:
Thief caught on camera stealing $2,000 motorcycle in Santa Elena

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police in Santa Elena are investigating the theft of a motorcycle valued at $2,000 after surveillance footage reportedly captured a helmeted individual making off with the vehicle late Sunday night.

The cycle’s owner reported that he parked his black Lifan 125-5 motorcycle outside his rented residence on Peter August Street around midday on October 11.

The man told police he fell asleep later that night and forgot to move the motorcycle into his fenced yard. When he woke around 6:30 a.m. Monday, the vehicle was missing.

After reviewing surveillance footage with his landlord, the owner reportedly discovered that an individual dressed entirely in white and wearing a helmet had taken the motorcycle around 11:45 p.m.

The suspect was seen heading toward Orchid Street before turning in the direction of the Santa Elena Cemetery.

The motorcycle bears licence plate SIM-05698. Police are investigating.

World.title: IC WANTS SPENDING CHECK
World.content:
The scene in Black River after the town took a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa last October.

THE Integrity Commission (IC) has called for full documentation and independent review of 476 Government contracts valued at $5 billion that public bodies identified as related to Hurricane Melissa recovery, raising questions about how the spending will be reviewed as Jamaica rebuilds after the disaster.

The contracts were awarded in the final quarter of 2025, with most using emergency or single-source procurement methods.

In its special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, tabled in the House on Tuesday, the commission said 182 of the recovery-related contracts, valued at $3.9 billion, were awarded through emergency procurement.

Another 262 were awarded through single- source procurement, while 32 were awarded through restricted bidding. “These awards warrant full documentation and independent review by the relevant authorities, and will be examined further in the commission’s report on its special monitoring programme, which is ongoing,” Director of Investigation Kevon Stephenson wrote in the report.

The findings come against the background of a sharp rise in emergency contracting last year, as public bodies responded to urgent needs, including those arising from the hurricane. The commission reported that emergency contracts for the year totalled $16.3 billion across 588 contracts, a 63 per cent increase in value over 2024.

Of that amount, $10.5 billion, covering 331 contracts, was awarded in the final quarter of 2025. The report said $9.7 billion of that fourth-quarter spending, across 278 contracts, was awarded on or after October 28, 2025, when Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica.

Stephenson acknowledged in the report the necessity for emergency procurement, but said the circumstances created heightened risks that required scrutiny. “The DI (director of investigations) recognises that emergency procurement was necessary to preserve life and to restore essential services.

However, the period following the hurricane was one of heightened procurement risk, by reason of the scale of emergency contracting, the size of certain individual awards, the use of emergency methods for contracts other than those identified as related to recovery, and the exemption of emergency procurement from the ordinary rules,” he wrote.

The report also raised concerns about how some hurricane-related contracts were recorded. It identified 360 single-source awards in 2025, valued at $840 million, whose descriptions referred to a hurricane but which were recorded as ordinary single-source contracts.

Of those, 337 were made in the final quarter of the year. The commission cautioned that some of these awards might already be included among the 262 single-source contracts identified as related to recovery. However, the report said the records indicated that emergency spending may have been understated and that the identification of disaster-related contracts was incomplete.

The findings do not establish that the recovery contracts were improperly awarded or that the spending involved wrongdoing. Rather, the commission is calling for the relevant authorities to examine the awards and the records supporting them. The report also recommends stronger checks after emergency spending.

These include requiring public bodies to report on their procurement activities following a declared disaster and improving oversight of emergency contracts, including checks on whether the Government received value for money.

The commission’s special monitoring programme remains under way, with further examination of procurement connected to the hurricane response and recovery expected to be addressed separately.

World.title: ‘Every life has value’
World.content:
St Andrew North Central Member of Parliament Delano Seiveright gestures while making his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in Parliament on Tuesday. Behind him is Member of Parliament for St Andrew North Western Duane Smith. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

While celebrating sharp reductions in murders, shootings, and robberies in St Andrew North Central, Member of Parliament (MP) Delano Seiveright has urged Jamaicans to balance support for the police with accountability and respect for human life.

Seiveright, who represents the constituency, told the House of Representatives on Tuesday, during his contribution to the Constituency Debate, that murders and shootings across the St Andrew North Police Division had fallen by 70 per cent as at October 11, while robberies declined by 60 per cent and break-ins by 50 per cent.

He credited the reductions to the Government’s leadership and the work of the security forces, but argued that improvements in public safety must not weaken the need for independent oversight when people die in circumstances involving State institutions.

“I want to fully support our police officers in the lawful execution of their duties.

They face extraordinary dangers and deserve our respect.

But support must go hand-inhand with accountability and respect for human life.

I recognise Indecom’s [Independent Commission of Investigations] important role in independent oversight, and I now have a much better sense of the challenges Indecom is having,” Seiveright said.

His comments come amid continuing public debate over fatal shootings involving members of the security forces and the need to ensure such incidents are properly investigated.

Seiveright did not identify a particular fatal shooting in his contribution.

Instead, he made a broader appeal for fairness and accountability, arguing that every Jamaican should be concerned when someone dies in circumstances involving institutions entrusted with protecting life.

He drew on lessons from his childhood and his upbringing in the Church to explain why he believes respect for human life must remain central to the country’s approach to security.

Every Sunday, without fail, I attended Open Bible Church on Washington Boulevard, including Sunday school… There, I learned respect for human life and compassion.

Those values that stayed with me have never changed.

The great English poet, John Donne, once wrote, ‘Never send to know for whom the bell tolls, it tolls for thee.’ When a citizen dies in circumstances involving institutions entrusted in protecting life, it must concern every Jamaican.

Every life has value.

Every family deserves answers,” he added.

The MP’s position was that support for the security forces and demands for accountability should not be treated as opposing interests.

While the police must be able to carry out their duties lawfully, he said, citizens must also be protected by the law and entitled to fair treatment.

“Every citizen deserves the protection of the law.

We must support our security forces while insisting on due process and accountability, and justice must never depend on your address, your circumstances, or your standing in society.

Because the bell may toll for someone else’s family [today], tomorrow it could toll for ours,” Seiveright said.

World.title: Dry taps, deep crisis
World.content:
PORT MARIA, St Mary — For Annette Tullouch-Tracey, turning on a pipe and seeing water flow is a luxury she has not known in the 15 years she has called Frontier Heights Phase 2 her home.

Tullouch-Tracey, who is the treasurer of the Frontier Heights Citizens’ Association, told the Jamaica Observer that she is not alone in being frustrated with the lack of water.

“The water situation is very bad. We have to buy water from the truck all these years and it is very expensive.

This has been going on since they gave us the lot up there. We have never seen water in the pipe from the time we live there until now,” said Tullouch-Tracey. She told the Observer that what was already a daily water struggle has now become a crisis with the island in the grip of a debilitating drought.

“With the drought that is on things are getting very bad, because if we need water and call the water truck, it takes some days before we get it. When we get the rain we would catch the water for domestic use but now we have to buy water for everything, and it is very expensive.” Tullouch-Tracey added.

She pointed out that for years, residents have hoped for relief and that seemed likely 2018 when a team from the National Water Commission (NWC) visited the community. “They came up there about eight years ago and found the pipe laterals and said that they were going to work on the water and up to now we cannot see anything,” a frustrated Tullouch-Tracey said.

According to Tullouch- Tracey, when residents seek answers from the NWC they are told that it is waiting on the Housing Association of Jamaica to hand over the scheme to them. She said those hardest hit by the lack of piped water are the most vulnerable residents.

“This is very bad for the elderly and children because they have to go to other places to catch water and it is very hard to walk up the hill with it. The standpipe is a few metres from the houses and many times when you go there, there is no water or the pressure is very low,” Tullouch-Tracey claimed.

The citizens’ association executive said cost of survival is staggering for residents of the small community. “For the truck to bring a load of water up there is $15,000 and this might last for two or three weeks depending on how many persons are in the family.

Sometimes we cannot afford to buy water when it is finished [and we] have to talk to the truck driver and trust [credit] the water,” Tullouch- Tracey said with a heavy voice as she issued a plea to the authorities for assistance.

“Right now we would like the NWC, or the Member of Parliament [People’s National Party’s Omar Newell] to try their best to help us along, with the parish council. “We are suffering and they say water is life but they are taking the life out of us.

Please… [Minister of Water Matthew Samuda], we would appreciate it if you can do something for us. We have been waiting for too long now,” added Tullouch Tracey.

Vi c e – p resident of the Frontier Heights Citizens’ Association Celia Pryce-Valentine said she has lived in the National Housing Trust (NHT) scheme for more than 47 years and has not received a drop of piped water in her home for more than six years.

According to Pryce- Valentine, she orders trucked water as needed, while residents of the community are grateful whenever the rain falls to fill their tanks. “But after the rain, the suffering continues [as] the tanks run dry and the pipes remain empty,” said Pryce-Valentine.

“When we complain to the NWC we are met with a long list of excuses. A lot of nonsensical reasons [such as], ‘the tank needs to be replaced, other persons were given access to water from our line, persons illegally attaching to our system, not enough pressure due to a blockage in the main’,” added Pryce-Valentine.

She charged that the NWC attempted to fix the blockage but the work left residents shocked and angry. “If you are to visit you will see a two-inch pipe they used to bypass the blockage instead of unblocking the main pipe running in the water table.

They responded by attempting to use a bandage on a sore,” said Pryce-Valentine as she claimed that the result is a daily financial and emotional torture for every family in the scheme. “Most residents resort to buying water privately or ordering water, so it is costly and stressful as waiting time for the ordered water is long.

So it is affecting us negatively,” she explained. “The cost of water depends on the size of your storage. Mine cost $15,000 for a single load of 1,800 gallons. If I order water it takes longer than 10 working days, if I do not sit and wait for NWC for delivery.

I order water every week because of the long wait to receive it. Plus we do not get trucked water unless we protest and go straight to management,” a frustrated Pryce-Valentine said as she added her voice to those calling on the authorities to address their plight.

“I would plead with them to replace the tank as it is an important part of our system. Give the other scheme their own system and take them off ours. Clear the blockages so the pressure will go back to normal, and schedule a shared recorded timetable for trucking water every three weeks to our residents,” suggested Pryce Valentine.

She argued that Frontier Heights is a standalone NHT scheme, while Frontier Heights Phase 2 is a different scheme which was constructed under the now defunct Government programme, Operation Pride.

According to Pryce- Valentine, they are two different developments but residents of both are crying out for water.

World.title: KSAMC sets October 21 deadline for vending near parish church
World.content:
Deputy Mayor of Kingston Lorraine Dobson presiding over themonthly meeting of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation on Tuesday. (Photo: Renae Osbourne)

EFFECTIVE October 21, vending will no longer be permitted near Kingston Parish Church or directly in front of South Parade Arcade in downtown Kingston, the municipal authority declared on Tuesday.

The notice was served by Deputy Mayor Lorraine Dobson in the absence of Mayor Andrew Swaby during the monthly meeting of the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC).

Dobson noted that the restrictions had become increasingly necessary as there have been reports that some vendors continued to sell goods and loiter outside commercial premises despite renting spaces inside 65 Mall Arcade.

“Rather than using those spaces for their intended purpose, these vendors reportedly store their goods and other items while continuing to sell their merchandise on the street.

KSAMC’s Commercial Service Department can verify the rental arrangement for its arcade and maintains a register of vendors who have rented spaces there,” she said, adding that the information will help to identify the extent to which designated vending spaces are being underutilised.

The deputy mayor told the meeting that the KSAMC had met with vendors several times to discuss the issue and inform them of the forthcoming vending restrictions.

She noted that on Wednesday, September 9, Swaby visited vendors operating in the area, telling them that the current situation was unacceptable and could not continue.

“Prior to the meeting, photographs and videos documenting the prevailing conditions were taken.

These were subsequently shown to the vendors during the meeting to illustrate the concerns, particularly the practice of vending directly in front of Kingston Parish Church,” explained Dobson.

She added that the KSAMC then staged a walk-through of the South Parade area on Friday, September 11, during which the need for compliance with the planned measures was further reinforced.

Following sensitisation visits, Dobson said that the corporation proceeded to serve notices on Monday, October 5, to vendors, advising them of the imminent restrictions within the vicinity of Kingston Parish Church and South Parade Arcade.

She added that signs will be erected on Tuesday, October 20, to notify vendors and members of the public of the designated no-vending area.

“On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, the KSAMC will deploy 15 courtesy and two municipal officers to the area to facilitate compliance with the notices and prevent vending and loitering in the vicinity of Kingston Parish Church and directly in front of South Parade Arcade.

“These measures are part of the KSAMC’s commitment to maintaining public order, protecting the dignity and accessibility of all public spaces, and ensuring that designated vending areas are used for their intended purpose,” she said.

Dobson maintained that the initiative aims to regulate the state of vending within the Corporate Area, while ensuring that vendors receive a clear notice of the new limitations.

“Our approach has involved direct management of vendors, the use of photographic and video evidence to demonstrate a concern, the issuance of formal notices, and advanced communication of the measures to be implemented… The KSAMC will therefore proceed with the planned enforcement measures from October 21, 2026,” she advised.

World.title: Reggae Girlz fall 3-1 to Mexico as El Tri avenge loss
World.content:
Jamaicas defender #7 Mimi Van Zanten and Mexico's forward #11 Lizbeth Ovalle fight for the ball during the women's international friendly football match between Mexico and Jamaica at La Corregidora Stadium in Santiago de Queretaro, Queretaro State, Mexico on October 13, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Girlz were beaten 3-1 by Mexico in the second game of their two-game international series in Querétaro, Mexico on Tuesday as the hosts rebounded after losing 3-4 on Friday.

Jamaica made four changes to the starting team from Friday’s games, bringing in Chantel Swaby, Kayla McKenna, Trudi Cater and Solai Washington. However, the Girlz produced a lacklustre effort, especially in the first half when they conceded two goals.

Team captain Khadija Shaw, who played all 90 minutes on Friday, was not on the match card on Tuesday. To add to the loss, Jamaica’s captain on the night, Allyson Swaby was carted off in the second half after an injury to her right foot.

An own goal in the sixth minute gifted Mexico the early lead, a result of a clumsy mix-up between goalkeeper Rebeca Spencer and her defenders that saw a back pass from Swaby roll under Spencer’s foot and across the goal line.

Spencer was well placed in the 19th minute to block a powerful shot from point blank range taken by Lizbeth Ovalle and a minute later Maricarmen Reyes missed from about three yards, lifting the ball over the cross bar.

Another mistake by the Jamaican defence gifted Mexico the second goal in the 32nd minute as Reyes ran between two defenders to volley a cross from the left flank inside the right post.

Ovalle made the score 3-0 in the 58th minute with a stunning left footed free kick from about 25 yards that gave substitute goalkeeper Liya Brooks no chance.

Kalyssa van Zanten pulled a goal back for Jamaica in the 60th minute, when her well taken shot from just on the edge of the 18-yard box flew high into the far left corner.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Legend confirmed as new JPL title sponsor in $300 million deal
World.content:
Wisynco Group CEO Andrew Mahfood (second right) and CEO of Professional Football Jamaica Limited, Owen Hill (right) share a toast to Legend’s title sponsorship of the Jamaica Premier League with fellow football stakeholders (from left) Craig Butler, Donovan White, Peter Higgins and Dave Cameron. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Wisynco Group brand Legend was officially confirmed as the new title sponsor of the Jamaica Premier League (JPL) on Tuesday, in a long-term deal valued at $300 million – described as the largest investment the company has made in local sport.

Speaking at the launch of the Legend Jamaica Premier League at the AC Hotel on Tuesday night, Wisynco CEO Andrew Mahfood said the partnership represented a significant vote of confidence in the country’s football product, with ambitions extending beyond branding to greater fan engagement, stronger club visibility and more opportunities for young Jamaicans.

“This partnership — Wisynco’s largest investment in Jamaican sport — is a long-term vote of confidence in local football,” Mahfood said, to rounds of applause.

“Let me be clear, we are not here for one season. We are here to help build something meaningful and lasting,” he added.

The announcement marks a major commitment by the Jamaican-owned manufacturer and distributor to the local game, with Mahfood insisting that Wisynco’s involvement is about helping to build a stronger and more sustainable football product.

He said the partnership with the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), Professional Football Jamaica Limited and the league’s clubs builds on Wisynco’s existing support for the Women’s Premier League, the Reggae Boyz and the Reggae Girlz.

“At Wisynco, we believe in the power of sport to unite communities, inspire young people, create opportunity, and bring out the best of the Jamaican spirit,” Mahfood said. “Football is part of our DNA and we see how it strengthens communities and opens doors for the next generation.”

Mahfood believes there is a natural connection between Legend, a Jamaican brand produced by Wisynco, and the ambitions of the country’s footballers, clubs and supporters.

He pointed to the qualities of passion, authenticity, determination and pride associated with the brand as characteristics that also define Jamaican football.

“Every player is pursuing a dream. Every club represents a community. Every supporter believes in something greater,” he noted.

He continued: “That relentless pursuit of excellence is what being a Legend is all about.”

While Legend assumes the title sponsorship, Mahfood explained that the partnership would extend across several Wisynco brands, each expected to contribute to different aspects of the league experience.

Worthy Park Rum Mix will support the adult matchday experience, while Mamba Stout is expected to connect with supporters. M.POWA will target ambitious young Jamaicans, and Powerade will focus on preparation, hydration and recovery.

“Together, our brands will help take the JPL from good to great,” Mahfood said.

However, the Wisynco chief executive stressed that the company’s ambitions were not limited to having its brands displayed at matches and around league venues.

He said the focus would be on improving the overall football experience, creating stronger connections between clubs and their communities, and giving the competition greater visibility.

“Our ambition goes beyond signage and branding,” Mahfood said. “We want stronger fan engagement, greater visibility for clubs, and deeper community support.”

Most importantly, he said, the partnership should help younger Jamaicans view football as a genuine pathway to opportunity.

The investment comes at a time when stakeholders continue to look for ways to strengthen the domestic game, improve its commercial appeal and create a more compelling product for supporters, sponsors and players.

“Jamaica has the talent. The clubs have the passion. And our players have the ambition to take Jamaican football even higher,” he said.

Mahfood described the launch as more than the unveiling of a new title sponsor, saying it represented an opportunity to elevate Jamaican talent and communities through a stronger league.

“Tonight, we launch more than a league — we launch a bigger stage for Jamaican talent, Jamaican communities, and Jamaican dreams,” he said.

“The whistle is about to blow. The next chapter starts now. Welcome to the Legend Jamaica Premier League. Let’s make it Legendary,” he concluded.

World.title: Seprod shareholders approve stock split, share issuance
World.content:
The Seprod corporate offices in Kingston.

Seprod Limited is set to split its shares in the coming weeks, preceding a potential new equity offer to raise fresh capital to reduce its debt balances.

All three resolutions at the company’s virtual extraordinary general meeting (EGM) were approved by shareholders on Monday. As a result, the company’s authorised share capital will be adjusted from one billion ordinary shares to 1.9 billion ordinary shares, effectively lifting the ceiling of how many shares can exist.

Subsequently, the company’s directors will set a date for its ordinary shares to be split five-to-one. This will result in the authorised share capital rising to 9.50 billion ordinary shares while the existing share count will move from 910,945,538 ordinary shares to 4,554,727,690 ordinary shares.

If an investor holds 12,500 ordinary shares of Seprod at Tuesday’s closing price of $79.82, those shares are worth $997,750. A five-to-one stock split would increase the number of shares held to 62,500 ordinary shares with each share valued at $15.96. As a result, an investor holds more shares at a lower nominal price while retaining the same value of shares.

This reduced share price will benefit the company which has hinted at re-entering the markets for fresh capital. The third resolution empowered the directors to allot and issue new ordinary shares for an additional public offer (APO), rights issue or private placement at price(s) deemed fit. The resolution spoke to the net proceeds being applied as the directors see fit, including the repayment of debt by the company and its subsidiaries.

Chairman Paul B Scott reiterated the debt reduction strategy at Monday’s EGM, a point which Seprod has emphasised during 2026. At the company’s July 29 annual general meeting, Scott explained that the group aims to cut its consolidated debt load from $51.21 billion to $47 billion by year end.

The focus on debt reduction was recently rewarded by CARICRIS (Caribbean Information & Credit Rating Services Limited) which revised its outlook on the manufacturing and distribution conglomerate from negative to stable. The ratings agency reported a negative outlook in October 2025 based on the group’s financial flexibility being constrained due to the growing debt levels to fuel the acquisition-led growth. At the time, CARICRIS expected Seprod’s debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) to remain challenged over the next 12 to 15 months.

“The stable outlook is premised on the high likelihood that Seprod’s financial flexibility will continue to improve over the next 12-15 months. This is underpinned by the refinancing of short-term debt into a longer-tenor bond, stronger cash balances, improved capitalisation and an increased focus on deleveraging,” CARICRIS noted as it expects the group’s effective DSCR to remain above 1.0 times.

Seprod’s standalone debt has moved from $13.92 billion in 2022 to $15.88 billion in 2025, with $8.45 billion of this debt in the form of bonds maturing between December 2027 to July 2031. Seprod’s core Jamaican operations and subsidiaries have seen their aggregate debt balances move from $17.13 billion to $19.46 billion.

Meanwhile, subsidiary Musson International Dairies Limited refinanced an $854.35 million bond in December 2025 through the issuance of a new $3 billion bond in November 2025. This included a $1.53 billion tranche with a 9.75 per cent interest rate and a $1.47 billion tranche with a 10.25 per cent interest rate.

However, Seprod’s consolidated debt balance has moved from $33.01 billion in 2022 to $51.21 billion in 2025. The higher debt load is due to its subsidiary A S Bryden & Sons Holdings Limited (ASBH) which has been the vehicle used to expand Seprod’s presence across the English-speaking Caribbean over the last four years.

Aside from ASBH taking on US$60.72 million debt facility for the amalgamation process in June 2022, it has also consolidated the debt load of the various subsidiaries it has acquired over the years. As a result, ASBH’s consolidated debt has risen from $15.88 billion in 2022 to $26.24 billion at the end of 2025.

Despite the relatively large, consolidated debt load, Seprod’s financial risk profile continues to be recognised as good by the ratings agency based on operating revenue growth, improved capitalisation and adequate liquidity. Management also intends to avoid new debt for the remainder of 2026 as it cuts the debt on its balance sheet. The report noted that Seprod is expected to repay $8 billion in maturing debt from internal cash flows over the next year.

“Notably, Seprod has consistently met its debt obligations in full and on time. Moreover, should the need arise, the Group can comfortably utilise its portfolio of liquid assets which includes short-term marketable securities of circa J $4.9 billion as at December 2025,” the CARICRIS report noted.

Seprod sold its stake in subsidiary International Biscuits Limited (IBL) in February 2026, with an inflow of $1.71 billion from the sale. That sale formed part of its portfolio optimisation strategy as it retained distribution rights for IBL products up to February 2031, with the option to renew. According to documents from the Companies Office of Jamaica, Kevin Donaldson, Wade Mars and Ravi Rochlani were appointed directors of IBL on February 28.

“So, we didn’t consider it sensible over the long term to be in a market that we are competing with our customers. So, strategically we felt divesting it would be a good choice,” Scott explained at Seprod’s July 2026 AGM.

Seprod is now moving to integrate its latest Barbadian acquisitions while leveraging its larger distribution platform across the region to improve product penetration and cross-selling opportunities. The company has implemented artificial intelligence (AI) driven analytics to enhance real time monitoring of the business while ASBH moves towards warehouse consolidation in Trinidad & Tobago. It is also set to benefit from the efficiencies from the recent introduction of its new Benhill machine for its dairy business.

With Seprod receiving shareholder approval at Monday’s EGM, the board is also empowered to issue new Seprod shares as consideration for acquisitions in the future. Seprod previously received permission from shareholders to issue new shares as the directors saw fit at its September 2023 AGM.

Seprod increased its stake in ASBH from 50 to 80 per cent in July 2026 by issuing new Seprod ordinary shares in exchange for the ASBH shares tendered by investors. This move resulted in Seprod director Anthony Mark Hart becoming the 10th largest shareholder in Seprod. Hart was previously issued ASBH shares in December 2024 as consideration for his shares in Caribbean Producers (Jamaica) Limited (CPJ).

“CariCRIS expects continued good performance from Seprod over the next 12 to 15 months supported by continued revenue growth from recent acquisitions, planned new product launches, expected benefits from its operational modernization initiatives and broadly stable macroeconomic conditions across its key markets,” the ratings agency noted.

Seprod’s stock price remains down five per cent in 2026 as of Tuesday, resulting in a market capitalisation of $72.71 billion. It has paid $1.21 in dividends totalling $1.10 billion during 2026.

World.title: Ophthalmologist visit under microscope as Ruel Reid and Co fraud trial continues
World.content:
Former Caribbean Maritime University President Professor Fritz Pinnock (left) and former Education Minister Ruel Reid (second left) about to enter the Corporate Area Parish Court in Half-Way-Tree, St Andrew, in October 2019 for a bail hearing. Both men, along with Reid’s wife Sharen and daughter Sharelle, as well as Jamaica Labour Party Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence, are facing multiple charges in a multimillion-dollar fraud case.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The court is expected to hear details of an August 2018 eye doctor visit by former Education Minister Ruel Reid when his fraud trial resumes on Wednesday as prosecution witness Connie Williams Champagnie continues her testimony on the stand.

Williams Champagnie, during examination-in-chief at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court, detailed the payment and record-keeping systems at her business, Optical Smart Limited, before telling the court that Reid had entered the establishment on August 15, 2018, for an eye exam with another customer known to her. She said he also bought two pairs of eyeglasses using two health cards and a debit card.

When asked how she knew Reid, Williams Champagnie said she had never met Reid prior to that day, but described him as a public figure, telling the court that she had recognised him from the news, as he was the education minister at the time of his visit in 2018.

Reid, his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle Reid, along with former head of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) Fritz Pinnock and Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence are on trial, accused of siphoning off around $25 million from the Ministry of Education and CMU between March 2016 and October 2019.

Williams Champagnie told the court that she, from about arm’s length on the day of his visit, had an unimpeded view of Reid for between five and 10 minutes.

When asked if she saw that same individual in the courtroom, she responded that she did, pointing out a man in the dock in a grey suit, glasses and a blue and red tie. The individual stood and identified himself as Ruel Reid.

The five defendants have pleaded not guilty to a litany of charges including that the former education minister and his family members instructed a domestic worker to set up an account in which millions were deposited.

It is alleged that money was funnelled through transfers to various accounts either owned or controlled by the accused, or handed over in cash, with the recipients either knowing, or reasonably should have known, it was criminal property, resulting in charges of acquisition of criminal property.

Pinnock and Reid are accused of using their roles as public servants to mastermind and effect a scheme in which individuals were being paid on a regular basis by CMU, without knowledge that they were being paid; and in which invoices for goods and services were generated, but not by the individuals being paid, who did not at any time provide the stated services or goods to CMU, resulting in charges of conspiracy to defraud.

The two are also charged with acts of corruption under Section 15 of the Corruption Act — Pinnock for allegedly facilitating the payment of monies from CMU by authorising fraudulent vouchers, and Reid, in his capacity as a minister, for causing money to be paid out from the ministry and CMU for work, goods, and services not provided.

— Dana Malcolm.

World.title: EU capitals weaken end-of-year deadline for budget deal
World.content:
Leaders are gathering in Brussels on Thursday and Friday to react for the first time to an Irish budget proposal that envisages €159 billion cuts. They will also discuss energy prices, enlargement, Ukraine and migration.

Several countries, including Italy and France, urged Costa’s team to drop a reference to “reaching a final agreement by the end of the year” from the Council conclusions, two EU diplomats who were briefed on the discussions told POLITICO on condition of anonymity.

During a parliamentary speech Wednesday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said that “we will not sign an agreement that is not beneficial to us just to meet a deadline,” adding “we will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy.”

There are also lingering concerns that Spain’s snap elections on Nov. 29 could work against the end-of-year deadline.

The new draft conclusions from Tuesday evening merely call for a “timely agreement,” adding that reaching a deal by the end of the year would allow EU funding to start flowing when the next budget takes effect in 2028. This is the same wording used in the Council conclusions from last June.

In another significant addition, EU leaders condemned U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel in the conclusions.

They also expressed “regret” towards U.S sanctions against the International Criminal Court and pledged to engage with Washington to reverse these measures.

Mathieu Pollet contributed to reporting.

World.title: Europe’s development aid dilemma
World.content:
The Commission is grappling with two goals that may be counterproductive: cutting migration and slashing development aid.

The EU executive’s argument is that a slash in development funding will likely result in people showing up at European borders in search of a better life. And that’s a problem for the bloc, since it’s looking to decrease migration numbers. On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart explain how the dilemma will be unpacked at the upcoming European Council this week.

Next, a shooting near the European Parliament in Brussels has EU officials — and everyone else, for that matter — on edge.

Finally, the U.K. under Andy Burnham is at a big inflection point when it comes to redefining its relationship to the EU. But the bloc doesn’t even seem to care.

World.title: EU’s cyber unit turns to AI to fend off ‘high-risk’ hacks
World.content:
Being able to respond quickly to cyberattacks is most crucial in “high-risk scenarios,” the EU executive’s internal cyber defenders warned, saying that the ability to detect an attack is “not sufficient if containment measures cannot be taken quickly enough.”

Officials at the in-house IT department, DG DIGIT, are planning to use automated “protective measures” in specific high-risk scenarios, it said. Those scenarios were redacted in the document, which was provided to POLITICO in response to a freedom of information request.

The plan does not amount to “uncontrolled automation” and there will be strict controls in place including human oversight, according to the document.

As well as laying out the response plan, the document sets out the cybersecurity challenges the Commission faces from AI.

The most advanced AI models are expected to “significantly increase the speed, scale and adaptability of cyberattacks” and the Commission must therefore have defenses in places for an environment where “attacks are likely to become faster, more frequent and more scalable,” it said.

Risks include situations where “malicious activity occurs outside EC [European Commission] normal working hours, spreads more rapidly across systems, or results in large-scale exfiltration or operational disruption before manual intervention can be organized by EC,” they said.

The Commission's cyber division has sought approval internally to move ahead with the plans, it said, though it’s not clear whether the plans have yet been put in place.

The Commission didn't respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Ukraine brings war effort to football’s Champions League
World.content:
“At this point we are not representing just Shakhtar Donetsk. We are representing the whole country,” said Palkin, ahead of four matches in London this fall and winter. “For us, it’s also to support Ukrainian people who left their homes and moved to London, to England. And therefore, these games completely change context. It’s very important every time to send messages to support Ukraine.”

Shakhtar’s survival among Europe’s elite is emblematic of Ukraine’s own endurance against Moscow’s bombardment. Forced out of Donetsk in 2014, the club has spent more than a decade moving between temporary host cities while keeping its Champions League ambitions alive throughout the war, despite the difficulty of attracting top European signings while based in a war zone.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Shakhtar Donetsk has played “home” matches in Poland and Germany. Club bosses are thrilled to be based in England for this season’s games against Greece’s AEK Athens, Portugal’s Sporting CP, Turkey’s Fenerbahçe and Spain’s Real Madrid. “[London] is the capital of the football world,” Palkin said.

“We don’t have pressure. We want to play football. We are 24/7 under stress in Ukraine. And we want to just go out and play for our fans, for Ukraine,” added Srna, a former star defender for Shakhtar Donetsk and the Croatian national team.

Invest in Ukraine

Large white letters adorn Shakhtar Donetsk’s orange and black jersey bearing the name of SCM, the country’s biggest private financial and industrial investment company, owned by Ukraine’s richest man and the club owner, Rinat Akhmetov.

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s unabating assault has cost tens of thousands of lives in Ukraine, and also caused hundreds of billions of dollars worth of damage to infrastructure across the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has crisscrossed the globe in recent months trying to maintain Western support for Kyiv, as it runs short on cash and critical air defenses.

World.title: How Europe can increase resilience to global shocks — live updates
World.content:
Follow updates from inside the room at our European Resilience Summit, where we’re discussing how Europe can strengthen its ability to prosper in an increasingly fragmented world.

Europe needs to find a new way of working.

In an increasingly fragmented and unpredictable world, the policy choices it makes in the years ahead will determine how well Europe competes, prospers, and protects its citizens’ interests.

Leaders face difficult questions. How can Europe finance its ambitions? Can it build globally competitive industries while preserving its social and economic model? How can it secure the technologies, energy, and defense capabilities needed to remain resilient in a more uncertain world? And what tradeoffs will Europeans be willing to accept in pursuit of greater strategic autonomy?

World.title: Corruption could become harder to catch under new EU budget, watchdog warns
World.content:
The warning comes as EU leaders continue fighting over the price tag for the EU’s post-2027 budget in Brussels this week — and as the auditors document an increase in misspending of taxpayer funds.

Yet separate from the budget’s bottom line is the debate over how that money gets divided. As a spending cycle marked by the pandemic, wars and climate-fueled disruption comes to a close, the Commission wants to make the next seven-year budget more agile by assigning about half of it — almost a trillion euros over seven years — to a single pot of money that countries can spend on objectives ranging from migration to agriculture and regional development.

Those agriculture and regional development funds — often delivered in the form of subsidies to farms and local projects — have long been vulnerable to fraud and misuse.

According to Murphy, giving capitals more leeway to shift spending would make spending even harder to track.

“There will be some flexibility, but at what cost?” he said in an interview. More of the oversight will depend on the checks each country has already put in place.

As it stands, misspending of the EU budget was on the rise last year, with errors affecting transactions for an estimated €5 billion according to the ECA’s latest report.

World.title: Prosecution calls Russell Brand 'ruthless' sexual predator at opening of sex assault trial
World.content:
Russell Brand behaved as a “ruthless” sexual predator when he assaulted six women over the course of a decade, a prosecutor said on Wednesday as she opened the rape and sexual assault case against the actor-comedian.

 

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault.

The charges involve six women and alleged offences between 1999 and 2009.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors at Southwark Crown Court in London that the six women, who do not know each other, were assaulted in “a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at (Brand’s) home address.”

She said that at the time Brand had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, and “women were simply a means to an end.”

“He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said.

Brand is on bail and arrived at court Wednesday to a crowed of photographers and video journalists. He said he felt “blessed.”

Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court, 6 October, 2026 AP Photo

“I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved,” Brand said. “That’s my prayer.”

Born to working-class parents in Essex in eastern England, Brand launched a successful stand-up comedy career as a teenager.

He became a household name as a television presenter on MTV, Channel Four and the BBC, also penning newspaper columns and two autobiographies.

He then made a foray into Hollywood, starring in several hit films, and was in a brief, but high-profile, marriage to US pop star Katy Perry.

Now remarried and living in Florida with his young family, he has gained a new following as an influencer, with 6 million subscribers on YouTube, 10.1 million on X and 4.9 million on Instagram.

World.title: MEPs urge EU to shield International Criminal Court from US sanctions
World.content:
Fifty-eight members of the European Parliament have urged the European Commission to shield the International Criminal Court (ICC) from US sanctions that threaten to disrupt its operations.

 

In a letter sent on Tuesday and seen by Euronews, the MEPs called on Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to defend the Netherlands-based court against what they described as “an attack by a foreign power on an entity on EU territory”, warning of "devastating" consequences.

US President Donald Trump’s administration announced sanctions against the ICC last Friday, following repeated criticism of the court over its arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and its investigation into the conduct of US troops in Afghanistan.

After an initial six-month grace period, the sanctions could severely hamper the court's operations by barring US banks and companies from doing business with it, although exemptions are envisaged for some telecommunications, software and payment services.

Given the dominance of US firms in global finance and technology, the restrictions could leave the ICC struggling to pay its bills and conduct financial transactions.

European banks, insurance companies and other intermediary firms with business interests in the US could also be affected, potentially facing secondary penalties if they continue working with the ICC.

The MEPs called for the use of “all instruments at our disposal” to shield the ICC from the sanctions. In particular, they urged the Commission to activate the EU's Blocking Statute, a mechanism designed to protect European companies and individuals from the extraterritorial effects of foreign sanctions.

The statute can prevent foreign court rulings based on specified laws from being enforced in the EU and allows European companies to seek compensation for losses caused by their extraterritorial application.

The Commission can add foreign laws to those covered by the statute, subject to scrutiny by the European Parliament and EU member states.

The letter was drafted by European People’s Party (EPP) MEP Dirk Gotink and Socialists and Democrats (S&D) MEP Aurore Lalucq, and signed by lawmakers from the EPP, S&D, Renew Europe and the Greens/EFA groups.

The signatories warned that the sanctions threatened Europe's ability to protect its own citizens and institutions.

In a statement last Saturday, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the threat of sanctions against the ICC as “not acceptable”, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to international law. However, the EU has yet to take concrete action.

The ICC has 125 member states. The United States signed the Rome Statute, which established the court, but never ratified it.

World.title: How Germany is training medical staff to fight Ebola
World.content:
Just two days ago, Louise Gotze was in the Ugandan city of Entebbe with her team, sharing her knowledge with around 30 doctors and nurses. She spoke to healthcare professionals about how to care for Ebola patients without becoming infected themselves.

 

"These training sessions are absolutely essential to ensure that staff do not become infected and that they know how to work safely when they are in the red zone, meaning the area where patients are being treated," Gotze told Euronews.

Around 200 healthcare workers are currently known to have become infected as a result of their work.

According to Charité doctor Maximilian Gertler, between 800 and 1,000 patients are currently infected or receiving treatment at medical facilities in the Ituri and North Kivu regions.

Gotze has travelled to the Ebola crisis region seven times this year to train local healthcare professionals. In Berlin, she works as an intensive care nurse in the special isolation unit at Charité hospital. Another trip is being planned.

The ultimate goal is to establish a network of trained healthcare professionals across East Africa who can, in turn, pass on their knowledge to others.

Some 9,000 people are now infected with Ebola. Experts say the spread is still not under control. Euronews / Donogh McCabe

How the international community is fighting Ebola

Germany is sending teams to several countries, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya and Uganda, as the virus does not stop at national borders.

"We are currently training a group of around 120 doctors from the partner states of the East African Community," explained epidemiologist Gertler from Berlin's Charité hospital.

"Graduates of our programme from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have also started conducting training sessions themselves in Kinshasa to prepare for the possibility of cases emerging in the capital."

Epidemiologist Maximilian Gertler confirmed that the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is still not under control.

The number of infections has now risen to 9,000, with 4,000 deaths reported. According to Gertler, the fatality rate in this outbreak stands at 50%.

Simulation in Berlin: How Ebola patients are treated

He stands in front of a tent containing a height-adjustable hospital bed and other equipment needed to treat Ebola patients. But here in Berlin, in the courtyard of the Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, there is no real patient.

Instead, a mannequin is being used to demonstrate how people with Ebola are examined and treated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Germany's Development Minister Reem Alabali-Radovan and the Secretary-General of the East African Community, Stephen Patrick Mbundi, are also present.

The climatic conditions in the country, which lies close to the equator, make the work more difficult. Protective clothing can only be worn safely for around 45 to 60 minutes.

More than 10,000 protective suits are used every day and must then be burned to prevent contamination. Only protective goggles, rubber boots and aprons made from more durable materials last longer.

A simulation at the Development Ministry shows how protective equipment is used. Euronews / Donogh McCabe

Plastic walls with openings for arms also offer a solution.

"An innovative concept that the WHO and its partners have increasingly developed in recent years involves fitting the walls of these often tent-like structures in treatment facilities with transparent screens. This allows staff to care for and monitor patients without the need for protective equipment," Gertler explained.

Behind these walls, healthcare workers do not need to wear full protective gear and can still monitor the condition of several patients at the same time.

"This can significantly reduce the number of staff who need to remain in protective clothing continuously," Gertler said.

€21 million for protective equipment and training

Since the Ebola outbreak began in June, Germany's Development Ministry has increased its support by €21 million, including funding for protective equipment.

Germany's commitment is important for global health, according to Development Minister Reem Alabali-Radovan (SPD).

"We cannot prevent outbreaks of infectious diseases and pandemics unless we take active measures. That means it remains important that we continue to invest in global health," Alabali-Radovan said.

The outbreak in eastern DR Congo has already spread to other countries. Kenya has so far recorded one death, while Uganda has reported several dozen infections.

A healthcare worker walks inside a treatment centre for Ebola patients in Beni, 7 October, 2026 AP Photo

"Ebola has broken out in regions that are also affected by crises and conflicts. This means medical staff sometimes have to treat patients under life-threatening conditions, if they are even able to reach the affected areas," Alabali-Radovan stressed.

"We are trying to take the necessary measures to ensure that the outbreak does not spread across the entire region," Ambassador Stephen Patrick Mbundi, Secretary-General of the East African Community, said.

Gertler explained that the international campaign to prevent the further spread of the Ebola virus focuses on patient isolation and treatment, as well as public awareness.

According to Gertler, trust in "all kinds of state institutions" is relatively low in the "civil war-torn region". The population is not accustomed to a functioning healthcare system. Every year, 50,000 people die from infectious diseases such as malaria, cholera and measles. Some people are sceptical about the increased focus on Ebola, as fewer people have died from the virus so far.

"Awareness-raising is needed within communities, and these efforts must reach the people," Gertler stressed.

Alabali-Radovan thanked German personnel for their efforts and called for continued international cooperation to contain the outbreak.

Health workers and officials stand outside a Ebola isolation facility at The Nairobi Hospital, 7 October, 2026 AP Photo

Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo

The Ebola outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in mid-May this year. By July, the number of confirmed cases had already exceeded 2,000, with 754 deaths reported. The total number of infections has now risen to more than 9,000, and according to WHO figures, the virus has killed over 4,000 people.

Some 2,269 people have survived Ebola. The outbreak is considered the most severe and fastest-growing in the country's history.

In May 2026, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

During an international aid operation, two US citizens became infected and were brought to Germany for treatment in specialised isolation units.

Both doctors were later discharged in good health. According to the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), whether an infected person recovers depends "to a large extent on how good the medical treatment is."

There are still no approved vaccines against the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, although one vaccine candidate is currently undergoing testing.

World.title: EU's methane rules face one-year delay, sparking environmental backlash
World.content:
The European Commission proposed on Wednesday to push back the first deadline for importers to demonstrate compliance with EU methane rules, giving companies until May 2029 to demonstrate that their supplies meet equivalent EU standards.

 

The proposal follows pressure from industry and governments concerned about compliance costs and energy security, but falls short of calls from some EU countries for a three-year delay.

Environmental groups condemned the move, arguing that the methane rules pose no threat to Europe's energy security and that the current supply crisis stems instead from the US-Israeli war against Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Under the proposal, importers would have until 31 May, 2029, to demonstrate that their fossil fuel supplies in 2028 met equivalent EU standards for monitoring, reporting and verifying methane emissions.

EU governments and industry have pushed for a delay amid turmoil in energy markets, while climate campaigners accuse Brussels of weakening a recently adopted law without tackling the underlying causes of the crisis.

EU countries adopted methane rules in May 2024, introducing requirements to measure, report and verify emissions from the energy sector as part of efforts to curb one of the most potent greenhouse gases.

But the latest energy crisis, which has driven up prices and threatened diesel and gas supplies, has fuelled concerns that the rules could aggravate shortages.

French President Emmanuel Macron recently joined industry calls to delay the requirements, which were due to take effect in early 2027.

"It is also important not to weaken European production capacities while preparing for long-term supply difficulties," Macron said in a letter to the Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

The United States, the EU's largest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG), has also repeatedly complained about the impact of the rules on American energy companies.

Suspending penalties

The Commission had already offered significant flexibility, including a three-year suspension of certain penalties, in a concession to industry. But it had stopped short of formally postponing the compliance deadline.

The EU methane law requires fossil fuel importers to provide information on emissions associated with production.

In practice, importers may need to collect reliable data from producers operating thousands of kilometres away, at the other end of a complex supply chain.

Importers argue that they still face legal uncertainty despite the proposed suspension of penalties, and have called for more time and clearer obligations.

Environmental groups, however, warn that even a limited delay could pave the way for further concessions, while doing little to improve Europe's energy security.

They also argue that reopening the legislation risks penalising companies and producing countries that have already invested in monitoring and reporting systems, while undermining confidence in EU rules.

Related Eleven EU countries call for methane rules pause amid energy security fears

Jack Corscadden, senior Campaigner at Environmental Investigation Agency, said there was no demonstrable link between the implementation of the EU methane rules and the current energy supply challenges.

“After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires, the Commission is failing European citizens by delaying this vital piece of climate legislation to appease fossil fuel producers and exporters," Corscadden said.

Esther Bollendorff, fossil free program manager at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, said that delaying the EU methane rules made no economic or strategic sense.

"At a time of yet another energy price crisis and tensions on the gas market, methane mitigation could unlock over 40 billion cubic meters of gas from the EU’s main fossil fuel suppliers - more than half the volume of US LNG imported by the EU in 2025," Bollendorff said.

The Commission's proposal still requires approval from the European Parliament and EU governments. It is set to be discussed by EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on Thursday, alongside broader concerns about European competitiveness and soaring energy prices.

World.title: Climate change is putting Europe’s brain health at risk
World.content:
Climate change is emerging as a growing threat to brain health, as rising temperatures and other environmental pressures add to the burden of neurological health conditions.

 

Neurological disorders, ranging from migraines to dementia and Parkinson’s disease, affect around one in three people over their lifetime, according to estimates cited by neurologist Ulf Kallweit, who is also a co-chair of the environmental influences task force at the European Academy of Neurology. Combined with mental health conditions, they accounted for an estimated global economic burden of €1.5 trillion in 2019.

“Everybody is somehow affected or knows somebody who is affected by a neurological disorder,” Kallweit told Euronews Health on the sidelines of the European Health Forum Gastein.

As climate change drives temperatures higher, the situation could deteriorate further, he warned, worsening existing conditions and potentially increasing the risk of developing neurological disorders.

But the trajectory is not inevitable. Policymakers can help limit the risks through measures that reduce exposure to heat and pollution and improve the environments in which people live.

Heat puts the brain under pressure

One of the clearest concerns is the relationship between high temperatures and stroke.

The number of stroke cases rises as temperatures climb above 30°C, Kallweit said, warning that heat-related strokes, which he said currently account for around 1% of all stroke cases, could represent 5 to 8% within the next 20 to 30 years.

Heat can also affect brain health indirectly by disrupting sleep.

Tropical nights, when temperatures remain above 20°C overnight, make it harder for the body to cool down. This can interfere with deep sleep and prevent people from recovering properly overnight.

“Everybody who experienced the last summer knows that sleep gets worse in these kind of heat nights,” Kallweit said.

Prolonged sleep disruption may have more serious consequences than a few restless nights.

“If you don't sleep well, not maybe one night, but for a longer time, there's a huge increase, let's say, for the risk of getting a stroke or also becoming demented,” he said.

Rising temperatures are also changing the geographical range of some infectious diseases, including those transmitted by ticks and mosquitoes. Some of these infections can affect the nervous system. Lyme borreliosis, for example, is transmitted by infected ticks and can cause neurological complications.

Malaria, meanwhile, remains a concern in discussions about the future spread of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe.

“Malaria is still not fully on yet there, but maybe in five or 10 years it may also affect us in southern parts of Europe,” Kallweit said.

Where you live matters

The risks are not shared equally.

Children, pregnant women, older people and those with pre-existing health conditions can be particularly vulnerable to extreme heat and other environmental pressures.

If they live in deprived neighbourhoods, their health risks rise further. Recent research has found that people living in socioeconomic deprivation have poorer indicators of brain health, including lower total brain volume and more signs of vascular damage.

Climate change could compound these existing inequalities.

“If you have heat and you cannot afford an AC, then you are more bothered,” Kallweit said. Access to healthy food, housing conditions and the surrounding environment can also shape people's health, he added.

Urban environments are particularly important. Noise, pollution and stressful living conditions can all affect wellbeing, while access to green spaces may offer some protection.

Therefore, improving access to green spaces is one potential way to support brain health.

“Going out to the forest one hour per week decreases your stroke risk by 3% or dementia risk by 4%,” Kallweit said.

Kallweit urged people to spend time in green surroundings and to protect their sleep by limiting exposure to light, noise and other disturbances.

But individual measures are only part of the answer. Public policy can help determine whether people have access to cooler homes, quieter neighbourhoods and cleaner air.

Kallweit called for safeguards against pollution and toxic substances, as well as changes to the way buildings are designed.

“How buildings are constructed should be reconsidered because they're still looking very much to the south, where the sun is entering,” he said, adding that such architecture “may be changed in the future.”
