En él se han alojado personajes ilustres como Oscar Wilde, que buscó inspiración en sus habitaciones con vistas al mar, o la actriz Sofia Loren, regresando a su tierra natal con la elegancia de quien conquistó Hollywood sin olvidar sus raíces. Destinar parte del viaje a subir a su azotea para tomar un aperitivo o degustar un delicioso ágape mediterráneo contemplando una de las vistas más estremecedoras del Vesubio y el golfo de Nápoles justifica por sí sola la visita a este lugar.

Podría decirse también que el Excelsior es un personaje más del gran teatro napolitano. Su conexión con las artes y con el cine es muy estrecha, ya que tanto su interior como los exteriores se han inmortalizado en producciones como Viaggio in Italia (1954), de Roberto Rossellini, o Il giudizio universale (1961), de Vittorio De Sica. Sorrentino eligió la Via Partenope para rodar la última escena de su superproducción, donde la protagonista podría perfectamente descender por la escalinata del Excelsior con esa elegancia atemporal que solo poseen los grandes personajes del cine italiano.

La entrada del Hotel Excelsior de Nápoles. Michael Piepgras (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

El exterior del hotel nos lanza directamente a uno de los paseos más mágicos y representativos de Nápoles: el paseo marítimo. Transitar por esta extensa avenida acariciada por el mar Tirreno es imprescindible para tomarle el pulso a una de las capitales con más personalidad de Europa. Caminar por aquí al atardecer es adentrarse directamente en el imaginario de Sorrentino. Nápoles y la protagonista de la película comparten el mismo nombre y el mismo destino: una belleza deslumbrante que hechiza a quien la mira, pero que esconde una profunda melancolía. A lo lejos, la silueta imponente del Vesubio descansa como un gigante dormido y, en el centro del recorrido, el Castel dell’Ovo parece flotar sobre el agua en el islote de Megaride, que remite al origen mítico de la ciudad.

Posillipo, el escondite de la burguesía

Vista de la bahía de Marechiaro, en la colina de Posillipo. mauritius images / Alamy / CORDON PRESS

Famosa por su gran diversidad de marisquerías y elegantes coctelerías, Posillipo es una colina salpicada de villas y majestuosos palacios que miran al mar y parecen danzar al son de una de las canciones napolitanas más famosas de la historia: Marechiare (1885), de Francesco Paolo Tosti. Precisamente, descendiendo de Posillipo hacia Marechiaro se puede tomar una instantánea de la mítica fenestella (la pequeña ventana que inspiró la popular serenata). Una visita fundamental para comprender el glamur residencial de los años sesenta y setenta y contemplar el que era el escondite de la alta sociedad y el lugar donde Sorrentino sitúa la impresionante mansión donde nace y vive la protagonista de su Parthenope.

La galería Umberto I y el teatro San Carlo

Dejamos atrás estos rincones de postal para acercarnos a la zona del casco antiguo y descubrir dos edificios relacionados también con la época dorada napolitana, ambos junto a la majestuosa plaza del Plebiscito.

El interior de la Galleria Umberto I de Nápoles, unas galerías del siglo XIX. Zachary Frank (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

La Galleria Umberto I forma parte, igual que el Lungomare, de la gran intervención urbanística llamada Risanamento que tuvo lugar entre finales del siglo XIX y principios del XX, y cuyo objetivo era reconstruir los barrios más degradados de la ciudad. Igual que sucede hoy, esta obra maestra ha sido siempre un punto de encuentro de la sociedad napolitana. Ya en la Belle Époque, bajo su majestuosa cúpula de cristal y hierro se reunían caballeros con sombrero de copa y damas ataviadas con vaporosos vestidos para tomar un café o un limoncello tras disfrutar de una ópera en el cercano teatro San Carlo, el teatro de ópera en funcionamiento continuo más antiguo del mundo (desde 1737).

El patio de butacas del teatro di San Carlo de Nápoles. Dimitar Chobanov (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Para los amantes del chisme, en los bajos de la Galleria se encuentra el Salón Margherita, el homólogo del Moulin Rouge de París, que se puede visitar con reserva previa, aunque, al ser una propiedad privada, solo ofrece visitas guiadas exclusivas.

La cartuja de San Martino, en Vomero

Otro lugar fundamental para comprender la dualidad de Nápoles y contemplar el conjunto de esta sinfonía urbana es la colina del Vomero. Desde allí desafía al horizonte la cartuja San Martino, un antiguo complejo monástico que es una joya del barroco napolitano y que hoy alberga un museo con obras de arte, carruajes históricos y una de las colecciones de belenes tradicionales napolitanos más famosas del mundo. “En la parte alta de la colina de Vomero se encuentra también el castillo de San Elmo, construido en 1300 por los franceses con una función militar. Desde su inmensa plaza de armas se vislumbra una de las vistas panorámicas más completas de Nápoles, ya que abarca 360 grados. La ladera de la colina aloja también una viña histórica replicada en muchas pinturas de Nápoles”, explica la guía.

El Castel Sant'Elmo, una cartuja situada en la colina del Vomero. Engin Korkmaz (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Bagnoli, poesía en estado puro

No podemos poner el broche de oro a este recorrido por el Nápoles más sorrentiniano y hechizante sin visitar Bagnoli, uno de los barrios con más sabor y encanto. Muy cerca de Pozzuoli (lugar de procedencia de la oscarizada Sofia Loren), late uno de los rincones más cautivadores de ese Nápoles que se muestra sin filtros ni artificios, que te entrega su alma.

Una imagen de postal en la que decenas de barcas de pescadores se balancean en un coqueto y pequeño puerto, abrazadas por escarpados acantilados y edificios antiguos erosionados por la huella del tiempo y la humedad del Tirreno. Al frente, el pequeño islote de Nisida completa una panorámica de ensueño. Aquí espera el histórico restaurante Cicciotto, una elección perfecta para quienes quieran probar platos marineros como el pescado crudo o a la plancha, marisco, sus inimitables buñuelos o especialidades como los schiaffoni con langosta y los linguine con cangrejo.

Fundado en 1942 en la bahía de Marechiaro, su encantador nombre evoca la imponente y robusta figura de su fundador, Vincenzo Capuano. Lo que realmente no tiene parangón es el final de fiesta: cuando el nonagenario Vincenzo toma las riendas y empieza a entonar, mesa a mesa, canciones típicas napolitanas. No se me ocurre una mejor forma para cerrar este viaje “a ese Nápoles que, si no sabe cantar, puede, por una necesidad del corazón, y con amable intención, desafinar impunemente”, como lo describía Matilde Serao en El vientre de Nápoles (1884).

Deslizarse hoy por el bellísimo paseo marítimo, cruzar el umbral del majestuoso Excelsior y perderse por sus barrios históricos es transformarse en un personaje de esa gran película inacabada que es Nápoles. Un lugar donde el pasado de anteguerra, los dorados años cincuenta, sesenta y setenta y el presente más vibrante caminan de la mano. En Parthenope, Sorrentino filma su ciudad con la mirada de quien conoce cada rincón pero aún puede maravillarse ante ellos, como un amante que redescubre constantemente el rostro amado.

World.title: De Bilbao a A Coruña, una vuelta por el norte de España para disfrutar del mejor arte
World.content:
Las aperturas del Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao y Faro Santander se añaden a los centros culturales nacidos las últimas décadas entre el País Vasco y Galicia. Excusa perfecta para recorrer una zona que se ha convertido en uno de los epicentros mundiales del arte contemporáneo

Con la aportación del genio de arquitectos de la talla de Frank Gehry, Norman Foster, Renzo Piano, Oscar Niemeyer y David Chipperfield, las recientes aperturas del Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao y de Faro Santander confirman el interés cultural que ofrece el norte de España.

Para demostrarlo, trazamos una singular ruta cultural que se extiende desde el País Vasco hasta Galicia, una zona que se ha convertido en uno de los epicentros mundiales del arte contemporáneo. Un viaje con mucho arte que se inició hace 29 años con la apertura del Guggenheim Bilbao.

Más información Por los lugares de Goya: de Fuendetodos a Madrid pasando por Zaragoza

Guggenheim Bilbao

Levantado hace 29 años en una zona degradada del Nervión, el arriesgado edificio de Frank Gehry no ha perdido su aura. Todo lo contrario. La creación el arquitecto canadiense-estadounidense está considerada el edificio contemporáneo de mayor trascendencia. Su influencia ha sido tal que ha impulsado la transformación de una ciudad industrial en declive, hasta ser referente mundial de innovación urbana. Es el llamado Efecto Bilbao.

Antes de entrar en esta ágora del arte contemporáneo, hay que echarle un vistazo desde el puente de La Salve. Sus arcos rojos, del artista Daniel Buren, son contrapunto de los fríos tonos del titanio del Guggenheim. Desde sus alturas, la vista pasea por las escamas metálicas del enorme pez —“lata de Sardinas”, lo llaman los bilbaínos—, doradas por la luz del otoño bilbaíno.

El Guggenheim Bilbao y, a la izquierda, los arcos rojos del artista Daniel Buren en el puente de La Salve. m. subirats (Alamy / cordon press)

En el inicio de la escalinata que conduce a la entrada del muso pocos resisten la tentación de tirarse unas fotos a los pies de Puppy, gigantesco ramo de flores al que Jeff Koons dio forma de entrañable Westie. Ya en el centro del esbeltísimo atrio central se impone doblar el cuello y vislumbrar sus alturas. “La Flor” lo bautizó el arquitecto por la disposición de sus láminas de cristal. En la distancia, los visitantes que transitan por las aéreas pasarelas asemejan hileras de hormigas. Es parada obligada el mirador sobre La materia del tiempo, desmesurada instalación de Richard Serra para la que Gehry tuvo que diseñar un espacio suficiente para albergar su inmensidad.

'La materia del tiempo', de Richard Serra, en el museo Guggenheim de Bilbao. ilyas Ayub (Alamy / cordon press)

Alrededor del museo y en lo que fue un espacio industrial que olía a abandono, una sucesión de zonas verdes invita al paseo. Por ellas transita el tranvía de Bilbao, que sigue el viejo trazado ferroviario de los trenes cargados de productos y desechos de siderurgias y astilleros. Recorrer la línea entre las estaciones de Atxuri y la del nuevo estadio San Mamés es buena manera de conocer cómo le ha cambiado la cara al Botxo. No lejos aguarda Azkuna Zentroa, la impactante restauración de la vieja alhóndiga que la magia de Philippe Starck convirtió en centro de ocio y cultura.

Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao

No hay que abandonar Bilbao sin la visita a su última gran novedad: la reapertura del Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao, inaugurado el 5 de octubre después de una reforma a cargo de Luis María Uriarte y Norman Foster que se ha prolongado cuatro años. Son 6.900 metros cuadrados donde destacan el impresionante atrio de entrada y el transgresor nuevo cuerpo Agravitas, rematado por una terraza de 700 metros cuadrados de vistas impagables.

El Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao, un edificio diseñado por Norman Foster y Luis María Uriarte. Nigel Young (BILBAO MUSEOA)

Con 150 nuevas obras, se incluyen trabajos de 55 mujeres, como un lienzo de Frida Kahlo. Destaca el centenar de piezas aportadas por el mecenas Plácido Arango. Obras de Eduardo Chillida, Cristina Iglesias, Susana Solana, Jorge de Oteiza, Juan Muñoz y Richard Serra, entre otros, ocupan los nuevos espacios. No opacan el severo fulgor del Guernica de Agustín Ibarrola, a propósito del cual Miguel Zugaza, director del museo, advirtió a los periodistas en la presentación de la ampliación: “Estamos satisfechos con nuestro Guernica. Aquí (en el montacargas) el de Picasso no entra ni en diagonal”, disipando la polémica sobre el traslado de la obra del malagueño, hoy en el Reina Sofía, en Madrid.

La reapertura del Bellas Artes confirma el esplendor cultural de Bilbao iniciado con el Guggenheim. Desde ahora inseparables, ambos museos ofrecen una entrada conjunta a precios ventajosos.

Faro Santander

Exterior del Faro Santander. BELÉN DE BENITO (FARO SANTANDER)

La rehabilitación del británico David Chipperfield de la antigua sede del Banco de Santander despierta admiración desde su inauguración, el pasado 7 de septiembre. Faro Santander es la primera obra museística realizada en España por el arquitecto premio Pritzker. Se ha transformado por completo el histórico edificio Pereda, que tiene su origen en dos bloques independientes. El primero se construyó en 1795 para viviendas, el segundo llegó en 1921. Albergaron un hotel, el club de regatas de la ciudad, hasta que pasó a ser la sede bancaria en 1923. Se unieron en los años cincuenta con un gran arco.

Las obras se han prolongado ocho años. Vaciado el conjunto por completo, solo se han respetado las fachadas. La novedad más reseñable está en el citado arco. Concretamente en el cubo de cristal encajado en su interior. Ha permitido unir las plantas de ambos bloques, logrando una continuidad de la que carecían, sin ocultar las vistas al exterior. “El arco es un potente gesto que conecta el edificio con su entorno”, señaló Chipperfield en la inauguración.

Dos esculturas en una de las terrazas del nuevo Faro Santander. JUAN BARAJA

La cuarta planta alberga uno de los puntos fuertes del museo: las obras maestras de la Colección Banco de Santander. De momento se exponen 69 piezas de las más de 1.200 que la componen. No son demasiadas, pero apabullan. El Sansón y el león, de Rubens, enfrentado a tres obras contemporáneas: Niña sentada en la sala con bancos, de la santanderina María Blanchard, un Tàpies y una pieza de Ángela de la Cruz de idéntico rojo al del perizoma que cubre la desnudez del héroe. Resumen de la vida que quiere darse al proyecto expositivo, en las siguientes salas conviven Velázquez, El Greco, Murillo, Goya, Lucas Cranach el Viejo, Alonso Cano, Tintoretto y Zurbarán con Barceló, Millares, Picasso, Miró y Chillida, entre otros.

Algunas de las obras de la Colección Banco Santander expuestas en Faro Santander. BELÉN DE BENITO (FARO SANTANDER)

El morbo de Faro se encuentra estos primeros meses en las exposiciones temporales. La consagrada a la surrealista Leonora Carrington (hasta el 31 de enero de 2027), en la que se recogen las terribles experiencias que sufrió en España. Otra ofrece una selección de las obras de la Colección Gelman Santander. Se trata del conjunto de 161 obras maestras de artistas mexicanos reunidas por Jacques Gelman y Natasha Zahalka, pareja de origen ruso establecida en México en la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Catalogadas Monumento Artístico por el Gobierno Mexicano, 93 de ellas se muestran en Faro. Esta muestra estará abierta hasta el 10 de enero de 2027, razón suficiente para visitar Santander estas semanas y contemplar las obras de Diego Ribera, David Alfaro Siqueiros, José Clemente Orozco, Rufino Tamayo, Graciela Iturbide, Tina Modotti… y Frida Kahlo. Absolutamente de moda la mexicana, el público hace cola para admirar, retratar y tirarse selfis ante Diego en mi pensamiento, Autorretrato con monos, El abrazo de amor de entre el Universo, la Tierra, yo, Diego y el señor Xólotl, Autorretrato con trenza y el resto de sus 18 obras expuestas.

Centro Botín

Exterior del Centro Botín, inaugurado en junio de 2017 en Santander, con diseño de Renzo Piano. Stéphane ABOUDARAM (CENTRO BOTÍN)

Al otro lado de los jardines de Pereda destaca el inconfundible hermano de Faro, el Centro Botín. Si en el primero se tuvo especial cuidado en conservar su imagen neoclásica, en el Centro Botín no fue necesario, pues se construyó en un espacio vacío. Inaugurado en junio de 2017, con diseño de Renzo Piano, este rompedor edificio de dos volúmenes se sitúa en el borde del muelle de Albareda. Unidos por terrazas, escaleras y pasarelas que se adentran en la bahía, tiene piel de cristal, acero y 270.000 piezas cerámicas que otorgan al edificio un aspecto inconfundible, causa de que los santanderinos le llamen “el Radiador”.

Se reparten su espacio exposiciones temporales —hasta el 25 de octubre puede verse la de la poco conocida Marisol, enigmática artista encuadrada en el pop— y una selección de piezas de la colección del Banco de Santander.

Una de las obras expuertas en 'MARISOL: Cuando todo está por comenzar', muestra que se puede ver en el Centro Botín. CENTRO BOTÍN

Es buena idea darse un paseo por el muelle de Calderón, que conserva muestras del patrimonio de la ciudad, como el Palacete del Embarcadero y la Caseta de Bombas. No puede pasarse por alto el homenaje a los raqueros: cuatro entrañables figuras de bronce del escultor José Cobo que recuerdan a los niños de la clase humilde santanderina, que esperaban en la orilla de la bahía a que los paseantes arrojaran una moneda al agua para zambullirse y sacarla a la superficie entre los dientes.

El Palacete del Embarcadero, en Santander. NATALIA PEREVERZIEVA (GETTY IMAGES)

Más allá, a los pies del Palacio de Festivales, se alzan las Naves de Gamazo. Antiguos talleres navales, datan de 1908. Quedaron en desuso a finales del siglo XX, hasta que Puertos del Estado las cedió a la Fundación ENAIRE, del Ministerio de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible. Tras una profunda transformación, abrieron en 2021 como primera sede permanente de la fundación fuera de Madrid. Hasta el 17 de enero acoge Persona, que reúne más de 80 retratos realizados por Estela de Castro a animales rescatados de centros de recuperación y entidades protectoras.

El Palacio de Festivales de Cantabria, en Santander. Andrzej Rostek (GETTY IMAGES)

Centro Niemeyer, en Avilés

Sorprende que una pequeña ciudad como Avilés tenga algo tan mayúsculo. Todo se inició en 1989, cuando el premio Príncipe de Asturias de las Artes recayó en el arquitecto brasileño Oscar Niemeyer. En agradecimiento, este regaló al Principado el proyecto de un centro cultural, con la única condición de que se construyese cerca del mar. Se escogió Avilés para recuperar su degradada zona industrial. El centro abrió en la primavera de 2011, despojando a la urbe de la triste grisura que la cubrió décadas para vestirlo con la optimista blancura de Niemeyer. Recorrer su amplia plaza es entender las palabras del brasileño, que señaló su obra como “una plaza abierta a todo el mundo, un lugar para la educación, la cultura y la paz”.

El exterior del Centro Niemeyer, en Avilés (Asturias). Carranza

La singular forma del auditorio le han hecho ganarse el sobrenombre con el que algunos lo conocen y que evita su descripción: “el huevo duro”. La Cúpula es una semiesfera en cuyo interior destaca una voluptuosa escalera. El arquitecto aseguró que la diseñó inspirándose en las curvas de la mujer carioca. El edificio polivalente alberga cafetería, sala de cine y oficinas. Sobre el resto de construcciones destaca la torre. En sus alturas aguarda el deleite de la gastronomía convertida en un bien cultural, que ofrece el exclusivo restaurante Yume.

Fundación MOP (A Coruña)

Antes de 2022, A Coruña daba la espalda al muelle de Batería. Cerradas a cal y canto, las verjas impedían ver poco más que el tránsito de los grandes cruceros internacionales que atracan a diario en el puerto de la capital gallega. Desde entonces, el Centro MOP ha barrido el polvo de la vieja cementera aquí situada, transformando el lugar en destino de cabotaje obligado del circuito de las grandes exposiciones internacionales.

La Fundación MOP, ubicada en el muelle de Batería de A Coruña. THE MOP FOUNDATION

Ha sido posible por el empeño de Marta Ortega, presidenta de Inditex, en impulsar la difusión del octavo arte y su relación con la moda. La nómina de artistas que ha desfilado por el estandarte de The MOP Foundation confirma su calado: Peter Lindbergh, Steven Meisel, Helmut Newton, Irving Penn, David Bailey, Annie Leibovitz, Paolo Roversi y, a partir del 21 de noviembre, David Sims.

No solo son estos artistas la razón de que el MOP se haya convertido en referencia mundial. También lo es el exquisito proyecto de recuperación de la arquitecta coruñesa Elsa Urquijo, que ha logrado fusionar la espesa esencia industrial que reinó en el pasado con un minimalismo contemporáneo. Sin cambiar el exterior, donde se ha creado una irresistible terraza, el silo mantiene sus ásperas formas. En su interior, las mesas de la cafetería comparten espacio con la vieja maquinaria y en los racks de almacenamiento reposan libros de fotografía. Sentarse aquí a tomar un café con un libro entre las manos frente al Atlántico es buena manera de entretener una tarde.

Interior de The MOP Library. YAGO CASTROMIL (THE MOP FOUNDATION)

Al lado se abre una de las salas más formidables de la instalación: la librería. Adaptada al volumen circular del interior del silo, sus anaqueles colman las paredes hasta el techo. Una rampa asciende hasta los libros situados en lo más alto. Especializada en fotografía, permite una consulta gratuita de sus más de 5.500 libros, revistas, catálogos y otras publicaciones, sin descuidar una esmerada sección infantil. La vecina nave acoge las exposiciones, todas gratuitas. Sus montajes son auténtico espectáculo. Instalaciones inmersivas, proyecciones, rincones que reproducen el universo donde trabajan los artistas… muchos repiten la visita solo para disfrutar otra vez las puestas en escena. Da pena que la estricta programación del centro impida prolongarlas.

World.title: De escuchar música a dormir sin ruido: estos son los auriculares que recomendamos para cada situación después de haberlos probado
World.content:
Hemos reunido en una sola guía los ganadores de nuestras comparativas, que incluyen desde modelos inalámbricos hasta opciones gaming y de traducción de idiomas

Escuchar música mientras paseamos, aislarnos del ruido en el transporte público, atender una llamada sin tener que sacar el móvil del bolsillo o sumergirnos en un videojuego; los auriculares se han convertido en compañeros habituales de nuestro día a día y nos permiten disfrutar del sonido (o cancelarlo) en situaciones muy diferentes. Sin embargo, no todos están pensados para lo mismo. Mientras algunos priorizan la comodidad y la autonomía, otros buscan ofrecer una experiencia más inmersiva y hasta los hay capaces de traducir distintos idiomas.

Con tantas opciones sobre la mesa, encontrar el modelo adecuado puede resultar complicado. El presupuesto, el tipo de conexión o la cancelación de ruido son algunos de los aspectos que conviene valorar antes de elegir. En EL PAÍS Escaparate hemos probado todo tipo de auriculares y, por ello, hemos reunido en esta guía los modelos que más han destacado en su categoría para ayudarte a encontrar los que mejor encajan contigo.

Auriculares inalámbricos

Los auriculares inalámbricos nos permiten prescindir de los cables al transmitir el sonido mediante tecnologías como Bluetooth. Dentro de esta sección encontramos opciones para prácticamente todos los gustos y bolsillos.

Auriculares inalámbricos económicos

Si buscas unos auriculares inalámbricos por menos de 30 euros, te alegrará saber que hay modelos que ofrecen prestaciones interesantes sin necesidad de gastar demasiado. Estos de Btootos nos convencieron por su comodidad, la cancelación de ruido y una autonomía de hasta ocho horas con una sola carga. Además, la calidad del sonido y la claridad de las llamadas nos parecieron dos aspectos muy prácticos para el uso diario.

Auriculares inalámbricos Btootos. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares inalámbricos con cancelación de ruido

Los auriculares inalámbricos con cancelación de ruido son una buena opción para escuchar música o ver películas sin que el sonido ambiental interfiera demasiado. En nuestra selección destacó este modelo de Soundcore, un superventas que acumula más de 12.000 reseñas en Amazon. Su cancelación de ruido de hasta 42 dB nos pareció especialmente útil en lugares como el transporte público.

Auriculares inalámbricos con cancelación de ruido de Soundcore. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares inalámbricos deportivos

Los auriculares deportivos inalámbricos deben ofrecer una buena sujeción y resultar cómodos incluso durante los entrenamientos más intensos. En nuestra comparativa, los Shokz OpenRun fueron los ganadores gracias a su innovador diseño de conducción ósea, que transmite el sonido mediante vibraciones a través de los huesos del cráneo sin cubrir los oídos.

Auriculares inalámbricos deportivos Shokz OpenRun. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares inalámbricos invisibles

Los auriculares invisibles destacan por su tamaño reducido y su diseño discreto pensado para quienes prefieren que apenas se noten al llevarlos puestos. En nuestra comparativa, los JLab Go Air Pop+ fueron los ganadores por su buena calidad de sonido y las posibilidades de personalización del audio, que permiten ajustar la experiencia de escucha a las preferencias de cada usuario.

Auriculares inalámbricos invisibles JLab Go Air Pop+. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares true wireless

Tras semanas de pruebas, nuestra experta eligió los Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2.ª generación) como sus auriculares true wireless favoritos por su excelente calidad de sonido y su eficaz cancelación activa de ruido. Dos características que los convierten en una opción especialmente interesante para quienes buscan una experiencia auditiva envolvente.

Auriculares true wireless Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2.ª generación). CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares con cable USB-C para móvil

Los auriculares USB-C para móvil son una alternativa para quienes prefieren una conexión por cable y no quieren depender de la batería, como sí ocurre con un modelo inalámbrico. Después de testar varias opciones, estos de Panasonic fueron los que más nos gustaron por su diseño ergonómico, la facilidad de uso de sus controles y una experiencia sonora que, en conjunto, fue la más completa de todos los modelos analizados.

Auriculares USB-C para móvil de Panasonic. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares para niños

Los auriculares para niños están diseñados para adaptarse a la cabeza de los más pequeños y ofrecer una experiencia de escucha cómoda y adecuada a su edad. A la hora de elegirlos, conviene fijarse en aspectos como el límite de volumen, la autonomía y la resistencia. En nuestra comparativa, los Belkin SoundForm Mini 2 fueron los ganadores gracias a sus hasta cincuenta y cinco horas de autonomía, su diseño plegable y la posibilidad de que dos menores escuchen el mismo contenido a la vez gracias a la función Rockstar Mode.

Auriculares para niños Belkin SoundForm Mini 2. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares de concierto para niños

Para acudir a espectáculos musicales y otros entornos ruidosos, los auriculares de concierto para niños son una opción ideal pues ayudan a reducir la exposición a los sonidos más fuertes. De todos los modelos analizados, los Vanderfields Kids KM-2 fueron los mejor valorados en este sentido.

Auriculares de concierto para niños Vanderfields Kids KM-2. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares para ordenador

Los auriculares para ordenador son especialmente útiles para trabajar, hacer videollamadas o mantener reuniones sin depender de los altavoces del equipo. Después de poner a prueba varios, los Jabra Evolve2 65 fueron los elegidos como ganadores por su calidad de sonido, su diseño ergonómico y su capacidad para reducir el ruido ambiental, una ventaja especialmente interesante en oficinas concurridas.

Auriculares para ordenador Jabra Evolve2 65. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares gaming

Dentro de las opciones para ordenador, los auriculares gaming están diseñados para ofrecer una experiencia de juego más inmersiva y facilitar la comunicación con otros jugadores durante las partidas. De los cuatro modelos analizados, los Logitech G Pro X fueron nuestros favoritos por su ajuste cómodo, su buena calidad de sonido y un micrófono con tecnología específica para optimizar la voz.

Auriculares gaming Logitech G Pro X. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares para dormir

Los auriculares para dormir están diseñados para resultar cómodos durante el descanso y reducir las molestias provocadas por el ruido ambiental. Tras semanas de pruebas, los de Anker fueron los ganadores de nuestra comparativa gracias a su comodidad y a la cancelación activa de ruido, que ayuda a atenuar sonidos como los ronquidos de quien duerme a nuestro lado.

Auriculares para dormir Soundcore de Anker. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares sumergibles

Diseñados para escuchar música mientras nadas, los auriculares sumergibles deben ofrecer una buena resistencia al agua y mantener una reproducción clara bajo la superficie. Como los ganadores de nuestra comparativa ya no están disponibles, hemos escogido los segundos clasificados: un modelo de Creative que destaca por su calidad de construcción y por ofrecer un sonido nítido incluso debajo del agua.

Auriculares sumergibles de Creative. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Auriculares traductores

Tras probar varios auriculares traductores, nuestros favoritos fueron los Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max por combinar una traducción casi simultánea con funciones avanzadas de audio, cancelación activa de ruido y prestaciones que también resultan útiles en el día a día.

Auriculares traductores Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max. CORTESÍA DE AMAZON

Preguntas frecuentes sobre auriculares

¿Qué hay que tener en cuenta al comprar unos auriculares?

Antes de elegir unos auriculares, conviene valorar para qué vamos a utilizarlos, la comodidad, la calidad del sonido y el presupuesto. Si optamos por un modelo inalámbrico, también es importante revisar la autonomía y el tiempo de carga. Para usos concretos, como hacer deporte, jugar o dormir, interesa prestar atención a características específicas, como la sujeción o el diseño.

¿Son mejores unos auriculares inalámbricos o con cable?

Depende de las preferencias de cada persona. Los inalámbricos ofrecen más libertad de movimiento y evitan los cables, aunque obligan a estar pendiente de la batería. Los modelos con cable no necesitan recargarse y pueden resultar prácticos para quienes buscan una conexión sencilla y estable.

¿Qué significa que unos auriculares sean true wireless?

Los auriculares true wireless (TWS) son completamente inalámbricos, lo que significa que los dos auriculares funcionan sin ningún cable que los una entre sí ni al dispositivo de reproducción. Normalmente se conectan por Bluetooth y se guardan en un estuche que permite transportarlos y recargarlos.

[Recuerda que si eres usuario de Amazon Prime, todas las compras tienen gastos de envío gratuitos. Amazon ofrece un período de prueba gratuito y sin compromiso durante 30 días.]

*Todos los precios de compra incluidos en este artículo están actualizados a 14 de octubre de 2026.

World.title: Auditors: €9.5bn needed to put roads and railways on war footing
World.content:
The Netherlands needs to invest nearly €10 billion to make its road and rail infrastructure fit for war, auditors have warned in a critical report.

The Court of Audit said investment was needed to upgrade motorways and rail lines to ensure military vehicles and supplies can be transported across the country.

“Shortfalls in the maintenance budget mean that on an everyday basis, infrastructure is so outdated that it can no longer be used properly,” the auditors said.

“This leads to limitations on use, such as traffic travelling at lower speeds or with lighter loads, which military transport also has to contend with.”

The Netherlands’ key strategic position on the edge of the North Sea makes it a crucial link in the chain for military supplies to Nato partners. A broken bridge or subsidence on the railway line could have far-reaching consequences, the auditors warned.

Last year junior infrastructure minister Thierry Aartsen called for a review of the railway lines between the Netherlands and the Baltic states, after researchers warned that the network was prone to sabotage.

Railway sabotage

A month ago saboteurs brought the network to a standstill by fastening steel pipes and other objects to rail lines, in a co-ordinated campaign that was blamed on farmers angry with the government’s plans to tackle the nitrogen emissions crisis.

Altogether the audit office says the country needs to spend an extra €9.5bn, including €5 billion to meet Nato standards by widening military corridors, raising clearance heights and strengthening bridges.

They added that the list was incomplete because it does not include spending on waterways or how much was needed to maintain military corridors in their current state.

The figure is far greater than the €1.5bn the cabinet announced in its 2027 budget for repairs to roads and bridges over the next decade. All Nato countries agreed at last year’s summit in The Hague to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP, including 1.5% on critical infrastructure.

World.title: ASML posts record quarter as AI demand outpaces expansion plans
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch chip-machine maker ASML had a record third quarter, with sales of €11.7 billion and net profit of €5 billion. That is well up from the €2.1 billion profit last year.

ASML is benefiting from the boom in AI, with customers continuously raising their forecasts for how many machines they will need.

That puts pressure on ASML to make more machines. The company had planned to raise capacity by 30% in 2027, with a possible further 30% in 2028, but now says even that will not fully meet customer demand.

Sales of upgrades for existing machines also rose above expectations, reaching €3.3 billion, helping push the profit margin to 57.5%.

ASML expects fourth-quarter sales of between €14.2 billion and €15.2 billion, and between €44 billion and €45 billion for the full year. Shareholders will receive an interim dividend of €1.88 per share in November.

World.title: VeiligThuis denied plea for extra funding for domestic abuse
World.content:
Domestic abuse reporting network VeiligThuis had its request for an additional

€70 million rejected by parliament on Tuesday, after the organisation said it was being overwhelmed with reports and could not handle the workload.

Waiting lists have been growing substantially for years, and how a case is handled depends on the region where you live.

MPs voted against immediately granting more money. First, parliament wants the cabinet to look at the “role, position and capacity” of VeiligThuis to see how best to improve it. A motion calling for that investigation was passed a year ago.

MPs agreed the motion needs to be implemented now, but that more money is not the solution until the problems are better understood.

Pro MP Lisa Westerveld said the previous and current cabinets are responsible for the delay. “This is not primarily a matter of money, but of doing what was promised.”

In the past year, serious child abuse incidents have sparked national outrage and drawn attention to the lack of sufficient resources and care.

World.title: Senate votes to axe penalty payments for asylum applicants
World.content:
Senators voted on Tuesday to scrap all penalty payments to asylum seekers whose applications are delayed beyond the legal six month deadline.

This means that anyone applying for asylum status in the Netherlands and has to wait more than the maximum term of 6 months for a decision, will not be financially compensated for having to wait longer than promised.

The decision was agreed with a large majority; asylum minister Bart van den Brink announced recently that the immigration service IND had paid out almost €100 million in penalties for missing deadlines in the first seven months of 2026.

The IND said penalty payments do nothing to speed up decisions.

The legal changes agreed in the senate also introduce rules allowing authorities to detain people who are deliberately refusing or avoiding leaving the country despite having an application rejected. It also makes it easier to declare foreign nationals convicted of crimes “undesirable”.

The changes do not include another idea, first proposed by the right-wing PVV, which would formally criminalise illegal residence. This caused controversy in April when it was voted down, as it could mean anyone without their residency paperwork sorted out (including foreign nationals whose permits lapsed) could be prosecuted.

D66 senator Boris Dittrich told Dutch News at the time that the law, if passed, could open the door to a future right-wing cabinet “hunt down all illegal immigrants.”

Van den Brink has since proposed a narrower bill that would only criminalise rejected asylum seekers who actively “frustrate” their return, with a maximum penalty of six months in jail.

World.title: Alkmaar moves protest against Israeli fans amid safety concerns
World.content:
The mayor of Alkmaar, Anja Schouten, has ordered two demonstrations against Thursday’s Europa League match between AZ and Hapoel Be’er Sheva to be moved away from the stadium because of concerns about potential disorder.

Hundreds of people are expected to attend the protests against the participation of Israeli clubs in European competition, which have been organised by pro-Palestinian groups Boycott 4 Palestine and Week 4 Palestine.

The protests were originally due to take place outside the main entrance to the AFAS Stadium, but Schouten ordered the demonstrators to gather near the Kooimeer roundabout, the main road junction leading to the stadium, instead.

“It is not possible to take adequate management measures to prevent disorder and separate fans going to the stadium from demonstrators,” Schouten said.

“This [new] location allows us to facilitate the safe arrival and departure of demonstrators. We also need to prevent confrontations taking place with other groups.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Week.4PalestineNL (@week.4palestinenl)

In a briefing note to councillors, the mayor said there were indications that supporters of the Israeli club were planning to travel to Alkmaar in spite of the ban.

“There are fears that protesters will come into conflict with each other, with supporters’ groups or with the police, that vandalism could ensue, or that the safety of people attending the match could be endangered,” she wrote.

Schouten came under fire from opposition parties on the city council last week for her decision to ban Israeli supporters from travelling to the match. AZ Alkmaar cancelled ticket sales to visiting fans in the wake of the mayor’s decision.

Amsterdam riots

She said the decision was based on public order concerns rather than “political considerations”, following the riots surrounding a Europa League game between Ajax and Maccabi Tel Aviv in Amsterdam two years ago.

Schouten said it was “virtually impossible” to keep groups apart outside the stadium, especially as many visiting fans were expected to stay in Amsterdam for the game.

Alkmaar had originally said Israeli supporters were welcome at the game, but the mayor changed her mind after her counterpart in Amsterdam, Femke Halsema, made an “urgent” appeal not to allow a repeat of the scenes in the capital in 2024.

VVD councillor John van der Rhee accused Schouten of succumbing to a “powerplay” by the mayor of Amsterdam.

World.title: PSV punished for missed chances as Leipzig claim narrow CL win
World.content:
Peter Bosz was left ruing missed chances after his PSV team lost 1-0 in Leipzig to move down the Champions League table.

Ivan Perisic missed a penalty in the 18th minute during a bright start for the visitors, after RB Leipzig defender Ridle Baku was penalised for handball.

But in the second period PSV were on the back foot and Brajan Gruda fired in the winner in the 75th minute with a shot that took a deflection off the luckless Perisic’s back.

“I thought we were the better team for a lot of this match,” Bosz told Ziggo Sport afterwards. “The first 30 to 35 minutes were all us, but towards half-time we started to struggle.

“Leipzig had some big chances but so did we. We played a settled game and could keep the ball for longer.”

Brazilian defender Mauro Junior also said his team deserved more from the game. “We created enough chances, but at this level you have to take them,” he said.

The result extends a winless run for PSV in Germany dating back nearly 50 years to 1977, when they beat Eintracht Braunschweig 2-1. Since then they have lost 14 matches and drawn three, against Bayern Munich in 1986, Werder Bremen in 1995 and Bayer Leverkusen last year.

It also leaves PSV in 25th place out of the 36 teams in the Champions League table, with five of those below them still to play their second-round matches. Those teams include Feyenoord, who take on Italian club Como in Rotterdam on Wednesday evening.

Next week PSV face another tricky test away to Portuguese champions Porto, coached by former Ajax manager Francesco Farioli.

World.title: Weekly regional transport strikes begin, to run until Christmas
World.content:
Regional bus and train services across most of the country are disrupted by strikes as of Wednesday morning, which trade unions CNV and FNV organised over pay and working conditions.

Staff at regional operators Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Transdev and Keolis are taking part. National rail operator NS is running a normal service.

City transport in Amsterdam and The Hague, run by GVB and HTM, is not affected because it falls outside the regional pay deal. In Rotterdam, RET trams and metro trains are running but its buses are not. Few or no buses and trams are expected to run in Utrecht.

The strikes could continue every week until Christmas unless the unions’ demands are met. They want higher wages, quicker access to permanent contracts for staff, and better working schemes for older employees.

They will announce each week’s strike day only shortly beforehand, assuming their demands aren’t met. They also plan to pick a different day each week, so operators can’t prepare emergency timetables and the same passengers are not hit every week.

World.title: Woman, 29, goes missing in Amsterdam on bike with unknown man
World.content:
Police say they are concerned for the safety of a woman who went missing in Amsterdam after she was seen cycling with an unknown man more than a week ago.

Hajar, 29, left the Rai area in the direction of Buitenveldert last Sunday, October 4. Police said she and the man were riding a black ladies’ bike.

She is described as between 1.65m and 1.70m tall with dark curly hair and dark eyes. The day before she went missing she was wearing a tiger print dress and white New Balance shoes, but it is not clear if she was still wearing the same outfit when she left Rai.

“The police and Hajar’s family are concerned about her welfare,” a police spokesman said.

We cannot do what we do without your support. Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year. Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8 — Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks. While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast. Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028. Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia. The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president. Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions. PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M — Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026 Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in. The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so. Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge. Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present. The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK. The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present. The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding. 1294/2026 Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo — Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026 Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him. However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government). Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions. Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal. Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK. Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026 Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry. Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”. However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”. This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force. ❗️Policja szarpie posłów oraz zgromadzonych obywateli pod TK ❗️ pic.twitter.com/eGPRFQJnAX — Oskar Szafarowicz (@Szafarowicz2001) October 14, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Man charged with plotting attack on Polish PM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot. The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist. Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026 On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”. On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences. “The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years. Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns. Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect. Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force. At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026 Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts. On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”. "Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026 In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty. A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison. “He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine. “In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre. 🇵🇱🤝🇳🇴 Strategiczne partnerstwo Polski i Królestwa Norwegii oficjalnie przypieczętowane. ✍️ Podpisano deklarację o strategicznym partnerstwie między obu państwami, stanowiącą efekt wieloletniej współpracy oraz wspólnoty interesów biznesowych, geopolitycznych i moralnych. 🛡️ W… pic.twitter.com/vBrWrdC8oT — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 12, 2026 The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries. Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries. Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation. “The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.” The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”. Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors. Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe. “Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine. Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed. It will be followed by two more new frigates as part of a €3.5bn programme to modernise the ageing Polish fleet https://t.co/093Fx2WSM7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Poland has in recent years also moved to strengthen its ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. This year, Polish and Norwegian companies announced plans to develop a new anti-drone system for Poland in the wake of incursions of Russian drones into Polish airspace. Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic. Poland will manufacture the missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is buying from South Korea. The Norwegian government says that Polish production "will strengthen security of supply for Norway and other European customers of the system" https://t.co/NIJj7owK45 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 29, 2026 Poland has also moved closer in recent years to Sweden, with which it signed a strategic partnership in 2024. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Last year, at Poland’s suggestion, NATO launched a new military mission to protect critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: Germany detains Turks suspected of sabotaging Starlink station in Poland on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia. On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”. He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”. Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026 Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA). He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life. Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”. The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion. Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military. A fire last night at a Starlink ground station in Poland that is used to provide internet services to Ukraine was caused deliberately and "the modus operandi is clearly Russian", says digital affairs minister @KGawkowski https://t.co/p2DEn7XexF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026 On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not. He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects. Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation. “We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.” Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 On Tuesday morning, German newspaper Handelsblatt reported confirmation from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Baden-Württemberg that two Turkish men had been detained on Monday in the town of Nürtingen at the request of the Polish authorities. The office did not provide further details, but Handelsblatt reports that the two suspects are due to be brought before a judge today. Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons. Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024. Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga. W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq — TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026 According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks. The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life. Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services. However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement. Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack. Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw. Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years. Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted. Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism. That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025 In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory. A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe. Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland. Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region.
