World.title: Engineers must remain accountable for AI use – expert
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in engineering education should not replace analytical thinking or an understanding of physical processes, and engineers must remain accountable for the results of using AI, Aldo Canova, a representative of the Department of Energy at Italy’s Polytechnic University of Turin, said at the opening ceremony of the 20th IEEE International Conference on Application of Information and Communication Technologies (AICT2026) in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

“It is important to maintain an analytical approach. In my applied electromagnetics courses, I teach students analytical methods, even through simple examples. This is necessary primarily to ensure that they have a solid understanding of physics, fundamental equations, and mathematical models. This will enable them to formulate appropriate prompts for artificial intelligence and have the tools to verify its results,” he said.

According to Canova, without such an understanding, students may accept AI-generated answers without critically assessing them or checking their accuracy.

He also emphasized the importance of engineers taking responsibility when using AI in their professional activities.

“When students graduate from university and start designing a bridge or a power plant, they can continue to use artificial intelligence to perform certain tasks. However, they must understand that they, as engineers, are responsible for the results, not artificial intelligence. AI is not accountable,” Canova noted.

He added that students should view AI as a tool while recognizing their own responsibility for the results of its application.

The 20th IEEE International Conference on Application of Information and Communication Technologies (AICT2026) is being held at ADA University in Baku. Azerbaijan is hosting the conference for the seventh time, and this year’s event marks the 20th anniversary of the AICT series under the slogan “20 Years of Connecting Science, Technology, and Society.”

The event is jointly organized by ADA University, relevant IEEE units in Azerbaijan, the Polytechnic University of Turin, George Washington University, Nazarbayev University, United Arab Emirates University, Tashkent University of Information Technologies, Kazakh-British Technical University, Tbilisi State University, Georgian Technical University, SDU University, the Nikola Tesla Institute of Electrical Engineering, and the Alessandro Faedo Institute of Information Science and Technologies.

The conference aims to facilitate knowledge exchange in information and communication technologies and discuss the sector’s latest developments. It brings together researchers, academics, and industry representatives.

World.title: Baku hosts kelaghayi procession from Maiden Tower to Baku Boulevard (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. Baku has come alive with the colors of national traditions: a colorful “Kelaghayi” procession has set off from the Maiden Tower, featuring representatives of civil society organizations and everyone who appreciates Azerbaijan’s cultural heritage, Trend’s correspondent reports.

Participants in traditional costumes are marching along the route from Icherisheher to Fountain Square to Baku Boulevard, attracting the attention of residents and visitors to the capital. They are taking photos with passersby, smiling, singing songs, and turning a stroll through the city into a true celebration of national culture.

The main goal of the event is to promote the Kelaghayi, a traditional Azerbaijani women’s headscarf, which is not merely part of the national costume but also a symbol of beauty, identity, and the continuity of generations.

The Kelaghayi’s special value is underscored by its international recognition: in 2014, the traditional art of crafting and wearing this headscarf, as well as its symbolism, were inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. This highlights the uniqueness of Azerbaijani traditions and the importance of preserving them.

Kelaghayi bridges the past and the present and serves as a reminder that preserving cultural values is an investment in the future. Thanks to such initiatives, national traditions are being revitalized, and Azerbaijan’s heritage is becoming more accessible to the younger generation and attracting the interest of the country’s guests.

World.title: TransLogistica Kazakhstan 2026 opens in Astana with 230 companies
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. The 29th Kazakhstan International Exhibition on Transport and Logistics, TransLogistica Kazakhstan 2026, has opened at the EXPO International Exhibition Center in Astana, bringing together 230 companies from 20 countries.

According to the Ministry of Transport of Kazakhstan, the opening ceremony was attended by Kazakhstan's Vice Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov.

The exhibition features 101 Kazakh companies and 129 international participants, including logistics operators, representatives of railway and port infrastructure, manufacturers of transport and warehouse equipment, and developers of IT solutions.

This year's event includes 36 new exhibitors and, for the first time, the Turkish Service Exporters Association, which brings together more than 700 companies. A podcast zone titled "People Who Move the World" has also been introduced to facilitate discussions with industry leaders.

The business program, running from October 14 to 16, will focus on international transport corridors, logistics hubs, warehouse logistics and the adoption of modern technologies.

Key events include the panel session "Central Asia: A New Logistics Hub," the third BreakBulkKazakhstan conference, the fifth Kazakhstan Warehouse Logistics Conference and the ninth New Silk Way International Transport and Logistics Business Forum. The program will conclude with the Expert Talks session "FUTURE CHECK: Kazakhstan's Transport and Logistics in 2035."

The exhibition is held with the official support of Kazakhstan's Ministry of Transport and leading industry organizations. It is organized by Iteca and Atakent-Expo in cooperation with international partner ICA Events.

TransLogistica Kazakhstan 2026 aims to strengthen international business ties, expand partnerships and promote modern solutions in the transport and logistics sector.

World.title: Social media, AI pose cognitive risks and enable manipulation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. Excessive use of social media and automated systems can lead to a decline in human cognitive abilities and create opportunities to manipulate users’ behavior for commercial and other purposes, Erol Gelenbe, an IEEE member and professor at the Institute of Theoretical and Applied Informatics of the Polish Academy of Sciences, said at the opening ceremony of the 20th International Conference on Application of Information and Communication Technologies (AICT2026) in Baku on Wednesday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

“The results of the PISA assessment in secondary education have, for the first time, shown a significant decline in performance across most OECD countries. This is directly linked to the spread of social media: people spend time browsing information online instead of devoting sufficient time to learning and developing the ability to solve complex problems independently. Excessive dependence on automated systems also carries the risk of people losing their own capabilities. The danger is that we will increasingly lose our abilities if we rely on automated systems that tell us what to do. I consider this the main risk,” Gelenbe said.

He also drew attention to the possibility of manipulating users’ behavior through artificial intelligence systems. According to him, large software and hardware systems known as AI systems contain vast numbers of parameters whose modification can affect how they behave. When deliberately exploited, these mechanisms may cause systems to influence and manipulate people rather than help them.

“This has already happened over the past seven or eight years, when Facebook used established principles of cognitive science to adaptively modify users’ responses, particularly those of young people, to create addiction,” Gelenbe said.

He emphasized that the main risks stem both from the underdevelopment of human capabilities due to excessive dependence on technology and from the potential for companies and other actors to use digital systems to pursue their own economic, political, and other objectives.

The 20th International Conference on Application of Information and Communication Technologies (AICT2026) is being held at ADA University in Baku.

Azerbaijan is hosting the conference for the seventh time. This year’s event marks the 20th anniversary of the AICT conference series under the slogan “20 Years of Connecting Science, Technology, and Society.”

The event is jointly organized by ADA University, relevant IEEE units in Azerbaijan, Politecnico di Torino, George Washington University, Nazarbayev University, United Arab Emirates University, Tashkent University of Information Technologies, Kazakh-British Technical University, Tbilisi State University, Georgian Technical University, SDU University, the Nikola Tesla Institute of Electrical Engineering, and the Alessandro Faedo Institute of Information Science and Technologies.

The conference aims to facilitate knowledge exchange in information and communication technologies and discuss the sector’s latest developments. It brings together researchers, academics, and industry representatives.

World.title: Zelenskyy says partners not warning Ukraine of incoming ballistic missiles
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he received no early warning from international partners about incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv.

Russian forces struck the Ukrainian capital with ballistic missiles on Tuesday, killing two people in a high-rise apartment, then hitting a critical thermal power plant in the second attack in 24 hours.

"Once again, no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically thermal plant No. 4," Mr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.

Mr Zelenskyy said it was unfair that Kyiv was enduring attacks without warnings from partners.

"According to our intelligence, the Russians are preparing further ballistic missile launches.

"The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound to abide by what the president of the United States said," he added, referring to US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire at the weekend.

"And it is certainly unfair that they are destroying our energy infrastructure while Ukraine is not even receiving warnings about ballistic missile launches."

Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) said it was unfair for Ukraine to operate without warning of strikes from its partners. (Supplied: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service)

Mr Zelenskyy had earlier said Ukraine had again received no warning from Western partners before a previous overnight attack on the capital.

Mr Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence, even as he pressured Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries.

Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries.

Starlink limited in Ukraine

On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials confirmed SpaceX had introduced a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, disrupting combat drone missions that rely on the technology.

The satellite internet terminals from Elon Musk's company are crucial in guiding Ukraine's longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and eastern Ukraine, which have assisted in disrupting Russian logistics.

"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.

Beskrestnov said SpaceX had stopped the operation of its military-grade version above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h).

Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the south-east, said units had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," the Rapid Reaction Corps said in a statement.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular US business hours.

Although it was not immediately clear why Starlink's service was throttled, the move comes as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Starlink does not work inside Russia, and the Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication.

Two killed in struck apartment

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strike on a nine-storey building had killed two people and injured 21. Sixteen people were being treated in hospital, and four were in serious condition.

Emergency crews were battling fires in apartments throughout the building, and residents were being evacuated.

Russia ignoring 'energy ceasefire': Zelenskyy The Ukrainian president says if Moscow wants Kyiv to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, as demanded by Donald Trump, then it should stop hitting key infrastructure.

Ukrainian authorities confirmed on Wednesday morning that the hours-long missile and drone attack that unfolded overnight, primarily targeting Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, had damaged 30 energy facilities.

At least 600,000 people were left without power, according to Mr Zelenskyy.

Unconfirmed energy ceasefire

Mr Trump, who lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week in a bid to lower politically sensitive fuel prices, has said that both sides agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.

Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed this.

Vladimir Putin did not confirm whether the energy ceasefire had been agreed upon. (AP: Dmitri Lovetsky)

"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Mr Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"Russia does not consider the American president's statements strong."

Russia's defence ministry said on Wednesday it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets.

World.title: Cracking firetrucks, $1b funding shortfall identified in Victorian audit
World.content:
Victoria's auditor-general has found more than $1 billion in extra investment is needed to provide critical upgrades to the state's fleet of aging fire trucks.

A report released by the auditor-general on Wednesday examined whether the fleet of more than 3,000 fire trucks were fit to meet the state's firefighting needs.

The audit found almost 60 per cent of Country Fire Authority (CFA) and Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) trucks were more than 15 years old, despite FRV internal documents recommending fire trucks be replaced at that age.

Auditor-General Andrew Greaves found $1.5 billion in investment was needed between 2024-25 and 2033-34 to maintain and replace the trucks that make up the multi-agency firefighting fleet.

He found only $390.4 million — about a quarter of what was needed — had been allocated in grant and budget funds so far, an investment shortfall of more than $1 billion.

"It clearly shows that we have more work to do," Premier Ben Carroll said.

Cracking issue put crews 'at direct risk'

A recent Labor election promise to deliver 150 new fire trucks by 2030 was not considered in the audit, but United Firefighter Union boss Peter Marshall said that offer was only a fraction of what was needed.

He said the report demonstrated what firefighters had been saying for a long time.

"Those persons responsible for the budget cutting, the cost cutting, allowing firefighters to use equipment that was just not suitable and dangerous, they should be made accountable," Mr Marshall said.

The audit also found a widespread cracking issue among trucks managed by the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) had "put firefighters at direct risk".

The cracking problem became so widespread DEECA had to suspend more 54 per cent of its own fleet — nearly 350 trucks — ahead of the 2025-26 summer.

The audit found DEECA, the lead agency for bushfire prevention on public land and state forests, continued to use fire trucks with known cracks and also operated trucks over safe weight limits.

Treasurer knocked back funding requests

Former state treasurer Jaclyn Symes was forced to defend her record after the report pointed out that the FRV and CFA shrunk recent funding requests in response to the treasurer's instructions to limit asks in line with the government’s fiscal strategy.

The audit said FRV initially requested almost $160 million in fleet capital in 2024-25, which it found would have covered just over half of the investment required.

FRV's actual funding proposal was reduced to just $14 million, less than five per cent of what the audit calculated was needed.

Ms Symes said fiscal responsibility was necessary and that there was no "special treatment" for some organisations in need of state funding.

"[All government agencies] are asked to make sure that they bid for what they need, not necessarily everything that they want, because it's difficult decisions that need to be made," she said.

CFA fire trucks and volunteers fight fires in regional Victoria as well some outer-suburban growth areas. (ABC News: Kate Ashton)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the restrictions on Victorian fire services was proof the current government had "not managed the finances."

But Emergency Services Shadow Minister Danny O'Brien acknowledged the investment required was "a very big figure".

Mr O'Brien did not say if a Liberal-National government could commit to reaching the $1.5 billion investment the auditor said was needed, but said the opposition would have further announcements on this topic soon.

"We have been working on this for sometime, to trying to work out how we can afford to modernise our firefighting fleet," he said.

World.title: Michelin Guide dishes out first Australian stars to array of SA restaurants
World.content:
A spread of South Australian restaurants has achieved distinguished culinary honours by becoming the first venues in the nation to receive stars from world-renowned guide Michelin.

At a glitzy, red-carpet ceremony at the Adelaide Convention Centre on Wednesday evening, Michelin dished out one-star ratings to 10 SA eateries.

It also delivered a single, coveted two-star rating to Magill Estate Restaurant, which overlooks Penfolds Magill Estate.

The one-star winners are Anvers Restaurant, Maxwell Restaurant, Botanic, Arkhé, Esmay, Aurora at ILA, Hentley Farm, LVN Restaurant at Bird In Hand, Aptos and Skillogalee Barrel House.

"Tonight marks an historic milestone — the first time the Michelin Guide has recognised restaurants in Australia," Michelin Guide international director Gwendal Poullennec said.

"To every restaurant recognised tonight — congratulations.

"They are all putting South Australia on the world culinary map."

World-renowned Michelin Guide stars have been distributed to SA restaurants. (Reuters: Christian Hartmann)

The winners come from across some of South Australia's premium produce districts, including McLaren Vale, the Adelaide Hills and the Barossa Valley.

Magill Estate Restaurant chef Scott Huggins could barely contain his delight, saying it was a "dream that's come true".

"We looked at opening restaurants in France to achieve a Michelin star — that's how crazy it can be," he said.

"It's come to South Australia, so extremely lucky and honoured to be the first restaurant in Australia to achieve two stars.

" It's like buying a lottery ticket — just not knowing until the number's been read out how it's going to land. "

The Michelin Man at the Adelaide Convention Centre. (ABC News)

Dozens of other venues and individual chefs were recognised in various ways, with Shobosho chef Shakaan Abillion winning the inaugural young chef award.

"We now have 77 different venues being recognised by Michelin," SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said.

Esmay chef Alanna Sapwell said the honour of a star rating would fill her colleagues with pride.

"I just walked out and my whole team's just in tears, and I think I was just a little bit in shock before," she said.

"I would really love to see this spread throughout Australia because it should be inclusive."

Esmay chef Alanna Sapwell hopes the recognition spreads across the industry nationally. (ABC News)

Aptos chef Justin James, who hails from the US, likened the achievement to the Super Bowl and the Oscars, while Jake Kellie from Arkhé said SA was currently the envy of the national culinary scene.

"I was very fortunate [to be] in Sydney last night speaking with a lot of industry folk, and they're all very jealous that we've got this amazing opportunity to put South Australia on the world map," he said.

'This is life-changing'

The awards have been hyped for their potential to lure international tourists to South Australia.

The awards ceremony represents the first time Michelin has rated Australian restaurants in its guide, after entering a commercial agreement with the SA government.

The government said the price it paid was confidential for commercial reasons.

Mr Malinauskas said the recognition bestowed by the awards was "worth its weight in gold" and described the ceremony as a "special night for the hospitality industry" in Australia.

"Every restaurant represented here tonight, every chef, should be brimming with pride."

Australian food advocate Mandy Hall says the awards are "life-changing". (ABC News)

Earlier in the night, Australian food industry advocate Mandy Hall said achieving a Michelin star was "life-changing — there's no question".

"We already have global recognition — but to actually have the Michelin stamp and that star next to your name is amazing," she said.

"These people decide very early on in their life that they want to dedicate their life to this career — and when I say 'dedicate', they really do; they give it everything, they have relationships with all their producers, so this is life-changing."

World.title: India's 'cockroach' movement leaders detained for five days
World.content:
Two leaders of India's "cockroach" youth movement will serve five days in jail after being detained during a protest.

Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among a dozen people detained by police on Tuesday after they climbed over barricades to enter a historic site popular for protests in New Delhi.

Police said this week that the site, Jantar Mantar, was no longer an official protest venue and accused Das and Ranka of trespassing.

The arrests follow a sweeping police crackdown over the weekend aimed at preventing mostly young Indians from gathering to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The Cockroach Janta Party is demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner. (AP: Manish Swarup)

Police briefly detained thousands of demonstrators.

"Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it," opposition leader Rahul Gandhi wrote on X.

Protests intensify

Protests have intensified over an ongoing nationwide revision of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year.

India releases 'cockroach' leaders as movement calls for more protests In a social media post after his release, the founder of the movement said PM Narendra Modi was "an embarrassment to India."

Critics say the exercise is politically motivated and could disenfranchise millions of eligible voters.

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Abhijeet Dipke, the "cockroach" movement's founder, criticised Modi in a post on X.

"If you're so determined to crush dissent, have the courage to officially declare an Emergency instead of hiding behind these cowardly tactics," he wrote.

The "cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites.

Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience.

Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

AP

World.title: The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now
World.content:
This year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century. Keynote speaker Sam Roggeveen, director of the Lowy Institute's International Security Program, gave his lecture Four Forces: Australia in the New Asia this evening. This is an edited extract.

The biggest change to Australia's region since World War II is underway. Three forces are reshaping Asia and Australia's place in it: the decline of one empire, the rise of another, and the emergence of a powerful neighbour on Australia's doorstep.

Amid this regional shift, a fourth potent force is at play: an unmistakeable change in the character of Western liberal democracy, including in Australia.

These four forces present a challenge not just to our place in the world, but to our politics and identity; we are a Western nation perched alongside Asia as it enters a post-Western era.

We can't stop these international forces, but we have a choice to make about how we meet the challenge, a choice about whether we leave our fate in the hands of others or take the harder road towards self-reliance.

The 'material dethroning of the West'

It doesn't take much persuading these days to convince Australians that China is an important part of their future, because it is already so conspicuous in our daily lives. It is a major source of immigrants, students and consumer products, our largest trading partner, and it is credited with keeping Australia out of recession during the global financial crisis.

There is no mistaking the change in character of Western liberal democracy, Sam Roggeveen says. (Supplied)

But what China means to Australia is a fraction of what it means to the world. China is the largest trading partner to around 120 other countries, too. Roughly a third of all the physical objects produced in the world today are made in China. Its economy is now at least four-fifths the size of America's and may even be the largest in the world, depending on how you measure.

For the economic historian Adam Tooze, China's rise represents nothing less than "the material dethroning of the West as the central driver of world history".

Until not so long ago, China's economic rise was only good news. It was lifting hundreds of millions of its own people out of poverty, producing cheap goods for the world, and creating wealthy consumers for our goods and services. But China's rise was always going to create problems, including for our ally, the United States.

When the Cold War ended, the US became Asia's uncontested leader. The hope, at the time, was that China would simply go along with that arrangement. The plan in Washington was that even as China became richer, it would remain subordinate to the US. China would become something like Japan or Germany — economic powerhouses with no big independent foreign policy ambitions.

Clearly, that's not how things are turning out. China is building the world's biggest navy and quadrupling the size of its nuclear arsenal. It punishes American allies, including Australia, by imposing trade restrictions. Its behaviour in the South China Sea, where it has built artificial islands based on dubious legal claims, can be fairly described as territorial expansion. China is clearly not going to become a super-sized version of Germany or Japan.

We should assume China wants to lead in the region, and that means subordinating the US and its allies, and even pushing Washington out of Asia altogether. That's not because China is communist or because it's a dictatorship. It is those things, and that makes China harder to deal with. But this is a simple question of scale. China is big and big countries demand leadership.

Now, nothing up to this point would perturb any mainstream foreign policy commentator. But here's where I swerve off the beaten path. Because the consensus in Australia is that, whatever challenge China presents to us, the Americans will help us face it. In fact, our entire national defence is built upon this premise.

No previous US president could have prevented China's ascent, and no future US president is going to enter a competition with China that could lead to war. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

The US is weaker in Asia

China's rise has made America's position in Asia unsustainably weak. It used to be easy for America to make lavish promises to defend its partners and allies in Asia because no other country was strong enough to challenge it. That's not true anymore. It would now be incredibly costly for the US to meet the commitments it has made.

It is still assumed, on the Korean Peninsula and in Taiwan, and even in Japan and Australia, that the US will be willing to risk the lives of thousands of its troops, and perhaps even nuclear attacks on its own cities, to defend us. But the US simply has no vital reason to accept such risks. The sacrifice would not be worth it.

Now, it's important to stress: saying that America's position in Asia is weak is not the same as saying that America itself is weak. In fact, the United States has a reasonable claim to being the strongest and most secure nation in the history of the world. But that's part of our problem.

America has the world's biggest military, a huge economy, thousands of nuclear weapons, and is separated from China by a vast ocean. It is so secure that it simply doesn't need to be Asia's leader. It's nice to have, but not essential. So, when a challenger as big as China comes along, we should not assume that the US will bear the burden of resisting it.

If this is jarring, it's because it has happened relatively quickly. One of my predecessors as Boyer Lecturer, the distinguished Australian foreign policy thinker Owen Harries, titled his first address And Then There Was One, because in 2003 the US was the only superpower in the world. It's worth adding that Owen did not assume this would be a permanent condition.

You will note I haven't mentioned President Trump so far, who is so often the focus of our alliance concerns. And why not? He has threatened to annex Greenland, make Canada the 51st state, and throw Ukraine under the bus. Still, it's a mistake to focus on Trump because it invites us to believe that he was the cause of the power shift I am describing, and that things will return to something like "normal" after he leaves the world stage. They won't.

No previous US president could have prevented China's ascent, and no future US president is going to risk their nation's safety and prosperity by entering a competition with China that could lead to war.

So no, this is not a Trump phenomenon. It is a permanent shift.

The AUKUS deal came at exactly the moment when American reliability went into permanent decline.

AUKUS hits a jarring note

This is why AUKUS is such a jarring note in our national life. The agreement to supply Australia with eight nuclear-powered submarines, announced by the Morrison government in 2021 and now supported by the Albanese government, represents the biggest change to our alliance in its history. Yet it comes at exactly the moment when American reliability goes into permanent decline.

AUKUS is an illustration of one of the least attractive aspects of our national character: an insatiable desire to win the approval of Americans. Of course, the Americans sense this and they exploited it when we proposed AUKUS, which involves not just our biggest ever military purchase but billions of Australian dollars invested in US shipyards.

Listen to the Boyer Lecture Series on ABC listen Featuring distinguished speakers from across Australia, Singapore and Indonesia, this year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century.

In the 1930s, America built the gambling mecca of Las Vegas, an entire city in the desert dedicated to fleecing gamblers. If AUKUS demonstrates anything, it is that the Americans still have a talent for separating fools from their money.

Australia should be sceptical of both China and America as one rises and the other declines. And from this dual scepticism flows an obvious conclusion: we must do more to look after ourselves.

Once we accept that our relationship with the US will become more transactional, the natural instinct will be to find a partner to replace it. But there is no replacement.

The sheer scale of the Asia Pacific counts against an alliance-like security partnership with Tokyo. Japan is pre-occupied with security threats far closer to home, and lacks the military capacity and ambition to be a significant power in our part of Asia.

What about India? It is in a slightly different category because of its size and still untapped potential — one day, it will likely surpass the US in GDP terms. But India is also too far away from Australia to be a close security partner. It is difficult to imagine that any security threat to Australia would ever be so vital to India that New Delhi would offer us help, and the same is true for Australia in its dealings with India.

There is one nation which, although it will never replace the US, does have vital interests that align with ours. It is close to Australia and has vast economic potential, enough to resist being pulled into China's orbit.

Today, Indonesia is South-East Asia's leader and soon its economy will surpass ours. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

A great power on our doorstep

Indonesia matters to Australia because it is big and it is near.

Two hundred and ninety million people dispersed across an archipelago that covers Australia's northern approaches, and boasting consistent growth that will see it enter the top five economies in the world by the middle of the century.

Australia is about to have a great power on its doorstep.

For Australia's security, Indonesia ranks above every other nation. If we get this relationship wrong, the dangers are immense. Soon, Indonesia will be wealthy and strong, and we will not want it as an enemy.

We've had an antagonistic relationship with Jakarta before and even faced off against Indonesian troops in the so-called Konfrontasi of the early 1960s. But Indonesia was a poor country then, with little military power or influence on the regional stage. Today, Indonesia is South-East Asia's leader and soon its economy will surpass ours. From there, the gap will only widen.

For Australia, then, the stakes in the relationship continue to grow. The more powerful Indonesia becomes, the less we can afford a breach with Jakarta.

But if we get this relationship right, Indonesia offers a natural barrier against threats from third countries. And the good news is Canberra and Jakarta share one crucial interest: neither Australia nor Indonesia wants China to dominate our region. Right there is the kernel of a deeper partnership with Jakarta. It can be something like an alliance dedicated to ensuring that no outside power ever dominates the region we share.

Of course, that ambition remains distant and Jakarta may never be the partner we would like it to be. But with that vital interest in common, many barriers can be overcome, including the fact that Australia and Indonesia do not share what our politicians call "shared values".

If that sounds coldly transactional, then so be it. We Australians cherish our political traditions, but we've never insisted that our regional partners adopt our ways.

Only a 10th of Brits say Brexit has made their life better. (Reuters: Neil Hall)

Lessons from the UK

The United Kingdom is, like us, a liberal democracy and an island lying just off a powerful continent. Ten years ago, the UK comprehensively sabotaged its own economy and its relationship with its neighbours.

I don't need to dwell on the damage Brexit has done over the past decade: according to The Economist magazine, it has taken at least 2.5 per cent, or maybe as much as 8 per cent, off Britain's GDP. Only a tenth of Brits now say Brexit has made their life better.

Why did it happen? We're told it was about xenophobia and anti-European sentiment. Yet despite some truly ugly outbreaks of racial violence, Britain remains a fundamentally liberal and tolerant society. And don't forget, the defining message of the Brexit campaign was not about keeping foreigners out, it was about taking back control.

That slogan — take back control — is a clue to what's really going on, not just in the UK but in every Western democracy touched by the rise of right-wing populism, including ours. I think the lesson of Brexit is not that British voters were xenophobic, but that they distrusted their own elites.

In every Western democracy, the gap between voters and their political leaders has widened to a chasm because the connective tissue between voter and government has withered and decayed. That connective tissue is the political party.

The decline of the big centre-right and centre-left parties that dominated Western democratic politics in the second half of the 20th century is the signature political phenomenon of our time. Those parties represented well-defined constituencies. The centre-left clustered around unions and the working class. The centre-right around business, small and large, and the middle class. But every force that once tied big political parties to a defined constituency — unionism, manufacturing, religion, class and even race — has withered.

The effect on the big parties has been catastrophic. It was the weakening of the Conservative Party at the hands of its own Eurosceptics and Nigel Farrage's UKIP that triggered the Brexit referendum. Major parties have declined all over Europe too, creating openings for new political forces.

In Australia, the collective membership of the Labor and Liberal parties couldn't fill the MCG. At the 2007 federal election, 43 per cent of us put Labor first. By 2025, even though Labor won the election convincingly, that figure was 33 per cent. The trends are roughly the same for the Coalition. Our primary votes are now split an even three ways, with independents and small parties also getting roughly one third.

The result is that modern Australian governments achieve power whilst never really feeling that they are in charge.

If a government doesn't feel it has a mandate, it sets about trying to manufacture one. Perhaps you've noticed that the term "social licence" has crept into our political vocabulary — that's an implicit acknowledgement of the democratic deficit I'm describing.

Our governments launch endless enquiries and establish expert bodies to make decisions that were once considered to be within their own remit. These are all signs of governments desperately searching for new indicators of public approval and devising mechanisms to work around its absence. No truly confident government would feel the need.

The Howard government was the last under the old two-party settlement. Not coincidentally, that was also when Australia had its last major economic reform. If we have indeed become a timid nation, as Paul Keating argues, then I think this is why.

The missing piece is a sense of authority arising from democratic legitimacy. That's what instils courage and policy boldness in governments.

Our future without a powerful regional ally

For the first time in our history, we face a future without a powerful ally committed to regional supremacy.

We face a future in which Asia will be led by an Asian superpower, one that has interests and ambitions that clash with ours. And we face a future in which our close neighbour, Indonesia, will have greater national power than us. All of this in a political environment undergoing its biggest realignment since the creation of the Liberal Party in 1944.

The changes to our region demand not just a new defence strategy or a new foreign policy, but an ambitious national reform agenda dedicated to creating a truly self-reliant Australia.

Yet our domestic political malaise is frustrating our ability to meet the regional challenges. The major parties are exhausted and fragile; they lack the energy and authority to embark on such a journey. The last big wave of Australian reform, in the 1980s and 90s, was built on consensus between our major parties. If there is to be another wave of reform it will need to be built on the ashes of the two-party system.

Right now, the boldness Australia needs has no political home. The far right offers nostalgia for a wholly imagined monoculture. The left is pre-occupied with conservation and flirts with de-growth. The major parties offer technocratic tinkering. There is not a single political force in Australia today focused squarely on building Australia's wealth and strength.

The most telling evidence is that Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are now all, to one degree or another, retreating from immigration.

Loading

Immigration retreat also one from Asia

Given the temper of our immigration debate, perhaps the least popular argument one can make right now is for Australia to get bigger. But immigration is our national superpower, and we do multiculturalism better than any country on earth.

Although many factors go into producing a strong nation, sheer size is vital. When Singapore got rich in the 1970s, the world applauded. When China got rich in the 2000s, the world shook. The difference is scale.

Australia should recommit to immigration not because "diversity is strength", to use the prime minister's anodyne phrase, but because scale is strength. Retreating from immigration will make us materially weaker. It will also raise the drawbridge to talented and industrious Asians who want to make Australia home. It will cut us off from our region. A retreat from immigration is a retreat from Asia.

Yet our politicians now propose to take us to the precipice. If the political mood against immigration holds until the next election, voters will be invited to consign Australia to a shrunken, inward looking, future — our own version of the Brexit referendum.

But Australia can't afford to turn its back on Asia the way the UK turned its back on Europe. Creating the conditions for an Australia that stands strong and independent in Asia begins with a simple act of recognition: we must look after ourselves.

If that sounds confronting, then I would close by reminding you that Asia is a source of immense opportunity, as well as risk. Although we in the West are passing through a moment of profound cultural pessimism, in Asia the future is still a source of optimism. And no wonder — the people living in its gleaming new cities are, in some cases, only one generation removed from rural poverty.

Young Australians are travelling freely around the region and imbibing its culture. They see Tokyo's urbanism, China's cityscapes, Singapore's garden-city infrastructure. These cities evoke a sense of promise.

Australia should want to capture the spirit of progress that animates those places, to be a country where the future feels exciting and abundant, maybe even a little glamorous.

Let that sense of optimism guide Australia as we navigate the difficult choices ahead.

Sam Roggeveen's keynote lecture will be on ABC TV and iview at 3:25pm October 17 and iview. This lecture and others from Louisa Lim, Mari Pangestu and Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong will air on consecutive Sundays from October 18 on ABC Radio National's Sunday Extra program, at 8:05am.

World.title: Woman charged over crash that claimed life of 11yo girl
World.content:
A woman has been arrested over a two-car crash in which an 11-year-old girl was killed in Adelaide's south last month.

South Australia Police said the woman was driving a Nissan sedan in which the girl was a passenger when it was involved in a collision with a Subaru station wagon at Moana on September 22.

Emergency services were called to the scene on Commercial Road about 6:45pm.

The 35-year-old Christie Downs woman was taken to hospital in a serious condition, but the girl died at the scene.

The 37-year-old Seaford Meadows man who was driving the Subaru was also taken to hospital with minor injuries and was later discharged, police said.

Police said the driver of the Nissan was arrested today and was charged with aggravated causing death by dangerous driving and aggravated causing harm by dangerous driving.

The woman, who has lost her licence, was bailed to appear in the Christies Beach Magistrates Court in November.

Police said major crash investigators were continuing to examine the circumstances of the crash.

World.title: Shots fired in Tullamarine linked to road rage incident, police say
World.content:
Police are investigating reports of gunshots being fired in Melbourne's north-west in a confrontation investigators believe may be linked to an earlier road rage incident.

Emergency services were called to reports of a collision between two vehicles and gunshots in Tullamarine just after 3pm today.

No injuries have been reported.

Investigators believe the incident occurred after an earlier road rage incident involving the occupants of an Isuzu utility and a Hyundai SUV.

Police said the victims in the Isuzu made their way to Broadmeadows Police Station, while the alleged offenders ditched the Hyundai and fled in a getaway vehicle.

Police have established two crime scenes, one on May Street and one on Dawson Street.

Aerial footage shows the white Hyundai appears to have been crashed and abandoned, with detectives on the scene collecting evidence.

World.title: Alice Springs resident whose home was destroyed welcomes funding support
World.content:
Brooke Klarenbeek looked shell-shocked as she described the terrifying moment the roof tore off her family home during a wild storm that lashed Alice Springs on Monday afternoon.

"It just went bang," she said, wide-eyed.

" Like an explosion had just gone off. "

As she sat in her lounge room of 11 years, she was surrounded by furniture strewn with roofing debris, bathed in light from the space where her roof used to be, sodden insulation swaying from the beams above.

"[The roof] just got ripped off, parts of it are in our next door neighbour's yard ... then pretty much the whole, entire ceiling caved in on everything, in about 75 per cent of the house," she said.

Brooke Klarenbeek said it was like an explosion when the storm tore her roof off. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

She sheltered in a doorway, unsure what to do.

"It was hailing outside, didn't know whether [I] could go outside, didn't know what was happening out there," she said.

Long road ahead

Ms Klarenbeek is one of hundreds of residents whose homes or property were damaged during the surprise storm that brought 96 kilometre per hour winds and hail.

The event lasted about half an hour, tearing down trees and powerlines, leaving destruction in its wake.

Power was cut to 9,000 homes in the town of about 12,000 electricity customers, with 2,000 without power as of Wednesday morning.

Parts of Ms Klarenbeek's roof is in her neighbour's backyard. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"I'm not sure what the long-term plan looks like for where we're going to stay or how long all this is going to take ... the hard bit is just not knowing," she said.

Disaster relief welcomed

According to the Insurance Council of Australia, Ms Klarenbeek's insurance claim is one of 400 lodged in Alice Springs since the weather event.

"If you have had some debris impact your house or branches and that sort of thing, we really encourage home owners to get their claim lodged straight away," Insurance Council's Liam Walter says.

Many houses, cars and fences were damaged after Monday afternoon's severe storm swept through Alice Springs. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Ms Klarenbeek said she welcomed disaster recovery assistance funds being made available by the federal and NT governments.

"Every time we have a storm, everyone usually gets together and helps... but not everyone has that support," she said.

"That initial support straight away that you need, when you don't know what else to do, not the insurance five or 10 weeks later.

"Not everyone has the money to fix something straight away, but need it done."

Brooke Klarenbeek says 75 per cent of her house was destroyed in the storm. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

The assistance will support eligible households with a one-off payment of up to $16,901 for essential structural repairs where insurance will not meet repair costs.

The announcement also covers freight subsidies for primary producers, as well as asset assistance grants for non-profit organisations.

Local councils will also be supported in recovery.

"It's a bit of a relief," Ms Klarenbeek said.

"Not just for me but for other people as well ... $16,000 would go a massive way."

A nervous wait

After a nervous wait for her insurance company to assess her property, Ms Klarenbeek has now moved her belongings to a safe place in case of more wet weather.

She said she was still in shock as she looked around her home.

Ms Klarenbeek's house has been left uninhabitable after the storm in Alice Springs. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"You'll look up and you'll see sky, it's just insane to think that this is my home," she said.

"It's supposed to be feeling safe here."

World.title: Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat Lachlan Abbott Updated October 14, 2026 — 9:57pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Four burly men surround a construction executive at a table outside a Melbourne cafe to deliver a $6 million message, allegedly part of an extortion plot. A video, played in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, shows one of the group point out the security camera that captures the December 2024 meeting at Flemington’s Mama Bear Cafe where Amir Teymoori is accused of threatening to kill a major Victorian developer’s manager. “I’m going to f--- you up and your family,” Teymoori allegedly tells the man. Audio from the vision is muffled by the wind, but a man can be heard swearing and saying: “Are you gonna pay me or not?”



Teymoori can be seen covering his mouth as he talks before shouting at the construction firm director. Amir Teymoori outside court in January. Jason South Daniel Van Camp also speaks, taking off his sunglasses to tell the alleged victim: “This is not going away.” The 52-year-old is the son of John Van Camp, a prominent former union boss turned industrial relations manager at Grocon – one of Australia’s biggest private building companies before it collapsed in 2020. Gazanfer Bekirovski sits at the end of the table and only briefly speaks to the construction firm manager, at one point tapping him on the arm.



Travers Grubb does not appear to speak at all, tapping his foot for much of the meeting. But the construction manager, whose identity is suppressed for his safety, told the court the message from Teymoori was clear. Daniel Van Camp, Gazanfer Bekirovski, Amir Teymoori, and Travers Grubb were all initially charged with extortion. Jason South/Justin McManus The four men appeared at a two-day preliminary hearing charged with extortion with a threat to kill. But in a blow to police trying to clean up the construction industry, the case against Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb was dismissed as magistrate Stephen Ballek found insufficient evidence they were complicit with Teymoori’s alleged threat.



Prosecutors allege Teymoori made an unwarranted demand for $6.6 million, claiming to have bought the alleged victim’s company industrial peace with the CFMEU. The firm denies ever hiring Teymoori, and police say his claim to be a union mediator is false. Stills from CCTV played at Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday show Jonny “Two Guns” Walker (rear near lifts). Melbourne Magistrates’ Court Another video clip shown on Wednesday, and also released to this masthead by the court, reveals notorious ex-bikie Jonny “Two Guns” Walker attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024 with Van Camp, Grubb and Teymoori as the latter sought millions from a developer. Walker was not charged over the alleged extortion or mentioned in court.



He told The Age late on Wednesday that he was arrested and questioned as part of the investigation, but gave a no-comment interview, and police later told him he had no case to answer. “Hawk Taskforce made a song and dance over f---king bullshit,” Walker said. “I’ve really got no comment about the case at all. I know nothing about it.” An earlier version of this story said CCTV played in court showed Gazanfer Bekirovski attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024. In fact, it was Travers Grubb who attended the premises. The Age contacted him to ask why he appeared in CCTV, but he did not respond. Teymoori’s barrister, Damian Sheales, suggested the alleged extortion victim lied at one point in a fiery cross-examination on Tuesday.



The construction manager, however, maintained Teymoori told him at the Racecourse Road cafe two years ago: “I would f--- you up.” “It was said in the context of ‘if you don’t have your money, I’m going to f--- you up and your family’,” the witness said. “There was no ambiguity.” The court heard Teymoori brought up mothers and religion during the meeting now at the centre of the case against him. “The contact was unwelcome,” the alleged extortion victim said. “It’s not normal course to have four people approach you in the street in that manner.” Teymoori faces an additional charge of trying to obtain property by deception at the Cremorne office building on October 28, 2024.



Police allege he sent an invoice to the construction company demanding payment he wasn’t owed. He turned up to the firm’s headquarters and asked to see managers about his claim, the court heard. Teymoori pleaded not guilty after being committed to stand trial and will reappear at the County Court in November. Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb patted him on the back as they left court cleared of all charges. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLCarlton Blues Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating Sam McClure October 14, 2026 — 9:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AFL integrity unit is now investigating the circumstances surrounding the hospitalisation of players Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward following a night out at the weekend, which the club says the pair is “embarrassed” about. The league’s involvement represents a significant escalation in the controversy engulfing Carlton, with the AFL now examining the events that led to both players requiring medical treatment in the early hours of Sunday morning. Blues footy boss Chris Davies. AFL Photos Davies confirmed the development on Wednesday evening as the AFL trade period drew to a close, with the Blues facing questions about the conduct of their players and the circumstances surrounding the incidents. “It’s an AFL discussion at the moment and we’ll leave it there,” Davies said.



“The AFL are going through a process right now and ultimately, we’ll work with the AFL to get to the end of that. “We’ve been having discussions with the AFL over the last two or three days, clearly, to make sure that we are at the bottom of that.” Davies was then asked about the health of the two players. “That’s the most important thing – they’re OK now, a little bit embarrassed, I guess, to put the club in this position,” Davies said. He also confirmed another player had been present on Saturday night, “but not in the same situation”.



Lachie Cowan was taken to hospital via ambulance but has since been discharged. AFL Photos The investigation comes amid allegations of illicit drug use at a gathering at Hayward’s South Yarra home on Saturday night, although Carlton have not confirmed whether drugs were involved in either player’s hospitalisation. Reports had widely circulated on Sunday, suggesting that illicit drugs were allegedly involved as the players received medical care. This masthead cannot confirm that illicit drugs were involved in either incident. The AFL’s intervention means the matter is no longer exclusively an internal Carlton issue, with the league’s integrity department now involved in establishing what occurred and whether any breaches of competition rules or policies warrant further action. Both players have since been discharged from hospital.



Cowan, 21, was taken to The Alfred hospital after emergency services attended an address in South Yarra early on Sunday morning. Ambulance Victoria confirmed advanced life-support paramedics responded to an incident about 5.15am, with a man in his 20s transported to hospital in a stable condition. Carlton subsequently confirmed Cowan had received medical treatment and undergone observation before being discharged. Hayward, 27, separately admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. The former Sydney forward received stitches before being discharged. The Blues have maintained that the two players were hospitalised under separate circumstances.



In a statement issued on Sunday, Carlton said its immediate priority was the welfare of both players. “The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances,” the statement said. The investigation presents an early test of the football department leadership of Davies and chief executive Graham Wright, who are charged with establishing higher standards at a club attempting to rebuild its football program. Carlton has already begun its own inquiries into the weekend’s events, with the findings expected to be made available to the AFL. The involvement of the league’s integrity unit also raises questions about how any potential breaches would be dealt with under the AFL’s existing illicit drugs framework.



The AFL and AFL Players’ Association have agreed to a revised illicit drugs policy, including expanded hair testing and a greater emphasis on identifying and addressing repeated drug use. However, the new framework is not scheduled to come into effect until 2027, meaning the Carlton matter will be assessed under the competition’s existing rules and disciplinary processes. Will Hayward was named Carlton’s best clubman this season, as well as winning the coaches’ and Spirit of Carlton awards. Getty Images The investigation does not necessarily mean either player will face disciplinary action, with the league yet to establish publicly whether any wrongdoing has occurred. Nevertheless, the episode has again exposed the challenges confronting the AFL in managing player behaviour away from football clubs, particularly during the off-season.



Carlton have endured previous off-field controversies, including the illicit drugs case involving Elijah Hollands, adding to the pressure on the club to demonstrate that player welfare and behavioural standards are being taken seriously. The timing is particularly uncomfortable for the Blues, who have spent the trade period reshaping their playing list and attempting to build momentum ahead of the 2027 season. Hayward arrived at Carlton from Sydney last year and played 21 games in his first season in navy blue, while Cowan has established himself as an important young defender. Cowan played 24 games in 2026 and has become a regular member of Carlton’s backline. The latest controversy threatens to overshadow the club’s list-management work, with Davies now confronting questions extending well beyond recruiting and the composition of Carlton’s playing list.



The central issue for the Blues is no longer simply the medical treatment required by two players on Sunday morning, but what led to those hospital visits and whether the circumstances reveal a broader failure of judgement or conduct. Those are questions the AFL’s integrity unit will now seek to answer. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.content:

This is rather curious: “When I opened my plastic-wrapped Herald on Monday Oct 12, and spread it on the kitchen bench, I noticed that the photo of Ben Roberts-Smith had been carefully removed from the front page,” reports Sue Lyall of Vaucluse. “The tear was just around his image and carefully done so that no other part of the page was cut or missing. I wonder how many other papers were tampered with by an unknown censor.”

Jack Dikian of Mosman takes the joystick: “HSC students: do your best, keep your nerve, and here’s hoping your recent Atari scores don’t influence your ATAR.”

“Driving past some local cattle herds over the weekend, I noticed that the bogongs (C8) seemed attracted almost magnetically to those dark-coloured beasts sitting around on the grass,” writes Mickey Pragnell of Kiama. “The lighter-coloured cattle were more mobile, moving around the pastures, and seemed to have none of the bogongs bothering them. I couldn’t think why, until I remembered that, of course, a strolling roan gathers no moths.”

“I had those same crêpes (C8) 20 years ago, but in Paris near the Notre-Dame Cathedral,” recalls Agostino Chiarella of Summer Hill. “A restaurant had set up a stall at night outside its premises on the footpath, and was selling crepes Suzette flambéed with Grand Marnier and served on paper plates. Delicious and cheap. Nearby, a person was roasting chestnuts on a metal garbage can lid atop a shopping trolley. The finer things in life.”

“Never mind being ‘shevelled’ or ‘gruntled’ (C8),” advises Nick Bencsik of Hunters Hill. “Is it possible to be just ‘whelmed’ if you’re neither over, nor underwhelmed?”

World.title: How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period Jake Niall October 14, 2026 — 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It might not play out on the ground in 2027, but Hawthorn and the Western Bulldogs were the finalists that gained the most ground during a trade period that was marked by an outbreak of honesty and rational negotiations. Zach Merrett, whose stranding at Tullamarine was the story of last year’s exchanges, was granted his wish to play under Sam Mitchell. Whereas Merrett’s failed escape in 2025 was a game of chicken between the Hawks and Bombers in which no one won, this time the deal was reached more than a week before the deadline and both clubs emerged as if they had signed a peace accord at Camp David, smiling and with bursting with goodwill. Zach Merrett in his new colours. The Hawks and Bombers struck a fair deal, one in which both sides might wonder if they could’ve done slightly better. Essendon gained the draft capital and some face – yes, a little less than they would’ve scored had the foes come to terms 12 months earlier. But if the Hawks go on to the win the flag in the next few years, they should be thanking the Suns on the podium, since it was their entirely pragmatic and logical decision to let Ben King leave as a free agent, without matching the seven-year $9 million deal, that allowed Hawthorn to consummate a trade with Essendon over Merrett that did not cost them vital organs.



Had the Suns matched and forced a trade, the Hawks did not have enough draft capital to land both King and Merrett. Or, they would have been forced to lose a player such as Noah Mraz, whom rival clubs had been eyeing. Their landing of King did cost the Hawks Aidan Schubert in what I would call a related party transaction (aka a side deal), as it happened. But to acquire two A-graders – one midfielder who can hit targets, and a key forward who can be counted on for 50 to 60 goals provided he stays upright – makes them the logical topweight in the 2027 premiership race. Zak Butters is now a key part of the Bulldogs’ star-studded midfield. Getty Images While the Bulldogs are coming from further back, the recruitment of Zak Butters, one of the game’s top five players, must vault them into genuine premiership contention, and that Butters purchase was buttressed, if you like, by the securing of Jordan Butts, who fills the club’s most gaping hole as a key defender. Allowing the usual alibis for injury, Hawthorn’s pass mark for next season will be reaching the grand final. The Bulldogs must make the top four and if they cannot do so (again, injury willing) with Butters sharing the centre square with Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards (plus Sam Darcy back in attack), then Luke Beveridge’s time will be just about up.



The Dogs, like Hawthorn, were blessed to take a high-worth free agent from a club (Port Adelaide) who finished low enough to take the compensation pick (No.5) rather than force a trade. Ben King has joined Merrett at the Hawks. AFL Photos But there was a trade, of course. It just wasn’t officially involving Butters, even though the whole deal was predicated on Port losing Butters and gaining a raft of picks. A coincidental deal. Port received a pile of early picks and handed back a heap of draft choices that were less valuable on the face of it. It was ticked off by the AFL, perhaps because so many clubs and picks (and two barely players) were involved (“flood the zone with picks” to borrow from Steve Bannon) that no one could be bothered ascertaining how uneven or “commercial” and standalone it really was. Side deals aside, there were a few notable themes:



1. The rise of the older player Geelong’s policy of getting high-quality players aged around the 30 mark, as either free agents (Toby Greene) or needs-based trades (Jordan Ridley, who is 27, and Rowan Marshall) continued, and their policy has been adopted by Collingwood (Lachie Neale, Jesse Hogan) and even Carlton (Lachie Whitfield). The Cats would fancy themselves capable bridging the gap between the top few and themselves. Collingwood possibly would think so, albeit they have fewer kids. The Magpies were fortunate to come up short, so to speak, in their offer to Richmond for Jayden Short and kept their draft picks. They had no need for another half-back flanker who is 30. Scott Pendlebury’s passage to Gold Coast was the extreme example of how the AFL gun players’ career spans are imitating other professional sports, such as tennis and the NFL, and extending beyond 35, albeit “Pendles” has really been hired as on-field assistant coach. 2. The mega-buck deals



If old players are easier to acquire, their appeal is heightened by the incredible contracts that mid-career stars can command in a market in which few top-liners are available. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 Bombers, Demons make key last-minute moves before the trade buzzer It is staggering to consider that King’s $9 million contract with Hawthorn is slightly more than half of what the Bulldogs have committed to Butters ($17 million to $17.5 million), which is now the game’s largest contract over nine years. Nick Blakey, meanwhile, on nearly $12 million over eight years, has become the richest defender in the competition thanks to the combination of the Pullman scandal and North Melbourne’s desperate need (matched by two other clubs) to land their first A-grader from another club since Wayne Carey was strutting around. 3. The end of warehousing players



Brisbane eventually parted with Keidean Coleman before deadline, no longer able to hold a talented running defender whose spot was locked up by super veteran Dayne Zorko. The Lions had little choice but to trade midfielder Sam Marshall to the Saints on similar grounds. In both cases, the Lions received more than adequate draft compensation. Hawthorn was compelled to let Schubert leave, in the knowledge that he might develop into a capable key forward, once they had King secured and – in defiance of expectation – persuaded Calsher Dear to re-sign for another two years. Those two clubs owned the deepest lists, perhaps, in 2026. It is not possible, if it ever was, to hold players, and build depth when individuals are trying to build careers. When Thomas Murfett sensed something was wrong with his plane on Saturday morning, he did what any experienced pilot would. The 63-year-old circled around the Muchea airfield where he had just taken off and looked for a suitable place to land. Tom Murfatt had a lucky escape on saturday when his plane crashed in Muchea. But as the RV-6A light aircraft that he built himself 30 years ago began to stall, he realised he had no hope of making it back to the airstrip. “He was just doing a few practice circuits before he and his friend were going to fly to Bunbury,” Murfett’s wife Melanie said.



“On the second round they felt that something wasn’t right with the aircraft so they came back around to look for somewhere to land. When he knew he wasn’t going to make the runway, he started worrying about people on the ground as he was right next to the Brand Highway.” Murfett - who crash-landed in a paddock - told his wife that he didn’t have much time to think “or do - your body just takes over and you just do what you can”. Murfett suffered multiple broken bones during the crash. The pilot, who has decades of experience, told her he could feel that something “felt not quite right” but that what happened after was a blur. The next thing he knew was that he had crash-landed and he couldn’t get out of the wreckage.



Murfett suffered a broken arm in the crash that needs surgery, a broken leg “that will take a couple of surgeries”, five broken ribs, a lung puncture and a fractured back. His friend, who was a passenger in the plane with him on Friday, also suffered broken ribs but has already been discharged from hospital. The wreckage left ofTom Murfett’s plane. 9News Perth Murfett, however, is bed-bound and “in pretty good spirits”. “He’s just laying back and [saying] ‘I don’t have to do anything, everyone is waiting on me now’,” Melanie laughed, before adding that he will “probably” go up in a plane again as soon as he’s able.



Police were called to Muchea just before 10.30am on Saturday morning with reports that a single-engine light aircraft had crashed near a private airfield off Brand Highway near Nolan Road. Melanie thanked everyone that rushed to help Murfett get medical assistance he needed, including emergency services. With 9 News Perth.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie would be handed powers to terminate protected industrial action under the Queensland government’s long-awaited overhaul of workplace laws. The government is also set to hold a parliamentary inquiry into Labor’s 2022 efforts to scuttle the role of LNP-linked “red unions” in the state, and review its union encouragement policy. Unions have said they will take time to consider the proposed changes, but warned the workers’ compensation scheme amendments would make it harder for frontline staff to get support. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie says the IR reforms will begin to shift the balance back in Queenslanders’ favour. Cameron Atfield Bleijie’s update came as he announced the Crisafulli LNP’s response to a review of industrial relations law and the workers’ compensation scheme, both tabled in parliament on Wednesday.



The review, conducted by former Bleijie-appointed WorkCover chair Glenn Ferguson and Industrial Relations Commissioner Gary Black, made 104 recommendations, Bleijie told parliament. Seventy-five recommendations have been accepted in full, while 14 were accepted in principle, six were noted, and nine were rejected, he said. A bill will be introduced on Wednesday night to action the LNP response. “These reforms, accepted by the government for implementation, will begin to shift the balance back in Queenslanders’ favour, bringing us into line with other jurisdictions – including the national government with the Fair Work Act – while protecting important rights and entitlements for Queensland workers,” Bleijie said. In his speech to parliament on Wednesday afternoon, he said the changes would save small business $1.46 billion annually by preventing workers’ compensation scheme premiums from increasing.



He said more details on the bill would be forthcoming with its full introduction, but he expected pushback and misleading claims from the Labor opposition and union movement, which has previously accused Bleijie of a “blind agenda of ideology”. Related Article Exclusive

Queensland government Unions lash out after Bleijie’s Friday night workplace board purge “Queenslanders are used to these Labor scare campaigns, which have been proven time and time again to be false,” Bleijie said. “I want to be clear about what we’re not doing: we are not accepting all recommendations made by the independent review. In doing so, the government is protecting a number of key entitlements for workers.” Elements that would feature in the bill, he said, included: A fit and proper person test for union officials seeking right of entry powers on worksites.

More “freedom” around who can represent workers in industrial disputes and wage negotiations.

Increased maximum penalties for WorkCover fraud.

A regulator-appointed representative who reasonably believes fraud has occurred would be given powers to suspend lump-sum compensation while it is investigated.

Requiring employment to be the major significant contributing factor in a psychological injury claim.



The government response document provided further detail about the accepted recommendations. These included a review of the state’s union encouragement policy, which lays out a proactive approach to allowing workers to organise, and a parliamentary committee probe of the amendments of the former Labor government, and how industrial law treats incorporated entities such as those under the Red Union banner. “We look forward to submissions during the parliamentary committee process with respect to freedom of association, because the Liberal Party is the party of freedom,” Bleijie said. The government has also accepted a recommendation to hand Bleijie, as industrial relations minister, similar powers to those of his federal counterpart to terminate protected industrial action. Such a move would only be open to Bleijie if he was satisfied the action was threatening or would threaten to endanger the life, safety, health or welfare of part of the population, cause damage to the state economy, or “would otherwise be contrary to the public interest”.



Related Article Perspective

Queensland government Can Queensland workers count on the LNP’s respect? This year they’ll find out Announcing the work earlier this year, including the required five-yearly review into the workers’ compensation scheme, the Crisafulli government cited an increase in psychological injury claims. The party had taken only a limited number of industrial relations policies to the election. Unions had claimed the review would be used to wind back protections for workers. In a statement on Wednesday afternoon, Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said requiring work to be the major contributing factor for a psychological injury claim “risks shutting workers out of compensation and access to the support they need”. King said the broader sweep of recommendations “needed to be considered in totality by the QCU, unions and other stakeholders”.



Civil Contractors Federation Queensland chief executive Damian Long said the reforms would provide a boost to the infrastructure sector in the lead-up to the 2032 Olympics. “Aligning Queensland’s industrial relations laws with national standards and strengthening expectations around lawful conduct will provide greater confidence and certainty for businesses delivering the infrastructure projects our state relies on,” Long said.
