Warning: This story contains graphic content. A woman admitted fatally stabbing her ex-girlfriend to her new prison lover while police listened on a hidden microphone, a court has been told. Tara Morrison was killed in Busselton in 2024. Facebook Hannah Louise Glover, 30, and James Anthony Sorgiovanni, 29, have pleaded not guilty to the murder of Tara Marie Morrison, 38, at a Busselton home in April 2024. The pair, who were a couple, are accused of repeatedly stabbing Morrison in her head, neck, body and hands.



A woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told the court that Glover confided details about the “brutal attack” while the pair were in the same prison cell in the months after the alleged murder. “Hannah disclosed to me about why she did it … she saw Tara give her daughter liquid fantasy (GHB),” she told the WA Supreme Court on Wednesday. “Then Hannah told me that Jimmy held Tara’s hand behind her back and that’s when Hannah grabbed her by the hair and stabbed her in the neck.” The woman used her right hand and made a stabbing motion three times to replicate for the jury what Glover did when they were speaking in a cell. “She dragged Tara throughout the house,” she said.



“There was an entrance door, and she said there was, like, blood splatter on it. “The blood that came from Tara’s body.” Police found Morrison’s body at Glover’s home in her daughter’s wardrobe. She had about 40 wounds, along with grazes and bruising that could indicate she was restrained. Blood was found splattered on the walls, doors and the floor.



Glover allegedly told the woman she used four knives during the attack. The court has previously been told Glover, Sorgiovanni and Morrison had been using illicit drugs before the killing. Glover and Sorgiovanni had been in a relationship for a few months, and before that, Glover was in a relationship with Morrison. “He’s a f---ing evil c---,” Glover said of Sorgiovanni in one of the covert police recordings played in court. “He only targets single mum … because he’s psychotic.”



Glover alleged Sorgiovanni had power over her, suggesting he made her kill Morrison. “I had no control,” she said. “Then I got back with Tara and that made him crazy.” Glover dabbed tears from her eyes in the dock as the recordings were played in court. “(Morrison) was obsessed with me and it was causing stuff between me and (Sorgiovanni),” she can be heard saying in another one. “She wanted to be with me.”



Glover also said Morrison was “so f---ed up” and was using her to get access to her daughter. She could be heard making stabbing noises on the police recording when talking about the alleged murder. “All I wanted to do was love my baby and protect her … and now look at me, I’m not in prison,” Glover said on the recording. The trial continues. AAP

World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat Lachlan Abbott Updated October 14, 2026 — 9:57pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Four burly men surround a construction executive at a table outside a Melbourne cafe to deliver a $6 million message, allegedly part of an extortion plot. A video, played in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, shows one of the group point out the security camera that captures the December 2024 meeting at Flemington’s Mama Bear Cafe where Amir Teymoori is accused of threatening to kill a major Victorian developer’s manager. “I’m going to f--- you up and your family,” Teymoori allegedly tells the man. Audio from the vision is muffled by the wind, but a man can be heard swearing and saying: “Are you gonna pay me or not?”



Teymoori can be seen covering his mouth as he talks before shouting at the construction firm director. Amir Teymoori outside court in January. Jason South Daniel Van Camp also speaks, taking off his sunglasses to tell the alleged victim: “This is not going away.” The 52-year-old is the son of John Van Camp, a prominent former union boss turned industrial relations manager at Grocon – one of Australia’s biggest private building companies before it collapsed in 2020. Gazanfer Bekirovski sits at the end of the table and only briefly speaks to the construction firm manager, at one point tapping him on the arm.



Travers Grubb does not appear to speak at all, tapping his foot for much of the meeting. But the construction manager, whose identity is suppressed for his safety, told the court the message from Teymoori was clear. Daniel Van Camp, Gazanfer Bekirovski, Amir Teymoori, and Travers Grubb were all initially charged with extortion. Jason South/Justin McManus The four men appeared at a two-day preliminary hearing charged with extortion with a threat to kill. But in a blow to police trying to clean up the construction industry, the case against Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb was dismissed as magistrate Stephen Ballek found insufficient evidence they were complicit with Teymoori’s alleged threat.



Prosecutors allege Teymoori made an unwarranted demand for $6.6 million, claiming to have bought the alleged victim’s company industrial peace with the CFMEU. The firm denies ever hiring Teymoori, and police say his claim to be a union mediator is false. Stills from CCTV played at Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday show Jonny “Two Guns” Walker (rear near lifts). Melbourne Magistrates’ Court Another video clip shown on Wednesday, and also released to this masthead by the court, reveals notorious ex-bikie Jonny “Two Guns” Walker attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024 with Van Camp, Grubb and Teymoori as the latter sought millions from a developer. Walker was not charged over the alleged extortion or mentioned in court.



He told The Age late on Wednesday that he was arrested and questioned as part of the investigation, but gave a no-comment interview, and police later told him he had no case to answer. “Hawk Taskforce made a song and dance over f---king bullshit,” Walker said. “I’ve really got no comment about the case at all. I know nothing about it.” An earlier version of this story said CCTV played in court showed Gazanfer Bekirovski attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024. In fact, it was Travers Grubb who attended the premises. The Age contacted him to ask why he appeared in CCTV, but he did not respond. Teymoori’s barrister, Damian Sheales, suggested the alleged extortion victim lied at one point in a fiery cross-examination on Tuesday.



The construction manager, however, maintained Teymoori told him at the Racecourse Road cafe two years ago: “I would f--- you up.” “It was said in the context of ‘if you don’t have your money, I’m going to f--- you up and your family’,” the witness said. “There was no ambiguity.” The court heard Teymoori brought up mothers and religion during the meeting now at the centre of the case against him. “The contact was unwelcome,” the alleged extortion victim said. “It’s not normal course to have four people approach you in the street in that manner.” Teymoori faces an additional charge of trying to obtain property by deception at the Cremorne office building on October 28, 2024.



Police allege he sent an invoice to the construction company demanding payment he wasn’t owed. He turned up to the firm’s headquarters and asked to see managers about his claim, the court heard. Teymoori pleaded not guilty after being committed to stand trial and will reappear at the County Court in November. Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb patted him on the back as they left court cleared of all charges. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLCarlton Blues Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating Sam McClure October 14, 2026 — 9:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AFL integrity unit is now investigating the circumstances surrounding the hospitalisation of players Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward following a night out at the weekend, which the club says the pair is “embarrassed” about. The league’s involvement represents a significant escalation in the controversy engulfing Carlton, with the AFL now examining the events that led to both players requiring medical treatment in the early hours of Sunday morning. Blues footy boss Chris Davies. AFL Photos Davies confirmed the development on Wednesday evening as the AFL trade period drew to a close, with the Blues facing questions about the conduct of their players and the circumstances surrounding the incidents. “It’s an AFL discussion at the moment and we’ll leave it there,” Davies said.



“The AFL are going through a process right now and ultimately, we’ll work with the AFL to get to the end of that. “We’ve been having discussions with the AFL over the last two or three days, clearly, to make sure that we are at the bottom of that.” Davies was then asked about the health of the two players. “That’s the most important thing – they’re OK now, a little bit embarrassed, I guess, to put the club in this position,” Davies said. He also confirmed another player had been present on Saturday night, “but not in the same situation”.



Lachie Cowan was taken to hospital via ambulance but has since been discharged. AFL Photos The investigation comes amid allegations of illicit drug use at a gathering at Hayward’s South Yarra home on Saturday night, although Carlton have not confirmed whether drugs were involved in either player’s hospitalisation. Reports had widely circulated on Sunday, suggesting that illicit drugs were allegedly involved as the players received medical care. This masthead cannot confirm that illicit drugs were involved in either incident. The AFL’s intervention means the matter is no longer exclusively an internal Carlton issue, with the league’s integrity department now involved in establishing what occurred and whether any breaches of competition rules or policies warrant further action. Both players have since been discharged from hospital.



Cowan, 21, was taken to The Alfred hospital after emergency services attended an address in South Yarra early on Sunday morning. Ambulance Victoria confirmed advanced life-support paramedics responded to an incident about 5.15am, with a man in his 20s transported to hospital in a stable condition. Carlton subsequently confirmed Cowan had received medical treatment and undergone observation before being discharged. Hayward, 27, separately admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. The former Sydney forward received stitches before being discharged. The Blues have maintained that the two players were hospitalised under separate circumstances.



In a statement issued on Sunday, Carlton said its immediate priority was the welfare of both players. “The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances,” the statement said. The investigation presents an early test of the football department leadership of Davies and chief executive Graham Wright, who are charged with establishing higher standards at a club attempting to rebuild its football program. Carlton has already begun its own inquiries into the weekend’s events, with the findings expected to be made available to the AFL. The involvement of the league’s integrity unit also raises questions about how any potential breaches would be dealt with under the AFL’s existing illicit drugs framework.



The AFL and AFL Players’ Association have agreed to a revised illicit drugs policy, including expanded hair testing and a greater emphasis on identifying and addressing repeated drug use. However, the new framework is not scheduled to come into effect until 2027, meaning the Carlton matter will be assessed under the competition’s existing rules and disciplinary processes. Will Hayward was named Carlton’s best clubman this season, as well as winning the coaches’ and Spirit of Carlton awards. Getty Images The investigation does not necessarily mean either player will face disciplinary action, with the league yet to establish publicly whether any wrongdoing has occurred. Nevertheless, the episode has again exposed the challenges confronting the AFL in managing player behaviour away from football clubs, particularly during the off-season.



Carlton have endured previous off-field controversies, including the illicit drugs case involving Elijah Hollands, adding to the pressure on the club to demonstrate that player welfare and behavioural standards are being taken seriously. The timing is particularly uncomfortable for the Blues, who have spent the trade period reshaping their playing list and attempting to build momentum ahead of the 2027 season. Hayward arrived at Carlton from Sydney last year and played 21 games in his first season in navy blue, while Cowan has established himself as an important young defender. Cowan played 24 games in 2026 and has become a regular member of Carlton’s backline. The latest controversy threatens to overshadow the club’s list-management work, with Davies now confronting questions extending well beyond recruiting and the composition of Carlton’s playing list.



The central issue for the Blues is no longer simply the medical treatment required by two players on Sunday morning, but what led to those hospital visits and whether the circumstances reveal a broader failure of judgement or conduct. Those are questions the AFL’s integrity unit will now seek to answer. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period Jake Niall October 14, 2026 — 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. It might not play out on the ground in 2027, but Hawthorn and the Western Bulldogs were the finalists that gained the most ground during a trade period that was marked by an outbreak of honesty and rational negotiations. Zach Merrett, whose stranding at Tullamarine was the story of last year’s exchanges, was granted his wish to play under Sam Mitchell. Whereas Merrett’s failed escape in 2025 was a game of chicken between the Hawks and Bombers in which no one won, this time the deal was reached more than a week before the deadline and both clubs emerged as if they had signed a peace accord at Camp David, smiling and with bursting with goodwill. Zach Merrett in his new colours. The Hawks and Bombers struck a fair deal, one in which both sides might wonder if they could’ve done slightly better. Essendon gained the draft capital and some face – yes, a little less than they would’ve scored had the foes come to terms 12 months earlier. But if the Hawks go on to the win the flag in the next few years, they should be thanking the Suns on the podium, since it was their entirely pragmatic and logical decision to let Ben King leave as a free agent, without matching the seven-year $9 million deal, that allowed Hawthorn to consummate a trade with Essendon over Merrett that did not cost them vital organs.



Had the Suns matched and forced a trade, the Hawks did not have enough draft capital to land both King and Merrett. Or, they would have been forced to lose a player such as Noah Mraz, whom rival clubs had been eyeing. Their landing of King did cost the Hawks Aidan Schubert in what I would call a related party transaction (aka a side deal), as it happened. But to acquire two A-graders – one midfielder who can hit targets, and a key forward who can be counted on for 50 to 60 goals provided he stays upright – makes them the logical topweight in the 2027 premiership race. Zak Butters is now a key part of the Bulldogs’ star-studded midfield. Getty Images While the Bulldogs are coming from further back, the recruitment of Zak Butters, one of the game’s top five players, must vault them into genuine premiership contention, and that Butters purchase was buttressed, if you like, by the securing of Jordan Butts, who fills the club’s most gaping hole as a key defender. Allowing the usual alibis for injury, Hawthorn’s pass mark for next season will be reaching the grand final. The Bulldogs must make the top four and if they cannot do so (again, injury willing) with Butters sharing the centre square with Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards (plus Sam Darcy back in attack), then Luke Beveridge’s time will be just about up.



The Dogs, like Hawthorn, were blessed to take a high-worth free agent from a club (Port Adelaide) who finished low enough to take the compensation pick (No.5) rather than force a trade. Ben King has joined Merrett at the Hawks. AFL Photos But there was a trade, of course. It just wasn’t officially involving Butters, even though the whole deal was predicated on Port losing Butters and gaining a raft of picks. A coincidental deal. Port received a pile of early picks and handed back a heap of draft choices that were less valuable on the face of it. It was ticked off by the AFL, perhaps because so many clubs and picks (and two barely players) were involved (“flood the zone with picks” to borrow from Steve Bannon) that no one could be bothered ascertaining how uneven or “commercial” and standalone it really was. Side deals aside, there were a few notable themes:



1. The rise of the older player Geelong’s policy of getting high-quality players aged around the 30 mark, as either free agents (Toby Greene) or needs-based trades (Jordan Ridley, who is 27, and Rowan Marshall) continued, and their policy has been adopted by Collingwood (Lachie Neale, Jesse Hogan) and even Carlton (Lachie Whitfield). The Cats would fancy themselves capable bridging the gap between the top few and themselves. Collingwood possibly would think so, albeit they have fewer kids. The Magpies were fortunate to come up short, so to speak, in their offer to Richmond for Jayden Short and kept their draft picks. They had no need for another half-back flanker who is 30. Scott Pendlebury’s passage to Gold Coast was the extreme example of how the AFL gun players’ career spans are imitating other professional sports, such as tennis and the NFL, and extending beyond 35, albeit “Pendles” has really been hired as on-field assistant coach. 2. The mega-buck deals



If old players are easier to acquire, their appeal is heightened by the incredible contracts that mid-career stars can command in a market in which few top-liners are available. Related Article Live

AFL 2026 Bombers, Demons make key last-minute moves before the trade buzzer It is staggering to consider that King’s $9 million contract with Hawthorn is slightly more than half of what the Bulldogs have committed to Butters ($17 million to $17.5 million), which is now the game’s largest contract over nine years. Nick Blakey, meanwhile, on nearly $12 million over eight years, has become the richest defender in the competition thanks to the combination of the Pullman scandal and North Melbourne’s desperate need (matched by two other clubs) to land their first A-grader from another club since Wayne Carey was strutting around. 3. The end of warehousing players



Brisbane eventually parted with Keidean Coleman before deadline, no longer able to hold a talented running defender whose spot was locked up by super veteran Dayne Zorko. The Lions had little choice but to trade midfielder Sam Marshall to the Saints on similar grounds. In both cases, the Lions received more than adequate draft compensation. Hawthorn was compelled to let Schubert leave, in the knowledge that he might develop into a capable key forward, once they had King secured and – in defiance of expectation – persuaded Calsher Dear to re-sign for another two years. Those two clubs owned the deepest lists, perhaps, in 2026. It is not possible, if it ever was, to hold players, and build depth when individuals are trying to build careers. When Thomas Murfett sensed something was wrong with his plane on Saturday morning, he did what any experienced pilot would. The 63-year-old circled around the Muchea airfield where he had just taken off and looked for a suitable place to land. Tom Murfatt had a lucky escape on saturday when his plane crashed in Muchea. But as the RV-6A light aircraft that he built himself 30 years ago began to stall, he realised he had no hope of making it back to the airstrip. “He was just doing a few practice circuits before he and his friend were going to fly to Bunbury,” Murfett’s wife Melanie said.



“On the second round they felt that something wasn’t right with the aircraft so they came back around to look for somewhere to land. When he knew he wasn’t going to make the runway, he started worrying about people on the ground as he was right next to the Brand Highway.” Murfett - who crash-landed in a paddock - told his wife that he didn’t have much time to think “or do - your body just takes over and you just do what you can”. Murfett suffered multiple broken bones during the crash. The pilot, who has decades of experience, told her he could feel that something “felt not quite right” but that what happened after was a blur. The next thing he knew was that he had crash-landed and he couldn’t get out of the wreckage.



Murfett suffered a broken arm in the crash that needs surgery, a broken leg “that will take a couple of surgeries”, five broken ribs, a lung puncture and a fractured back. His friend, who was a passenger in the plane with him on Friday, also suffered broken ribs but has already been discharged from hospital. The wreckage left ofTom Murfett’s plane. 9News Perth Murfett, however, is bed-bound and “in pretty good spirits”. “He’s just laying back and [saying] ‘I don’t have to do anything, everyone is waiting on me now’,” Melanie laughed, before adding that he will “probably” go up in a plane again as soon as he’s able.



Police were called to Muchea just before 10.30am on Saturday morning with reports that a single-engine light aircraft had crashed near a private airfield off Brand Highway near Nolan Road. Melanie thanked everyone that rushed to help Murfett get medical assistance he needed, including emergency services. With 9 News Perth.

PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Deputy premier to get strike-breaking powers under overhaul of Qld labour laws Matt Dennien October 14, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie would be handed powers to terminate protected industrial action under the Queensland government’s long-awaited overhaul of workplace laws. The government is also set to hold a parliamentary inquiry into Labor’s 2022 efforts to scuttle the role of LNP-linked “red unions” in the state, and review its union encouragement policy. Unions have said they will take time to consider the proposed changes, but warned the workers’ compensation scheme amendments would make it harder for frontline staff to get support. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie says the IR reforms will begin to shift the balance back in Queenslanders’ favour. Cameron Atfield Bleijie’s update came as he announced the Crisafulli LNP’s response to a review of industrial relations law and the workers’ compensation scheme, both tabled in parliament on Wednesday.



The review, conducted by former Bleijie-appointed WorkCover chair Glenn Ferguson and Industrial Relations Commissioner Gary Black, made 104 recommendations, Bleijie told parliament. Seventy-five recommendations have been accepted in full, while 14 were accepted in principle, six were noted, and nine were rejected, he said. A bill will be introduced on Wednesday night to action the LNP response. “These reforms, accepted by the government for implementation, will begin to shift the balance back in Queenslanders’ favour, bringing us into line with other jurisdictions – including the national government with the Fair Work Act – while protecting important rights and entitlements for Queensland workers,” Bleijie said. In his speech to parliament on Wednesday afternoon, he said the changes would save small business $1.46 billion annually by preventing workers’ compensation scheme premiums from increasing.



He said more details on the bill would be forthcoming with its full introduction, but he expected pushback and misleading claims from the Labor opposition and union movement, which has previously accused Bleijie of a “blind agenda of ideology”. Related Article Exclusive

Queensland government Unions lash out after Bleijie’s Friday night workplace board purge “Queenslanders are used to these Labor scare campaigns, which have been proven time and time again to be false,” Bleijie said. “I want to be clear about what we’re not doing: we are not accepting all recommendations made by the independent review. In doing so, the government is protecting a number of key entitlements for workers.” Elements that would feature in the bill, he said, included: A fit and proper person test for union officials seeking right of entry powers on worksites.

More “freedom” around who can represent workers in industrial disputes and wage negotiations.

Increased maximum penalties for WorkCover fraud.

A regulator-appointed representative who reasonably believes fraud has occurred would be given powers to suspend lump-sum compensation while it is investigated.

Requiring employment to be the major significant contributing factor in a psychological injury claim.



The government response document provided further detail about the accepted recommendations. These included a review of the state’s union encouragement policy, which lays out a proactive approach to allowing workers to organise, and a parliamentary committee probe of the amendments of the former Labor government, and how industrial law treats incorporated entities such as those under the Red Union banner. “We look forward to submissions during the parliamentary committee process with respect to freedom of association, because the Liberal Party is the party of freedom,” Bleijie said. The government has also accepted a recommendation to hand Bleijie, as industrial relations minister, similar powers to those of his federal counterpart to terminate protected industrial action. Such a move would only be open to Bleijie if he was satisfied the action was threatening or would threaten to endanger the life, safety, health or welfare of part of the population, cause damage to the state economy, or “would otherwise be contrary to the public interest”.



Related Article Perspective

Queensland government Can Queensland workers count on the LNP’s respect? This year they’ll find out Announcing the work earlier this year, including the required five-yearly review into the workers’ compensation scheme, the Crisafulli government cited an increase in psychological injury claims. The party had taken only a limited number of industrial relations policies to the election. Unions had claimed the review would be used to wind back protections for workers. In a statement on Wednesday afternoon, Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said requiring work to be the major contributing factor for a psychological injury claim “risks shutting workers out of compensation and access to the support they need”. King said the broader sweep of recommendations “needed to be considered in totality by the QCU, unions and other stakeholders”.



Civil Contractors Federation Queensland chief executive Damian Long said the reforms would provide a boost to the infrastructure sector in the lead-up to the 2032 Olympics. “Aligning Queensland’s industrial relations laws with national standards and strengthening expectations around lawful conduct will provide greater confidence and certainty for businesses delivering the infrastructure projects our state relies on,” Long said. World.title: Ability to pay shouldn’t decide kids’ education
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Ability to pay shouldn’t decide kids’ education October 14, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Photo: Megan Herbert SCHOOLS That independent and religious schools should not be supported by government funding is an idea worth pursuing here (“Radical plan to end private school fees”, 14/10). Many independent and religious schools have facilities that state-financed schools can only dream about: concert halls, pools, gymnasiums, staffed libraries, etc.

Private (ie independent) schools in England do not receive government funding but rely on parents or guardians to meet the cost of educating their children. It is a choice every family makes.

I liken this way of equity in education to transport choices. You can use public transport at minimum cost or you can pay for a taxi at your own expense. The ability to pay high fees should not be the determining factor to receive a good education.

Gillian Yung, Kew Funding non-government schools is standard

The only reason a proposal to remove fees in non-government schools is portrayed as radical (“Radical plan to end private school fees”, 14/10) is that we have been fed 60 years of propaganda that Australia is unique in funding such schools when doing so is standard practice throughout the OECD. Finland fully funds them but bans them from charging fees. England fully funds those that do not charge fees. New Zealand almost fully funds those that charge very low fees.

Cutting all funding to fee-charging schools is politically untenable, but a smart party that wanted to win the coming state election would offer a substantial increase in funding to the Catholic sector and low-fee independent schools that agreed to cap their fees, and enrol the same proportion of disadvantaged students as the government sector.

We all accept that the public health system funds non-government doctors via Medicare and non-government chemists via the PBS. We ought to accept that the public education system can include schools that are not owned or run by the government.

Chris Curtis, Hurstbridge



Tech study doesn’t need to be a trade-off

Your correspondent (Letters, 14/10) provides a clear-sighted view of the technical v academic school debate. She rightly argues that “good schools have great teachers who create opportunities for everyone”.

Adequate funding of public schools would enable teachers to provide such opportunities so all students can reach their full potential. It isn’t just a matter of manual training or academic pursuits. All students should have access to the education that suits them. For many, that will include learning from both streams. I want tradies to not only competently fix my home but to understand the wider world in which they live and vote.

Judy Williams, Beaumaris Don’t repeat the mistakes of the ’90s

The reference by your correspondent (Letters, 14/10) to “in the past, narrow offerings at technical schools cut off many working-class students from hopes of a university education” has a historical import. It recalls the late 1980s and the early 1990s when social and political pressure was placed on students to stay at school to year 12. Many were, in effect, “parked” at school in a context of being stigmatised if they didn’t want to go to university. It appears that a “class” issue still remains in secondary schooling, however, the educational failure of the 1990s shouldn’t be repeated.

Des Files, Brunswick End the right to discriminate at faith-based schools

Allegra Spender’s Private Member’s Bill to stop faith-based schools being able to fire and expel students and staff based on sexuality, gender identity, pregnancy and marital status cannot be enacted soon enough. As for the Australian Christian Lobby’s claim that this is about freedom, not discrimination, I believe most Australians, including gay Catholics like me, realise this is about their freedom to discriminate.

As a former teacher working in independent and faith-based schools, I know only too well how the constant threat of firing disables a teacher to challenge homophobia and transphobia in the classroom. The data proves that affirmation, friendship and volunteerism are vital enablers for queer young people to thrive. All schools should have a duty of care to proactively make schools safe so that all students can learn and all teachers can teach.

Olivia Brozecki, Howlong, NSW THE FORUM Complicated issues

The article, “Barrister’s claims on sexual assault spark outcry” (14/10), raises a number of important issues. Firstly, it is clear that a sexual assault may still have been committed regardless of whether a conviction has occurred. Given the high bar required to convict – proof beyond reasonable doubt – as a matter of logic, there must be victim-survivors where there has been no conviction.

On the other hand, it is also hard to refute the claim that not all persons who allege sexual assault are telling the truth. There are many instances where this has been clearly established, including cases of simple recantation. Nobody knows what percentage of allegations are in fact false (whether intentionally or mistakenly), and the “guestimate” of 5 per cent is itself unreliable; it is an estimate of proven false allegations. Research on this aspect reveals there are a large number of allegations which are in the “don’t know” basket.

The tension between establishing a “victim” before the criminal law and a victim in fact is unresolvable. The reasons for this include the very requirements of the criminal law, and the fact that false allegations do occur.

Con Differding, Torquay



Perverse logic

Re “Barrister’s claims on sexual assault sparks outcry” (14/10): What’s next? Unless murderers confess, the victims will be deemed “alive”?

Les Aisen, Elsternwick More training required

Reframing Melbourne barrister Geoffrey Steward’s starting-point assertion that “some women lie” — a determinative framing that shapes how the story is told thereafter — the more honest and empirically grounded starting point would be to say that a significant proportion of sexual assaults are committed by men who know they have not obtained a woman’s active consent, and many others who remain silent about the abusive conduct of their peers.

Because the correct framing is supported by every available dataset: high prevalence, low reporting, minuscule conviction rates, and a well-documented pattern of bystander silence that shields perpetrators.

In this context, it goes without saying that annual refresher legal education for lawyers, judges, police officers, and all court-adjacent personnel ought to be mandatory to dismantle the rape myths that continue to be consciously and/or unconsciously rehearsed in courtrooms across Australia to the grave detriment of victim-survivors of a heinous, yet persistently underestimated, crime.

Jelena Rosic, Mornington Growing pains

Ross Gittins makes some valid points in trying to untangle the twaddle peddled by politicians about immigration (“Immigration is too easy a scapegoat”, 14/10). But he’s still an economist peddling the line we have to have continued population growth for the sake of caring for an ageing population and propping up the economy.

This is the same old macroeconomic theory that doesn’t match the fact that planning approvals for massive new subdivisions on the city fringe, or high-rise redevelopment in the inner suburbs, have not ensured the resulting capital gains from these developments fund new schools, kindergarten and health services to support the people who live in those dog boxes with no room for a tree and veggie garden. So the basic infrastructure is not funded, private profits are pocketed, and another generation is worse off than the one before.

Not to mention what this form of growth is doing to the planet.

Bernadette George, Mildura Related Article Note From The Editor How The Age chooses which letters to publish Treaty repeal essential

I disagree with your correspondent that repealing the Indigenous Treaty is a retrograde step (Letters, 14/10). In fact, many people see its repeal as essential.

Despite Victorians rejecting the Voice referendum, then-premier Jacinta Allan proceeded with the Treaty without seeking a public plebiscite. A poll was entirely justified as parts of the Treaty radically alter parliamentary government in this state. An Indigenous council was established that could second-guess the decisions of an elected government. Such an arrangement effectively re-engineers our democracy.

Claims the Treaty is necessary for the Indigenous to have their views represented inside the tent could be equally applied to any other group. That is why we have a parliament where all voices can be heard. There are better means of addressing Indigenous disadvantage.

Martin Newington, Aspendale



Liberals’ insult

The Liberals’ policy to repeal the current act and abandon the Treaty is an insult to First Nations people. It refuses to acknowledge the harm done to them since we invaded their country. I, like many, will refuse to vote Liberal while this policy exists.

Andrew O’Brien, South Yarra Booing shameful

On the anniversary of the Voice to parliament referendum, the shameful booing of the Welcome to Country at the weekend’s Australia Cup final (“FA boss condemns booing at cup final”, 13/10) shows not only how far we have to go to achieve reconciliation with First Nations people, but also how sadly we are moving further away from a unified Australia.

Divisive politics from One Nation and Jess Wilson’s Liberals, who have made a point of promising to tear up Victoria’s Treaty, have a lot to answer for. A unified Australia cannot be built by turning reconciliation into a political wedge.

James Alexander, Fitzroy Damning indictment

Heidi Everett’s story of homelessness in the streets of the city (“I walk city streets just to stay safe”, 14/10) is a damning indictment on our society’s failed public housing system that has been sold off and dismantled by successive governments over the past 40 years.

Data shows Victoria has 40,000 public housing applicants on the priority waiting list. That is, people like Everett who desperately need and deserve housing within a short period of time, but who are actually waiting up to 20 years.

It is time governments ensured multinational corporations paid their fair share of tax so we can properly fund public housing, health services, aged care and the NDIS.

Jeff Fiedler, Castlemaine Help the homeless

Included in Heidi Everett’s compelling account of her life on the streets was a plea to help the homeless. Her suggestions included various ways to help the homeless find places to cook their own food, and where to find somewhere to camp or sleep.

Coincidentally, The Age featured a full-page ad authorised by more than 100 social sector organisations pleading with the prime minister to restore Ask Izzy’s funding. Not-for-profit organisation Infoxchange operates Ask Izzy, which supports more than 38,000 community organisations delivering vital services. The Ask Izzy website/app provides information for people seeking help for assistance services.

This is not only useful for homeless people who do have a phone, it is very practical tool for passers-by in the community who have been approached for help (as I have on occasions) by vulnerable people who don’t know where to seek assistance in their area.

I’d like to know why the federal government is ceasing funding to provide such vital information.

Sally Davis, Malvern East No going back

Your correspondent (Letters, 14/1) says if Josh Frydenberg re-enters politics, a “difficult tasks await him” (leadership?). The party has moved right, but it’s more a deep-dive into the far-right to reclaim voters lost to One Nation.

Scrapping net zero when global warming is expected to reach 1.8C in the not-too-distant future is just mind-blowingly stupid. There is no way Frydenberg could be successful in Kooyong without a commitment to net zero and renewable energy. Nuclear power: don’t even think about it.

Frydenberg would also be aware only 23 per cent of voters under 40 voted for the Coalition in 2025.

There is no way back to the political centre for the Coalition this side of the 2028 election, nor, I believe, for Frydenberg.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne





Make the switch

Many people have made the switch to reduce their transport costs as electric vehicles now lead car sales. Cheaper renewable options help the household budget and as Shane Wright reports, according to the IMF, “the sharp lift in renewable energy sources” has protected the global economy, too (“Australia is facing the sharpest jobless rate rise in developed world”, 14/10).

What is the Coalition waiting for? Many Australian households have moved to renewables manage their costs. If the Coalition wants to be the better economic managers, they could get moving, too.

Jenny Kashyap, Bentleigh. Easy decision

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese just keeps digging holes for himself with his inability to make decisive decisions. Despite widespread support, he caved to the gambling industry; with AI glasses, he has vacillated. Now with the abhorrent live-stream of the execution in the United States, Albanese is looking at what can be done to stop it, which is an admirable sentiment but not actual action (“Big tech, media warned over live-streamed US execution”, 13/10).

Prime minister, just ban it. Tell the telcos and other providers that they must not allow it into Australia. Sure, people with VPNs will find ways around it, but surely Albanese can make a stand on this matter with a simple clear-cut decision.

Ross Hudson, Mount Martha Stay in your lane

The Greens remind me of the car in front that’s weaving all over the road (“Split emerges in Greens over military aid to Ukraine”, 14/10). Could they please stay in their lane and campaign for social justice and the environment? That’s already a lot. Let the Ukrainians make up their own minds about defending themselves or rolling over to Russia.

Di Cousens, Upwey AND ANOTHER THING ... Eggs

The ACCC investigation into a potential eggs cartel could end up in boiled eggs.

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South



Photo: Matt Golding I now eggspect to see eggceptional and eggspansive letters about the bad egg industry!

Myra Fisher, Brighton East America

The prospect of a live-streamed execution means we confront the morality of the deed. Averting our gaze makes us complicit.

Peter Bennett, Clifton Hill Having watched the prolonged death of democracy live-streamed from the Oval Office, Australians have no appetite to watch another American execution.

Ken Machin, Grovedale It’s not a good idea to tell narcissists to “look in the mirror”. That’s probably where it all started. Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills



Potholes

Rocky road is my favourite chocolate treat, but the rocky roads I am forced to drive on are not nearly as palatable.

Tris Raouf, Hadfield Some years ago, the Brunswick council repaired all the potholes in a quiet suburban street, and installed speed humps the following week.

Martin Harris, Heidelberg Furthermore

Pity the poor bloke down on the beach going insane, trying to measure the rise in sea levels.

Gerry Lonergan, Reservoir I am always amused by the classification of “world-class” when applied to luxury units or cruise ships. In many parts of the world, people live in shanty towns with no running water or sewerage, and huts made of thatch and adobe, or tents. A different world perhaps?

Julie Christensen, Blackburn North I can understand the complexities and absurdities of world politics, but I have never understood the AFL trade period.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill

Warning: This story contains graphic content. A woman admitted fatally stabbing her ex-girlfriend to her new prison lover while police listened on a hidden microphone, a court has been told. Tara Morrison was killed in Busselton in 2024. Facebook Hannah Louise Glover, 30, and James Anthony Sorgiovanni, 29, have pleaded not guilty to the murder of Tara Marie Morrison, 38, at a Busselton home in April 2024. The pair, who were a couple, are accused of repeatedly stabbing Morrison in her head, neck, body and hands.



A woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told the court that Glover confided details about the “brutal attack” while the pair were in the same prison cell in the months after the alleged murder. “Hannah disclosed to me about why she did it … she saw Tara give her daughter liquid fantasy (GHB),” she told the WA Supreme Court on Wednesday. “Then Hannah told me that Jimmy held Tara’s hand behind her back and that’s when Hannah grabbed her by the hair and stabbed her in the neck.” The woman used her right hand and made a stabbing motion three times to replicate for the jury what Glover did when they were speaking in a cell. “She dragged Tara throughout the house,” she said.



“There was an entrance door, and she said there was, like, blood splatter on it. “The blood that came from Tara’s body.” Police found Morrison’s body at Glover’s home in her daughter’s wardrobe. She had about 40 wounds, along with grazes and bruising that could indicate she was restrained. Blood was found splattered on the walls, doors and the floor.



Glover allegedly told the woman she used four knives during the attack. The court has previously been told Glover, Sorgiovanni and Morrison had been using illicit drugs before the killing. Glover and Sorgiovanni had been in a relationship for a few months, and before that, Glover was in a relationship with Morrison. “He’s a f---ing evil c---,” Glover said of Sorgiovanni in one of the covert police recordings played in court. “He only targets single mum … because he’s psychotic.”



Glover alleged Sorgiovanni had power over her, suggesting he made her kill Morrison. “I had no control,” she said. “Then I got back with Tara and that made him crazy.” Glover dabbed tears from her eyes in the dock as the recordings were played in court. “(Morrison) was obsessed with me and it was causing stuff between me and (Sorgiovanni),” she can be heard saying in another one. “She wanted to be with me.”



Glover also said Morrison was “so f---ed up” and was using her to get access to her daughter. She could be heard making stabbing noises on the police recording when talking about the alleged murder. “All I wanted to do was love my baby and protect her … and now look at me, I’m not in prison,” Glover said on the recording. The trial continues. AAP

World.title: National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds debate in Queenstown
World.content:
Analysis - National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds turned up to Queenstown ready for a bit of rough and tumble on Wednesday evening.

The ASB Great debate featuring cross-party finance spokespeople has a history of getting a bit rowdy, and while it's often the large audience responsible for a lot of that, this year it was the panelists leading the charge.

In addition to Willis and Edmonds the 800-strong southern crowd got served up Act's David Seymour, New Zealand First's Shane Jones, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, and newcomer Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity party.

Stood side-by-side in the middle of the panel of five, Willis and Edmonds scrapped it out about the government's Investment Boost and Labour's plan to scrap it and replace it with a policy that targets small businesses.

Debate moderator TVNZ's Jack Tame asked Edmonds what a business like Coronet Peak, which has benefitted from Investment Boost's tax support for businesses would do without it, Edmonds fired back "I don't have to copy Nicola, we are two very different people" to huge applause from the crowd.

In an unusual twist, Swarbrick and Jones paired up regularly throughout the debate, and were highly amused by the scrap playing out in the middle of the panel, leading Jones to pipe up and suggest the Green co-leader "offer some clarity".

Edmonds held her ground against Willis however, saying in her opening remarks she would be the next finance minister: "Not Chlöe Swarbrick and not Nicola Willis - Barbara Edmonds the MP for Kenepuru will be."

Seymour summarised the Willis and Edmonds showdown saying: "It's like two bald men fighting over a comb in the middle there."

Jones also received some big laughs in his opening remarks when he detailed how slow and clogged up the economy had become, shouting: "Look at my beloved fast-track, it's turned into a constipated beast."

Tax was also a big talking point with Wong, Edmonds, and Swarbrick given a shot at pitching their respective land, capital gains, and wealth tax proposals to the audience.

The debate descended into sledges and lots of shouting as Willis and Seymour took their turns picking holes in them all.

Swarbrick revved up at Willis, who said Labour would introduce a capital gains tax (CGT) and Swarbrick who wants a wealth tax would "kick the door wide open" and expand it.

Given an opportunity to respond, Swarbrick harked back "to a time even I can remember" when National criticised the international visitor levy, only to then increase it when in government.

Seymour was highly amused by that, quipping: "I love how Chlöe said she was old enough to remember something that happened in 2018."

A new coalition also came out of the tax debate when Wong, Edmonds, Jones and Swarbrick were all asked whether they would support a bed tax for Queenstown if in government, and it was a unanimous yes from them all, much to the delight of the crowd.

Another big laugh came when Willis and Seymour were in the thick of a debate on breaking up the supermarkets and Jones interrupted to say: "Now you know what our Cabinet meetings are like."

Seymour - not one to miss an opportunity - replied: "One person has to bring the basic economics to Cabinet, that's exactly what it's like!"

One of the final topics rounding out the debate was the issue of superannuation and how the country will afford it in years to come.

All of the politicians were asked if they supported being part of a cross-party review on the country's retirement future.

Seymour said he would entertain it with a yes, but noted he was disappointed it wasn't a big feature of the debate overall, given what a significant issue it is.

Wong was supportive, saying Opportunity needed to be in Parliament and in the room "to be the broker in a heated environment where people don't agree and have proven not to hold themselves accountable to long-term plans".

Edmonds acknowledged Willis who had agreed to the idea with her at the weekend. Willis returned that and said she too wanted to celebrate Edmonds on that front but added she was disappointed the conversation hadn't happened during this term, which she blamed on Labour.

Swarbrick was also in the 'yes' camp but said the "missing piece" in this election was also talking about investment in climate change adaptation and planning.

World.title: Greens 'unapologetic' at Mongrel Mob meeting as National cries foul
World.content:
Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson is defending some of her candidates meeting with the Mongrel Mob, saying the party will engage with all communities.

National is crying foul at a social media post from Mongrel Mob lifetime member Harry Tam, which shows the Greens' Hūhana Lyndon and Michel Mulipola, along with Oriini Kaipara and Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke from Te Pāti Māori, at a whānau, health, and wellbeing election hui.

National's justice spokesperson Paul Goldsmith said the Greens and Te Pāti Māori were "prioritising" gangs over victims.

"They profit off misery and addiction by peddling meth in our communities and they make victims of Kiwis up and down the country."

Goldsmith said National stood with victims, not the gang members who made them victims.

"I have one simple question for these candidates. Did you ask any of the Mongrel Mob members you met what they did to get patched? Because their victims know."

But Davidson said it meeting with gangs was not a new thing.

Embedded content removed for printing https://www.facebook.com/harry.tam1/posts/pfbid0Zus1t93kRDvLfB6oM4EtZFM13iEj5YZ4ivnVi8XQPn9GQYxDLZyCornAujGqNYNHl

"We are unapologetic about making sure that we can engage with all communities, especially communities who are living on the margins. So we're proud, and we have done that year and year again," she said.

"And actually, those communities are the very people who hold the solutions to being able to live good lives, so it's not a new thing, and we're not apologising for making sure that everyone has a chance to engage in democracy and has access to politicians."

Davidson said the Greens also met with victims.

"We do consistently, as we meet with people who have been harmed by the decisions of this very government, by the policy decisions to restrict housing support, with young people, we meet with the people who have been harmed by this government every single day."

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the best way to stop the cycle of gang violence and criminality was to understand what was driving it in the first place.

Asked if victims of gang violence would be upset about the visit, Swarbrick said the Greens were trying to understand the needs of every New Zealander.

"I completely accept your point with regard to victims and victimisation and the need for us to end the cycle of violence and the cycle of criminality and the cycle of gangs in this country."

"The way that we best do that is that we understand what is driving that in the first place and we stop that cycle."

Swarbrick said there were people "on the margins" who were swept up in cycles of criminality and victimisation.

"They too need to be de-radicalised, they need to be reconnected with services that allow them to reintegrate with society," she said.

Te Pāti Māori also responded to questions about the photos.

"Regardless of how our people choose to meet with us, whether it's at the marae, on the netball courts, in a town hall, or at a community hauora day, Te Pāti Māori will be there," a spokesperson said in a written response.

"We do not judge, they have whakapapa. We do not separate our people into those who are easy to stand beside and those who are difficult. Our role is to engage with all Māori, listen to their concerns, and advocate for better outcomes for our communities. We are unapologetic about that."

Posting on Instagram, Kaipara said the kaupapa was about the health and wellbeing of the Mob community.

"Many will raise eyebrows, throw stones, and cast judgement over our visit, but the truth is, every member of a gang is a member of a whānau, a whakapapa, and a part of New Zealand society."

Kaipara said being present did not mean endorsing everything.

"It means recognising that whānau do not stop being whānau because of a patch."

Labour's Barbara Edmonds was asked about the meeting on Wednesday afternoon and said each party made their own decisions.

"Labour doesn't have particular rules around it, but if I can just address the fact that gang members are part of our communities.

"I'm a local MP where we have gangs and we have people that belong to gangs and their families in our communities. So, I'm not going to speak any further on that."

She said Labour also meets with victims of crime as well, and in response to criticism from National that it showed Labour wouldn't take crime seriously and isn't putting victims first, Edmonds said it was "just more petty sort of politicking at a time when actually the cost of living is the number one issue for most people in this country".

World.title: Aquaculture sector urged to seize export opportunities in India
World.content:
A growing middle class makes India one of the world's largest and fastest-growing seafood markets, the aquaculture industry has been told.

The government wants to quadruple the value of the country's farmed seafood exports over the next decade, but those in the sector say there needs to be better collaboration between government departments to enable growth.

Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade policy and negotiation manager Sara Meymand told Aquaculture NZ's annual conference in Nelson on Wednesday that Australia's seafood exports to India had increased by almost 300 percent since a partial free trade agreement was signed in 2022.

New Zealand's seafood exports to India fell by 67 percent during the same time.

The New Zealand-India Free Trade Agreement will come into effect next week with the current 33 per cent tariff on key fish and seafood exports to be phased out over seven years.

Meymand said it was a huge opportunity for the sector.

"This is a real moment, a real opportunity to lean into a market that is just huge. You're talking about a middle class alone that's 700 million people, so that's more than all of the EU (European Union) more than all of ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations), it's the Indian middle class that will be wanting your stuff."

The 1285-hectare open ocean salmon farm, Hananui, off the northern coast of Rakiura Stewart Island was the first aquaculture project to gain fast-track approval in August. RNZ / Samantha Gee

The government wants to see the aquaculture industry's contribution to the economy reach $3 billion by 2035. Its annual export revenue is currently about $750 million.

Meymand said there were many challenges for food exporters at present but, with a growing global middle class, health was becoming a major focus for many people.

"The demand for premium high-quality nourishing food is on the rise and New Zealand aquaculture, one of the most scalable export innovation stories we have, is well positioned to make the most of this opportunity."

About 1200 commercial marine farms - mostly greenshell mussels, oysters, and salmon - are operating across the country.

A 1285-hectare open ocean salmon farm off the northern coast of Rakiura/Stewart Island was the first aquaculture project to gain fast-track approval in August.

Hananui, led by Ngāi Tahu Seafood, is expected to produce more than 14,000 tonnes of salmon a year, provide about 450 jobs and generate more than $310 million dollars in annual sales.

Awarua Rūnaka Ltd chairman Barry Bragg said the project had been 11 years in the making and was part of a plan to make Murihiku Southland a leader in aquaculture.

The Blue Endeavour Salmon Farm in Cook Strait. RNZ / Samantha Gee

When Rio Tinto announced it planned to close the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter near Bluff in 2020, it sent shockwaves through the region, with leaders forced to consider how to ensure there would be jobs into the future, he said.

Hananui was one of many aquaculture projects it had worked to get consented.

The first bid for the open ocean salmon farm was declined by an independent panel in 2023, with Ngāi Tahu appealing that decision in the High Court, before choosing to rework the proposal and submit it under the Fast-track Approvals Act.

Ngāi Tahu Seafood general manager Aaron Endacott said diversification into aquaculture was a strategic priority.

The next stage with Hananui was to create a detailed business case and test the commercial viability of the project, he said.

"This will include updating capital and operating assumptions, feed costs, as well as revisiting market conditions to understand a realistic price per kg that we can expect for the product produced."

Government support had been fundamental and was needed for critical regional infrastructure, coordinated research and enabling regulatory framework, while "alignment between government departments would be nice as well", said Endacott.

Yesterday, members of Ngai Tahu Seafood and Awarua Rūnaka travelled to Blue Endeavour, the country's first open ocean farm, in the Cook Strait.

The Blue Endeavour Salmon Farm in Cook Strait. Supplied / New Zealand King Salmon / Jim_Tannock

The government had invested $29m over five years in the New Zealand King Salmon aquaculture project.

Chief executive Carl Carrington said the company would share the lessons its learned with the industry in a bid to help it grow.

"Part of the deal is that we share the do's and the don'ts and what we've learned from it with other industry players, you know, what's the expression, the early bird gets the worm, but it's the second mouse gets the cheese and in this instance it'll be for the benefit of Ngāi Tahu, they'll be able to be much more efficient than we've been."

About 70,000 king salmon were transferred to the Blue Endeavour farm as a test earlier this year.

One of the pens will be fully stocked with 100,000 salmon this summer and once running at full capacity, the farm is expected to more than double NZ King Salmon's annual revenue.

Carrington said there needed to be better cohesion between government departments.

"It's an issue and that's a message that we are giving the government, get your act sorted as a cohesive unit because right now it's it's got the potential to kneecap investment."

Te Aupōuri Fisheries Management general manager Penetaui Kleskovic said getting consent for marine projects was expensive, complex, and uncertain - and change was needed, especially in the laws governing the sector.

"We need clear and predictable pathways for responsible marine farming, whether through reform of the existing RMA or a dedicated marine farming legislative approach," he said.

"We can't keep telling Maori to become economically independent while maintaining systems that make economic development unnecessarily difficult, we need a system that protects our environment without paralysing our ambition."

He said in the Far North, iwi leadership wanted to see more than just a financial return.

"We want jobs, we want infrastructure, we want young people developing their skills and local businesses securing contracts and in communities like Houhora, Pukinui, Whangaroa, Mangonui, Kaitaia, those opportunities, they matter enormously.

"One new job can change the circumstances of an entire whanau."

World.title: Internal documents warn of food safety risk after MPI said none existed
World.content:
New Zealand Food Safety assessments found health risks associated with a pesticide on food, despite telling the public there were none, documents obtained under the Official Information Act reveal.

The annual 2022-2023 New Zealand Food Safety (NZFS) report showed the pesticide methamidophos was detected on one grower's silverbeet at 360 times the legal limit, or maximum residue limit (MRL).

The pesticide was not authorised to be used on silverbeet at the time, and its use was banned in New Zealand in 2024.

Internal documents show the silverbeet had already been harvested and distributed by the time the grower was contacted by NZFS, and no recall was issued.

The NZFS risk assessment showed the exposure was more than twice what could be safely eaten in 24 hours without presenting a health risk. However, the watchdog's public reports stated there were no food safety risks that year.

RNZ revealed in 2025 that NZFS had not issued a fine, prosecution or recall for food with illegal levels of potentially harmful agrichemicals in at least five years, despite dozens of breaches.

At the time, NZFS deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said none of the 75 breaches posed food safety risks.

"For each of these detections we conducted a rigorous scientific food safety assessment to ensure there was no risk to consumers, which is standard practice," Arbuckle said in a statement.

NZFS documents obtained by Greenpeace under the Official Information Act (OIA) show the ministry identified health risks it did not report publicly in at least one case.

NZFS intially declined Greenpeace's July 2025 OIA request for copies of the formal investigations into 30 pesticide breaches discovered during the annual Food Residues Survey Programme, on the grounds it would require substantial collation or research.

But when Greenpeace then requested three specific investigation and risk assessment reports - of glyphosate breaches in 2015-16, acephate breaches in 2017-19 and methamidophos breaches in 2022-23 - NZFS declined the request for information on the glyphosate and acephate breaches, arguing the documents did not exist or could not be found, though it provided brief risk assessments in both cases.

NZ Food Safety also supplied the investigation and risk assessment for the 2022-23 methamidophos breach, which found that residue on a silverbeet sample was above the ARfD or "acute reference dose", which is the amount a person can eat in 24 hours without appreciable health risk.

The methamidophos residue was 106 percent of the reference dose for adults and 232 percent of the reference dose for children.

New Zealand Food Safety's risk assessment concluded this meant "a human health food safety risk for children cannot be excluded" and that 64 grams of silverbeet would be dangerous for a 23 kilogram child.

According to the United Nation's Rotterdam Convention on hazardous chemicals, methamidophos is an "extremely toxic organophosphate which causes serious adverse effects to human health".

The World Health Organisation classifies it as Class 1B toxicity - highly hazardous.

Greenpeace executive director Russel Norman said NZ Food Safety told the public there were no food safety issues - but their own risk assessment warned the breach was more than twice the safe level for children.

"Every parent across the nation would feel a chill going up their spine reading the internal risk assessment stating their children were at risk from food highly contaminated with dangerous pesticides. Meanwhile the government agency responsible for protecting food safety was telling people that everything was safe. It wasn't," he said.

NZ Food Safety's 2022-23 Food Residue Survey Programme found illegal residues in nine percent of the food samples tested.

Norman said the number of non-compliant tests and the number of non-compliant food samples were quite different.

"In 2022-23, they tested 300 food samples out of the billions of food samples that New Zealanders eat every year. They did 500 tests on each of those food samples, so it sounds like there's a lot of testing underway, then they say 'we only found bad results on 0.02 per cent of all of those'," he said.

"What they don't make clear to people is that nine per cent of all the food samples had illegally high levels of pesticides, so one in 11 of the fresh food items in your shopping trolley were found to have illegally high levels of pesticide residues on them."

Greenpeace believed there was a conflict of interest in New Zealand Food Safety sitting within the Ministry of Primary Industries (MPI), which has a dual role promoting exports and regulating agriculture.

"This creates tensions because if MPI finds serious wrongdoing it can damage the 'clean green' export brand. MPI is chronically exposed to industry capture and the temptation to downplay or hide bad news," Norman said.

"Having the food safety agency located within a government mega-ministry committed to promoting agribusiness exports is a particularly problematic conflict of interest."

He said the group wanted the food safety role to sit within the Ministry of Health, focused on protecting human health from pesticides.

Norman also pointed to NZFS's move away from testing for glyphosate after finding a third of wheat samples had levels exceeding the limit allowed, some by 50 times, during 2015 testing.

In its 2016 report, MPI said "none of the wheat samples posed any food safety risks".

Since then, NZ Food Safety has not tested for glyphosate.

Norman obtained NZFS's risk assessment of the glyphosate breaches under the OIA, which was three pages long and heavily redacted.

"They found very high levels of glyphosate and so their response was to never test again. The risk assessment was very short and concluded everything was fine.

"We don't know how much glyphosate is in our food because the regulators simply stopped testing it once they found very high levels.

"If you had a regulator that was actually concerned about food safety and consumers' health rather than about the reputation of agribusiness, when it found high levels of glyphosate - much higher than are legally allowed - you'd think the response would have been to pay even more attention to the issue."

New Zealand Food Safety deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said while it identified "potential food safety risks" from the methamidophos breach, following a "rigorous risk assessment, these detections were not found to pose a food safety risk".

While a NZFS toxicologist assessed a food safety risk could not be excluded for chronic or ongoing exposure, "in this instance the exposure would have been a one-off", Arbuckle said.

Arbuckle said studies had shown that washing silverbeet before eating could reduce residues by a quarter and that methamidophos breaks down in temperatures above 80°C.

"Given the above context, it was considered that there was no immediate or ongoing food safety risk," he said.

Arbuckle said the grower was contacted to "establish the facts" and "educated about the rules and our expectations".

"In our experience, the few occasions in which MRLs have been breached have been accidental or the result of incorrect use. Farmers and growers do not intentionally use these compounds in such a way that residues would exceed MRLs and there are generally no advantages to them doing so," Arbuckle said.

"NZFS takes a stepped approach to enforcement that is proportionate to the risk to consumers and in line with international best practice. Each case is considered separately and takes into consideration the circumstances."

In a statement, the New Zealand Vegetable Council said 99.9 percent of plant-based food sold in New Zealand was compliant with the Food Act according to New Zealand Food Safety's most recent testing.

World.title: Walters explains choice of Walsh over Tedesco for World Cup opener
World.content:
Kevin Walters has declared the battle for Australia's fullback berth remains wide open despite Reece Walsh winning the nod over James Tedesco to start in the Kangaroos' World Cup opener.

Walters claimed ahead of Thursday night's clash with New Zealand that Tedesco, the captain as Australia lifted the trophy four years ago, would have a chance to prove his worth in the group-stage game against Fiji in Brisbane on October 25.

Walsh, the hero of last year's Ashes whitewash, will don the No.1 jersey at Sydney's Allianz Stadium, but as for whether the Brisbane Broncos star will be first choice later in the tournament, Walters is keeping an open mind.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The Kangaroos coach indicated he had chosen to rest Tedesco and playmaker halfback Sam Walker following their exploits in the Sydney Roosters' NRL grand final win.

"I feel it's in the best interest of the team they get a spell this week and they'll play next week," Walters said on Wednesday.

"To be honest, I haven't decided that (fullback) position yet, that's why we're here, and they'll both get an opportunity.

"They're both Clive Churchill medallists, the last two, so I look at it that way. I'm very fortunate to have both of them in the team.

"They're different players, but I love what they both bring to the team. Teddy's the more experienced custodian and Reece is on the way up as such."

Walsh has retained his place after his heroics in last year's Ashes. (Getty Images: PA Images/Mike Egerton)

The one drawback to Walsh is his fitness, with Thursday's opener his first competitive match in close to two months after sustaining an ankle injury in clubland.

"He (Walsh) has had a good preparation and there's a few players in that position themselves, so it's good to get them around the group," Walters said.

Walsh will be part of a relatively settled Kangaroos spine, with Cameron Munster at five-eighth and Harry Grant at hooker.

Halfback Mitchell Moses is the only new addition to the key playmaking roles.

Moses was on last year's Ashes tour but didn't take the field, with the Parramatta skipper an understudy to Nathan Cleary, who has missed this World Cup following his compound ankle fracture.

Tedesco last played for Australia in 2023. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"He's a very influential player, an experienced player, particularly his kicking game around the halves will be invaluable," Walters said.

"He gets his opportunity and I'm sure he's looking forward to taking it as well.

"They (Munster and Moses) are very calm and know what we need to do in different situations."

The Kangaroos have not lost to New Zealand on Australian soil since 2015, and while the Kiwis have a monster forward pack, Walters insists his side have the firepower to match them.

"It's a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they're not mugs," the Kangaroos coach added.

"We've got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, that's what the World Cup is all about: seeing the best players on the world stage."

AAP
